meanings.Chinese: quzhe qianjin, bi kai, duobi, qipian

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'lī' means to cling to, adhere, hide within, or dissolve into something. Because it carries an indicator letter 'ṅ' (līṅ), it takes Atmanepada endings in the active voice. When used with a causative affix (ṇic), it changes to mean 'causing someone or something to dissolve or hide'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakara (present tense), prathama purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The deer hides in the forest.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (causative voice), Lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The boy hides things in the cave.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: līṅ śleṣaṇe. śleṣaṇam aliṅganam saṃśleṣo vā. ṅittvād ātmanepadī. anit. layate, liliyate, letā, leṣyate.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: līṅ śleṣaṇe. śleṣaṇaḥ saṃśleṣaḥ. anudāttaṅita iti ātmanepadam. layate.

meanings.English: to cling to, adhere, melt, dissolve, or hide
meanings.Bengali: lege thaka, mile jaoya, lukiye thaka

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'trap' means to feel shy, to be bashful, or to feel ashamed. It functions naturally in the Atmanepada (self-referential) voice because feelings of modesty or shyness occur within oneself. When causative markers are applied, it shifts to mean causing someone to feel ashamed or embarrassing them.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakara (present tense), prathama purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The boy feels shy when seen by everyone.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (causative), Lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: His improper speech embarrasses others.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: Madhaviya Dhatuvritti clarifies that 'trapūṣ lajjāyām' possesses an anudatta vowel marker indicative of Atmanepada endings. It conjugates as trapate in the present tense, trepe or tatrape in the perfect, and exhibits characteristic vṛddhi or guna according to standard set-dhatu rules.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes under 'trapūṣ lajjāyām' that this root denotes inward hesitation or modesty (lajja). It is classified under the anudatteta group of Bhvadi, ensuring middle voice (Atmanepada) personal terminations in primary non-causative conjugations.

meanings.English: to be ashamed, to feel shy, to be modest

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root glai means to become exhausted, weary, or to lose cheerfulness. In standard active voice (Kartari Prayoga), it takes Parasmaipada endings with the present base glaya- (e.g., glayati - he feels weary). When converted into the causative form by adding the nic affix, it becomes glapayati or glapayati, changing the meaning to 'causes to feel tired' or 'exhausts someone'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Active voice (Kartari Prayoga), Present tense (Lat), 3rd person singular
scenarios.example_english: The traveler, fatigued by the heat, feels weary.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative form (Nic-pratyaya), Present tense (Lat), 3rd person singular
scenarios.example_english: The intense sunshine exhausts the plant.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: Madhaviya Dhatuvritti analyzes glai with the semantic indicator harsaksaye (loss of enthusiasm, vigor, or cheerfulness). It derives the present stem glayati through adesha substitutions and notes the application of specific phonological rules in past participles (glana) and periphrastic forms.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin in Kshiratarangini explains glai in the sense of loss of joyful energy and vitality. He highlights the substitution of ai to a (adestva) before non-sarvadhatuka affixes and notes the anit nature of the root across its parasmaipada conjugations.

meanings.English: to feel tired, to languish, to lose vigor, to become despondent
meanings.Hindi: thakna, klanta hona, utsahahin hona, murjhana
meanings.Bengali: klanto howa, utsahohin howa, mlan howa
meanings.German: ermatten, erschopft sein, den Mut verlieren
meanings.French: languir, se fatiguer, perdre son entrain
meanings.Chinese: juan dai, pi fa, sang shi re qing

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'kṛṣ' means to plough, scratch, or pull. In Parasmaipada (karṣati), it represents the general act of ploughing the field or dragging an object. In Ātmanepada (karṣate), it emphasizes the action performed for the agent's own sake or drawing something toward oneself. Adding the causative suffix Nic (karṣayati) gives the meaning of causing someone to pull or till.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga (Parasmaipada, Lat-lakara, Prathama-purusha, Ekavacana)
scenarios.example_english: The farmer ploughs the field with a plough.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga (Ātmanepada, Lat-lakara, Prathama-purusha, Ekavacana)
scenarios.example_english: The boy pulls the rope towards himself.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic-pratyaya, Kartari Prayoga, Lat-lakara)
scenarios.example_english: The master has the oxen plough the field.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'kṛṣī vilekhane' belongs to the Bhvādi class. With the marker ī (īkāra-it), it indicates specific accent and morphological traits. In Sarvadhatuka environments, it undergoes guna to produce 'karṣati' and 'karṣate'. Sayanacharya clarifies that vilekhana fundamentally signifies tearing the soil (bhūmer vidāraṇam) and by extension pulling or attracting (ākarṣaṇam).
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines 'kṛṣ' under vilekhana as breaking or furrowing the earth with tools like a plough. He notes that while the primary sense in the Dhatupatha is agricultural furrowing, secular and Vedic usage extends the semantic domain to dragging, drawing, and attracting.

meanings.English: To plough, furrow, pull, drag, draw

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'cyu' means to move, slip, trickle, or fall from a position. Because it has an anubandha 'ṅ' (cyuṅ), it naturally takes Atmanepada verb endings in the basic active voice. When expressing making something drop, move, or fall (causative), the suffix 'ṇic' is added, turning the root into 'cyāvayati' (or 'cyāvayate'), where it can take Parasmaipada endings to mean causing to fall, remove, or displace.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (Basic Active Voice, Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana)
scenarios.example_english: The fruit falls from the tree.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (Causative, Kartari prayoga, Parasmaipada)
scenarios.meaning: causes to fall, removes, or displaces
scenarios.example_english: The king removes the enemy from his position.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'cyuṅ' is catalogued in the Bhvadi-gana with the meaning 'gatau' (in the sense of motion, movement, or falling away). Being ṅit (marked with silent ṅ), it is anudātteṅlakṣaṇa-ātmanepada. It is anit (devoid of iṭ augment in standard non-sārvadhātuka environments like liṭ, lṛṭ, luṅ). In the present tense, it forms cyavate, cicyuve in liṭ, cyotā in luṭ, and acyoṣṭa in luṅ.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'cyuṅ gatau' as indicating movement, dropping, or slipping down from a steady state. Being ṅit, its fundamental forms are Atmanepadi (cyavate). Guna occurs before sarvadhatuka affixes yielding 'cyav-'. In causative contexts with Nic, vriddhi takes place yielding 'cyāvayati'.

meanings.English: to move, to fall down, to drop, to slip, to deviate
meanings.Hindi: girna, khisakna, vicyut hona, gati karna
meanings.Bengali: cholyachol kora, pore jaoya, bicyuto howa

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'jṛbh' (appearing as 'jṛmbh' due to the marker 'ī' causing 'num'-agama) means to yawn, expand, or stretch one's limbs. In its basic middle voice (Atmanepada), it denotes someone yawning or stretching naturally. When used with a causative affix (Nic), it shifts meaning to causing someone to stretch, relax, or yawn.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Lat lakara (present indicative), prathama-purusha, eka-vacana, Atmanepada (Kartari)
scenarios.example_english: The sleepy boy stretches and yawns due to fatigue.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (Causative), Lat lakara, prathama-purusha, eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The gentle breeze causes the blossoms to open up.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root is given as 'jrbhi gatraviname' in the Bhvadi gana. The 'i-kara' as an it-marker indicates the insertion of 'num'-agama before the final consonant by 'idito num dhatoh' (Panini 7.1.58), yielding the base 'jrmbh-'. It is anudatteta, hence strictly Atmanepadi in active voice.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'jrbhi gatraviname' signifying bodily relaxation, yawning, or stretching of the limbs. The resulting inflected base is 'jrmbhate' in the present tense, taking 'num' regularly.

meanings.English: to yawn, stretch the limbs, expand, open up
meanings.Hindi: jamhai lena, angadai lena, vikasit hona
meanings.Bengali: hai tola, anga-moramora deoya, bikashito haoya

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'rādh' (rādhā) belonging to the first conjugation (Bhvādi) specifically conveys the meaning of injuring, striking, or harming (hiṁsā). It operates in the Parasmaipada voice in standard active usage, directly acting upon a direct object (the one harmed or killed).

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga (Active Voice, Lat Lakara, Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana)
scenarios.example_english: The hunter harms the deer.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic-pratyaya, Lat Lakara, Prathama Purusha, Bahuvacana)
scenarios.meaning: cause to harm / cause to injure

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: rādhā hiṁsāyām. rādhati, arātsīt. The root rādhā with the it-marker ā belongs to the Bhvādi class and signifies hiṁsā (injuring, destruction). Because it takes a sap-vikaraṇa, it conjugates regularly as rādhati.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: rādhā hiṁsāyām. rādhati. Kshirasvamin notes this root in the Bhvādi list denoting destruction or harm, distinct in meaning from the Divādi and Svādi roots of similar phonological form denoting accomplishment or propitiation.

meanings.English: to harm, to injure, to hurt, to kill
meanings.Bengali: hiṁsā karā, āghāta karā, badha karā

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'dakṣ' inherently means to grow, thrive, or act with speed and capability. It is conjugated in the Atmanepada. When used in simple present active voice (kartari prayoga), it takes the Atmanepada personal endings like '-te' (dakṣate). In causative constructions (ṇic), it forms 'dakṣayati', meaning to cause to grow or to make competent.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara (present tense), prathama-purusha, eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The boy excels and acts competently in all tasks.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (ṇic-pratyaya), Lat lakara, Parasmaipada, prathama-purusha, eka-vacana
scenarios.meaning: causes to grow or makes someone competent/skilled
scenarios.example_english: The teacher makes the student capable in all fields of knowledge.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'dakṣँ' belongs to the Bhvadi class with anudatta it marker indicating Atmanepada inflection. Its recorded semantic scope is 'vṛddhau śīghrārthe ca' (in the sense of growth/expansion and quickness/dexterity). Forms like dakṣate, dadakṣe, and dakṣiṣyate are derived systematically under standard Paninian sutras with it-agama.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'dakṣa vṛddhau śīghrakāritve ca'. The root conveys both material/physical growth (vṛddhi) and agility or promptness in executing actions (śīghrakāritva), from which the classical nominal 'dakṣa' (dexterous/expert) is derived.

meanings.English: to grow, increase, act promptly, be dexterous or capable
meanings.Telugu: peruguta, samarthyamu kaligi unduta, vegamugaa cheyuta
meanings.Hindi: badhana, samartha hona, shighrata se karya karna
meanings.Bengali: briddhi paoa, dakhata labha kara, druta karya kara
meanings.German: wachsen, gedeihen, geschickt sein, flink handeln
meanings.French: grandir, prospérer, agir rapidement, être habile
meanings.Russian: rasti, procvetat, byt umelym, deystvovat bystro

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'stṝ' means to spread, strew, or cover. Since it is marked with an indicator 'ñ' (ñit), it takes Parasmaipada when the result of the action benefits someone else, and Atmanepada when the result of the action is intended for the subject. In the Bhvadi class, it takes the standard 'śap' infix and strengthens the vowel 'ṝ' to 'ar', forming 'starati' (Parasmaipada) and 'starate' (Atmanepada).

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Parasmaipada (Kartari prayoga, action oriented outward)
scenarios.example_english: The devotee spreads flowers before the deity.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Atmanepada (Kartari prayoga, action oriented toward the agent / self-benefit)
scenarios.meaning: Spreads or prepares a seat/bed for oneself
scenarios.example_english: The sage spreads a kusha-grass mat for his own meditation.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: Madhaviya Dhatuvritti glosses 'stṝñ ācchādane' as covering, expanding, or spreading over an area. Being marked with 'ñ' as an it-marker, it is Ubhayapadi. In Sarvadhatuka tenses with the 'śap' vikarana, the root vowel undergoes guna replacement to 'ar', yielding forms like 'starati' and 'starate'. In Ardhadhatuka tenses, appropriate guna or dirgha processes apply according to general sandhi and it-agama rules.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes in Kshiratarangini that 'stṝñ' conveys 'ācchādana' (covering, enveloping, scattering over). The presence of the anubandha 'ñ' establishes its dual-voice inflection (Ubhayapada). He contrasts its Bhvadi conjugation ('starati/starate') with its Kryadi homophonic usage ('stṛṇāti/stṛṇīte'), highlighting the primary sense of spreading a layer across a surface.

meanings.English: to spread, to cover, to strew, to scatter over

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'dṛ' with the marker 'ṅ' belongs to the first conjugation group (Bhvādi) and is used in the Ātmanepada to mean showing disrespect, disregarding, or slighting someone or something. When used in the causative (Nic), it conveys causing someone to be disregarded or humiliating them.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Bhvādi Ātmanepada kartari prayoga (Present indicative 3rd person singular with śap)
scenarios.example_english: The foolish person disregards the word of the wise.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Ṇic-pratyaya (Causative base with Ātmanepada/Parasmaipada affix)
scenarios.example_english: The wicked person causes everyone to be slighted.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti notes that root 'drṅ' has the it-marker 'ṅ' which secures the Ātmanepada voice by 'anudāttaṅita ātmanepadam'. It operates in the sense of 'anādara' (disregard or contempt). The root undergoes guna before śap leading to 'darate'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin states in Kshiratarangini that 'drṅ' is aniṭ and ātmanepadi indicating lack of respect or neglect ('avajñā'). Forms such as 'darate' are derived regularly in Sarvadhatuka environments.

meanings.English: to disregard, to disrespect, to slight, to neglect
meanings.Hindi: anādar karnā, tiraskār karnā, upekṣā karnā
meanings.Bengali: anādar karā, tiraskār karā, upekṣā karā

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'sru' belongs to the Bhvadi class and means 'to flow' or 'to trickle'. In the standard active voice (Parasmaipada), it describes liquid moving or oozing on its own. When the causative suffix Nic is added, it switches to causative meaning 'to cause to flow' or 'to pour/shed'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakara (present tense), prathama-purusha ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: Pure water flows from the mountain.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: nic-pratyaya (causative), Lat lakara, prathama-purusha ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The sad boy sheds tears from his eyes.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'sru~ gatau' is anudattet and anit. It undergoes guna substitution (u -> o) followed by av-adesha before sarvadhatuka affixes, forming 'sravati'. In lit, it forms 'sasrava', 'sasratuh', 'sasruh'. In lun, it takes the form 'asravit'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'sru gatau' primarily denotes continuous movement characteristic of fluids (dravatva-purvika gatih). It is anit and parasmaipadi throughout the un-augmented conjugational tenses.

meanings.English: to flow, to trickle, to ooze, to stream

canonical_dhatvartha: gatikshepanayoḥ (in the senses of moving/going and throwing/propelling/driving)

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'aj' means 'to drive', 'to lead', 'to throw', or 'to move'. It belongs to the 1st Gana and is Parasmaipada. In the basic present tense, it conjugates simply as ajati, ajataḥ, ajanti. In complex non-present tenses (like lit or lut), Paninian rules substitute the root 'aj' with 'vi' (ajervyaghañapoḥ), but in present everyday usage, it directly means driving cattle or throwing/moving objects forward.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga (Present Tense, 3rd Person Singular, Parasmaipada)
scenarios.example_english: The cowherd drives the cows to the forest.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga (Present Tense, 3rd Person Plural, Parasmaipada)
scenarios.example_english: The soldiers shoot (throw forward) arrows towards the enemies.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti analyzes 'aja gatikshepanayoḥ' as a halanta Parasmaipadi root. In Sarvadhatuka environments, 'shap' affix is added yielding 'ajati'. In Ardhadhatuka suffixes (except ghañ and ap), Panini rule 2.4.56 'ajervya-ghapoḥ' substitutes 'aj' with 'vi' (e.g., vayati, vetum, vitum), showing specialized stem alteration.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin explains that 'aj' conveys both intransitive/transitive motion (gati) and casting or driving forward (kshepana). He notes the historical development where forms outside the four non-perfect/non-aorist systems largely merge into 'vi'.

meanings.English: to drive, to propel, to go, to throw

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'tvañc' belongs to the first group of verbs (Bhvadi Gana) and conveys the fundamental meaning of moving, going, or walking. It is conjugated in the Parasmaipada voice with the thematic infix 'śap' (a), producing present-tense forms like 'tvañcati' (he/she/it moves or goes). When used in the causative (Nic), it means 'to make someone move' or 'to propel' (tvañcayati).

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga (Active Voice), Lat Lakara (Present Tense), Prathama Purusha (Third Person), Ekavacana (Singular)
scenarios.example_english: The deer moves swiftly in the forest.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga (Active Voice), Lan Lakara (Past Imperfect), Prathama Purusha (Third Person), Ekavacana (Singular)
scenarios.example_english: The traveler walked slowly along the path.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti identifies 'tvancu gatau' as an udit root ending in a palatal consonant in the cavarganta section of the Bhvadi gana. Being udit (having 'u' as an it-marker), the augment it is optional before the gerund suffix ktva by the rule 'udito va' (yielding tvancitva or tvaktva). In the present tense with sap, it retains the nasal marker and derives 'tvancati', with lit form 'tatvanca'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes under the cavarganta roots that 'tvancu' denotes motion (gati). It follows the standard thematic inflection of the first conjugation, taking parasmaipada affixes. Because it is marked with udit-tva, it optionally admits it-agama in ktva-pratyaya forms while remaining regularly set in general universal environments.

meanings.English: to go, to move, to wander

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'dā' (dāṇ) means 'to give'. In the present tense (kartari prayoga), it takes the special substitute form 'yaccha-' before Sarvadhatuka affixes, forming 'yacchati' (he/she gives). When used in the causative (Nic), the root retains its base shape to form 'dāpayati' (causes someone to give).

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga, lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana (with yaccha-adesha)
scenarios.example_english: The king gives wealth to the beggar.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: nic pratyaya (causative), lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: causes to give / makes someone give
scenarios.example_english: The father makes the boy give charity.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: dāṇ dāne. anit, parasmaipadī. 'pāghrādhmāsthāmnādāṇ...' ityādinā yaccha-ādeśaḥ. yacchati, dadau, dātā, dāsyati, adāt.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: dāṇ dāne. yacchatīti rūpam. ṇakāra anubandhaḥ parasmaipada-niyamārthaḥ viśeṣaṇārthaśca. yacchati, ayacchat, dadau, dāsyati.

meanings.English: to give, bestow, donate, offer

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'vāś' means to cry out, howl, chirp, or bellow like birds or animals. Because it is naturally Ātmanepada, it takes endings like -te (vāśate) when animals or people utter characteristic sounds. When used in the causative (ṇijanta) form with -aya-, it changes to both padas (vāśayati / vāśayate), meaning 'to cause to cry or sound'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga, laṭ lakāra, prathama puruṣa, ekavacana (base Ātmanepada)
scenarios.example_english: The bird chirps melodiously in the tree.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: ṇijanta (causative), kartari prayoga, laṭ lakāra, prathama puruṣa, ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: causes (an animal or bird) to cry or roar
scenarios.example_english: The boy makes the dog bark/howl.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'vāśṛ~ śabde' belongs to the Bhvādi gaṇa as an anudāttet, ātmanepadī, and seṭ dhātu. The marker 'ṛ' indicates the application of the relevant aorist or augment options without affecting its primary verbal classification. It denotes the production of characteristic sounds by animals, birds, or weeping beings, conjugating as vāśate, vavāśe, vāśitā, and vāśiṣyate.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'vāśṛ śabde' specifically for animal vocalisations and cries. It takes Ātmanepada affixes throughout primary tenses (vāśate). In lit lakāra it reduplicates to produce vavāśe, and in sananta (desiderative) it yields vivāśiṣate.

meanings.English: to roar, cry, bellow, chirp, or make animal sounds

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root krip (realized systematically as klip/kalp) means to be capable, fit, suitable, or to bring about. In the standard present tense (Lat lakara), it functions in the Atmanepada taking the form kalpate to signify being ready, suitable, or capable. In causative usage (Nich), it produces kalpayati, meaning to arrange, fashion, prepare, or make capable.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Lat (Present Indicative), Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana, Atmanepada
scenarios.meaning: is capable / is suitable / serves to
scenarios.example_english: Knowledge becomes suitable through humility.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nich-pratyaya (Causative), Lat, Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The student arranges the assignment.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root kripu samarthye is read with the anubandha u. By rule 'kripo ro lah', the 'r' sound is substituted by 'l' throughout the standard derivations, producing kalpate. The meaning denotes capability, adequacy, or becoming conducive to a result.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes kripu in the sense of samarthya (competence, fitness, or adequacy). The letter 'r' turns to 'l' regularly to yield forms like kalpate, ciklipe, kalpta / kalpita, and in future tenses kalpsyate / kalpsyati.

meanings.Bengali: samartha haoya, jogya haoya, kalpana kora

meanings.French: etre capable, convenir, etre propre a, façonner

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'raṭ' conveys shouting, making a loud sound, or learning/repeating aloud continuously. In its standard active form (Kartari Prayoga with Parasmaipada), it describes a subject uttering or calling out loudly. When modified by the causative suffix (ṇic), it forms 'rāṭayati', meaning to cause someone to cry out or recite loudly.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Active Voice (Kartari Prayoga), Present Tense (Laṭ-lakāra), 3rd Person Singular
scenarios.meaning: Calls out loudly / cries aloud / recites repeatedly
scenarios.example_english: The child cries out loudly due to fear.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative Form (Causal ṇic affix), Present Tense (Laṭ-lakāra), 3rd Person Singular
scenarios.meaning: Causes to cry out or repeat loudly
scenarios.example_english: The teacher makes the student recite the verse aloud.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya explains 'raṭa paribhāṣaṇe' as denoting distinct or loud verbal articulation (uccaiḥ śabda-karaṇam). Being an anudāttet Parasmaipadī root of the Bhvādi class, it takes the standard Śap vikarana to yield 'raṭati', forms its periphrastic and simple futures with iṭ-āgama as 'raṭitā' and 'raṭiṣyati', and takes the perfect form 'rarāṭa'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes that 'paribhāṣaṇam' represents verbalization, clamor, or lamenting loudly. The derivation follows standard Bhvādi rules without guṇa modification of the root vowel 'a' in unaugmented non-sarvadhātuka contexts, retaining its seṭ status throughout non-conjugational tenses.

meanings.English: to shout, to cry aloud, to recite repeatedly

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The verbal root 'guṇ' primarily conveys the act of inviting, calling upon, or addressing someone politely. In standard active usage within the Bhvādi-gaṇa, it takes Ātmanepada endings where the internal vowel 'u' strengthens to 'o' by guṇa sandhi before the sap-pratyaya, yielding forms like 'goṇate'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Laṭ lakāra, Prathama puruṣa, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The householder invites the guest for hospitality.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Ṇijanta (causative), Kartari prayoga, Laṭ lakāra, Prathama puruṣa, Ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: causes to invite / sends an invitation through someone
scenarios.example_english: The king causes his allies to be invited through a messenger.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: guṇa āmantraṇe. Anudāttettvād ātmanepadaṃ bhavati. Guṇādeśe kṛte goṇate iti rūpam. Āmantraṇam nāma abhimukhīkaraṇapūrvakaṃ saṃbodhanam.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: guṇa āmantraṇe. Goṇate, jugoṇe, goṇitā. Āmantraṇam niyogapūrvakaṃ saṃbhāṣaṇam ityarthaḥ.

meanings.English: to invite, to call, to address politely

canonical_dhatvartha: gatisravanayos (in the senses of motion and hearing/listening)

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'kati' means to move (go) or to listen/hear. It is an 'idit' root (having an 'i' marker), which causes a nasal 'n' to be inserted into the root, forming 'kantate'. It inherently belongs to the Atmanepada class.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakara (present tense), 3rd person singular, Atmanepada
scenarios.example_english: The boy listens to the teacher's words.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (causative), Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, 3rd person singular
scenarios.meaning: causes someone to go / makes someone listen
scenarios.example_english: The father makes the son walk along the path.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti notes 'kati gatisravanayos' as an idit root, establishing the insertion of the num-agama (nasal letter) across all verbal forms by 'idito num dhatoh', leading to forms like kantate and cakante.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin explains that this root operates in two main senses: going (gati) and hearing (sravana). Being anudatta-it, it conjugates systematically in Atmanepada with num augmentation.

meanings.English: to go, to move, to hear, to listen

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'dhmā' means to blow into something (like blowing a conch shell to make a sound) or blowing air to ignite/kindle a fire. In the present tense, the root irregularly substitutes 'dham-', giving forms like 'dhamati'. When used in the causative sense (making someone blow or melting metals with intense air), it becomes 'dhmāpayati'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga (present active indicative, lat lakāra)
scenarios.example_english: The boy enthusiastically blows the conch shell.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: ṇijanta (causative active indicative, lat lakāra)
scenarios.meaning: causes to blow / kindles / melts by blowing
scenarios.example_english: The blacksmith kindles the fire using bellows.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: dhmā śabdāgnisaṁyogayoḥ. 'pā-ghrā-dhmā-sthā-mnā-dāṇ-dṛśyarti-sarti-śada-sadāṁ piba-jighra-dhama-tiṣṭha-mana-yaccha-paśrtya-ṛccha-dhāva-śīya-sīdāḥ' iti dham-ādeśaḥ. dhamati, dadhmau, dhmātā, dhmāsyati, adhmāt. śabde agnisaṁyoge cāvartate.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: dhmā śabdāgnisaṁyogayoḥ. dhamati śaṅkham agniṁ vā. dhmānaṁ phūtkāra-pūrvaka-vāyu-saṁyogaḥ. nijante dhmāpayati.

meanings.English: to blow, to produce sound by blowing, to kindle fire
meanings.Bengali: phuṁk deoyā, śaṅkho bājāno, āgun jvālāno

canonical_dhatvartha: shleshana-kridanayoḥ (to embrace, cling, shine, or play)

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'las' primarily means to shine, flash, frolic, or embrace. In basic active forms (Parasmaipada), it describes someone or something glittering, shining, or playfully moving. When a causative suffix (Nic) is added, it turns into 'lasayati' or 'ullasayati', meaning to cause to shine, to brighten, or to gladden.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga (Present tense, 3rd person singular)
scenarios.example_english: The light of the moon shines in the sky.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti analyzes 'lasa' in the sense of 'shleshana' (clinging/embracing) and 'kridana' (playing/reveling), pointing out the usage of upasargas like 'ud' (ullasati) to convey radiating, joy, and emergence, taking standard Bhvadi Guna and Shap vikarana without root modification in Sarvadhatuka stems.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines 'lasa' as conveying both bodily play/embrace and luminous manifestation, highlighting forms such as 'lasati', 'alasiit', and nominal derivations like 'lasana' and 'vilasa' denoting playful charm or splendor.

meanings.English: to shine, play, flash, embrace

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root gādh expresses two related actions: establishing oneself firmly in a place (finding solid ground or standing firm) and keenly wishing to acquire something (desiring/coveting). In its standard form, it stays in the Ātmanepada voice, reflecting that the state of being settled or the yearning belongs to the subject itself.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakara (present tense), Prathama purusha (3rd person), Ekavacana (singular)
scenarios.meaning: Stands firm, finds a foothold, or seeks/desires
scenarios.example_english: The righteous person stands firm in moral duty.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (causative), Lat lakara (present tense), Prathama purusha (3rd person), Ekavacana (singular)
scenarios.meaning: Causes someone to settle down firmly or establishes someone
scenarios.example_english: The teacher firmly establishes the student in knowledge.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti glosses gādhṛ with the canonical meaning pratiṣṭhālipsayoḥ. Pratiṣṭhā signifies sthiti (stability, firm footing, or settlement), while lipsā signifies labdhum icchā (the desire to obtain). Being ṛdit, it takes Ātmanepada terminations and seṭ augment iṭ in non-sarvadhatuka affixes, forming jāgādhe in the perfect and gādhitā in the periphrastic future.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin analyzes gādhṛ as indicating both physical/social stability (taking firm ground or finding refuge) and the mental disposition of seeking acquisition. It forms the standard present tense stem as gādhate through the affixation of the general thematic marker Śap.

meanings.Chinese: Zhan wen jiao gen, an dun, ke qiu

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'ḍhauk' means to approach, go near, or present oneself. In standard usage, it takes Atmanepada endings (ḍhaukate) to describe movement toward something. When used with causative affixes (Nic), it shifts to Parasmaipada (ḍhaukayati), meaning 'to bring near' or 'to present/offer'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga, laṭ lakāra, prathama puruṣa, ekavacana (ātmanepada)
scenarios.example_english: The student approaches the teacher.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: ṇijanta (causative), kartari prayoga, laṭ lakāra, prathama puruṣa, ekavacana (parasmaipada)
scenarios.example_english: The devotee offers a fruit to the deity.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'ḍhaukṛ' is read with an anubandha 'ṛ' indicating the application of specific kṛt affixes (such as aṅ in appropriate contexts). It denotes 'gati' (movement, approaching), is marked as anudātteta (ātmanepada), and is seṭ (takes iḍ-āgama in ardhadhātuka affixes).
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'ḍhaukṛ gatau' as an Atmanepadi root belonging to the Bhvadi class, yielding forms like ḍhaukate, ḍuḍhauke, and ḍhaukitā, signifying approaching or drawing near.

meanings.English: to approach, to go near, to arrive

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'plu' means to float, jump, leap, or swim. It belongs to the first group of verbs (Bhvadi gana) and is used in the Atmanepada voice. In simple present tense, the root vowel 'u' changes to 'o' and then to 'av' before adding endings (e.g., plavate). When converted to causative (Nich), it uses Parasmaipada or Atmanepada (plavayati / plavayate) to mean 'causes to float' or 'inundates/washes'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara (Present Indicative), Prathama purusha, Eka-vachana
scenarios.example_english: The fish floats happily in the water.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nich pratyaya (Causative), Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Eka-vachana
scenarios.example_english: The flood inundates the fields.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: plun gatau. anudattetvadanudattopadeshah. plavate, pupluve, plota, plavishyate. gativiseshe plavane prayujyate.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: plun gatau. anit atmanepadi. plavate, plavanam plavah. ap-tat-purvakasya santaranarthata.

meanings.English: to float, to swim, to leap, to inundate

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'prath' means to spread, expand, or become well-known and famous. As a standard Atmanepada verb of the first conjugation, it describes the natural process of something extending itself or renown radiating out. When used in the causative form (nic), it takes the meaning of actively making something famous, publishing, or spreading out information or objects.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga (active voice), lat-lakara (present tense), prathama-purusha eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The fame of a virtuous person spreads everywhere.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: nic-pratyaya (causative), kartari prayoga, lat-lakara, prathama-purusha eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The poet spreads his renown through his poetry.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: pratha prakhyane. prakhyanam prasiddhih vistarashca. anudattettvad atmanepadi. prathate, paprathe, prathita, prathitum ityadi rupani bhavanthi.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: pratha prakhyane. prakhyanam prasiddhy-arthatvam vistararthatvam ca. set atmanepadi ca bhavati. paprathe, prathitah.

meanings.English: to spread, extend, become famous or renowned

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'mruñc' primarily expresses the action of going, gliding, or moving quietly. In standard usage, it takes Parasmaipada endings in the present tense (mruñcati). When used with a causative suffix (Nic), it shifts meaning to causing someone or something to move or advance.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga, lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The deer moves through the forest.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: nic pratyaya (causative), lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: causes to move or directs movement
scenarios.example_english: The cowherd causes the cow to move along.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'mruñcu' belongs to the Bhvadi class and is read with the semantic tag 'gatau' (in the sense of going or motion). It is anudattopadesha / anit according to primary traditions, forming its base with internal nasal retention as mruñcati in Sarvadhatuka environments.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'mruñcu gatau', grouping it along with tvañcu and ksañcu in the series of motion-signifying roots ending in ca-varga. Forms like mruñcati and the reduplicated perfect mamroñca are listed under this heading.

meanings.English: to go, to move, to glide

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The verbal root 'syand' means to flow, ooze, trickle, or stream. In its basic form, it takes Atmanepada endings ('syandate') to describe natural motion of liquids. In causative usage, it describes causing liquid to flow or rain down.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (Present indicative 3rd person singular, Atmanepada)
scenarios.example_english: Cool water streams down from the rock of the mountain.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (Causative Parasmaipada 3rd person singular)
scenarios.example_english: The cloud from the sky causes rain to stream down.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: syandu prasravane. anudatteta atmanepadinam. udittvad vet, tena syandita syanta iti roopadvayam. sasyande, syandisyate ityadi.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: syandu prasravane gatau ca. sravanam dravasya calanam. syandate jalam, kshiram syandate.

meanings.English: To flow, stream, ooze, or trickle
meanings.Chinese: Liu dong, di liu, liu tang

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root sṝ primarily denotes injuring, hurting, or destroying in the first conjugation (Bhvādigaṇa). Being an aniṭ Parasmaipada root, it undergoes guṇa in strong tenses like the present tense (sarati) and takes vṛddhi in the causative form (sārayati), where it shifts the meaning to causing destruction, tearing down, or driving away.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga, laṭ-lakāra, prathama-puruṣa, eka-vacana (Bhvādigaṇa)
scenarios.example_english: The brave warrior strikes down the enemy.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: ṇic-pratyaya (causative), kartari prayoga, laṭ-lakāra, prathama-puruṣa, eka-vacana
scenarios.meaning: causes to destroy / causes to be crushed or driven away
scenarios.example_english: The commander causes the enemies to be routed.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: Mādhavīya Dhātuvṛtti identifies the root sṝ under the meaning of hiṃsā (harm, injury, destruction). In the sārvadhātuka forms, it takes the standard guṇa replacement of the final ṝ to ar (sarati). In the perfect tense (liṭ), reduplication yields sasāra. Being an aniṭ root, intermediate iṭ-āgama is barred in ardhadhātuka affixes beginning with val consonants where applicable.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kṣīrataraṅgiṇī glosses sṝ with hiṃsāyām and notes its parallel behaviour to other ṝ-ending roots of the Bhvādigaṇa like jṝ and tṝ. It establishes the differentiation between sṛ (gatau) and sṝ (hiṃsāyām), detailing the regular derivation paths in standard lakāras.

meanings.English: to injure, to harm, to crush, to destroy
meanings.Hindi: hiṃsā karnā, mārnā, cōṭ pahũcānā, naṣṭa karnā
meanings.Bengali: hiṃsā karā, āghāt karā, binaṣṭa karā

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'las' means to shine, flash, play, or embrace. In standard usage, it takes Parasmaipada endings (e.g., lasati - shines/plays). When used with a causative suffix (Nic), it changes to 'lasayati', meaning 'causes to shine' or 'displays/manifests'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakara (present tense), Prathama purusha (3rd person), Ekavacana (singular)
scenarios.example_english: Lightning flashes in the sky.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (causative), Lat lakara (present tense), Prathama purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The sunlight causes everything to sparkle.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'lasa shleshana-kridana-pradyotaneshu' is placed in the Bhvadi class. It is Parasmaipadi and Set. Madhava notes that the root denotes shining, sporting/embracing, and radiance (lasati, alasiit, lasishyatis).
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin interprets 'lasa' primarily in the sense of 'khelane' (sporting/playing), 'diptau' (shining), and 'shleshane' (embracing/clinging). It forms 'lasati' regularly with the Shappratyaya.

meanings.English: to shine, glitter, play, or embrace

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'hras' primarily denotes the action of making a sound or producing noise. In the basic present tense, it follows the standard Bhvadi first-conjugation pattern adding 'a' (sap) before the active endings, yielding 'hrasati'. When converted to a causative form (nic), it means 'to cause someone or something to make a sound'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, prathama-purusha, eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: A bird makes a sound in the forest.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (Causative), Lat lakara, prathama-purusha, eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The boy causes the musical instrument to sound.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti identifies 'hrasa sabde' under the Bhvadi-gana. It is an akarmaka root signifying the production of audible sound, conjugating with the affix sap in active voice to form hrasati, hrahraasa in lit, and exhibiting an it-agama throughout the non-sarvadhatuka forms due to its set classification.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes in Kshiratarangini that 'hrasa' belongs to the sabdartha (sounding) series of Bhvadi roots alongside dhrasa and bhrasa. It retains Parasmaipada inflection and takes normal guna/vriddhi transformations where applicable in secondary conjugations.

meanings.English: to sound, to make a noise

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'sthā' means to stand, stay, or stop moving. In the present tense, it transforms into 'tiṣṭhati'. When prefixes like 'anu' are added, it takes Atmanepada ('anutiṣṭhate') and means to follow or practice. When combined with the causative suffix Nic, it becomes 'sthāpayati' meaning to establish or place something.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga (active voice), simple present (lat lakara)
scenarios.example_english: The boy stands on the road.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: ṇic pratyaya (causative), kartari prayoga
scenarios.example_english: The father places the book on the table.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'ṣṭhā' has initial dental replacement of cerebral 'ṣ' by rule 'dhātvādeḥ ṣaḥ saḥ'. The meaning 'gatinivṛtti' indicates the stoppage or absence of motion. By the rule 'pāghrādhmāsthā...', the base 'tiṣṭha' replaces 'sthā' in Sarvadhatuka environments.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'ṣṭhā gatinivṛttau' as an anit, parasmaipadi root. In combination with upasargas like 'pra', it signifies departure or setting out ('prasthāna'), showing semantic shifts driven by preverbs.

meanings.English: to stand, to stay, to remain, to stop

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root jṛṣ means to grow old, decay, or lose vitality through aging. Because it is an intransitive Parasmaipada root, it describes an internal state or automatic bodily progression rather than an action performed onto an object.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: lat-lakara (present indicative), prathama-purusha, eka-vacana, active voice (kartari prayoga)
scenarios.example_english: The body wastes away with old age.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: nijanta (causative), lat-lakara, prathama-purusha, eka-vacana
scenarios.meaning: causes to decay / causes to grow old
scenarios.example_english: Disease causes the body to decay.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root jṛṣī is cited in the sense of vayohāni (loss of youth or decay with age). The terminal īkāra is an anubandha indicating specific svara and aorist morphophonemic rules. It takes standard Bhvadi guna in the sarvadhatuka stems to yield jarṣati.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin lists jṛṣī vayohānau among halanta roots ending in ṣakāra, explaining vayohāni as the waning of strength, vitality, and lifespan.

meanings.English: to grow old, to decay, to waste away with age
meanings.Hindi: būḍhā honā, jīrṇa honā, kṣīṇa honā
meanings.Bengali: vṛddha haoyā, jīrṇa haoyā, kṣaya prāpta haoyā

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'tṛp' means to be satisfied, pleased, or content. In the basic active form (Parasmaipada), it describes a person experiencing fullness or satisfaction from food, drink, or knowledge. When used with a causative affix (Nic), it shifts the meaning to 'making someone satisfied' or 'gratifying/feeding' someone.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga (Present Active, Parasmaipada, Lat Lakara, Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana)
scenarios.meaning: He/she becomes satisfied or gets pleased.
scenarios.example_english: The boy becomes satisfied with milk.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic Pratyaya, Present Active, Lat Lakara, Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana)
scenarios.meaning: He/she satisfies, pleases, or gratifies someone else.
scenarios.example_english: The mother satisfies the child with food.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti notes that 'tṛpa tṛptau' denotes satisfaction and contentment. It takes 'num' augment in certain classes or forms (as tṛmpati in Tudadi/Bhvadi variations) and undergoes regular guna of 'ṛ' to 'ar' yielding 'tarpati' and 'tarpayati' in causal formations. It also discusses its optional i-karana (vet status) in ardhadhatuka affixes.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin analyzes 'tṛp' in the sense of 'tṛptau' (satiety/contentment). The vritti highlights its alternation between guttural and retroflex nuances in derivations like 'tarpaṇa', its behavior in the aorist and desiderative systems, and its syntactic government of instruments or genitives to indicate the source of satisfaction.

meanings.English: to be satisfied, to be content, to please

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'bhram' means to wander, roam, or revolve. In the simple active present tense (Kartari Prayoga), it takes standard 1st-class endings to mean moving about aimlessly. By Paninian option, it can also take the 4th-class affix (shyan) to mean being confused or dizzy. When used in the causative (Nic), it shifts to mean causing someone or something to spin or rotate.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga, Lat Lakara (Present Tense), 1st class standard conjugation (Shap)
scenarios.example_english: The deer roams in the forest.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic-pratyaya), Lat Lakara
scenarios.example_english: The boy spins the wheel.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'bhramu' is categorized under Bhvadi-gana in the sense of physical motion (calana) as well as unsteadiness or confusion (bhranti). By the rule 'va bhrasa-bhlasa-bhramu-kramu-klamu-trasi-truti-lasah' (3.1.70), it optionally takes the 'syan' affix in Sarvadhatuka forms, yielding both 'bhramati' and 'bhramyati'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes that 'bhramu calane' indicates rotary motion, moving in various directions, or error/delusion of mind. The root exhibits optional it-agama in certain Ardadhatuka formations and alternates between standard 1st class and 4th class thematic stems in the present system.

meanings.English: to wander, roam, spin, revolve, be confused
meanings.Chinese: you dang, xuan zhuan, mi huo

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'śas' means to hurt, injure, or cut down. It belongs to the 1st conjugation (Bhvadi-gana) and takes standard Parasmaipada endings. When someone performs the act of hurting or striking, 'śasati' is used. When made into a causative form with the Nic suffix, it means to cause someone to strike or slaughter.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga (Present Active indicative 3rd person singular, Lat Lakara)
scenarios.example_english: The hunter slaughters the deer in the forest.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Lun Lakara (Aorist indicative with An affix due to Rdit marker)
scenarios.example_sanskrit: śūraḥ aribhiḥ saha yuddhe śatruṁ aśasat.
scenarios.example_english: The warrior struck down the enemy in battle.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root śasṛ is categorized under hiṁsā (injuring, slaying, or cutting). Being marked with anubandha ṛ (ṛdit), it obligatorily takes the 'aṅ' substitute in the Aorist tense (Luṅ), producing the form 'aśasat'. In normal present usage, it conjugates as śasati, śasataḥ, śasanti.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'śasṛ hiṁsāyām' as a root denoting destructive or lethal injury (vadha/chedana). It forms the perfect reduplicated stem 'śaśāsa' (and 'śaśaṁsa' under certain contextual alternates) and adheres to Parasmaipada inflections.

meanings.English: to injure, hurt, kill, or cut down

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'sphat' signifies bursting, breaking open, or splitting. In the active voice (Parasmaipada), it describes something bursting or opening up directly. When used with causative affixes (nic-pratyaya), it denotes causing an object to split, crack, or burst open.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat-lakara (present tense), prathama-purusha, eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The ripe fruit bursts open.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (causative voice), Lat-lakara (present tense), prathama-purusha, eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The carpenter splits the wood.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'sphata bhedane' belongs to the Bhvadi-gana. The meaning 'bhedana' implies breaking, bursting, or cleavage. It takes Parasmaipada endings and requires the intermediate 'i' augment (idagama) in non-sarvadhatuka forms where applicable.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'sphata bhedane' as denoting separation or splitting into parts. The root exhibits simple Guna-free stem inflection in standard Sarvadhatuka environments yielding 'sphatati'.

meanings.English: to burst, split, crack, break open

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'pan' means to praise, commend, or admire. In classical grammar, it regularly functions in Atmanepada and optionally takes the suffix 'aya' (producing panayati/panayate or panate). In everyday usage, it denotes honoring or extolling good virtues.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The noble person praises the virtuous one.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Svarthika 'aya' pratyaya, Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The student extols the teacher's virtues.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti explains 'pana stutau' as expressing praise and admiration. By the sutra 'aya-daya ardhadhatuke va', the affix 'aya' is optionally applied in Sarvadhatuka contexts, leading to forms like panate and panayate.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes that 'pana' is restricted to the sense of praise ('stutau'), distinguishing it from 'pana' which can also convey commercial transaction ('vyavahara'). It is anudattet and inherently takes Atmanepada endings.

meanings.English: to praise, applaud, admire, or extol

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'dāś' means 'to give', 'to offer', or 'to grant' (especially in the context of offerings, gifts, or serving with devotion). In simple present tense (Parasmaipada), it forms 'dāśati', meaning someone gives or offers something to someone. When converted to the causative form with the affix 'ṇic', it becomes 'dāśayati', meaning to cause someone to offer or give.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Simple present tense (laṭ lakāra), third person singular in Parasmaipada (active voice)
scenarios.example_english: The devotee offers an oblation to the deity.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (ṇic pratyaya), simple present tense (laṭ lakāra), third person singular
scenarios.meaning: Causes to give / makes someone offer
scenarios.example_english: The teacher causes the student to give charity.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: dāśṛ dāne. ṛkāro viśeṣaṇārthaḥ. dāśati, dadāśa, dāśitā, dāśiṣyati. sakarmakaḥ, seṭ, parasmaibhāṣī. dānam arpaṇaṃ ca asya arthaḥ.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: dāśṛ dāne. dāśati. havirādīnāṃ dāne prayujyate. dāśaḥ ityādi rūpāṇi asyaiva bhavanti.

meanings.English: to give, to offer, to grant, to present
meanings.Russian: davat, prinosit v dar, darit, odaryavat

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'dasi' (daṃs) means 'to see', 'to perceive', or 'to show/manifest'. Because it has an indicatory short 'i' (idit), a nasal (anusvara/num) is inserted before the final consonant, forming 'daṃsati' in the basic present tense. When used with causative affixes, it means to cause someone to see or to display something clearly.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakara (present tense), prathama-purusha (third person), ekavacana (singular)
scenarios.example_english: The sage perceives the truth.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (causative), kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, prathama-purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The teacher reveals the path to the student.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: dasi darśane. idittvān num. daṃsati. darśana-vyāpāre 'sya prayogaḥ.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: dasi darśane. ididayaṃ daṃsati, didaṃsiṣati. darśanārthe sakarmakaḥ.

meanings.English: to see, perceive, view, manifest

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'gaj' means to make a roaring or loud sound, to trumpet like an elephant, or to be proud/intoxicated. In basic Parasmaipada form, it describes the subject producing a sound or roaring. When used with a causative suffix (Nic), it means to cause someone or something to roar or resound.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana (Simple present active)
scenarios.example_english: The lion roars loudly in the forest.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (Causative), Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: causes to resound / makes something roar
scenarios.example_english: The cloud makes the vault of the sky resound.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti analyzes 'gaja shabde ca' as an unaccented, vowel-ending root (akaranta upadesha) belonging to the Bhvadi gana. It takes the Parasmaipada terminations in active voice. Because it is marked as Set, it admits the augment it in non-sarvadhatuka affixes like it-agama (e.g., gajita, gajitum). The meaning 'shabde' encompasses roaring, trumpeting, and deep resonant vocalization.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin in Kshiratarangini notes that 'gaj' denotes making sound ('shabdana'), intoxication, or loud clamor. Derived nominals such as 'gaja' (elephant) stem directly from this root due to their characteristic trumpeting and majestic pride. It follows the standard pattern of shabdanartha Bhvadi roots forming gajati, jagaja, gajita.

meanings.English: to sound, to roar, to trumpet, to be intoxicated or proud
meanings.French: rugir, barrit, retentir, faire du bruit

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'rah' means to abandon, leave behind, or separate from. In standard active voice (Parasmaipada), it describes an agent who leaves or gives up something or someone. When used in causative forms, it conveys making someone abandon or empty a space.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakara (present tense), Prathama purusha (third person), Ekavacana (singular)
scenarios.example_english: The sage abandons delusion.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (causative), Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: causes to leave / causes to abandon
scenarios.example_english: The guru makes the student give up fault.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti analyzes 'raha tyage' as a root denoting abandonment or relinquishment. It forms present stem 'rahati' by taking the standard 'sap' vikaranapratyaya of the Bhvadi class. In the perfect tense (lit), reduplication produces 'raraha' and 'rahatuhi'. Being set, it admits the intermediate augment 'it' in Ardhadhatuka affixes such as the past participle 'rahita'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines 'raha' in the sense of 'tyaga' (leaving, deserting, or loneliness/seclusion from which derivatives like 'rahas' and 'rahita' arise). The root operates regularly in Parasmaipada without special stem alterations in Sarvadhatuka forms.

meanings.English: to leave, to abandon, to forsake, to quit

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root mlecch means to speak indistinctly, utter unclearly, or speak a foreign/incomprehensible tongue. In the active voice (Parasmaipada), it describes a subject speaking vaguely or inarticulately. When converted to the causative form (nic), it means to cause someone to speak indistinctly or to distort speech.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga (active voice), lat-lakara (present tense), prathama-purusha, eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The child speaks indistinctly due to drowsiness.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: nic-pratyaya (causative), kartari prayoga, lat-lakara, prathama-purusha, eka-vacana
scenarios.meaning: Causes to speak unclearly / renders speech incomprehensible.
scenarios.example_english: He distorts his speech out of fear.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: mlecha avyaktayam vaci. asphuta-uccarane ityarthah. bhvadir udattah parasmaipadi set. mlecchati, mimleccha, mlecchita, mlecchisyati.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: mlecha avyakte. avyaktam aspashtam bhasate ityarthah. mlecchati, mimlecchatu ityadi.

meanings.English: to speak indistinctly, to speak an unintelligible or foreign tongue
meanings.Hindi: aspat bolna, avyakt boli bolna, mleccha bhasha bolna
meanings.Bengali: aspashta bhabe bola, abodh bhashay katha bola
meanings.Chinese: fayin buqing, shuo bu dong de hua

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root hve means to call, invite, summon, or challenge. Because it has an indicatory marker n (nit), it can be conjugated in both Parasmaipada and Atmanepada. When the caller calls someone for someone else or generally, Parasmaipada is used; when calling for one's own sake or when challenging an opponent in competition, Atmanepada is traditionally preferred.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari parasmaipadam (general action / for another)
scenarios.example_english: The mother calls the child home.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari atmanepadam (spardhayam / kartrabhipraye kriyaphale)
scenarios.example_english: The wrestler challenges another wrestler to a combat.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: hven spardhayam ahvane ca. nitvad ubhayapadi. spardha sangharsah, ahvanam akarah. sap-pratyaye gune 'av'-adese ca 'hvayati', 'hvayate' iti bhavatah. ardhadhatuke 'hva' ityasya 'va' ityadesah kvacid bhavati, kiti tu samprasaranam 'hu' iti rupasiddhir bhavati.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: hven spardhayam ahvane ca. spardha utkarseccha, ahvanam svarasabdabhimukhibhavanam. sisyadin ahvayati, yuddhartham spardhaya ca hvayate. anidayam dhatu.

meanings.English: to call, summon, invite, or challenge
meanings.Hindi: bulana, pukarna, ahvana karna, chunauti dena

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root kvan means to make a ringing, jingling, or musical sound, like bells, anklets, or lutes. In the standard active voice (Parasmaipada), it describes the object itself ringing (kvanati). In the causative form (Nic-pratyaya), it describes a person playing an instrument or making something jingle (kvanayati).

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga (Present Active, 3rd Person Singular, Lat)
scenarios.example_english: The anklet tinkles.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (Causative, Kartari Prayoga)
scenarios.example_english: The musician plays the lute.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti explains 'kvana sabde' under the Bhvadi class as denoting inarticulate musical or jingling sounds (avyakta-dhvani). Being in the Parasmaipada section, it takes standard kartari sap-vyanjana inflections yielding kvanati, akvanit, and kvanisyati with an it-agama.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes in Kshiratarangini that 'kvana' belongs to the series of acoustic roots alongside svana and dhvana, primarily applied to resonant, pleasant instrumental or metallic sounds such as the ringing of bells and strings.

meanings.English: to sound, to tinkle, to ring, to jingle
meanings.Bengali: shabda kara, jhankarita haoya, baje utha
meanings.Chinese: fa chu ding dong sheng, ming xiang

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'śardh' denotes the natural physiological action of expelling downward wind or breaking wind. In simple active voice (Parasmaipada), it shows a person or animal passing gas. In causative forms with the Nic suffix, it expresses causing or prompting relief/emission of digestive gas.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, prathama-purusha, eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The man suffering from indigestion breaks wind.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic-pratyaya), Lat lakara, prathama-purusha, eka-vacana
scenarios.meaning: causes to expel wind / induces discharge of gas
scenarios.example_english: The medicine causes the trapped gas to be expelled.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'śardh' is categorized under the Bhvadi-gana with the meaning 'utsarge' (specifically indicating apānavāyutyāga, the excretion or expulsion of flatus). It forms 'śardhati' in the present tense, taking the Guna vowel change and standard Parasmaipada inflections.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines the root as 'utsarge kutsite ca śabde', showing the physical expulsion of apāna wind accompanied by a low, unpleasant sound.

meanings.English: to break wind, to fart, to discharge flatulence
meanings.Kannada: apana vayu bidu, vayu visarjane madu

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'dhvañc' belongs to the first conjugation (Bhvadi gana) and means to move or go. In its standard active form (Parasmaipada), it describes an agent moving or going forward. When converted into the causative form (nic), it signifies causing someone or something to move or directing movement.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakara (present tense), prathama purusha (third person singular)
scenarios.example_english: The deer moves through the forest.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (nic-pratyaya), Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara (present tense)
scenarios.meaning: Causes to move or drives forward
scenarios.example_english: The cowherd makes the cow move.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti explains dhvanca in the sense of gati (motion). As a set root in the Bhvadi class, it takes the standard shap vikarana and forms dhvancati in the present tense, retaining the nasal in Sarvadhatuka environments.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes in the Kshiratarangini that dhvanca denotes movement (gatau). It conjugates regularly with Parasmaipada terminations, producing dhvancati, dadhvanca, and dhvancita.

meanings.English: to go, to move

transitivity: Sakarmaka / Akarmaka (Transitive when meaning to steal, Intransitive when meaning to move)

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'gluc' belongs to the first conjugation (Bhvadi-gana) and takes Parasmaipada terminations. In its simple present form (Kartari Prayoga), it undergoes guna strengthening of the vowel 'u' to 'o' before the thematic affix 'shap', yielding 'glocati'. It carries two distinct senses: stealing (surreptitious taking, which is transitive) and moving/going (which is intransitive). When converted into the causative (Nic), it becomes 'glocayati', meaning 'causes someone to steal or go'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga, Lat Lakara, Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana (Simple Present Active)
scenarios.example_english: The thief steals the wealth at night.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic Pratyaya (Causative), Lat Lakara, Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: Causes to steal / Directs to move away
scenarios.example_english: The master causes the servant to proceed to the forest.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti identifies 'glucI~' with the meaning 'steye gatau ca' (in the sense of theft and motion). It explains that the 'I' marker indicates the prohibition of nasal insertion or specific nit-operations, and notes that like 'grucI~', it undergoes guna of the penultimate 'u' in Sarvadhatuka affixes, forming 'glocati', 'aglocat', and 'jugloca' in Lit.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin in Kshiratarangini groups 'gruc' and 'gluc' together as synonyms denoting stealthy movement and theft ('steye gatau ca'). He notes the interchangeability of 'r' and 'l' (ralayoraikyam) between 'gruc' and 'gluc', detailing forms such as 'glocati' and the reduplicated perfect 'jugloca'.

meanings.English: to steal, to go, to move stealthily

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'kap' means to tremble, shake, or move. It is conjugated in Atmanepada to indicate an intrinsic involuntary trembling or moving action of the subject.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat-lakara, Prathama-purusha, Eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The leaf on the tree shakes due to the force of the wind.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (Causative), Lat-lakara, Prathama-purusha, Eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: Fear causes the boy to tremble.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: kapate calane iti anudattettvad atmanepadam. dharanamiti kecit, calanartho'yam. cakara cakape, kapita ityadi set-tvam.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: kapi calane. kampate ityarthah. anudatteta atmanepadina kapate, cakape ityadi.

meanings.English: to tremble, shake, or move

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'trap' means to feel shy, bashful, or embarrassed. In its basic form (Atmanepada), it shows the subject experiencing modesty or shame. When used with the causative affix nic, it turns into 'trapayati' or 'trapayate', meaning to make someone feel shy or ashamed.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga (present indicative 3rd person singular, Atmanepada)
scenarios.example_english: The young boy feels shy in the presence of the teacher.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: nic-pratyaya (causative present indicative 3rd person singular)
scenarios.meaning: causes to feel ashamed / makes one shy
scenarios.example_english: Lying makes the child feel ashamed.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: trapusr lajjayam. anudattetvadanudattopadeshacca atmanepadi. lajjayam vridayamityarthah. trapate, tetrape. radibhyo nishthayamitinishedhe prapte trapasphurasancanamanitityanitkaryam.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: trapusr lajjayam. trapate. lajja vrida. atmanepadi seshanivrittyarthah. trapita trapta iti ca rupa-vikalpah.

meanings.English: to feel shy, to be ashamed, to feel modest

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'daks' means to grow, thrive, prosper, or to be quick and capable. Because it is an Atmanepadi root, it takes middle endings like -te, -ete, -nte. When used in the causative (Nic), it takes Padas based on who benefits or follows standard Ubhayapada causative rules, meaning to cause to grow or to train someone to be capable.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, prathama-purusha, eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The boy prospers and becomes capable through knowledge.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (causative), Lat lakara, prathama-purusha, eka-vacana
scenarios.meaning: causes to grow or makes skilled/efficient
scenarios.example_english: The teacher makes the disciple skilled and capable.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: daksa vriddhau shighrarthe ca. anudattettvad atmanepadi. dakshate, daksamcakre, daksita, daksishyate. vriddhih abhivridhhih, shighrarthah tvararthah.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: daksa vriddhau shighre ca. daksate. vriddhau siddhih, shighratvam pravinyam. tato dakshah samarthah pravinah.

meanings.English: to grow, to prosper, to be capable or act quickly
meanings.Hindi: badhana, vriddhi pana, kushal ya chatur hona
meanings.Bengali: briddhi pawa, unnati labh kora, daksha howa
meanings.German: wachsen, gedeihen, geschickt oder schnell handeln
meanings.French: grandir, prosperer, etre habile ou prompt
meanings.Russian: rasti, procvetat, byt umelym ili bystrym

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'drā' expresses moving in a disgraceful, distressed, or frightened manner, such as running away or fleeing in terror. In simple active voice (Parasmaipada), it describes the subject fleeing or roaming helplessly. When the causative suffix (ṇic) is applied, it means causing someone to run away or putting an enemy to flight.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga (active voice), laṭ-lakāra (present tense), prathama-puruṣa, eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The terrified servant flees in distress.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: ṇyanta (causative), kartari prayoga, laṭ-lakāra, prathama-puruṣa, eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The brave warrior puts the enemies to flight.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti explains 'drā kutsāyāṃ gatau' as indicating despised or reproachable movement, primarily denoting the act of fleeing (palāyana) under panic or roaming in utter degradation. Forms include drāyati, dadrāu, and adrāsīt.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes under 'drā kutsāyāṃ gatau' that kutsitā gati denotes moving in a condemned, ruined, or disordered manner (palāyate ityarthaḥ). Being anit and akarmaka, it forms non-copious intransitive paradigms in primary conjugation.

meanings.English: to run away, to flee, to wander in distress
meanings.Hindi: bheebhit hokar bhagna, durdasha me bhatakana
meanings.Russian: bezhat v strakhe, skitat'sya v bedstvii

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'kuṭ' means to be crooked, to bend, or to act deceitfully. In normal active voice (Parasmaipada), it describes the subject naturally bending, curling, or acting in a crooked manner. When using the causative suffix (Nic), the form becomes 'koṭayati', which means to make something bend or curve intentionally.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga, Lat Lakara (Present Tense), Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: A wicked person always acts deceitfully in interactions.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic-pratyaya), Lat Lakara, Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The worker bends the wooden stick.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti records 'kuta kautilye' in the Bhvadi class. Guna of the penultimate 'u' takes place before Sarvadhatuka affixes yielding 'kotati'. It is characterized as a Set root with Parasmaipada inflection.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin interprets 'kuta' in the sense of crookedness (kautilya) in shape or moral behavior, noting the regular vowel strengthening (guna) to 'o' in the present stem.

meanings.English: to be crooked, to bend, to curl, to act deceitfully
meanings.Tamil: valavu adaiyudhal, konalaga iruthal, kodiya muraiyil nadathal
meanings.Hindi: tedha hona, mudna, kutil vyavahar karna
meanings.French: etre tordu, se courber, agir avec fourberie
meanings.Chinese: wan qu, bian wan, bu cheng shi

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'kram' primarily means to step, walk, stride, or advance. In simple active voice without prefixes, it takes lengthened forms in Parasmaipada (krāmati), meaning 'he strides'. When combined with prefixes (upasargas) or used to denote self-motivated progression or enterprise, it switches systematically between Parasmaipada and Atmanepada, altering shades of meaning from peaceful stepping to attacking, crossing, or advancing.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Atmanepada (Kartari prayoga, showing continuity or self-motivated stride)
scenarios.meaning: He strides forward or proceeds steadily
scenarios.example_english: The boy proceeds along the path.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic pratyaya)
scenarios.meaning: Causes someone or something to step or advance
scenarios.example_english: The teacher makes the student advance to higher levels.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti categorizes 'kramu' under 'padavihare' (movement of feet/striding). It highlights that because of the 'u' marker (udit), it allows optional it-agama in select kit-affixes. It details the conditions under which lengthening of the vowel occurs in Parasmaipada (krāmati) and analyzes rules governing prefix interactions (such as 'vi-ati-kram', 'a-kram', and 'pra-kram').
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines 'padavihara' as step-by-step movement or walking with feet ('padabhyam caranam'). He notes the udit nature of the root and outlines the derivation of derived nominals like krama, kranti, and vikrama, clarifying contextual shifts between transitivity (crossing an obstacle) and intransitivity (walking).

meanings.English: to step, stride, walk, advance, cross over
meanings.Telugu: adugu veyu, kramincu, munduku sagu, datu
meanings.Tamil: ettu vai, nadanthu sel, kadanthu sel, munneru
meanings.Hindi: kadam badhana, dag bharna, par karna, kramashah chalna
meanings.Bengali: pa barano, kramasho agano, atikram kara
meanings.French: marcher a grands pas, enjamber, avancer, franchir

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'hmal' belongs to the Bhvadi class and fundamentally means to move, waver, or shake. Because it denotes an intransitive action of motion or trembling, it takes Parasmaipada endings in its basic form. When used in the causative (nic) form, it changes from an intransitive verb into a transitive verb meaning 'to cause to move' or 'to shake something'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga (active voice, simple present tense, lat-lakara, 3rd person singular)
scenarios.example_english: The tree sways in the wind.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: nic-pratyaya (causative present tense, lat-lakara, 3rd person singular)
scenarios.example_english: The strong breeze causes the branches of the tree to shake.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti classifies 'hmala calane' as an intransitive root within the jvaladi subgroup of Bhvadi gana. It takes the affix sap in sarvadhatuka tenses producing standard forms like hmalati and jahmala in the perfect tense. Its semantic domain centers strictly on movement, wavering, and agitation.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin in Kshiratarangini notes that 'hmal' is grouped alongside jval, hval, and vmal as roots expressing agitation, unsteady movement, or trembling (calanartha). He explains the regular inflectional patterns following the canonical Bhvadi rules.

meanings.English: to move, to shake, to waver, to tremble

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'trap' expresses the emotion of feeling shy, modest, embarrassed, or ashamed. By default, it operates in the Atmanepada voice (e.g., 'trapate'). When converted to a causative form using the Nic affix, it takes the meaning of putting someone to shame or making someone feel shy.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakara (present tense), Prathama purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The child feels shy in the assembly.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic-pratyaya), Parasmaipada, Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: causes someone to feel ashamed / puts to shame
scenarios.example_english: The teacher makes the student feel ashamed due to misbehaviour.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The anubandha 'ū' in 'trapūṣ' indicates its anudatta property leading to Atmanepada designation. 'Lajjā' is explained as modesty, hesitation, or bashfulness arising from respect, decorum, or avoidance of improper actions.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes the root under 'trapūṣ lajjāyām' as an anudattet verb yielding 'trapate' in Sarvadhatuka formations and discusses standard reduplication in lit ('tatrape') and variable it-agarna in ardhadhatuka suffixes.

meanings.English: to be ashamed, to feel bashful, to be modest

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root kṣam means to endure, tolerate, or forgive. In its primary Bhvadi Atmanepada form (kṣamate), it expresses bearing difficulties patiently or forgiving someone. When converted to the causative form (kṣamayati), it means to cause someone to forgive, to pacify, or to ask for patience.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Bhvādi-gaṇa, Kartari prayoga, Laṭ-lakāra, Prathama-puruṣa, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: A virtuous person always forgives an offense.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Ṇij-anta (Causative), Kartari prayoga, Laṭ-lakāra, Prathama-puruṣa, Ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: Causes to forgive / asks for pardon / pacifies
scenarios.example_english: The student, realizing his fault, asks the teacher for forgiveness.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root kṣamūṣ is read with the anubandha ūṣ, indicating it belongs to the Atmanepada series in the Bhvadi gana. Its primary semantic scope is sahane (tolerating, patience, enduring hardship, and granting pardon). In Ardhadhatuka forms, it admits optional iṭ according to standard sutras.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes kṣamūṣ sahane as indicating forbearance and patience (titikṣā). The anubandha denotes intrinsic Atmanepada usage in its primary conjugation, yielding kṣamate in the present tense.

meanings.English: to endure, to tolerate, to forgive, to be patient

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'khaj' means to churn, agitate, or stir liquids, as well as to move. In the basic active voice (Parasmaipada), it describes someone stirring or churning something (e.g., milk or water). When converted into the causative form (Nic), it conveys making someone else churn or cause vigorous agitation.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Lat lakara, Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana (Basic Parasmaipada present tense)
scenarios.example_english: The cowherd girl churns the curd.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya, Lat lakara (Causative present tense)
scenarios.example_english: The mother makes the girl stir the milk.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'khaja manthane' belongs to the Bhvadi class and is inflected in Parasmaipada. In the Dhatupatha, its primary sense is 'manthana' (churning, stirring, or shaking). In the present tense, it takes the Shap vikarana without guna due to short penultimate vowel constraints, yielding forms such as khajati, akhajat, and khajishyari (with i-agama as it is Set).
