vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'khaja manthane', indicating motion coupled with churning or mechanical agitation of fluids. The derived noun 'khaja' or 'khajika' refers to a churning stick or ladle used for stirring.

meanings.English: to churn, stir, agitate

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'khūrd' means to play, frolic, or hop playfully. In its simple form (Kartari Prayoga), it is used in Parasmaipada to describe someone playing or jumping happily. In the causative form (Nich-pratyaya), it changes to mean making someone or an animal play and leap about.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga (present tense, active voice, 3rd person singular)
scenarios.example_english: The child plays and hops playfully in the garden.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: ṇic-pratyaya (causative present, 3rd person singular)
scenarios.meaning: causes to play / makes (someone) leap playfully
scenarios.example_english: The mother makes the baby play and jump happily.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: khūrda khelane. khelanam krīḍā gatiśca. seṭ parasmaipadī. khūrdati, cukhūrda, khūrditā, khūrdiṣyati.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: khūrda khelane. khelanaṃ vilāsaḥ krīḍanaṃ vā. dīrghavān set ca bhavati. khūrdati mṛgaḥ.

meanings.English: to play, to sport, to leap playfully

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'sad' transforms its stem to 'sīd-' before common present-tense endings to mean sinking down, sitting, drooping, or feeling dejected. When prefixes (upasargas) are added, it takes on well-known everyday meanings: 'ni + sad' becomes 'niṣīdati' (sits down), 'pra + sad' becomes 'prasīdati' (becomes happy or pleased), and 'vi + sad' becomes 'viṣīdati' (becomes despondent or sorrowful).

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat-lakara, Prathama-purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The tired traveler sinks down in the shade.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Upasarga 'pra' with Lat-lakara, Prathama-purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The teacher is pleased by the humility of the disciple.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The anit root ṣadḷ is taught in three primary meanings: viśaraṇa (decay, splitting, or disintegration), gati (movement or approaching), and avasādana (exhaustion, sinking, or despondency). By Paninian rule 'pāghrā...ṣadaḥ sīdaḥ', the root substitutes 'sīda' in Sarvadhatuka environments bearing the Śit marker. The anubandha 'lṛ' governs specific augment behaviors in non-conjugational tenses.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin analyzes viśaraṇa as avayava-viśleṣa (loosening or falling apart of parts), gati as gamana (motion), and avasādana as kheda-nimajjana (weariness and sinking down). In the active present system, the dental 's' remains except where phonological rules apply with upasargas, and 'sad' becomes 'sīd' under the regular substitution rule before Śap.

meanings.English: to sink down, to perish, to sit, to become exhausted
meanings.Tamil: utkar, sorvu adai, azhindu po, kizhe irangu
meanings.Hindi: baithana, dukhi hona, kshina hona, tutana
meanings.Bengali: bosa, kshina haoya, abasadagrasta haoya, dhvamsa haoya

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'grans' (derived from the idit root 'grasi~') means to scratch, furrow, write upon, or incise. It operates in the Atmanepada voice, taking middle-voice endings such as '-ate' in the present tense (kartari prayoga). When expressing an action directed to scratching or engraving, it uses standard first conjugation (Bhvadi) thematic marker 'sap' (a).

scenarios.grammar_trigger: lat lakara, prathama-purusha, eka-vacana, kartari prayoga (Active/Middle voice)
scenarios.example_english: The farmer furrows the ground.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: lun lakara, prathama-purusha, eka-vacana (Aorist)
scenarios.example_english: The sculptor carved a letter on the rock.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: grasi vilikhane. Idittvannum. 'vilikhanam' ullikhanam lekhanam va. Atmanepadi. Gransate, jagranse, gransita, gransishyate, agransishta.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: grasi vilikhane. Ididayam numarthah. Vilikhanam nakha-kashthadibhih kshatanam, lekhanam va. Gransate.

meanings.English: To scratch, furrow, scrape, incise, or engrave
meanings.Kannada: Giru, gachchu, bareyu, uttu salu madu
meanings.Telugu: Geeyu, ravvanta guchchu, chekku, dunnadamtho chaluvulu cheyu
meanings.Tamil: Kiruru, keeru, varaindu eluthu, uzhavu sal amai
meanings.Hindi: Kuredana, khurochana, likhana ya rekhankita karana
meanings.Bengali: Achada kata, khoncha deoya, ankana kora

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'has' fundamentally means to laugh, smile, or mock. In simple kartari prayoga (active voice), it expresses a person laughing or smiling. When used with a causative affix (Nic), it changes from intransitive to transitive, meaning 'to make someone laugh' or 'to amuse someone'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana (Simple Active Voice)
scenarios.example_english: The boy laughs with his friend.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (Causative), Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The jester makes everyone laugh.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti explains 'hasa hasane' as denoting the act of laughter or smiling (hasanam vikasanam mukhaprasadascha). Being marked without anuvadaka anubandhas, it takes standard shap vikarna and Parasmaipada endings yielding hasati, jahasa, hasita.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'hasati hasane mukhollase' indicating joyful facial expansion and laughter. It takes the set augment 'it' in ardhadhatuka environments, forming hasita, hasitum, and hasitavan.

meanings.English: To laugh, to smile, to mock

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'mā' means to measure, quantify, or assess. In its default Ātmanepada form (māte), it denotes the subject carrying out measurement for themselves or an inherent measure. When conjugated in the Causative (māpayati), it takes the sense of causing someone to measure, surveying land, or laying out/constructing according to measure.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Bhvādi Ātmanepada Lat Lakāra (Present Tense, 3rd Person Singular)
scenarios.example_english: The farmer measures the grain with a measuring vessel.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Ṇic-pratyaya) Parasmaipada Lat Lakāra
scenarios.meaning: causes to measure / builds / lays out by measure
scenarios.example_english: The royal architect lays out and constructs the city.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: māṅ māne. anudāttettvād ātmanepadam. māte, mamāte, mamire ityādi. ākārāntasyānudāttetaḥ sato 'niṭtvam.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: māṅ māne. mānam paricchedaḥ. māte, mamāte. ṇici māpayati. anudāttaṅitvādātmanepadam bhavati.

meanings.English: to measure, to mete out, to quantify, to value

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root kshīb expresses the action of becoming intoxicated, exhilarated, or wildly excited. In its basic active voice (Kartari Parasmaipada), it describes a subject getting drunk or losing composure through arrogance or intoxicants. In the causative form (Nich-pratyaya), it denotes causing someone to become intoxicated or exhilarated.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (Present indicative active, 3rd person singular, Lat lakara)
scenarios.meaning: He or she gets intoxicated or acts recklessly with excitement
scenarios.example_english: The intoxicated man acts wildly.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nich-pratyaya, Lat lakara)
scenarios.meaning: Causes someone to become intoxicated or excited
scenarios.example_english: The sweet wine intoxicates him.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root kshība is classified in the Bhvadi-gana having the meaning of mada (intoxication, exhilaration, or pride). Being an anudattopadesha-free consonant-ending root with id-agama, it follows standard Parasmaipada inflection taking the shap vikarana to yield kshībati.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes kshība in the sense of intoxication and pride (made). It forms regular Parasmaipada forms such as kshībati, chikshība, kshībitā, and accepts the intermediate augment it in ardhadhatuka environments.

meanings.English: to be intoxicated, to be excited or proud

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The verbal root takk belongs to the first conjugation (Bhvadi-gana) and is used in the Parasmaipada. It expresses the action of laughing or chuckling. In standard primary usage, the subject itself performs the act of laughing (takkati). When converted to the causative form (nic), it takes the sense of causing another to laugh or entertaining someone (takkayati).

scenarios.grammar_trigger: lat-lakara (present indicative), prathama-purusha, eka-vacana, kartari prayoga (Parasmaipada)
scenarios.example_english: The child laughs with great joy.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: nic-pratyaya (causative), lat-lakara, prathama-purusha, eka-vacana
scenarios.meaning: causes to laugh / makes someone laugh
scenarios.example_english: The jester makes everyone laugh.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: takka hasane. udattah parasmaibhashah set. takkati, tatakka, takkita, takkishyati, atakkīt. hasanartho bhavati.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: takka hasane. takkati. hasatityarthah. set, parasmaipadi, akarmakah.

meanings.English: to laugh, to chuckle, to smile

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'mruc' primarily means 'to go' or 'to move'. In the standard active voice (Parasmaipada), it describes a subject moving toward a destination. When used with causative suffixes (Nic), it changes to mean causing someone else to move or depart.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga (Present Active, Lat Lakara, 3rd Person Singular)
scenarios.example_english: The traveler goes to the village.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic Pratyaya (Causative, Lat Lakara, 3rd Person Singular)
scenarios.example_english: The father makes his son go to the village.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: mrucu gatau. UdattaH parasmaipadaH set. Laghupadhadirghabhavatve gunah, mrocati, mumroca, mrocita, amrocat.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: mrucu gatau. GatyarthaH. Guna-siddham ropam mrocati ityadi. Mloc-mruc-dvayamapi gatavarthe vartate.

meanings.English: to go, to move

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'pis' means 'to go' or 'to move'. It belongs to the first conjugation group (Bhvadi-gana) and takes Atmanepada (middle voice) endings in its basic form. In the causative (Nic) form, it expresses causing someone or something to move.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: lat lakara, prathama-purusha, eka-vacana (Atmanepada)
scenarios.example_english: The deer moves in the forest.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: nic-pratyaya (causative), lat lakara, prathama-purusha, eka-vacana (Parasmaipada)
scenarios.meaning: He/She makes someone go or sets in motion.
scenarios.example_english: The man makes the horse move.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: pisṛ gatau. ṛdit. anudāttetvāt ātmanepadam. pisate, pipese, pesitā, pesiṣyate. ṛditkaraṇaṃ 'aṅgalyāsaṃbhuktau' iti aṅvikalpārtham.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: pisṛ gatau. pisate. pipise vā pipese. ṛditatvāt caṅi hrasvo na bhavati iti kechit.

meanings.English: to go, to move, to glide

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'spardh' means to compete, rival, or vie with someone. Since it belongs to the Atmanepada category, the effort and ambition of competing or asserting superiority is centered on the agent. When used with causative markers, it signifies making someone compete or pitting rivals against each other.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Lat Lakara (Present Tense), Prathama Purusha (Third Person), Ekavacana (Singular), Kartari Prayoga (Active Voice)
scenarios.example_english: Arjuna competes with Karna.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Lan Lakara (Past Tense), Prathama Purusha (Third Person), Ekavacana (Singular), Kartari Prayoga (Active Voice)
scenarios.example_english: The runner competed fiercely for the victory.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The entry defines 'spardha sangharshe', where sangharsha denotes the competitive striving to excel above another ('aham-ahamika'). Being anudattet, the dhatu takes Atmanepada affixes by default in the active voice and is classified as set for augment it.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines sangharsha as 'parasparotkarshabhipraya'—the mutual desire to demonstrate superiority or outdo a peer. Standard inflections include spardhate, paspardhe, and spardhita.

meanings.English: To compete, to vie with, to rival, to challenge
meanings.Hindi: Hod lagana, mukabala karna, spardha karna

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root mish means to sprinkle, wet, or moisten an object. As a standard Parasmaipada verb, it takes simple active endings to indicate someone pouring or sprinkling liquid onto something. When used in the causative (Nic), it signifies making someone else sprinkle or causing a substance to be moistened.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga, lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The gardener sprinkles the tree with water.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: nic pratyaya (causative), lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The farmer gets the field sprinkled by the servant.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: mishi secane - idit-rahitah shakaranto dhatu. mishati, mimesha, meshita, meshishyati. secanam nama jaladi-dravya-samparkena ardri-karanam.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: mishi secane - mishati. seshicati yan-rupam. meshayati iti niji rupam. ardrata-sampadana-vishyakah.

meanings.English: sprinkling, moistening, wetting

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'kan' belongs to the first group of verbs (Bhvadi-gana) and takes Parasmaipada endings. It conveys three interrelated actions: shining/radiating light, desiring or loving, and moving. When used in the simple present tense, the 'i' marker falls away, producing 'kanati'. Adding the causative suffix (Nic) forms 'kanayati', meaning 'to cause to shine' or 'to cause to desire'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga (Active Voice), Lat-lakara, Prathama-purusha, Eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The gem shines with brilliance.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic-pratyaya), Lat-lakara, Prathama-purusha, Eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The sunlight brightens everything.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti analyzes 'kani' with the marker 'i' as an indicator of semantic extension across dipti (radiance), kanti (desire, beauty, or love), and gati (movement). It forms 'kanati' in the present tense with standard Guna-less base application and takes the 'it' augment in non-conjugational tenses.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes in Kshiratarangini that 'kani diptikantigatisu' shares semantic characteristics with roots expressing brightness and desire. The root remains Parasmaipadi and undergoes normal affixation under Bhvadi general rules without lengthening of the vowel in simple tenses.

meanings.English: to shine, to love, to wish, to go

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'dhvras' means to move crookedly, zig-zag, or walk in an erratic and deceptive manner. In basic active form (dhvrasati), it shows a subject moving in a curved or uneven path.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakara (present tense), prathama-purusha ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The snake moves crookedly on the path.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (causative), Lat lakara
scenarios.meaning: Causes someone or something to move crookedly
scenarios.example_english: The crookedness of the path causes the elephant to move in a zig-zag path.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'dhvrasu' is listed under the Bhvadi class in the sense of 'gatikautilyayoh' (crooked or deceitful movement). It is Parasmaipadi, vowel-ending in 'u' as an it-marker, takes the augment it (set), and yields standard active forms such as dhvrasati and dadhvrāsa without internal nasalization.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'dhvrasu gatikautilyayoh', explaining the action as 'kutila-gatih' (crooked motion). The root maintains the conjunct 'dhvr' throughout its basic sarvadhatuka conjugational paradigms like dhvrasati, dhvrasatah, dhvrasanti.

meanings.English: to move crookedly, to meander, to go in a zigzag manner
meanings.Chinese: wan qu xing jin, bu zheng er xing

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The verbal root 'dhu' means to shake, tremble, or agitate. In normal active usage, it describes something vibrating, shaking, or fluttering on its own. When made causative (Nic), it shifts to mean actively shaking something else or agitating it vigorously.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga, lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana (atmanepada)
scenarios.example_english: The leaf of the tree trembles due to the wind.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: nic pratyaya (causative), lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The strong wind causes the branches of the tree to shake.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The anubandha 'ñ' indicates Ubhayapada by Paninian rule 'svaritañitaḥ kartrabhiprāye kriyāphale'. In the Sarvadhatuka environment with Sap pratyaya, the root vowel 'u' undergoes Guna to 'o' and then Av-adesha before vowel-initial affixes, producing regular forms like dhavati and dhavate in the sense of trembling or shaking (kampane).
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin interprets 'dhuñ kampane' as denoting physical agitation, motion, and vibration. It forms anit bases in Bhvadi and is systematically distinguished from the ninth-class (Kryadi) root dhūñ kampane which yields dhunāti / dhunīte.

meanings.English: to shake, to tremble, to agitate

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root kṛp (often alternating phonetically with kḷp) belongs to the 1st conjugation (Bhvadi) and is strictly Atmanepada in its primary conjugation. Its core meaning is to be capable, fit, suitable, or able. In basic forms, it describes an inherent ability or readiness. When used with causative affixes or preverbs, it shifts to mean designing, imagining, arranging, or bringing about an outcome.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Lat (Present Indicative), Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana, Atmanepada
scenarios.meaning: is capable, is fit, or succeeds
scenarios.example_english: The intelligent student is capable of accomplishing the task.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic (Causative) + Upasarga 'pra', Parasmaipada, Lat, Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The teacher devises a new method.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: Madhaviya Dhatuvritti analyzes the root as 'kṛpū samarthye'. It is anudattet and anit, taking Atmanepada endings by default. Sayana highlights the phonetic relationship with the root kḷp ('kṛpo ro lah') and details its forms in the four universal tense-mood systems, confirming its application in contexts of adequacy, suitability, and functional power.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines the root under the semantic field of 'samarthya' (capability, competence, and readiness). He notes that the verbal base indicates the capacity or readiness of an agent or entity to manifest an action or fulfill a purpose.

meanings.English: to be capable, to be fit, to be adequate, to succeed
meanings.Hindi: samartha hona, yogya hona, sakshama hona
meanings.French: etre capable, etre propre a, convenir

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root kladi has an indicatory vowel 'i' (idit), which causes a nasal insertion (num-agama), turning the stem into 'kland-'. As an Atmanepada root in the Bhvadi class, it conjugates as 'klandate' in the present tense, denoting calling out, lamenting, or crying. In the causative form (nic), it takes the meaning of causing someone to weep or shout.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat-lakara, Prathama-purusha, Eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The distressed girl weeps and laments.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (Causative), Lat-lakara, Prathama-purusha, Eka-vacana
scenarios.meaning: causes someone to cry out or weep
scenarios.example_english: Cruel words cause her to lament.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root kladi is idit, thus taking the num-agama by rule 'idito num dhaatoh', yielding the verbal base kland-. It is inflected in the Atmanepada with standard set-characteristics in ardhadhatuka environments, giving forms like klandate, caklande, and klanditaa.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines the semantic domain as calling (aahvaana) and weeping (rodana). Being idit, the insertion of the penultimate nasal is permanent across conjugational and derivative categories, giving the present form klandate.

meanings.English: to call out, to weep, to lament

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'dā' (dāṇ) belongs to the Bhvadi class and means 'to give' or 'to bestow'. In the basic present and continuous systems (Sarvadhatuka tenses), the entire root changes its base form to 'yaccha-'. The recipient of the given object is put in the Dative case (Chaturthi Vibhakti).

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Present Tense (Lat Lakara), 3rd Person Singular (Prathama Purusha Ekavacana)
scenarios.example_english: The king gives wealth to the poor person.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Imperative Mood (Lot Lakara), 2nd Person Singular (Madhyama Purusha Ekavacana)
scenarios.example_english: O friend, give me the pen.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti identifies 'dāṇ dāne' as a root terminating in a long vowel ā with the indicatory letter ṇ. By the Paninian sutra 'pāghrādhmāsthāmnādāṇdṛśyaṛtisaśadsadāṃ pibajighradhamatiṣṭhamananyacchapaśyarcchadhāśīyasīdāḥ' (7.3.78), the root 'dāṇ' gets replaced by the stem 'yaccha' before Sarvadhatuka affixes, forming forms such as yacchati, ayacchat, and yacchetu.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin records 'dāṇ dāne' as an anit Parasmaipada root of the Bhvadi class. He distinguishes this root from the 3rd class root 'ḍudāñ dāne' (which forms dadāti) by highlighting that 'dāṇ' takes the special stem substitute 'yaccha' in Sarvadhatuka environments and does not undergo reduplication like Juhotyadi roots.

meanings.English: to give, grant, bestow, donate

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'kard' means to make an unpleasant, contemptible, or harsh sound (like croaking or screeching). In its basic active form (Parasmaipada), it describes a subject naturally producing a jarring or unpleasant noise. When used with a causative suffix (kardayati), it conveys making someone or something produce such an unpleasant sound.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana (active simple present)
scenarios.example_english: The frog croaks harshly in the mud.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (causative present)
scenarios.meaning: causes to make an unpleasant noise
scenarios.example_english: The boy causes the musical instrument to screech jarringly.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'karda' is grouped under Bhvadi-gana with the semantic designation 'kutsite śabde' (in making a contemptible or harsh sound). It is anudattopadesha-varjita and set, taking the kartari sap vikaraṇa yielding the regular base kardati.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines 'karda' in the sense of 'kutsita-śabda' (unpleasant or derogatory sound). Being a set root with standard guna-free base formation in the sarvadhatuka stems, it conjugates as kardati, kardataḥ, kardanti.

meanings.English: to make an unpleasant or harsh sound, to croak, to screech
meanings.Telugu: karkashamugā dhvani cheyu, asahyamaina shabdamu cheyu
meanings.Tamil: aruvrukkaththakka oli ezhuppu, karaparappaana oli seyyu
meanings.Hindi: kutsit ya karkash dhvani karna, bura shabda nikalna
meanings.Bengali: karkash ba kutsit shabda kora, bikat dhvani kora
meanings.German: ein unangenehmes Geraeusch machen, kraechzen, kreischen
meanings.French: emettre un son desagreable, coasser, grincer
meanings.Chinese: fa chu nan ting de sheng yin, guaza, wawa jiao

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'gard' means to speak contemptuously, utter abusive words, or shout harshly. Because it belongs to the Atmanepada class, the action reflects an internal attitude or posture of disdain during speech.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (Present indicative, third person singular, Atmanepada)
scenarios.example_english: The wicked person always speaks contemptuously.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Bhave prayoga (Impersonal passive)
scenarios.example_english: Contemptuous words are uttered by that untruthful one.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti specifies 'garda kutsitayam vaci' indicating base speech or abusive vocalization. It conjugates with intermediate 'i' (it) affix where applicable, forming standard Atmanepada forms like gardate, jagarde, and gardisyate.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin categorizes 'garda' under the subset of roots ending in 'da' signifying defective or reprehensible sound production (kutsitasabda / kutsitavani), emphasizing its inherently derogatory vocal nature.

meanings.English: to speak contemptuously or abusively

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'kū' means to make an indistinct sound, to coo, or to hum. Because it is marked with an indicator 'ñ' in the traditional Dhatupatha list, it conjugates in the Atmanepada (middle voice) as 'kuvate'. When using the causative suffix (Nic), it changes to 'kāvayati' meaning to cause someone or something to make a sound.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Atmanepada, Lat lakara (present tense), prathama-purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The cuckoo coos on the tree.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (causative), Parasmaipada, Lat lakara, prathama-purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: causes to make a sound / causes to coo
scenarios.example_english: The boy makes the bird chirp.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti analyzes 'kūñ shabde' as an Anit root belonging to the Bhvadi class. Being anudattett/nit, it assumes Atmanepada terminations. In Sarvadhatuka forms with Shap (a), the u-karanta stem undergoes guna and uvad-adesha yielding 'kuvate', 'kuvete', 'kuvante'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes under 'kūñ shabde' that this root denotes subtle vocalization, chirping, or indistinct humming. In ardhadhatuka operations, Anit rules apply where appropriate, generating forms like cukuve in the perfect tense (Lit).

meanings.English: to make an indistinct sound, to coo, to chirp, to hum
meanings.Kannada: dhvani madu, koogu, chilipili dhvani madu
meanings.German: girren, gurren, toene von sich geben

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'sphur' fundamentally means to throb, quiver, flash, or burst forth into view. In the basic active voice (Parasmaipada), it describes an eye twitching or lightning flashing on its own. When used with the causative affix (nic), it conveys causing something to vibrate, manifest, or shine brilliantly.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), lat-lakara (present tense), prathama-purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The eye twitches.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (nic-pratyaya), kartari prayoga, lat-lakara, prathama-purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: causes to throb / displays / manifests brightly
scenarios.example_english: The lightning causes brightness to flash forth.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti notes that 'sphura sphurane' signifies subtle motion, throbbing, trembling, and manifestation (calana, spandana, prakasana). It conjugates standardly in the Bhvadi class without Guna in basic Sarvadhatuka forms due to anit rules, producing 'sphurati', and in Lita it takes reduplication forming 'pusphora'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin states that 'sphura' denotes pulsation, shaking, or sudden shining ('sphuranam calanam diptirva'). It follows the standard Parasmaipada inflection of roots ending in consonants with penultimate short vowels.

meanings.English: to throb, quiver, flash, radiate
meanings.Bengali: furok kora, kompit haoa, jholmol kora

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The verb root 'pat' means to go, wander, or move. In simple active voice, it shows a subject moving or walking. When combined with the causative suffix nic, it shifts to mean making someone or something move or go.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakara (present tense), 3rd person singular
scenarios.example_english: The deer wanders in the forest.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (causative), Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, 3rd person singular
scenarios.example_english: The cowherd drives the cows forward.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'pata' is read in the sense of motion (gatau). Being halanta with short 'a' as anudatta it-marker, it takes Parasmaipada affixes and takes intermediate 'i' (it-agama) in the non-sarvadhatuka ardhadhatuka forms, producing forms like patati, papata, patita.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'pata gatau' under the class of simple verbs of motion. It takes normal guna in specific non-sarvadhatuka sets and forms regular parasmaipada conjugations.

meanings.English: to go, to move, to wander

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'khya' means to tell, narrate, or make something known. In the basic active voice (Parasmaipada), it describes an agent narrating or speaking a story. When augmented with prefixes like 'pra' (prakhya) or used in causative forms, it conveys making something famous or widely celebrated.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana (active indicative present)
scenarios.example_english: The sage narrates the story.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: nic pratyaya (causative present with prefix pra)
scenarios.example_english: The king proclaims the royal decree.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti explains 'khya kathane' as signifying the act of recounting, enumerating, or revealing facts. It notes that the root takes anit status and undergoes typical a-karanta substitutions in non-sarvadhatuka environments.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines 'khya kathane' as public declaration or verbal recounting ('kathana'). The vritti details its forms in the simple present such as 'khyati' and highlights its derived nominals like 'khyati' (fame, cognition) and participial forms.

meanings.English: to tell, narrate, declare, recount

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'pru' means to jump, leap, or move gracefully. Because it possesses the marker ṅ (ṅit), it exclusively takes Atmanepada endings in its basic form (pravate). In the causative (nic), it takes āy-augment and becomes prāvayati / prāvayate, meaning to cause someone to leap or move forward.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, prathama-purusha, eka-vacana (Atmanepada via anudatta-nita atmanepadam)
scenarios.meaning: He/she/it leaps, jumps, or moves forward.
scenarios.example_english: The deer leaps in the forest.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Hetumarti nic (causative), Lat lakara, prathama-purusha, eka-vacana (Parasmaipada)
scenarios.example_english: The boy makes the horse leap forward.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: pruṅ gatau - ṅitvād ātmanepadī. śap, guṇaḥ, avādeśḥ - pravate. aniṭkārikāsu 'śricyupludrupruśvāśca' ity anena aniṭtvam. liṭi puprive. luṅi aproṣṧa.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: pruṅ gatau. ṅitvāt taṅ. pravate, puprive, protā. gatir iha viśikhagativat plutigatir vā lakṣyate.

meanings.English: to leap, to jump, to move, to glide

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'kṛṣ' fundamentally means to scratch, furrow, plough, or drag/attract. Because it is marked with an elided svarita accent (svaritet), it belongs to Ubhayapada, meaning it takes Parasmaipada endings when the action is general or performed for someone else, and Atmanepada endings when the fruit of the action directly benefits the subject. Adding the causative suffix (ṇic) changes the meaning to 'causing someone to plough or pull'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Bhvadi / Kartari Prayoga (Parasmaipada)
scenarios.example_english: The farmer ploughs the field with two oxen.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Bhvadi / Kartari Prayoga (Atmanepada)
scenarios.example_english: Seeking the harvest, he tills his own field.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nich-pratyaya (Causative / Parasmaipada)
scenarios.meaning: causes to plough / causes to drag
scenarios.example_english: The landowner has the ground ploughed by the farmhand.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: Sayana explains 'kṛṣa vilekhane' as signifying the scratching or breaking up of the earth (bhūmer udghātanam/vidāraṇam) as well as pulling or attracting (ākarṣaṇam). Because it possesses an elided svarita accent, it operates in both padas (svariteto kartrabhiprāye kriyāphale ātmanepadam). In non-sarvadhatuka forms, it demonstrates specific sandhi variations with the sibilant and retroflex consonant clusters, yielding forms such as karkṣyati or krakṣyati.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines 'vilekhana' as the action of furrowing or dividing the soil with a ploughshare (halādinā bhūmer lekhanaṁ vidāraṇam). He highlights related semantic extensions including dragging, drawing lines, and physical attraction. The root forms standard nominal derivatives such as kṛṣi (agriculture), kṛṣaka (farmer), and karṣaṇa (drawing or tilling).

meanings.English: to plough, to furrow, to drag, to pull, to attract
meanings.Bengali: chash kara (jami chasha), tana, akarshan kara

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'iksh' fundamentally denotes visual perception or observation ('to see' or 'to look'). As an Atmanepada verb in the Bhvadi class, its primary third-person singular present form is 'ikshate'. When combined with upasargas (prefixes) like 'pra' or 'pari', it yields specialized meanings such as viewing a performance or examining thoroughly.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakara (present tense), prathama purusha (third person), ekavacana (singular)
scenarios.example_english: The boy looks at the moon.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Upasarga 'pari' + iksh (Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara)
scenarios.example_english: The teacher examines the lessons.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: iksha darshane. ikshate. anudattetvat atmanepadam. set. darshanam ihakshina vyaparah upalabdhirva.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: iksha darshane. ikshate, aikshishta, ikshita. pradiyogena parikshate prekshate ityadi siddhyati.

meanings.English: to see, to look at, to observe, to behold

transitivity: Sakarmaka (in the sense of praising) / Akarmaka (in the sense of rejoicing)

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'mand' means to praise someone or to rejoice/be delighted. It belongs to the 1st conjugation (Bhavadi gana) and takes Atmanepada endings. When used ordinarily, it expresses rejoicing or glorification. In causative (Nic) form, it expresses making someone joyful or causing someone to celebrate.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Lat (Present Tense), Prathama Purusha (3rd Person), Ekavacana (Singular), Kartari Prayoga (Active Voice)
scenarios.example_english: The devotee praises and rejoices in Hari with devotion.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic (Causative), Lat (Present Tense), Prathama Purusha (3rd Person), Ekavacana (Singular)
scenarios.example_english: The words of the friend gladden the king.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti analyzes 'madi' as idit, acquiring the penultimate nasal (num-agama) to form the base 'mand-'. It is marked with anudanatta-it, establishing its Atmanepada character. It functions in the senses of stuti (praise), harsha (joy), and moda (exhilaration), taking the suffix shap in Sarvadhatuka environments.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'madi stutiharṣayoḥ' with num-agama due to the idit marker, yielding 'mandate'. The root connotes both transitive adulation (stutau) and intransitive state of joy (harṣa-sukhe).

meanings.English: to praise, to rejoice, to delight, to be glad
meanings.Hindi: stuti karna, harshit hona, prasanna hona
meanings.Bengali: stuti kora, anandita howa, harshito howa

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'cak' means to be satisfied, contented, or to resist/recoil. In the active voice (Parasmaipada), it simply expresses the subject feeling contented or becoming full. When used with causative suffixes (Nic), it signifies making someone else satisfied or causing contentment.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Lat lakara, prathama-purusa, eka-vacana (Simple Active Present)
scenarios.example_english: The deer is satisfied after drinking water.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (Causative), Lat lakara, prathama-purusa, eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The mother satisfies the child with sweet pudding.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root caka is glossed under trpti (contentment/satisfaction) and prativestana (resistance/obstruction or coiling). Being a standard dental-initial velar-final Bhvadi root, it takes shap vikarana and forms simple active conjugations like cakati, cacaka, cakita.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes caka in the dual sense of trpti (satiety) and prativestana (covering/resisting). It conjugates regularly in Parasmaipada without guna of the short 'a' in simple sarvadhatuka stems.

meanings.English: to be satisfied, to be content, to resist or repel
meanings.Hindi: trpta hona, santusta hona ya rokana

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'gru' belongs to the first conjugation (Bhvadi gana) and is exclusively Atmanepada due to the indicatory letter 'ṅ' (Anudatta-ṅit). It expresses the action of going or moving. With the present tense marker 'śap' (a), the root vowel 'u' undergoes guṇa to 'o' and then changes to 'av', producing the primary form 'gravate'. In causative forms, the affix 'ṇic' adds the meaning of causing someone to move ('grāvayati').

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakara (present indicative), 3rd person singular
scenarios.example_english: The deer moves slowly in the forest.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Luṅ lakara (aorist past), 3rd person singular
scenarios.example_english: The traveler moved towards the city.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'gruṅ' is listed under the Bhvadi gana with the semantic indicator 'gatyarthaḥ' (signifying motion). Being ṅit, it takes Atmanepada affixes (anudāttaṅita ātmanepadam). The guṇa of 'u' followed by 'av' ādeśa yields 'gravate' in the present tense. It is seṭ, admitting the augment 'iṭ' in ardhadhatuka environments.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin categorizes 'gruṅ' alongside 'khruṅ' and 'gluṅ' in the sub-group of motion verbs (gatyarthāḥ). The morphological development conforms to regular u-ending roots of the first class, demonstrating standard ātmanepada terminations with iṭ-āgama in the non-sarvadhatuka tenses.

meanings.English: to go, to move

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The verbal root 'gai' denotes the action of singing or producing melodious sound. In standard active voice (Kartari Prayoga), it takes Parasmaipada endings to mean 'sings'. When the causative suffix (ṇic) is added, it takes the augment 'puk' to form 'gāpayati', meaning 'causes someone to sing' or 'teaches singing'. In the passive voice (Karmaṇi Prayoga), it undergoes vowel reduction to form 'gīyate' (is sung).

scenarios.grammar_trigger: lat-lakāra, prathama-puruṣa, eka-vacana, kartari prayoga (parasmaipada)
scenarios.example_english: The singer sings a melodious song.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: ṇic-pratyaya (causative), lat-lakāra, prathama-puruṣa, eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The teacher makes the disciples sing the hymn.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'gai' is listed in the Bhvādi-gaṇa with the canonical sense of 'śabde' (sound/singing). It is categorized as aniṭ and transitive (sakarmaka). By the rule 'ādeca upadeśe 'śiti' (6.1.45), the final diphthong 'ai' is replaced by long 'ā' before non-śit affixes and in initial operational stages, leading to forms such as 'gāyati' in sārwadhātuka environments with śap, 'jagau' in liṭ, and 'gātā' in luṭ.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin analyzes 'gai śabde' as the fundamental verbal root for melodious vocalization and song. He highlights the phonological changes where the diphthong yields ākāra ('ātvam') before specific affixes, yielding regular active derivations like 'gāyati', reduplicated perfect forms like 'jagau' / 'jaguḥ', and contracted participial forms like 'gīta'.

meanings.English: to sing, to chant, to praise in song

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'dhrā' describes three kinds of movement—such as flying, gliding, or moving along a path. In its basic active form (Parasmaipada), the subject moves or glides on their own. When used with a causative affix, it means directing or causing another to move or glide smoothly.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat-lakara (present indicative), 3rd person singular
scenarios.example_english: The bird glides in the sky.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (causative), Lat-lakara, 3rd person singular
scenarios.meaning: Causes to glide or move along
scenarios.example_english: The wind makes the leaf glide along.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'dhrā' belongs to the Bhvādi-gaṇa and is given in the sense of 'gatitraye' (three modes of movement). Being Parasmaipadi and Anit, it forms the present tense base 'dhrāya-' with the universal Śap-pratyaya, yielding the primary finite form 'dhrāyati'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kṣīrasvāmin elucidates 'gatitraya' as the threefold distinction of movement—namely upward (flying/rising), downward (dropping/descending), and transverse (gliding/horizontal moving). The root signifies smooth multi-directional motion.

meanings.English: to move, to glide, to fly in different directions
meanings.Hindi: calnā, uṛnā, vividha rūpoṃ meṃ gati karnā
meanings.Bengali: calā, oṛā, vividha gati prāpta howā

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root ksam means to tolerate, endure, or forgive. In its basic Atmanepada form (ksamate), the subject patiently bears a difficulty or forgives someone. When used in the Causative form (ksamayati), it means causing someone to forgive, asking for pardon, or pacifying someone.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Bhvadi Lat Lakara (Present Tense, Atmanepada, Prathama Purusha Ekavacana)
scenarios.example_english: The noble person endures criticism patiently.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic Pratyaya (Causative, Lat Lakara, Parasmaipada)
scenarios.meaning: causes to forgive / asks forgiveness / pacifies
scenarios.example_english: The student asks the teacher for forgiveness.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: Madhaviya Dhatuvritti records ksamus sahane in the Bhvadi gana. The anubandha us indicates specific morphological nuances in certain derivations. The root takes Atmanepada endings under normal conditions, yielding ksamate, caksame, and aksamista or aksanta, signifying mental forbearance, endurance of pain, and pardon of transgression.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin analyzes ksamus with the meaning of sahane (endurance and patience). He highlights that ksam refers to the capacity of the mind to remain unperturbed when confronted with adverse conditions or offenses, showing both physical endurance and moral forgiveness.

meanings.English: to endure, to tolerate, to forgive, to bear patiently

canonical_dhatvartha: gatau (in the sense of moving or going)

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'kṣviṅgh' belongs to the first conjugation (Bhvadi gana) and inherently means 'to move' or 'to go'. In its basic active form (Parasmaipada), it describes an agent moving on its own. When used with the causative suffix (-nic-), it switches to meaning 'causing to move' or 'propelling'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Bhvadi gana kartari prayoga (Parasmaipada, Lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana)
scenarios.example_english: The deer moves swiftly in the forest.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative form (Nic pratyaya)
scenarios.meaning: causes to move or drives forward
scenarios.example_english: The charioteer causes the horse to move.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: Madhaviya Dhatuvritti places ksvingha in the varganta series of roots meaning gatau (movement). It forms present tense ksvinghati by regular Shab-vikarana and maintains set characteristics in ardhadhatuka affixes like aksvinghit.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes this root among the cluster of onomatopoeic and movement-denoting velar-final roots (ksvinka, ksvinkha, ksvinga, ksvingha). It is identified as taking parasmaipada inflections unconditionally.

meanings.English: to go, to move, to advance

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'syand' means to flow, stream, or trickle like water in a river or tears from eyes. In the standard Atmanepada form (syandate), it expresses the natural motion of a liquid flowing smoothly. When combined with prefixes like 'pra-', it describes an abundant gushing or streaming forth.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Lat Lakara, Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana (Kartari Atmanepada)
scenarios.example_english: The cool river flows from the mountain.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Lat Lakara with upasarga 'pra' (Intensified action)
scenarios.example_english: Tears of joy stream forth from the eyes.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: syandu prasravane. prasravanam sravanam ksharanam ca ityarthah. syandate, asyandata, sisyande. ubhayapaditvam tu nittvat.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: syandir prasravane. prasravanam dravasya sravanam gatih. syandate jalam, nadyah syandante.

meanings.English: to flow, to trickle, to stream, to ooze

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'puṭ' means to fold, bind together, envelop, or bring multiple things into intimate contact (saṃsarga). When used in standard active voice (Parasmaipada), it describes folding or uniting objects. When used in causative (Nic), it signifies making someone fold, wrap, or join materials together.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga (Active Voice, Laṭ-lakāra, Prathama-puruṣa, Ekavacana)
scenarios.meaning: Folds, binds, or brings together into contact
scenarios.example_english: The devotee folds the leaves together for worship.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Ṇic-pratyaya (Causative, Laṭ-lakāra, Prathama-puruṣa, Ekavacana)
scenarios.meaning: Causes to fold, roll, or envelop
scenarios.example_english: The father makes the boy fold the clothes.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: puṭa saṃsarge. Bhvādiḥ parasmaipadī seṭ. Saṃsargaḥ saṃśleṣaṇam ekībhāvaḥ. Puṭati, puṭitaḥ, apuṭīditīti rūpa-siddhiḥ.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: puṭa saṃsarge. Puṭati saṃbandham upanayannityarthaḥ. Saṃśleṣe saṃgrahe ca vartate.

meanings.English: to fold, to wrap, to bind together, to connect

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'spad' (spand) means to twitch, quiver, or move very slightly. In its basic Atmanepada form (spandate), it denotes a natural involuntary twitch or throb experienced by a subject. In the causative form with Nic (spandayati), it means to cause something to stir, vibrate, or flutter.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakara (present tense), Prathama purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The left eye twitches.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (causative), Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The gentle wind makes the leaves quiver.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'spadi kiñciccalane' is idit, which causes the insertion of the nasal augment num (giving the base spand). Being anudattet, it takes Atmanepada affixes (spandate, paspande, spandita). The primary meaning is alpacalana (slight or subtle physical movement).
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines the root in the sense of 'calanam alpiyah' (a minute or fractional movement). Due to the 'i' marker (idit), the penultimate 'n' appears systematically across all primary tenses, remaining set and middle voice.

meanings.English: to quiver, to twitch, to throb, to move slightly

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'trap' expresses feeling shy, bashful, or modest. Being an Atmanepada verb, it depicts an internal emotional state experienced by the subject. When combined with the causative suffix nic, it shifts meaning to causing someone to feel embarrassed or shaming someone.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (present indicative 3rd person singular in Atmanepada)
scenarios.meaning: feels shy / is bashful / feels ashamed
scenarios.example_english: The boy feels shy in front of the sage.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (Causative formation)
scenarios.example_english: Speaking falsehood embarrasses a person.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'trapūṣ' belongs to the Bhvadi class and is used in the sense of lajja (shame, bashfulness, modesty). The final letter 'ṣ' and medial 'ū' are it-markers. It takes Atmanepada affixes (trapate, trape). In perfect tense it forms trepe or tatrape.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'trapūṣ lajjāyām' as an intransitive Atmanepada root indicating modesty and moral hesitation. In derived forms like participial trapita or nominal trapa, it consistently signifies bashfulness and embarrassment.

meanings.English: to feel shy, to be bashful, to feel ashamed, to be modest
meanings.German: sich schamen, verlegen sein, scheu sein
meanings.French: avoir honte, etre timide, eprouver de la pudeur

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'klīv' means to lack boldness, to be timid, or to act without courage. In simple present tense (Parasmaipada), it forms 'klīvati', expressing that someone behaves timidly or hesitates due to a lack of boldness.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat-lakara (present tense), prathama-purusha (3rd person singular)
scenarios.example_english: The boy acts timidly in the assembly.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (causative), Kartari prayoga, Lat-lakara, prathama-purusha
scenarios.example_english: Fear does not unman the soldier.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'klīvṛ' is marked with the indicatory letter ṛ (ṛdit) and is defined in the sense of adhārṣṭya (absence of boldness or courage). Being ṛdit, it takes specific aorist (luṅ) and augment operations without vowel lengthening in certain formations. The present stem inflects as klīvati, klīvataḥ, klīvanti.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'klīvṛ adhārṣṭye', signifying naisthuryābhāva or kātaryatva (timidity and absence of audacious boldness). It is an intransitive (akarmaka) root belonging to the standard Parasmaipada group of the Bhvādi class.

meanings.English: to be timid, to lack boldness, to act without courage
meanings.Hindi: darpok hona, dhrishtata na hona, kayarta dikhana
meanings.German: verzagt sein, schuchtern sein, unmutig handeln

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'gard' means to make an unpleasant, indistinct sound or to grunt. In its basic form (Atmanepada), it describes a person or animal making a guttural or ugly noise. When modified by the causative suffix (Nic), it shifts into Parasmaipada to express causing someone or something to emit an unpleasant sound.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga, laṭ lakāra (present tense, 3rd person singular, ātmanepada)
scenarios.meaning: grunts or makes an unpleasant sound
scenarios.example_english: The donkey grunts / brays unpleasantly deep inside the forest.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: ṇic-pratyaya (causative), kartari prayoga, laṭ lakāra (parasmaipada)
scenarios.meaning: causes to make an unpleasant sound
scenarios.example_english: The boy causes the toddler to produce an agitated, unpleasant cry.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: gardṛ kutsite śabde. anudāttaṅitvād ātmanepadī, seṭ. gardate, gagarde, garditā, agardiṣṭa. kutsito garhitaḥ śabdaḥ iti arthaḥ.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: gardṛ kutsite śabde. gardate, gagarde. kutsita-śabdana-kriyāyām ayam vartate.

meanings.English: to make an unpleasant sound, to grunt, to mutter coarsely
meanings.Hindi: asuhāvanī yā kutsit āvāz karnā, gurgurānā
meanings.German: ein unangenehmes Geräusch machen, grunzen, knurren
meanings.Chinese: fa chu bu yue er de sheng yin, di ming

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'phull' belongs to the 1st group (Bhvadi gana) and takes Parasmaipada endings. It conveys the action of blossoming, opening up, or blooming into fullness. When used directly in kartari prayoga (active voice), it describes flowers or smiles blossoming on their own. In causative forms (Nic), it shows causing something to expand or bloom.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara (Present active indicative, 3rd person singular)
scenarios.example_english: The flower blossoms in the forest.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (Causative active indicative, 3rd person singular)
scenarios.example_english: The spring season causes the lotus to bloom.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'phulla vikasane' is classified under Bhvadi gana as Parasmaipadi and Set. Its primary semantic scope is 'vikasana' (unfolding, opening, blooming). Forms include phullati, puphella/pophulla, phullitaḥ, and standard Bhvadi conjugational markers without vowel reduction.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines 'phulla' in the sense of 'vikasana' (expansion/flowering). It acts intransitively in basic active usage, referring naturally to flora and expanding features like eyes or smiles.

meanings.English: to blossom, to bloom, to expand

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'kuc' means to make a sound, to bend/shrink, or to trace a line/scratch. In standard active voice (Parasmaipada), the vowel 'u' takes Guna strengthening to become 'o', forming 'kocati' (he/she makes a sound or contracts). When used with a causative suffix (Nic), it becomes 'kocayati' or 'kucayati', meaning to cause to bend or to contract something.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga (Present Active, 3rd person singular)
scenarios.example_english: The branch of the tree bends (or creaks) due to the wind.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic, Kartari Prayoga)
scenarios.example_english: The child folds/crinkles the leaf.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'kuca' is listed in Bhvadi-gana under the multiple senses of sound-making (shabda), writing/line-drawing (rekha), motion (gati), and crushing or rubbing (vimardana). It takes the Guna modification of 'u' to 'o' before Sarvadhatuka affixes, giving the present tense form 'kocati'. It is an It-dhatu.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'kuca' with the varied meanings of sound, delineation, and contracting/rubbing. It forms the standard Parasmaipada inflection 'kocati', taking the augment it in non-conjugational tenses (e.g., cukoca, kocita).

meanings.English: to make a sound, to curve, to contract, to trace lines
meanings.Bengali: shobdo kora, shonkuchito howa, dag kata
meanings.German: einen Laut von sich geben, sich krummen, zusammenziehen
meanings.French: emettre un son, se courber, se contracter

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root svard belongs to the 1st conjugation (Bhvadi gana) and is conjugated in Atmanepada. It primarily means 'to taste', 'to relish', or 'to be savory and pleasing to the palate'. In the simple active present tense, it forms 'svardate'. When a causative suffix (Nic) is added, it forms 'svardayati', shifting the meaning to 'causes someone to taste' or 'sweetens/renders palatable'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The sweet fruit tastes pleasing in the mouth.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (Causative), Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: Makes palatable or causes to relish
scenarios.example_english: The mother sweetens the pudding with sugar.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: svarda asvadane. bhvadir atmanepadi seT. asvadanam asvadasampadanam anubhavo va. svardate, sasvarde, svardita, svardisyate iti rupani bhavanti.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: svarda asvadane. svardate. asvadanartho rucyartho va. svarditah, svardanam.

meanings.English: to taste, to relish, to be savory or pleasing to taste
meanings.Bengali: svada grahana kara, asvadana kara, svadishta haoya
meanings.French: gouter, savourer, etre agreable au gout
meanings.Russian: probovat na vkus, naslazhdatsya vkusom, byt vkusnym
meanings.Chinese: pin chang, pin wei, you feng wei

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'tuj' means to impart strength, to strike, or to protect and restrain. In active voice (Parasmaipada), the agent performs the action of strengthening, urging, or impelling another object, while in Middle voice (Atmanepada), the impact of strengthening, exerting force, or protecting reflects back upon the agent or is undertaken for the agent's own sake.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Bhvadi Gana Lat-lakara (Present Tense) Parasmaipada Prathama-purusha Ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: He/She gives strength or urges forward
scenarios.example_english: The warrior strikes or drives back the enemy.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Bhvadi Gana Lat-lakara (Present Tense) Atmanepada Prathama-purusha Ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: He/She exerts strength or protects for oneself
scenarios.example_english: The warrior strengthens his own forces.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: Madhaviya Dhatuvritti notes that 'tuja' in this entry is recited for the senses of strength (bala), imparting power (baladana), or checking/restraining (nirodha). It undergoes guna of the ik-vowel before Sarvadhatuka affixes, forming tojati and tojate.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin in Kshiratarangini explains that the root denotes dynamic exertion, impelling, or preservation of force, yielding regular Bhvadi conjugational forms with vowel strengthening in four universal tenses and moods.

meanings.English: to make strong, to urge, to strike, to protect, to restrain
meanings.Hindi: balashali banana, prerit karna, prahar karna, rokna
meanings.Bengali: balashali kara, prerana deoya, aghat kara, raksha kara

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'kṛṣ' means to plough, draw, scratch, or pull. In the basic first-conjugation present tense (Parasmaipada), the vowel 'ṛ' undergoes guna strengthening to 'ar', forming 'karṣati'. When used in causative (nic), it forms 'karṣayati' (causes to plough or drags).

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana (Basic active voice)
scenarios.example_english: The farmer ploughs the field.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (nic-pratyaya), Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara
scenarios.meaning: causes to plough / causes to draw
scenarios.example_english: The landowner causes the farmers to plough the field.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti explains 'kṛṣa vilekhane' as signifying the act of furrowing, scratching, or tearing up the earth (vilekhana). Being in the Bhvadi class with anubandha, it receives guna before sarvadhatuka affixes to yield 'karṣati', forming anit forms in the aorist and non-sarvadhatuka environments.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes in Kshiratarangini that 'vilekhana' refers to furrowing or drawing lines upon the soil (kṣetra-vidāraṇa). It takes Parasmaipada terminations naturally in the first gana and denotes physical drawing or furrowing.

meanings.English: to plough, furrow, draw, pull, scratch

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'khañj' (khaji) means to limp or move with an impaired gait. It takes an internal nasal (num-agama) resulting in the form 'khañjati' in present tense Parasmaipada. When used causatively with the 'nic' affix ('khañjayati'), it means to cause someone or something to limp.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara (present tense), prathama-purusha, eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The old person limps along with a walking stick.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (causative), Lat lakara, prathama-purusha, eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The stone causes the horse to limp.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti notes that 'khaji' possesses the idit marker which demands the insertion of num (nasal augment), yielding the base 'khañj'. The meaning 'gativaikalye' signifies defective movement or limping. Conjugated as khañjati, cakhañja, khañjitā, khañjiṣyati.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin explains that 'khaji gati-vaikalye' refers to the impairment of normal foot movement (padavighāta). As an idit root, the nasal augment is regular throughout all sarvadhatuka and ardhadhatuka non-kit/nit formations.

meanings.English: to limp, to walk with a halt or defective gait

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'ras' means to make a sound, howl, cry out, or bray (often used for the characteristic sound of animals like donkeys or jackals). It is conjugated exclusively in Atmanepada in the active voice. When used in the causative (Nic) form, it means to cause someone or something to cry out or make noise.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakara (present tense), prathama purusha, eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The donkey brays loudly.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (causative), Lat lakara, prathama purusha, eka-vacana
scenarios.meaning: causes to make a sound / causes to howl
scenarios.example_english: The boy makes the dog howl.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'rasa sabde' belongs to the Bhvadi gana. It takes the Atmanepada affixes due to its anudatta marker (anudattetvat atmanepadam). In the present tense, it forms 'rasate'. Being set, it takes the intermediate 'i' augment in non-sarvadhatuka forms where applicable, yielding forms like rasisyate and rasishta.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'rasa sabde' as an Atmanepadi root denoting vocalization or sound-making. It follows the standard Bhvadi formation with the Sap vikarana without root vowel modification (guna/vriddhi) since the vowel 'a' is already a long vowel.

meanings.English: to make a sound, howl, bray, cry out

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'kah' belongs to the first group of verbs (Bhvadi-gana) and means 'to give' or 'to bestow'. It takes active endings (Parasmaipada) in its base form. When we make it causative (by adding 'nic' to form 'kāhi'), it shifts meaning to 'causing someone to give' or 'making someone bestow'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga (Active Voice, Simple Present, Lat Lakara, 3rd Person Singular)
scenarios.example_english: The king gives wealth to the scholar.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (Causative Active Voice, Simple Present, Lat Lakara, 3rd Person Singular)
scenarios.example_english: The father makes the son give charity.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: Madhaviya Dhatuvritti confirms 'kaha dāne' as a root ending in 'h' (ha-kārānta) in the Bhvadi-gana. It is classified as Parasmaipadi and Set (takes intermediate 'i' in non-sarvadhatuka affixes). Key forms derived include kahati (present), cakhāha (perfect), kahitā (periphrastic future), and kahiṣyati (future).
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin in Kshiratarangini records 'kaha dāne' in the ha-anta division of Bhvadi. It conveys the sense of giving (utsarga/dāna) and follows standard bhvadi conjugation without internal root vowel elongation in the present tense (kahati).

meanings.English: To give, bestow, donate

canonical_dhatvartha: alpibhave (in the sense of becoming small, diminishing, shrinking, or bending)

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'krunc' means to shrink, diminish, or bend. In simple present tense (kartari prayoga), it takes standard Parasmaipada endings with the thematic affix 'a' (sap), yielding forms like 'kruncati'. When used in causative (nic), it takes the meaning 'to cause to shrink' or 'to diminish' (kroncayati/kruncayati).

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga, lat lakara, prathama-purusha, eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: Due to the cold, the cloth shrinks.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: nic-pratyaya (causative), lat lakara, prathama-purusha, eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: Heat causes the cloth to shrink.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: Madhaviya glosses 'krunca alpibhave' indicating reduction in size, bending, or becoming meager. The nasal 'n' is part of the dhatu and is retained in standard sarvadhatuka formations (kruncati, akruncat, kruncatu, kruncet), with guna optionally prevented or conditioned in ardhadhatuka contexts.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines 'krunca' under alpibhava (diminution/shrinking) and movement/bending (kutila-gati). It conjugates as kruncati in lat, with lit forms showing reduplication like cukronca or cukrunca depending on guna rules.

meanings.English: to diminish, to shrink, to become small, to bend
meanings.Bengali: shonkochit howa, chhoto howa, kshino howa

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'sphūrj' means to make a loud rumbling, roaring, or thundering noise. In standard active voice (Parasmaipada), it describes subjects like storm clouds or thunderclaps emitting deep sounds. When converted to a causative form (ṇic), it signifies causing a loud noise, blast, or reverberation.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga, laṭ lakāra (present tense, active voice, 3rd person singular)
scenarios.example_english: The cloud rumbles terribly in the sky.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: ṇic pratyaya (causative), kartari prayoga, laṭ lakāra
scenarios.meaning: causes to rumble / detonates / reverberates loudly
scenarios.example_english: The wind makes the thunderbolt crash violently.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya explains 'sphūrjā nirghoṣe' as indicating continuous deep sound or roaring (mahānirghoṣa). It belongs to the Bhvādi-gaṇa, takes Parasmaipada terminations, has the augment iṭ (seṭ), and yields forms like sphūrjati, pasphūrja, and sphūrjitā.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines 'sphūrjā nirghoṣe' under the velar/palatal consonantal series of Bhvādi, linking 'nirghoṣa' specifically to atmospheric phenomena like thunder, crashing waves, or explosions, forming primary derivatives such as sphūrjathu (clap of thunder).

meanings.English: to thunder, rumble, crash, roar
meanings.Bengali: gorjon kora, baj pora, bhison shobdo kora

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'blī' primarily conveys the action of moving along gracefully or covering/sheltering something. Because it carries an anubandha 'ṅ' (blīṅ) in the Dhatupatha, it strictly takes Ātmanepada affixes (such as -te, -ete, -nte). When turned into a causative verb using the 'ṇic' affix, it indicates causing someone or something to move or be covered.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakāra (present tense), prathama puruṣa (third person), ekavacana (singular)
scenarios.example_english: The deer moves softly in the forest.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nyanta (causative), Kartari prayoga, Lat lakāra, prathama puruṣa, ekavacana with Parasmaipada ending
scenarios.meaning: Causes to move or causes to be covered
scenarios.example_english: The herdsman guides the cow along the path.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'blīṅ' belongs to the Bhvādi class and is marked with the anubandha ṅakāra indicating exclusive Ātmanepada conjugation. Sayana explains its primary sense as motion ('gatau') as well as covering or gathering ('saṁvaraṇe'). In the present tense, after applying standard guṇa vowel strengthening and the śap vikarana, it forms 'blayate'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes the interchangeability of labials and dentals ('va-ba-yor abhedaḥ'), acknowledging textual variants between 'vlīṅ' and 'blīṅ'. The core semantic range emphasizes gentle motion and protective enveloping, conjugate forms remaining aniṭ in standard classical derivation.

meanings.English: To move, to go, to advance; to cover, to conceal

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root śuc means to feel sorrow, mourn, or grieve. In standard active voice (Parasmaipada), it describes a person experiencing grief. When used with the causative affix (nic), it means to cause someone to grieve or to lament over something.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakara (present tense), 3rd person singular
scenarios.example_english: The father grieves due to separation from his son.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (nic-pratyaya), Lat lakara (present tense), 3rd person singular
scenarios.example_english: This distressing news saddens the people.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti identifies the root 'śuca' in the sense of sorrow ('śoke'). Being ending with short a-kara for svarartha, the root undergoes guna of the vowel 'u' to 'o' before sarvadhatuka affixes like shap, producing forms like śocati, aśocat, and śocatu.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'śuca śoke', emphasizing its classification as parasmaipadi and intransitive (akarmaka) in its basic primary meaning of lamentation and grief, acquiring transitivity in causative or specific upasarga usages.

meanings.English: to grieve, to mourn, to sorrow, to lament
meanings.French: s'affliger, porter le deuil, se lamenter

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root bhrāś means to shine, flash, or glitter. In simple everyday Sanskrit, it takes Atmanepada endings to describe an object naturally glowing or shining forth with light. When converted to a causative (Nic) form, it switches to showing that someone makes something shine or illuminates it.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga, lat-lakara, prathama-purusha, eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The star shines in the sky.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: nic-pratyaya (causative), parasmaipada, lat-lakara, prathama-purusha, eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The sun illuminates the entire world.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'bhrāśṛ dīptau' belongs to the Bhvadi class. Being marked with 'ṛ' as an it-marker (ṛdit), it does not take lengthening or special guṇa augment where prohibited, and functions in the sense of prakāśana (radiating light or glowing). By the rule 'vā bhrāśa-bhrāṣa-bhramu-kramu-klamu-trasa-truṭi-laṣām', it optionally admits the Śyan affix in the universal non-causative system.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin explains 'bhrāśṛ dīptau' as signifying luminous expansion and shining (dīpti). It forms bhrāśate or optionally bhrāśyate in the sarvadhatuka system, indicating vivid light or luster, categorised as anit and anudattet/atmanepadi.

meanings.English: to shine, glitter, radiate light, sparkle
meanings.Hindi: chamakna, prakashit hona, deepti prapth karna
meanings.Bengali: jholmol kora, alo deoya, ujjwal hoya

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'kṝ' belongs to the Bhvadi class and means to scatter, disperse, or throw things in different directions. In normal active use, it expresses a subject directly scattering an object (like seeds or flowers). When used with prefixes or causative affixes, it indicates spreading widely or making someone scatter objects.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat-lakara (present tense), Prathama-purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The farmer scatters seeds in the field.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (causative), Lat-lakara (present tense), Prathama-purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The mother causes the child to scatter the flowers.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti defines 'kṝ vikṣepe' as an Aniṭ Parasmaipadi root of the Bhvadi class. Vikṣepa denotes the action of throwing apart or dispersing. In the presence of the sārvadhātuka affix Śap, it undergoes guṇa transformation (ṝ becoming ar), generating forms like karati, karataḥ, karanti.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin glosses 'kṝ vikṣepe' as an act of preraṇa (propulsion) and utsarjana (strewing or scattering). It is treated alongside ṝ-ending roots of the first conjugation, maintaining regular vocalic grade shifts in sārvadhātuka and ārdhadhātuka environments.

meanings.English: To scatter, to disperse, to strew

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'kuth' means to suffer pain, distress, or to undergo affliction and distress. In its standard active form (Parasmaipada), it describes experiencing anguish, suffering, or rotting/decay. In its causative form (kothayati), it means causing someone or something to suffer or undergo distress.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Lat lakara (Present tense), Prathama purusha (Third person), Ekavacana (Singular), Kartari prayoga (Active voice)
scenarios.example_english: The afflicted person suffers distress due to illness.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (Causative), Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: Injustice torments and causes distress to the people.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti explains 'kutha samkleshane' as indicating anguish, mental or physical distress, and affliction. It is classed under Bhvadi-gana, taking standard Parasmaipada terminations, with guna of the vowel occurring before sarvadhatuka affixes, forming kothati.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin in Kshiratarangini notes that 'kutha' conveys 'samkleshana' (distressing or being tormented). He confirms its set character and the development of forms like kothitum in the infinitive and cukotha in the perfect tense (Lit).

meanings.English: To suffer distress, to afflict, to rot or languish
meanings.Hindi: Klesh pana, kasht jhelna, sadna ya tadapna
meanings.Bengali: Klesha pawa, koshto pawa, pocha ba jorjoritha howa

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'vas' primarily means 'to reside' or 'to dwell'. In basic Parasmaipada form, it indicates the subject living in a place. When prefixes (upasargas) like 'upa' or 'adhi' are added, its meaning adapts to 'to observe a fast/stay near' or 'to inhabit a place' (making it transitive), and the causative form 'vasayati' means 'to settle or provide shelter to someone'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga (Present Active, 3rd Person Singular)
scenarios.example_english: The sage lives in the forest.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic-pratyaya, Present Active)
scenarios.example_english: The king accommodates the guest in the house.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'vasa nivase' belongs to the Bhvadi class and takes Parasmaipada terminations. It undergoes Samprasarana in the reduplicated perfect (lit) and past participle forms (e.g., uvasa, ushitah). It is classified as anit, forming vatsyati in the future tense with 'sa' following the conversion of 's' to 't' via Paninian sandhi rules.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'vasa nivase' as denoting dwelling or staying in an abode. He highlights the phonological changes like Samprasarana in weak environments (ushitah, ushitva) and the change of root-final 's' to 't' before 'sya' (vatsyati) and in the infinitive (vastum).

meanings.English: to dwell, reside, live, abide

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'ghūrch' expresses the action of wandering, reeling, or revolving. In basic active voice (kartari prayoga), it describes a person or object wandering or reeling by itself. When using the causative suffix (ṇic), it shifts the meaning to causing someone or something else to wander, stagger, or revolve.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana (simple present tense, active)
scenarios.example_english: The traveler wanders in the forest.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: nic pratyaya (causative), lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: causes to wander / makes reel or spin
scenarios.example_english: The wind makes the leaf spin in the sky.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'ghūrchā' is glossed as 'bhramaṇe' (in the sense of whirling, wandering, or roaming). Being marked with an anubandha indicator for parasmaipada, it conjugates as ghūrchati, jaghūrcha, ghūrchitā, and takes the intermediate augment 'iṭ' (seṭ).
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines 'ghūrchā bhramaṇe', explaining it as bodily motion in circular paths, wandering or staggering. Forms like ghūrchati and the krdanta derivative ghūrchitaḥ are derived accordingly.

meanings.English: to wander, to roam, to reel, to whirl

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'dhāv' has two primary meanings depending on context: to run/move fast, and to wash/cleanse. In everyday Sanskrit, it is used in Parasmaipada for running (where it is intransitive) and cleansing (where it is transitive). When using causative affixes, it means making someone run or having something cleaned.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga, laṭ lakāra, prathama puruṣa, ekavacana (parasmaipada)
scenarios.example_english: The boy runs quickly in the field.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: ṇijanta (causative), kartari prayoga, laṭ lakāra, prathama puruṣa, ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The father makes the horse run on the path.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti explains 'dhāvū gatiśuddhayoḥ' as functioning in the senses of swift motion (gati) and cleansing or purifying (śuddhi). It notes the retention of the long vowel and the application of standard Bhvadi vikarana 'śap', with regular seṭ characteristics in non-sarvadhatuka forms like dhāvitaḥ and dhāvitum.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin highlights the duality of the root's scope: motion (dhāvati aśvaḥ - the horse runs) and washing (vastraṃ dhāvati - cleanses the cloth). The commentary observes that when signifying cleansing, the root governs an objective accusative, whereas in the sense of running, it acts intransitively.

meanings.English: to run, to move swiftly, to wash, to purify

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'kuc' means to shrink, contract, curl, or bend. In the active voice (Parasmaipada), it describes a subject contracting or curling up on its own. When used with a causative affix (Nic), it changes the meaning to making something else shrink or contracting an object.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga, lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The leaf shrinks due to the cold.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: nic pratyaya (causative), kartari prayoga, lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The bear contracts its body.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: kuca sankocane - it is classified in the bhvadi-gana as an udattopadesha, Parasmaipada, and set root. Guna takes place in sarvadhatuka affixes yielding the form kocati, and in lit it forms cukoca.
