dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'parj' means to satisfy, nourish, or please someone. In its standard active form (Parasmaipada), the subject performs an action that satisfies or pleases another person or object. When used in the causative (Nic), it means to cause someone to satisfy or nourish.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara (present indicative active, 3rd person singular)
scenarios.example_english: The devotee satisfies the deities.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (causative), Lat lakara (3rd person singular)
scenarios.meaning: causes to satisfy / causes to nourish
scenarios.example_english: The mother causes the child to be satisfied with food.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'parja tarpane' belongs to the Bhvadi class, taking the standard Parasmaipada inflection. The canonical sense 'tarpana' signifies satisfying, gladdening, or refreshing by water, offerings, or food. It forms standard regular present forms like parjati, parjatah, parjanti with guṇa applicable where relevant.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines 'parja' in the sense of 'tarpane' (to gratify or propitiate). Being a set root with a short radical vowel followed by a conjunct, it forms its perfect tense as paparja and past passive participle as parjita.

meanings.English: to satisfy, to please, to nourish, to gratify

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'shrauk' means 'to go' or 'to approach/creep toward'. It belongs to the first group of verbs (Bhvadi-gana) and takes Atmanepada endings by default due to its marker (r-it). When used in standard active voice, it describes someone moving or going toward a location. When transformed into the causative (Nic), it means to cause someone to move or to dispatch someone forward.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat-lakara (present tense), Prathama-purusha (3rd person), Ekavacana (singular)
scenarios.example_english: The deer moves toward the forest.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (Causative), Kartari prayoga, Lat-lakara, Prathama-purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The cowherd causes the cow to move along the path.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root shraukr (gatau) is grouped in the Bhvadi-gana with dhaukr and traukr. Because it is marked with anudatta r-it, it takes Atmanepada terminations (shraukate). Being an id-dhatu (set), the augment it is applied in relevant ardhadhatuka forms such as shraukita and shraukitum.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes shraukr along with the series dhauka-trauka-shrauka under gati-arthaka (verbs of motion). It forms shraukate in the present tense, exhibiting standard Guna alteration where applicable and taking Atmanepada affixes consistently.

meanings.English: to go, to move, to approach

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'ras' means to taste, relish, or make a sound. When conjugated in active voice (kartari prayoga - Parasmaipada), it describes an agent tasting or enjoying a flavour. When used in causative form (Nich-pratyaya), it means causing someone to taste or making something delightful and tasty.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Lat lakara, Prathama-purusha, Eka-vacana (Simple Active Present)
scenarios.example_english: The boy tastes the sweet fruit.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nich-pratyaya) Lat lakara
scenarios.meaning: Causes to taste / enriches with flavor
scenarios.example_english: The mother has the child taste the sweet pudding.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: Rasa asvadane. Sakarmakah, set, parasmaipadi. Asvadanam jihvendriyena rasanubhavah shabdo va. Rasati, rarasa, rasita, rasishyati, arasit.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Rasa asvadane. Rasati madhuram. Asvadanam anubhavah. Svaradi-sanniveshat shabde api prayujyate.

meanings.English: to taste, to relish, to sound, to feel
meanings.Bengali: asvadan kara, chakha, ras grahan kara
meanings.Russian: probovat na vkus, degustirovat, naslazhdatsya vkusom
meanings.Chinese: pin chang, pin wei, chang shi

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'puṣ' (Bhvadi class) means to nourish, cherish, foster, or support. In the active voice (Parasmaipada), the vowel 'u' undergoes guna strengthening to 'o' before the class conjugational sign 'a' (śap), yielding 'poṣati' (he/she nourishes). In the causative construction (ṇic), it forms 'poṣayati', meaning to cause someone or something to be nourished or reared.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Bhvadi class Parasmaipada, Present Tense (Laṭ, Kartari Prayoga, Prathama Puruṣa, Ekavacana)
scenarios.example_english: The mother nourishes her son with affection.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Bhvadi class Causative (Ṇic, Kartari Prayoga, Prathama Puruṣa, Ekavacana)
scenarios.meaning: causes to nourish / causes to develop
scenarios.example_english: The farmer causes the crops to thrive in the field.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti analyzes 'puṣa puṣṭau' under the Bhvadi class. It notes that the final 'a' is an anubandha indicating Parasmaipada. As an udātta, it takes intermediate 'iṭ' in non-conjugational general tenses (seṭ). The base undergoes guna (u -> o) in sarvadhatuka environments: puṣ + śap + ti = poṣati.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin in Kshiratarangini states 'puṣa puṣṭau poṣati', explaining the sense of physical nourishing, bodily growth, and fostering. He distinguishes this Bhvadi formation (poṣati) from the Divadi class form (puṣyati) and the Kryadi form (puṣṇāti), emphasizing the simple thematized stem formation of the first gana.

meanings.English: to nourish, foster, support, cherish, cause to grow
meanings.Bengali: poshana kara, palana kara, briddhi kara

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'nard' means to roar, sound, or bellow loudly (like a lion or thunder). In standard active voice (Parasmaipada), it describes a subject making a roar. When used in the causative form (Nic pratyaya), it means 'to make someone roar' or 'to cause a sound to reverberate'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Active Voice (Kartari Prayoga, Lat Lakara, Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana)
scenarios.example_english: The lion roars loudly in the forest.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic pratyaya, Lat Lakara, Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana)
scenarios.example_english: Fear causes the elephant to bellow.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'narda' is listed under the Bhvadi class in the sense of making sound ('narda sabde'). It takes the Kartari Shap vikaran, retains the radical consonant cluster, and is marked as set with Parasmaipada inflection in the simple non-causative system.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'narda sabde', explaining that it denotes generic or deep, resonant vocalization such as roaring or bellowing, generating forms like nardati, nanarda, nardisyati, and anardit.

meanings.English: to roar, to sound, to bellow

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'bhraṃś' means to fall down, slip, or deviate from a status or path. In standard intransitive usage (Atmanepada), the subject slips or falls on its own. When the causative affix (ṇic) is added, it switches to Parasmaipada and means to actively drop, displace, or remove someone from a position.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (Basic Atmanepada)
scenarios.meaning: falls down or slips from a place
scenarios.example_english: The ripe fruit falls down from the tree.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (ṇic pratyaya, Parasmaipada)
scenarios.meaning: causes to fall, removes, or deposes
scenarios.example_english: The king removes the corrupt minister from his post.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: bhraṃśu adhaḥpatane. anudātta it anidit ca. bhraṃśate, babhraṃśe, bhraṃśiṣyate. adhaḥpatanaṃ galanaṃ cyutirvocyate.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: bhraṃśu adhaḥpatane. aniditvānnasya lopaḥ siddhiḥ kvacit. bhraṃśate skhalitvā patatītyarthaḥ.

meanings.English: to fall down, drop, slip, deviate
meanings.Bengali: pode jaoyā, bhrashto hoyā, khose podā

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root śrai means 'to cook', 'to boil', or 'to mature/ripen'. In standard usage (Kartari prayoga), it takes Parasmaipada affixes where the diphthong 'ai' changes to 'ā', producing forms like 'śrāyati' (he/she cooks or ripens). When used in the causative (Nic), it adds the augmenting consonant 'p' to become 'śrāpayati' (causes to cook or matures).

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakara (present tense), 3rd person singular
scenarios.example_english: The soup cooks thoroughly by the fire.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (causative voice), Lat lakara (present tense), 3rd person singular
scenarios.meaning: Causes to cook or ripens something
scenarios.example_english: The cook causes the rice to boil in the vessel.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'śrai' is classified under Bhvādi with the semantic value 'pāke' (in the sense of cooking, boiling, or processing by heat). By the rule 'ādeca upadeśe 'śiti', the root vowel 'ai' changes to 'ā' when followed by non-śit affixes or during general base formation with the standard śap vikarana yielding 'śrāyati'. It is anit (devoid of the augment iṭ) in Ardhadhatuka environments.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'śrai pāke' among the diphthong-ending Bhvadi roots. It undergoes qualitative transformation to 'śrā' before standard sarvadhatuka affixes, forming 'śrāyati'. In the causative formation, the pug-āgama rule operates yielding 'śrāpayati'.

meanings.English: to cook, to boil, to mature, to sweat/heat
meanings.Bengali: rānnā karā, pāk karā, siddha karā

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'gardh' means to desire intensely, crave, or covet something. In its basic Parasmaipada form (gardhati), it expresses an agent actively longing for or coveting an object. In the causative form (gardhayati), it conveys causing someone else to crave or desire something intensely.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga (active voice, lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana)
scenarios.example_english: The greedy person covets another person's wealth.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: nic pratyaya (causative active, lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana)
scenarios.meaning: causes someone to covet or crave
scenarios.example_english: The false enticement makes the child crave the fruit.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: gardha abhikanksayam. abhikanksa iccha visesah lipsa ityarthah. gardhati, jagardha, gardhita, gardhitum.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: gardha abhikanksayam. lipsayam ityarthah. gardhati, jagardha. anit-karika-anurodhat set.

meanings.English: to covet, to crave, to desire eagerly
meanings.Hindi: lalac karna, lobha karna, tivra iccha karna

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'kac' belongs to the first group of verbs (Bhvadi gana) and carries the basic sense of binding, tying, stringing together, or fastening. It is an 'idit' root (having 'i' as an indicator), which inserts a nasal 'n' sound before the consonant, forming stems like 'kancate'. In its regular middle voice (Atmanepada), it depicts an action of binding or stringing things together for oneself or as an inherent process. When converted into a causative verb (Nic) like 'kancayati', the meaning changes to actively causing someone or something to bind, string, or fasten together.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Lat lakara (Present Indicative), Prathama Purusha (3rd Person), Ekavacana (Singular), Kartari Prayoga (Active voice in Atmanepada)
scenarios.example_english: The garland maker strings (binds) the flowers together with a thread.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (Causative), Lat lakara (Present Indicative), Prathama Purusha (3rd Person), Ekavacana (Singular)
scenarios.meaning: Causes to bind, ties together, or fastens up
scenarios.example_english: The master makes the servant bind the bundle together.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti explains 'kaci bandhane' as an idit root, taking the num-agama (nasal infix) according to the rule 'idito num dhatoh', yielding forms such as kancate, kancete, kancante. In the perfect tense (Lit), it forms cakance. Because of being an idit, it is inherently set (takes it-agama in ardhadhatuka affixes). It functions transitively denoting the action of tying, binding, or intertwining.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin in the Kshiratarangini notes that 'kaci' conveys 'bandhana' (binding, linking, or restraining). He emphasizes the structural transformation via num-agama to yield 'kancate' and records its derivation alongside related roots of joining and fastening, highlighting its usage in both literal binding and metaphorical fastening or adorning.

meanings.English: to bind, to tie, to fasten, to string together, to restrain

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'rad' belongs to the 1st conjugation (Bhvadi gana) and takes Parasmaipada endings. Its core meaning is to dig, scratch, furrow, or gnaw. When used in active voice, it describes the subject scraping or cutting into an object. When modified by the causative suffix (nic), it takes the form 'radayati', meaning to cause to furrow, plow, or dig.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana (active present tense)
scenarios.example_english: The mouse gnaws the cloth.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: preranartha nic pratyaya, lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana (causative present tense)
scenarios.example_english: The farmer causes the field to be furrowed with a plow.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: rada vilekhane. vilekhanam kshananam khananam daranam va. set parasmaipadi. radati, aradat, radita.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: rada vilekhane. lekhana-bhedo vilekhanam, daranam ity arthah. radana iti dantasya nama yat vilekhanakari bhavati.

meanings.English: to gnaw, scratch, furrow, dig, or split

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'maṭh' means to dwell, inhabit, or reside in a place. In the active voice (Kartari Prayoga), it takes Parasmaipada endings to show someone staying or living somewhere. When used with the causative affix (ṇic), it shifts the meaning to causing someone to dwell or providing lodging/settlement for another person.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat-lakara (present tense), prathama-purusha (3rd person singular)
scenarios.example_english: The ascetic dwells in the forest.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (ṇic-pratyaya), Lat-lakara, active voice
scenarios.example_english: The king accommodates the community of ascetics there.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'maṭha' is classified under the Bhvadi class in the sense of 'nivāsa' (dwelling/residing). It is udātta, anudāttet, seṭ, and takes Parasmaipada affixes. Forms include maṭhati, mamaṭha, maṭhitā, and maṭhiṣyati. The nominal derivative 'maṭha' (a hermitage or monastery) is derived from this verbal root.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'maṭha nivāse' among the unaccented consonant-ending Bhvadi roots denoting habitation. In combination with primary affixes, it designates a hut, cell, or residence of students and ascetics.

meanings.English: to dwell, to reside, to inhabit

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'vañc' primarily means to move, wander, or go (often in a crooked or wandering path). In the basic active voice (Kartari Prayoga), it takes standard Parasmaipada endings. When combined with prefixes like 'vi' or used transitively/causatively, it shifts meaning to eluding, evading, or deceiving.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Lat (Present Tense), Kartari Prayoga (Active Voice), Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The deer wanders in the forest.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic (Causative) + Lat, Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The rogue deceives the person.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: vañcu gatyām. ukāro nāsikyo it. vakārādikāreṇa nakāralopa-abhāvaḥ. vañcati, vavañca, vañcitā. gativācī akarmakaḥ, kauṭilye tu sakarmakaḥ.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: vañcu gatyām. gatir iha kutilāpi gṛhyate. vañcati kuṭilaṃ gacchati ity arthaḥ.

meanings.English: To go, move, wander, evade, deceive

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'mas' means to hold, retain, or support. Being an Atmanepadi root, the primary verbal forms use middle endings (such as -te, -ete, -nte) to express that a subject holds or bears an object.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Lat lakara (present indicative), prathama-purusha (3rd person), ekavacana (singular), kartari prayoga (active voice)
scenarios.example_english: The tree holds the fruit.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Lat lakara (present indicative), prathama-purusha (3rd person), bahuvacana (plural), kartari prayoga (active voice)
scenarios.example_english: The pillars support the building.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'mase' belongs to Bhvadi gana and carries the canonical meaning of 'dharane' (holding, bearing, supporting). It is marked with an anudatta vowel marker 'e', making it inherently anit and restricted to Atmanepada. Conjugates as masate, mamashe, masita.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'mase dharane' among the anit Atmanepadi roots in Bhvadi. The radical 'a' does not undergo guna because it is already short 'a' followed by a conjunct or single consonant, leading directly to masate with standard shap-pratyaya.

meanings.English: to hold, bear, or retain

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'sphur' means to throb, twitch, pulsate, or flash. In simple active voice (Parasmaipada), it shows a part of the body or a light naturally twitching or flashing. When used with a causative affix (Nic), it changes into 'sphorayati', meaning to cause something to throb, burst, or quiver.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga (Present Active, 3rd Person Singular)
scenarios.example_english: The eye twitches.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic-pratyaya, Parasmaipada)
scenarios.example_english: The lightning causes the sky to flash.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'sphura' is listed in the sense of 'sphurana' (throbbing, vibrating, shaking, or shining forth). It takes the standard Bhvadi vikarana 'sap', with vowel lengthening/guna appropriately blocked or applied based on morphological conditions, yielding forms such as sphurati, visphurati, and pusphora.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'sphura sphurane', classifying it as an anit Parasmaipada root denoting sudden movement, vibration, or manifest shining (dipti/kampana). In combination with prefixes like 'vi', it indicates fierce trembling or intense radiance.

meanings.English: to throb, to twitch, to quiver, to flash

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root mlai means to wither, fade, or lose freshness and enthusiasm. In the normal active voice (Parasmaipada), it describes something withering or someone feeling exhausted. When used with a causative suffix (Nic), it changes to mean causing something to fade or wilt.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakara (present tense), prathama-purusa ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The flower withers due to the heat.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (nic-pratyaya), Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, prathama-purusa ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The intense heat of the sun causes the creeper to wither.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: mlai harsaksaye. 'harsaksayo mlani-bhavanam'. As an adanta/aiden root, it undergoes akara substitution in sarvadhatuka contexts before sap, forming mlayati. In lit lakara it forms mamlau, mamlatuh, mamluh. It is anit and akarmaka.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: mlai harsaksaye. Glossed as loss of bloom, languishing, or withering of cheerfulness. Forms include mlayati, mamlau, and mlana in the kta participle.

meanings.English: to wither, to fade, to droop, to lose vigor or enthusiasm

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'pan' means to praise, admire, or extol. Under Paninian grammar (sutra 'gup-dhupa-vicchi-pani-panibhyah ayah'), it obligatorily takes the affix 'aya' in sarvadhatuka tenses, forming 'panāyate' in the Atmanepada. It shows an action of admiring or singing praises of someone or something worthy.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat-lakara (present tense), prathama-purusha, ekavacana with optional/obligatory aya affix
scenarios.example_english: The devotee praises the virtues of Lord Hari.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat-lakara (present tense), prathama-purusha, bahuvacana
scenarios.example_english: The poets extol the valor of the king.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti notes 'pana stutau' as belonging to the group of roots beginning with 'gup' that take the special affix 'aya' (panāyate). In non-sarvadhatuka forms where 'aya' is optional, alternate root-forms can occur. The primary sense is exclusively praise or veneration.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin explains that 'pana' signifies 'stuti' (laudation/admiration). He groups it alongside 'paṇ', distinguishing 'pan' primarily in the sphere of pure praise without the connotation of commercial transaction.

meanings.English: to praise, applaud, admire, extol

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'vraj' means 'to go', 'to wander', or 'to travel'. It is conjugated in the Parasmaipada voice (vrajati = he/she goes). By adding the prefix 'pra-' (pravrajati), the meaning transforms to 'to go forth into ascetic life' or 'to renounce the world'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga (Present Tense, 3rd Person Singular)
scenarios.example_english: The traveler goes to the city.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Upasarga 'pra' + Kartari Prayoga
scenarios.meaning: renounces worldly life / goes forth as a monk
scenarios.example_english: The ascetic renounces the world and wanders into the forest.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti analyzes 'vraja gatau' as expressing directed movement and path-clearing. It details forms such as vavraja (Lit), avrajit (Lun), and derivations like vrajya and pravrajana.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'vraja' in the sense of continuous locomotion and pasturing, explaining how it derives both verbal paradigms and nouns like 'vraja' (a pasture/herdsman settlement).

meanings.English: To go, wander, travel, proceed

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'nam' means to bend down, bow, or show reverence. In simple active voice (kartari prayoga), it takes standard Parasmaipada endings to express an individual bending or bowing respectfully before elders or deities, or inanimate objects like branches bending. When the causative suffix (nic) is attached, it transforms into 'namayati', meaning 'to cause to bend' or 'to bend an object'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga (lat lakara, prathama-purusha, eka-vacana)
scenarios.example_english: The student bows to the teacher.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: nic-pratyaya (causative present indicative)
scenarios.meaning: causes to bend or bends something
scenarios.example_english: The wind bends the roadside tree.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya gloss defines 'nama prahvatve' as signifying the act of bowing or bending down (namribhavah). By the rule 'no nah', the initial 'na' transforms into dental 'n' in non-aupadeshika usage. It is classified as anit (lacking augment i) and governs the accusative case when bowing toward a respected person.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin interprets 'prahvatva' as both intentional respectful prostration/salutation by sentient beings (pranibhih pranama) and physical bending or drooping seen in trees and objects (apranibhir namanam).

meanings.English: to bow, to bend down, to salute, to prostrate

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'kud' (kuḍi~) primarily means to burn or scorch. Because it has an 'i' as an indicatory letter (idit), it takes an inserted nasal sound 'n' before the final consonant in its conjugated forms, becoming 'kuṇḍati' in the simple present tense (Parasmaipada). When used transitively, it shows the action of scorching or setting something on fire.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat-lakara, Prathama-purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The fire burns the piece of wood.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Lun-lakara (Aorist past), Prathama-purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The forest fire scorched the entire forest.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: kuḍi~ dāhe. iditvāt num-āgamaḥ. kuṇḍati, cukuṇḍa, kuṇḍitā, kuṇḍiṣyati. dāho jvalanaṃ santāpo vā. The root 'kud' is marked with indicatory 'i' which triggers the addition of 'num' (nasal infix), yielding forms such as kuṇḍati in Parasmaipada with the meaning of burning, heating, or scorching.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: kuḍi~ dāhe. idit, tena kuṇḍati. dāharthe prayujyamānaḥ ayam dhātuḥ sakarmakaḥ bhavati. Kshirasvamin notes the insertion of the nasal per the Paninian rule 'idito num dhātoḥ' yielding kuṇḍati in active present.

meanings.English: to burn, to scorch, to singe

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'kan' means to shine, to be pleasing/desire, or to move. In the standard active voice (Parasmaipada), it simply describes an object shining, desiring, or going. When combined with the causative suffix Nic, it means to cause someone to shine, to illuminate, or to cause to move.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Active voice (Kartari Prayoga), Present tense (Lat), 3rd person singular
scenarios.example_english: The gem shines in the assembly.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Preranaartha Nic), Present tense (Lat), 3rd person singular
scenarios.example_english: The lamp illuminates the mansion.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: kana dīptikāntigatiṣu - The root 'kan' is assigned three distinct semantic domains: dīpti (shining/radiance), kānti (beauty/desire/splendor), and gati (motion/attainment). As a standard Bhvadi Parasmaipadi root taking the sap-vikarana, it forms the present base 'kana-'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: kana dīptikāntigatiṣu - Kshirasvamin explains that this root operates across visual brilliance (dīpti), attractiveness (kānti), and physical motion (gati). Being anudatta-et by basic class characteristics, its set forms take the intermediate i (it-agama) in ardhadhatuka environments.

meanings.English: to shine, to wish or love, to go
meanings.Hindi: chamakna, chahana ya sundar lagna, chalna ya jana
meanings.Bengali: ujjval hawa, kamanā kara, gamana kara

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'dhāv' carries two primary meanings: 'to run / go quickly' and 'to wash / cleanse / purify'. When conjugated in Parasmaipada, it commonly expresses the motion of running or the action of cleansing. In the causative form with the affix 'ṇic', it shifts the sense to making someone run or causing something to be washed or cleansed.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Bhvādi-gaṇa Kartari Prayoga (Present Active, Parasmaipada, 3rd Person Singular)
scenarios.example_english: The horse runs fast.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (ṇic pratyaya), Kartari Prayoga
scenarios.example_english: The father makes the boy run.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'dhāvu~' is marked with the meanings 'gatau' (in the sense of motion/running) and 'śuddhau' (in the sense of purification/washing). It is seṭ and forms present tense bases such as 'dhāvati' and 'dhāvate' through standard guṇa-vṛddhi and vikarana 'śap'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'dhāvu gatau śuddhau ca', establishing both dynamic motion ('running swiftly') and physical/ritual cleaning ('mārjane śodhane'). Derivative nominal forms such as 'dhāvana' and 'dhauta' emerge directly from this classification.

meanings.English: to run, to move swiftly, to wash, to purify, to cleanse

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'phal' means to bear fruit, ripen, result, or succeed. In simple active present tense (Parasmaipada), it describes plants producing fruit or actions yielding a successful result. When used with a causative affix (nic), it means to cause something to bear fruit or to make an effort fruitful.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The tree bears fruit in due season.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (nic pratyaya), Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: causes to bear fruit / makes fruitful
scenarios.example_english: Hard work makes the effort fruitful.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: Madhaviya Dhatuvritti analyzes 'phala nispattau' as belonging to Bhvadi gana. It denotes completion, manifestation, or the fruition of action and growth. Forms derived include phalati, paphala, phalita, and phalitvan.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'phala nispattau' under the halanta Bhvadi class, highlighting the primary semantic sense of coming to fulfillment or ripening as a fruit (phalabhavena parinamah).

meanings.English: to bear fruit, yield results, ripen, succeed

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'kṣmā' expresses physical trembling, vibrating, or shaking. In its primary active sense, it takes Ātmanepada endings ('kṣmāyate' = trembles). In causative usage (putting into shaking motion), it takes the Niñ/Ṇic affix with -p- āgama yielding 'kṣmāpayati' (causes to tremble / agitates).

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga (Present Indicative, 3rd Person Singular, Ātmanepada)
scenarios.example_english: The tree trembles due to the fear of the gale.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic Prayoga, Present Indicative, 3rd Person Singular, Parasmaipada)
scenarios.example_english: The strong wind causes the branches of the tree to shake.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'kṣmāñ' is listed under the Bhvādi-gaṇa in the meaning of 'kampana' (shaking or vibrating). Due to the anubandha ñ-kāra, it accepts Ātmanepada affixes in kartari prayoga (forming 'kṣmāyate') and follows aniṭ inflectional principles in non-conjugational tenses.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kṣīrasvāmin notes 'kṣmāñ kampane' as expressing rapid trembling or tremor. In srvadhātuka contexts, it undergoes the required y-agama/vikaraṇa modifications resulting in the standard present base 'kṣmāya-'.

meanings.English: to shake, to tremble, to quiver

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'pard' describes the bodily action of expelling intestinal gas (flatulence) or making a vulgar sound. Belonging to the Bhvadi class with an anudatta marker, it strictly conjugates in the Atmanepada (middle voice) in normal active usage. When causative affixes (nic) are attached, it changes meaning to causing someone or something to expel flatulence.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakara (present indicative), 3rd person singular
scenarios.example_english: Due to indigestion, the boy breaks wind repeatedly.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (causative), Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, 3rd person singular
scenarios.meaning: causes to break wind / induces flatulence
scenarios.example_english: Impure food causes the stomach to produce flatulence.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti classifies 'parda' under 'kutsite sabde' and 'apanavayavotsarge'. Because the root is marked as anudattopadesha, it receives Atmanepada terminations exclusively in non-causative conjugations, producing the standard paradigm forms pardate, paparde, pardita, and pardishyate.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'parda kutsitadhvanau apanavayutsarge ca', confirming its semantic domain in expelling lower bodily air. It explains nominal derivations such as 'pardah' (an act of flatulence) and confirms that it behaves as a standard set root.

meanings.English: To break wind, to fart, to expel flatulence

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'kṣad' fundamentally conveys preparing or refining (saṃskāra) as well as dividing or carving portions (saṃvibhāga). Because it is anudāttet, it takes Ātmanepada endings in standard usage (kṣadate) when someone prepares food or allocates shares. In the causative form (kṣadayati), it signifies causing someone else to divide, prepare, or dress provisions.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The chef prepares and apportions the meal properly.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (Causative), Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: Causes someone to divide or carve
scenarios.example_english: The master causes the servant to distribute the goods.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root kṣada is glossed in the senses of refining/preparing (saṃskāra) and partition/distribution (saṃvibhāga). Being anudāttet, it declines in the Ātmanepada (kṣadate). The vritti notes that in Vedic usage, it frequently denotes slicing or preparing sacrificial offerings and food portions.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines the scope as 'saṃskāraḥ pariṣkāraḥ' (refinement, culinary preparation or embellishment) and 'saṃvibhāgaḥ pṛthagbhāvaḥ' (dividing, distributing into portions). It takes standard seṭ augment iṭ in non-sarvadhatuka contexts.

meanings.English: to divide, apportion, carve, or prepare (food)
meanings.Bengali: bhhag kora, bonton kora, sanskar kora

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'kṛp' belongs to the 1st conjugation (Bhvādi gaṇa) and takes exclusively Ātmanepada terminations. It primarily conveys the sense of ability, adequacy, competence, or strength (sāmarthye). When combined with causative affixes, it conveys making someone capable or empowering them.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga (active voice), laṭ lakāra (present tense), prathama puruṣa, ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The learned person is capable in all undertakings.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: ṇic pratyaya (causative), kartari prayoga, laṭ lakāra, prathama puruṣa, ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The teacher makes the student capable through knowledge.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'kṛpa' is indexed in the sense of sāmarthya (capability, strength, or competence). Being an anudāttet root in the standard Bhvādi sequence, it takes Ātmanepada affixes. In the present tense, guṇa vowel modification does not occur in simple forms due to the structural nature of short ṛ before consonants without specific lengthening conditions, yielding 'kṛpate'. It is seṭ in general ardhadhātuka environments.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines 'kṛpa sāmarthye' as denoting adequacy, power, or competence (śakti/samarthatva). He notes that its inflectional paradigm follows standard ātmanepada bhvādi patterns such as kṛpate, cakṛpe, kṛpitā, and kṛpiṣyate.

meanings.English: to be capable, to be able, to be competent
meanings.French: être capable, être en état de, avoir la force de
meanings.Russian: byt sposobnym, imet silu ili vozmozhnost

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'kākh' means to laugh or chuckle. In its basic Parasmaipada form, the subject performs the laughing themselves. When converted into a causative (Nic) form, it changes the meaning to causing someone else to laugh (e.g., telling a joke).

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (Present indicative 3rd person singular, Lat lakara)
scenarios.example_english: The boy laughs with his friend.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic-pratyaya, Lat lakara)
scenarios.example_english: The jester makes everyone laugh.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'kākhṛ' belongs to the Bhvadi class and is read with the anubandha 'ṛ' indicating 'hasane' (to laugh). Being an udātta-svarita sequence with an it-marker ṛdit, it conjugates as kākhati, cakākha, kākhitā, kākhiṣyati. It is classified as an it-taking root (seṭ).
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'kākhṛ hasane' as expressing mirth and laughter. He groups it alongside onomatopoeic guttural stems expressing facial or vocal expressions of amusement, confirming forms such as cakākha and kākhitum.

meanings.English: to laugh, to chuckle, to deride

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root kṣaj refers to obstructing or checking movement, as well as striking or overpowering. In the active voice (Kartari Parasmaipada), the subject performs the act of blocking or striking. When used with a causative affix (Nic), it signifies making someone obstruct or defend against an incoming force.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (present active 3rd person singular, Lat lakara)
scenarios.example_english: The brave warrior blocks the path.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (causative present active 3rd person singular, Lat lakara)
scenarios.example_english: The commander makes the soldiers hold back the advance.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya explains 'kṣaja gatipratighate' as denoting the obstruction or impedance of motion, as well as forceful injury or restraint. Morphologically, it forms 'kṣajati' with the standard thematic vikarana 'sap', with regular reduplication in perfect yielding 'cakṣaja'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines the dhatu under the sense of checking or repelling velocity ('gatipratighata') and inflicting harm. It highlights the formation of regular Parasmaipada terminations without nasalization.

meanings.English: to obstruct movement, check, strike, overpower
meanings.Hindi: gati rokna, badha dalna, prahar karna
meanings.Bengali: goti rodh kora, aghat kora, thamano

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'raṇ' means to produce a ringing, tinkling, or musical sound. In the standard active voice (Parasmaipada), it describes an object or ornament producing sound on its own. When used with the causative suffix (ṇic), it transforms into 'raṇayati', meaning to cause something to ring, strike, or sound.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga (Present Active, 3rd Person Singular)
scenarios.example_english: The anklet tinkles on the foot.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Ṇic Pratyaya, Present Active)
scenarios.example_english: The boy rings the bell.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti glosses 'raṇa kvaṇe' as denoting the generation of sound or jingling (kvaṇana-dhavani-rūpe). It details standard Bhvādi derivations with the sap-pratyaya yielding 'raṇati', reduplicated perfect forms 'rarāṇa', and periphrastic futures 'raṇitā'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin in Kshiratarangini treats 'raṇa kvaṇe' alongside other sonic roots like bhaṇa and cana, emphasizing its usage in the sense of sharp, musical, or resonant ringing sounds (kvaṇanārtha).

meanings.English: to sound, to ring, to tinkle, to chime

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root druph signifies feeling full, content, or satisfied (trpti). In simple active voice (Parasmaipada), the subject becomes pleased or contented on their own. When the causative suffix (nic) is added, it means causing someone else to feel satisfied or nourishing them.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga, lat-lakara, prathama-purusha, eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The child is satisfied with milk.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: nic-pratyaya (causative), lat-lakara, prathama-purusha, eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The mother satisfies the infant with sweets.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: drupha trptau. ayam bhvadih parasmaipadi udattah anit. trptih poshanam trptibhavo va. druphati, adrophit, drophita ityadi rupani bhavanti.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: drupha trptau. trup-trmph-druph-drmphity-ete catvarah parasmaipadinah trptyarthah. druphati, drophita, drophitum iti kshirasvami.

meanings.English: to be satisfied, to be pleased, to feel contented

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'rok' means to obstruct, restrain, or hold back. As an Atmanepada root of the Bhvadi class, it takes the 'te' ending in the present tense (rokate). When converted into a causative (Nic), it signifies making someone obstruct or causing an obstacle, taking both Parasmaipada and Atmanepada forms like rokayati or rokayate.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara (present tense), prathama purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The soldier obstructs the road.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic), Lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The king causes the flow of enemies to be stopped.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti explains 'rokṛ rodhane' as an anudattet, ātmanepadi root belonging to the bhvādi class denoting the act of hindering, holding back, or enclosing (rodhana). Due to the anubandha 'ṛ', it takes the intermediate augment 'i' (seṭ) in non-sarvadhatuka environments.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin in Kshiratarangini groups 'rokṛ' among the set of roots ending in 'k' expressing 'rodhane' (obstruction, blocking). He notes its regular Atmanepada conjugation like 'rokate, roroke, rokitā'.

meanings.English: to obstruct, to restrain, to block, to hinder

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'ej' conveys the action of trembling, shaking, or vibrating. In simple active voice (Parasmaipada), it describes a subject moving or trembling on its own. When the causative affix (nic) is added, it transitions to transitive usage meaning to agitate or cause something else to shake.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara (present tense), prathama-purusha, eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The boy trembles out of fear.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic-pratyaya), Lat lakara, prathama-purusha, eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The strong wind causes the branches of the tree to shake.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'ejṛ kampane' belongs to Bhvadi-gana, takes Parasmaipada affixes, and is anit/set classified as set with akarmaka valence. In standard derivations, it yields ejati, eje, and ejita. The semantic scope is defined as internal or physical oscillation and trembling.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'ejṛ kampane' denoting specific movement or vibration (gativishesha). The anubandha marker 'ṛ' indicates vowel gradation properties, producing forms such as ejati in the simple present and ejayati in causative constructs.

meanings.English: to tremble, to shake, to vibrate, to stir

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'svan' primarily denotes the action of paring down, chipping away, thinning, or cutting thin shavings (avatakshana). In the active voice (Kartari Parasmaipada), the subject performs the act of reducing or whittling an object. When modified by the causative affix 'nic', it denotes causing someone to pare or plane a material.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, prathama-purusha, eka-vacana (Simple Active Voice)
scenarios.meaning: Pares down, thins, or chips away
scenarios.example_english: The carpenter pares down the piece of wood.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (Causative), Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara
scenarios.meaning: Causes to pare down or chips through another
scenarios.example_english: The artisan causes his apprentice to pare the timber.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti glosses 'svana avataksane' as the process of peeling, thinning, or cutting away into thin layers (tanukaranam). Being set and belonging to the Bhvadi class, it takes the standard 'sap' vikarana yielding forms like svanati, sasvana/sasvana, and svanita.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes under 'svana avataksane' that 'avataksana' refers specifically to shaving, paring, or diminishing the thickness of an object (suksmi-karanam). It follows standard Parasmaipada inflection without idiosyncratic stem contractions.

meanings.English: to pare down, to chip away, to plane, to thin

canonical_dhatvartha: hiṁsāyām (in the sense of injuring, hurting, or harming)

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'riṣ' means to injure or inflict harm on someone or something. In standard active voice (Parasmaipada), the subject performs the act of harming. When converted into the causative form (nic), it signifies causing someone to inflict injury or damaging something through an agent.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga (active voice), lat-lakara (present tense), prathama-purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The wicked person harms everyone.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: nic-pratyaya (causative), lat-lakara, prathama-purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: Bad addiction ruins a man.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'riṣa' in the Bhvādi-gaṇa is documented in the sense of violence and injury (hiṁsāyām). Being in the first conjugation, it undergoes guṇa in sārvadhātuka environments yielding the base 'reṣa-', forming 'reṣati', 'reṣataḥ', 'reṣanti'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'riṣa hiṁsāyām' among roots expressing injury and destruction. It follows the regular Bhvādi inflection pattern in Parasmaipada with guṇa strengthening of the radical short vowel 'i' to 'e'.

meanings.English: to injure, harm, hurt, or destroy

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'śūla' means to ache, pain, or cause intense piercing suffering (like being poked by a sharp spear, known as a śūla). In normal active voice (Parasmaipada), it describes something aching or causing painful distress.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakara (present tense), prathama-purusha ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: Due to bad food, his stomach aches.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (causative), Lat lakara, prathama-purusha ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The severe fever torments the child.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'śūla' is classified under 'rujāyām' (in the sense of pain, disease, or infliction of severe distress). Conjugated with standard 'śap' vikarana in the first class, yielding 'śūlati'. In perfect tense (lit), it forms 'śuśūla'. As a set root, it takes the intermediate 'i' augment in ardhadhatuka forms such as 'śūlitā' and 'śūliṣyati'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin glosses 'śūla rujāyām' as conveying bodily piercing anguish or affliction (pīḍā). The root preserves its long vowel across sarvadhatuka formations (śūlati, śūlataḥ, śūlanti) and retains 'iṭ' in forms like 'śūlitum' and 'śūlitvā'.

meanings.English: to ache, to inflict pain, to torment, to pierce
meanings.Bengali: bēthanā haoyā, jantranā dēoyā, biddha karā

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'nat' means to dance, perform, or act on stage. In standard active voice (Parasmaipada), it describes a person performing a dance or theatrical role. When modified by the causative affix (nic), it signifies teaching someone to dance or directing/staging a dramatic performance.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Lat lakar (Present Tense), Kartari Prayoga (Active Voice), 3rd person singular
scenarios.example_english: The actor acts on the stage.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic-pratyaya), Present Tense, 3rd person singular
scenarios.meaning: causes to act / enacts / directs a performance
scenarios.example_english: The teacher makes the students perform on the stage.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti records 'naṭṛ nṛttau' as a Bhvadi-gana Parasmaipada root with penultimate 'ṛ' as an it marker. Being seṭ, it takes intermediate 'i' in non-sarvadhatuka environments (e.g., naṭitā, naṭiṣyati). It is noted as the morphological base for theatrical action and dramatic representation, distinct in formation from the 4th class root 'nṛt'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshiratarangini treats 'naṭṛ' in the sense of 'nṛttau' (dramatic dancing and mime), detailing its primary derivations such as 'naṭa' (an actor or performer) and explaining the absence of samprasarana or special vowel changes in the present stem.

meanings.English: to dance, to act on stage, to represent dramatically
meanings.French: danser, jouer un rôle, monter sur scène
meanings.Russian: tantsevat', igrat' rol', vystupat' na stsene

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'dal' primarily means to burst open, crack, blossom, or split into pieces. In simple active voice (kartari prayoga), it describes something opening up naturally (like a flower) or cracking. When converted into a causative verb (nic-pratyaya) as 'dalayati' or 'dalayati/dalayati', it means causing something to tear apart or actively crushing/breaking it into fragments.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga (active voice), lat-lakara (present tense), prathama-purusha eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: In the morning, the lotus blossoms.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: nic-pratyaya (causative), kartari prayoga, lat-lakara
scenarios.example_english: The boy breaks the fruit into pieces.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti glosses 'dala visarane' with the sense of bhedana (breaking, tearing apart) and vikasana (unfolding, blossoming). It forms 'dalati' with intermediate it-agama in ardhadhatuka forms such as 'dalita' and 'dalitum'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes under 'dala visarane' that the primary denotation is splitting or opening up (visarana = vidarana/sphutana). He highlights derived nominals like 'dala' (a petal, leaf, or broken portion/part).

meanings.English: to burst open, blossom, split, crack, tear into pieces
meanings.French: eclore, s'ouvrir, fendre, briser en morceaux

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'hṛṣ' means to rejoice, be happy, or experience a thrill (like goosebumps from joy). In standard active voice (Parasmaipada), it describes someone feeling joyful on their own. When used with a causative suffix (Nic), it shifts to 'harṣayati', meaning to cause someone else to rejoice or gladden them.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Bhvadi Gana, Lat Lakara (Present Tense), Parasmaipada, Kartari Prayoga (Active Voice)
scenarios.example_english: Seeing his friend, the boy rejoices.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic Pratyaya (Causative), Lat Lakara, Parasmaipada, Prayojaka Kartari
scenarios.example_english: Sweet speech gladdens everyone.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'hṛṣī' belongs to the Bhvadi class and is read with the meaning 'tuṣṭi' (satisfaction, joy, bodily bristling through joy). Because of its terminal ī-kara it takes standard Guna in Sarvadhatuka affixes yielding 'harṣati', with forms like jaharsa and aharṣat.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'hṛṣī tuṣṭau' denoting mental delight as well as the physical manifestation of bristling hair (romaharṣa). It behaves as an Anit root taking Parasmaipada affixes in Kartari prayoga.

meanings.English: to rejoice, to be gladdened, to thrill with joy

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root tuñc refers to shrinking, contracting, or moving in a restrained manner. In its basic active form (Parasmaipada), it describes an object or person contracting or retreating. When used with a causative affix (Nic), it signifies making something shrink or contracting something intentionally.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga (Present tense 3rd person singular)
scenarios.example_english: The child shrinks back out of fear.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic-pratyaya, Kartari Prayoga)
scenarios.example_english: The cold makes the limb contract.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root tuñci has an idit marker indicating an obligatory penultimate nasal (num-agama), yielding the base form tuñc-. It is conjugated in the Bhvadi class taking Parasmaipada endings with the sense of contraction (sankocha) and motion (gati).
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes tuñci as an idit root denoting sankoca (contraction or shortening) and gait, following the standard sarvadhatuka vikarana shap.

meanings.English: to shrink, to contract, to curb, to move slowly
meanings.Bengali: shukro ba sankucita haoa, goti kora

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'hval' means to shake, stumble, wobble, or deviate. In primary usage, it takes Parasmaipada endings to describe someone or something trembling, faltering, or wavering. When converted into a causative form (nic), it takes the meaning of causing to stumble or making something unstable.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga (present active indicative, 3rd person singular)
scenarios.example_english: The old person stumbles on the path with his foot.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: nic pratyaya (causative active, 3rd person singular)
scenarios.meaning: causes to wobble, dislodges, or shakes
scenarios.example_english: The strong wind causes the tree to wobble.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'hvala calane' is listed in the jvaladi sub-class of the Bhvadi gana. It takes the affix sap in sarvadhatuka contexts and forms 'hvalati'. It belongs to the class where optional viddhi/na-vriddhi rules in causative (jvalahvalahmalanam...) apply.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'hvala calane' as meaning shaking or moving out of course. In ardhadhatuka derivation, forms such as jahvala and hvalita appear following general it-agama rules.

meanings.English: to shake, stumble, wobble, falter, or go astray
meanings.Bengali: tholmole houa, heledole jaoa, thotmoth khora

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root pṛṣ means to sprinkle, moisten, or scatter drops of liquid. In simple active voice (Parasmaipada), it describes an agent sprinkling water or essence over an object. When modified into the causative form (parṣayati / prāṣayati), it conveys making someone sprinkle or causing an area to be wetted.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice, present tense 3rd person singular)
scenarios.example_english: The gardener sprinkles the tree with water.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (causative present tense 3rd person singular)
scenarios.example_english: The farmer causes the helper to sprinkle the field.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti outlines 'pṛṣu secane' as a root denoting the action of discharge of water drops or sprinkling (secana). The it-marker 'u' denotes specific anidit rules in participial formations, yielding forms like pṛṣati, paparṣa, and parṣitā or praṣṭā in various lakaras.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin analyzes 'pṛṣu secane' within the group of liquid-scattering roots, noting its basic semantic sphere of wetting (ārdrakaraṇa) and sprinkling (kṣepaṇa of drops), demonstrating vowel alternations in perfect and aorist stems.

meanings.English: to sprinkle, to wet, to moisten

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root kruc primarily indicates the action of moving, bending, or slipping away quietly. In basic active voice (Kartari Prayoga), it takes Parasmaipada terminations with guṇa strengthening the vowel 'u' to 'o' before the conjugational affix śap, yielding 'krocati'. When used in causative (Ṇic), it means making someone move or causing something to bend.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga (Present tense, 3rd person singular, Laṭ)
scenarios.example_english: The traveler moves along the path.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Ṇic-pratyaya (Causative active present, 3rd person singular)
scenarios.meaning: Causes to move or bends something
scenarios.example_english: The wind causes the branch to bend.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: Madhaviya Dhatuvritti lists krucā in the sense of motion (gatau) alongside klucā. It notes the regular guṇa modification of the penultimate short vowel 'u' to 'o' in the sārvadhātuka tenses (krocati), lit forms (cukroca), and classifies its it-status within the halanta anit series.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin explains krucā as gatyarthaka (signifying movement or curved gait), highlighting that it belongs to the group of roots ending in palatal consonants following short vowels, generating forms such as krocati, akrokṣģt, and krocitā.

meanings.English: to go, to move, to bend, to slip away

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'ghur' means to sound frightful, roar, snort, or appear menacing. Since it is Atmanepada in the primary Bhvadi conjugation, it takes endings like '-te' (ghurate) to describe a person or animal making a terrible or frightful sound. In the causative form, it describes making someone roar or causing something to sound dreadful.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakara (present tense), 3rd person singular
scenarios.example_english: The lion roars frightfully in the forest.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (causative), Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, 3rd person singular
scenarios.meaning: causes to sound terrible or terrifying
scenarios.example_english: The enemy causes the army to roar terrifyingly.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'ghurR' belongs to Bhvadi gana and is designated in the sense of 'bhimarthe' (frightfulness, terrible sound or appearance). It takes the Atmanepada affix, yielding forms such as ghurate, jughure, and ghorishyate, with it-agama applying in the non-sarvadhatuka environments.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'ghurR bhime' indicating creating dread or uttering an awful, frightening sound. The anubandha 'R' indicates that the root undergoes specific accent and marker properties, and it declines as an Atmanepadi root in this class.

meanings.English: to make a frightful noise, to roar, to snort, to be terrible
meanings.Kannada: bhayankaravagi ghurukisu, garjisu, bheekara dhvani madu
meanings.Bengali: gorjon kora, bhoyonkor shobdo kora, ghurgon kora
meanings.French: rugir d'une maniere effrayante, grogner, effrayer

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'hval' means to stumble, shake, or waver. In its standard active form (Parasmaipada), it describes someone or something wavering or stumbling on its own. When used with a causative affix (Nic), it shifts to an action where one person causes another thing to shake, tilt, or go off track.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakara (present tense)
scenarios.example_sanskrit: dhairyavan narah kleshe sati api margat na hvalati.
scenarios.example_english: A courageous person does not waver from the righteous path even during hardship.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (causative), Lat lakara
scenarios.meaning: Causes to shake, derails, or makes stumble
scenarios.example_english: The strong wind causes the old man to stumble from the path.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: hvalṝ calane. calanam kampa iti skhalanam iti va arthaḥ. ṛditvat can-pare nisedhadikah svaro bhavati. hvalati, jahvala, ahvalit.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: hvalṝ calane. hvalati skhalati kampate va. anit-karikasu na pathita ityatas set.

meanings.English: to stumble, to waver, to shake, to falter
meanings.Bengali: tolomol kora, hnochot khaoya, kompit howa

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'lāch' means to mark, brand, or distinguish with a sign. It is conjugated in Parasmaipada to indicate an agent applying a mark or distinguishing label onto an object. In the causative form, it signifies causing someone else to put a mark on an object.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat-lakara, Prathama-purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: Marks or puts a distinctive sign on
scenarios.example_english: The cowherd marks the cattle with a stamp.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic-pratyaya), Lat-lakara, Prathama-purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: Causes to mark or gets marked
scenarios.example_english: The owner has the horse marked by the servant.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: lācha lakṣaṇe. lakṣaṇaṁ cihnam aṅkanaṁ vā. seṭ parasmaipadī. lāchati, lalācha, lāchitā, lāchiṣyati.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: lāchṛ lakṣaṇe. aṅkayatītyarthaḥ. lakṣaṇaṁ cihnakaraṇam. lāchati, lāchitvā.

meanings.English: to mark, to distinguish, to brand, to label

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'dhukṣ' means to kindle, ignite, or revitalize. Because it is inherently an Atmanepadi root, its core present-tense form is 'dhukṣate' (he/she kindles or becomes revitalized). When used with upasargas like 'sam', as in 'sandhukṣate' or causative 'sandhukṣayati', it expresses stoking a fire or reviving someone's energy.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Lat lakara (Present tense), Prathama purusha, Ekavacana, Kartari prayoga
scenarios.example_english: The sage kindles the sacrificial fire.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (Causative), Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: Causes to blaze up, stimulates, or invigorates
scenarios.example_english: The friend's words reinvigorate his enthusiasm.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'dhukṣa' is glossed as 'sandīpane' (in the sense of inflaming, kindling, or stimulating). Due to being anudattet, it takes Atmanepada endings across the sarvadhatuka lakaras, yielding the primary form 'dhukṣate' and the lit form 'dudhukṣe'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines 'dhukṣa sandīpane' as 'sandīpanaṃ prajvalanaṃ poṣaṇaṃ ca' (kindling, causing to flame up, or fostering growth), illustrating the formation of standard Bhvadi conjugations with intermediate id-agama in ardhadhatuka environments.

meanings.English: to kindle, ignite, inflame, invigorate

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root svṛ means to make a sound, to praise/chant, or to suffer pain and affliction. In the active voice (Parasmaipada), it typically denotes making an audible musical or resonating sound, whereas in reflexive or middle usage (Atmanepada), it can indicate experiencing internal distress, pain, or producing sound for oneself. When used with the causative affix (Nich), it denotes causing someone to resound, utter, or torment.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara (Present tense), Prathama purusha, Ekavacana (Parasmaipada)
scenarios.example_english: The drum resonates loudly.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nich-pratyaya (Causative), Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The singer makes the lute resound.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti analyzes 'svṛ śabdo patāpayoḥ' as functioning in the dual semantics of producing sound (dhvani/shabda) and causing or experiencing affliction (rogadi-santapa/vedana). It notes the vocalic alternation in universal Sarvadhatuka environments yielding 'svarati' / 'svarate' with Guna substitution of the stem vowel 'r' to 'ar'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin in Kshiratarangini clarifies that svṛ denotes both articulation/chanting (svaryate/svarati) and bodily torment or distress (upatapa). He highlights the root's classification among vowels taking anit or set conditions in specific derived forms (svartum/svaritum) and its morphophonemic treatment in Vedic accents and general classical usage.

meanings.English: to sound, resonate, chant, or suffer pain/affliction
meanings.Kannada: dhvani madu, shabda madu, novannu anubhavisu
meanings.Telugu: dhvani cheyu, shabdamu cheyu, vedana padu
meanings.Hindi: dhvani karna, gunjana, shabda karna, dukh ya kasht jhelna
meanings.Bengali: shabda kara, dhvani tola, klesha ba bedana pawa
meanings.French: résonner, faire du bruit, chanter, souffrir
meanings.Russian: zvuchat, izdavat zvuk, oglasit, stradat ot boli

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root dhuksh fundamentally means to kindle, ignite, enliven, or nourish. In its base Atmanepada form (dhukshate), it expresses the action of flaring up, becoming invigorated, or kindling. When prefixed with 'sam' (sandhukshate) or used in the causative (sandhukshayati), it denotes active kindling or reviving something like fire, strength, or enthusiasm.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, prathama-purusha, eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The fire flares up in a moment.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (causative) with upasarga 'sam', Lat lakara, prathama-purusha, eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The wind kindles the fire.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti explains dhuksha in the sense of sandipana (kindling, inflaming, or nourishing). It is an Atmanepadi root with an indicatory vowel 'a', taking the theme affix shap to yield dhukshate in the present indicative.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes that dhuksha denotes sandipana (lighting up, enlivening, or stirring). It operates as a Set root yielding dhukshitam in the past participle and conjugated with intermediate 'i' in general non-conjugational tenses.

meanings.English: to kindle, ignite, enliven, or inflame
meanings.Hindi: sulagana, jalana, prerita ya uttejita karana

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'krath' belongs to the Bhvadi class and means 'to harm, injure, or kill'. It is primarily conjugated in Parasmaipada in active voice, meaning the subject executes the action of harming an object. When made causative (Nic-pratyaya), it denotes causing someone to harm or slaying through an instigator.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat-lakara (Active voice, Present indicative), Parasmaipada, Prathama-purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The hunter kills the deer in the forest.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (Causative), Kartari prayoga, Lat-lakara, Parasmaipada, Prathama-purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: He/she causes to kill or slays
scenarios.example_english: The king causes the enemy to be slain through the warriors.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: Madhaviya Dhatuvritti notes that the root 'kratha' is read in the sense of 'himsayam' (violence or injuring). It takes the standard Shap vikaranapratyaya of the Bhvadi class, resulting in regular guna/lengthening where applicable, taking set-agamas in ardhadhatuka affixes, forming krathati, cakratha, krathita, and akrathit.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin in Kshiratarangini explains 'kratha himsayam', grouping it with roots denoting destruction and harm. It takes simple Parasmaipada endings with set characteristics throughout ardhadhatuka tenses.

meanings.English: to harm, kill, or injure

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'vāñch' means to desire or wish for something. In its normal active form (Parasmaipada), it shows what a person desires directly. When used with a causative affix (Nic), it means to cause someone else to desire or wish for something.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakara (present tense), 3rd person singular
scenarios.example_english: The boy desires knowledge.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic pratyaya), Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara
scenarios.meaning: causes to desire / inspires a wish in
scenarios.example_english: The teacher inspires the student to desire wisdom.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root vāñchi is classified under the Bhvādi-gana with the meaning 'icchāyām' (in the sense of desiring or longing). Being an idit root (having an 'i' as an it-marker), it permanently retains the penultimate nasal augment (num-āgama), yielding forms like vāñchati, vavāñcha, and vāñchitaḥ.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines vāñchi in the sense of 'icchā' (wish/desire). The augment num is regular due to idit-tva, producing present indicative vāñchati and primary nominal derivatives such as vāñchā (desire, longing).

meanings.English: to desire, to wish for, to long for

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'jṛṣ' means to age, wear down, or decay. In its base active form (Parasmaipada), it describes a subject naturally growing old or losing physical strength. When converted to a causative form (ṇic), it changes from intransitive to transitive, meaning to wear out, exhaust, or cause someone to age prematurely.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat-lakara (present tense), Prathama-purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: With time, the physical body decays and grows old.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (ṇic-pratyaya), Kartari prayoga, Lat-lakara
scenarios.meaning: causes to decay / wears out / ages someone
scenarios.example_english: Excessive grief wears a person out and ages them.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: jṛṣī vayohānau. bhvādigaṇa-antargataḥ parasmaipadī seṭ. īdit-karaṇāt 'īditaḥ' iti niṣṭhā-tasya na natvam, kvacid iṭ-vikalpādikaṁ ca boddhavyam. guṇe kṛte 'jarṣati' iti rūpaṁ bhavati.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: jṛṣī vayohānau. vayaḥ parihāṇiḥ kṣayaḥ. jarṣati, jajarṣa, jarṣiṣyati. īdittvāt niṣṭhāyāṁ na natvamiti viśeṣaḥ.

meanings.English: to age, to decay, to grow old, to wither or lose vitality
meanings.Hindi: būḍhā honā, kṣīṇa honā, umra ḍhalanā
meanings.Bengali: bṛddha haoā, kṣīṇa haoā, boyos bāṛā

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'svaj' means to hug, embrace, or cling to someone. It is inherently an Atmanepada verb, expressing actions of close personal contact or mutual affection. When used with prefixes like 'pari-', it emphasizes embracing warmly.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara (Present tense), Prathama purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The mother embraces her son out of affection.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Upasarga 'pari' prefixation, Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara
scenarios.meaning: He or she embraces completely / warmly
scenarios.example_english: A friend embraces a friend with joy.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti analyzes 'ṣvañja pariṣvaṅge' as an anudatta-it, ātmanepada root. In sarvadhatuka affixes, the nasal is dropped according to standard Paninian deletion rules for non-it roots when marked (svajate). In kit/knit environments, the penultimate nasal is dropped (e.g., svakta, svañjita in certain secondary derivations).
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes in the Kshiratarangini that 'ṣvañja' governs contact and close physical attachment ('pariṣvaṅga'). It is anit and exhibits elision of the internal nasal before standard non-nasal endings, giving the present tense form 'svajate'.

meanings.English: to embrace, to clasp, to cling to, to encircle

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'dhre' means to diminish, decline, or waste away. Because it ends with the anubandha letter 'ṅ' in the Dhatupatha (dhreṅ), it strictly conjugates in the Atmanepada voice in the simple active present tense (Kartari). When making causative forms with the suffix 'ṇic', it switches to express causing something else to diminish or waste away.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Active Voice (Kartari Prayoga), Present Tense (Lat Lakara), 3rd Person Singular (Prathama Purusha Ekavacana)
scenarios.example_english: Due to the effect of illness, the body wastes away.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic Pratyaya), Active Present (Lat Lakara), 3rd Person Singular
scenarios.example_english: Grief diminishes his physical strength.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: dhreṅ kṣaye. anudātteṅitvād ātmanepadam. śap. dhrayate. eṅantatvād eca igghrasvādeśe prāpte 'aco 'ṇṇiti' ityādi-pravṛttau rūpa-siddhiḥ.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: dhreṅ kṣaye. kṣayo hāniḥ parikṣīṇatvam. ātmanepadī. dhrayate, didhre, dhretā.

meanings.English: to decline, to diminish, to waste away
meanings.Hindi: kshina hona, kam hona, ghata jana
meanings.Bengali: kshay paoa, rhāsa paoa, khaya haoya

canonical_dhatvartha: gatau (to go), dāne (to give), hiṃsāyām (to injure/strike)

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'kṣaj' belongs to the 1st conjugation (Bhvadi-gana) and is used in the Parasmaipada voice. Depending on context, it expresses moving, giving, or striking/injuring. When adding the causative suffix (Nic), the agent causes another entity to move, give, or strike.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Lat (Present Indicative), Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The warrior strikes the enemy on the battlefield.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (Causative), Lat, Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: causes to go or causes to give
scenarios.example_english: The king causes the gift to be given.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: kṣaja gatau dāne hiṃsāyāṃ ca. It is classified under the Parasmaipada section of Bhvadi-gana. The root takes the standard sap vikarana in sarvadhatuka tenses without internal modification of the vowel, producing forms such as kṣajati, kṣajataḥ, and kṣajanti.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: kṣaja gatyartho hiṃsārtho dānārthaśca. Kshirasvamin underscores the threefold semantic range encompassing motion (gati), injury (himsa), and donation/dispensation (dana), conjugated regularly with Parasmaipada terminations.

meanings.English: to go, to move, to give, to strike or injure
meanings.Bengali: jaoya, gamanan kora, dana kora, aghata kora

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'pan' means to praise, admire, or extol. By the special grammatical rule of Panini (sutra 3.1.28: gupu-dhupa-vicchi-pani-panibhya ayah), it mandatorily takes the suffix 'aya' in sarvadhatuka tenses, forming 'panāyate' in the Atmanepada voice. In causative or standard present constructions, it shows deep respect or admiration toward someone or something noble.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakara (present tense), 3rd person singular with obligatory 'aya' affix
scenarios.example_english: The seeker praises the divine virtues of God.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakara (present tense), 3rd person plural with 'aya' affix
scenarios.example_english: Scholars always praise the truth.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti lists the root as 'panī stomaviketanayoḥ' belonging to the Bhvadi class. Madhava explains that 'stoma' denotes praise or laudation (stuti), while 'viketana' signifies manifestation or showing special regard. He details the application of the 'aya' affix by the sutra 'gupūdhūpavicchipaṇipanibhya āyaḥ' (3.1.28), making the present tense form 'panāyate'. In non-sarvadhatuka forms, the affix 'aya' applies optionally according to 'āyādaya ārdhadhātuke vā'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin interprets 'panī' in the sense of 'stomaviketanayoḥ' (praise and clear recognition). He notes the inclusion of 'pan' alongside 'pan' and 'gup' within the specialized group taking the 'aya' pratyaya, yielding forms like 'panāyate' and derivative nominal forms like 'panāyita'.

meanings.English: to praise, to admire, to honor, to celebrate
meanings.Bengali: proshongsha kora, stuti kora, gunogaan kora

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'jvar' denotes falling ill, being afflicted with a fever, or burning with heat/distress. In active voice (Kartari Prayoga), it is conjugated in Parasmaipada as 'jvarati' (he/she suffers from fever). When used in the causative (Nic), it becomes 'jvarayati' meaning 'to cause someone to suffer fever or distress'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Simple Present (Lat Lakara, Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana)
scenarios.example_english: The sick boy suffers from fever due to the wound.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic Pratyaya, Lat Lakara)
scenarios.example_english: The intense heat causes fever in the traveler.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti analyzes 'jvara roge' as belonging to the Bhvadi class. It notes the special elongation and elision rules under Sutra 'jvaratvarasrivyavimavam upadhāyāsca' (6.4.20) in certain derived forms, demonstrating root operations in Kit-Ngit affixes.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin in Kshiratarangini explains 'jvara roge' as the condition of morbid heat and internal bodily distress caused by disease. It emphasizes its standard Parasmaipada inflection taking the Sap vikarana (jvarati).

meanings.English: to be afflicted with fever, to suffer from disease, to be distressed
meanings.Hindi: jvar se pidit hona, bukhar ana, rogagrast hona
meanings.Bengali: jvare bhoga, jvar asha, rogakranta howa
meanings.German: an Fieber leiden, fiebern, krank sein
meanings.French: avoir la fievre, etre malade, etre afflige de fievre

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'prath' means to become famous, expand, or spread out. By default in the 1st Gana, it is used in the Atmanepada voice (prathate). When we want to express that someone is actively causing something else to spread or making it famous, we add the causative suffix (Nic) to form 'prathayati'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, Prathama-purusha, Ekavacana (Atmanepada)
scenarios.example_english: The fame of a knowledgeable person spreads everywhere.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Prena/Nic), Parasmaipada, Lat lakara, Prathama-purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: causes to spread or makes something widely known
scenarios.example_english: The sun spreads light across the world.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya explains 'pratha prakhyane' as meaning prasiddhi (becoming famous or evident) and vistara (expansion). Since it is anudattet, it takes Atmanepada endings in standard active voice (kartari). It is a seṭ dhatu, taking an augment 'i' in non-sarvadhatuka forms like the periphrastic future and participles (prathita).
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes that 'prakhyanam' signifies unfolding, manifesting, and achieving widespread renown. He illustrates that the root implies both physical extension and metaphorical diffusion of glory or news.

meanings.English: to spread, to become famous, to unfold, to expand
meanings.Bengali: prasiddha haoa, choriye pora, bistrito haoa
meanings.German: sich verbreiten, beruehmt werden, sich entfalten

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'dhrāj' means 'to move', 'to glide', or 'to fly swiftly'. It is used in the Parasmaipada voice in active constructions. In its causative form (nic), it signifies 'causing to move' or 'propelling'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Active Voice (kartari prayoga), Present Tense (laṭ, 3rd person singular)
scenarios.example_english: The bird glides in the sky.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (ṇic-pratyaya), Present Tense (laṭ, 3rd person singular)
scenarios.example_english: The wind propels the cloud.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: dhrājī gatau. bhvādau parasmaipadī seṭ. dhrājati, dadhrāja, dhrājitā. gatyarthatvāt akarmakaḥ.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: dhrājī gatau. dhrājati. īkāraḥ svarasiddhi-prayojanaḥ. dhrājiḥ śīghragatau prasiddhaḥ.

meanings.English: to move, glide, fly swiftly
meanings.Hindi: calanā, vega se udanā yā jānā

transitivity: Dvikarmaka / Ubhayavidha (Intransitive in motion/emaciation, Transitive in conciliation)

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'klās' belongs to the first group of verbs (Bhvādi gaṇa) and takes standard Parasmaipada endings. It primarily describes physical movement (going/approaching) or pleasing/conciliating someone (rādhanam). In practical usage, adding personal endings like '-ati' gives active agentive forms like 'klāsati' (he/she moves or pleases).

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Laṭ (Present tense), Prathama puruṣa, Ekavacana, Parasmaipada
scenarios.example_english: The traveler walks along the path.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Luṅ (Aorist / Past tense), Prathama puruṣa, Ekavacana, Parasmaipada
scenarios.example_english: He pleased the master with his gentle words.
