scenarios.example_english: The child clings to the mother with deep affection.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: ṇic pratyaya (causative), Parasmaipada, lat lakara
scenarios.example_english: Affection causes the children to embrace one another.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'śuc̐' belongs to the Bhvadi gana and is glossed as 'abhiṣvaṅge' meaning close union, embrace, or deep attachment. Due to the anudatta it-marker on the final vowel, it takes Atmanepada affixes (śucate, śuśuce).
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'śuca abhiṣvaṅge' as denoting intense embrace, connection, or clinging. It conjugates with guna in sarvadhatuka contexts when applicable, yielding forms like śucate in the present tense.

meanings.English: to embrace, to cling to, to be attached

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'spand' means to throb, twitch, or move slightly. It takes Atmanepada endings in basic active usage (kartari prayoga) to describe an involuntary or gentle movement within an entity. When transformed into the causative (Nic) form, it expresses making something vibrate or causing a pulse.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat-lakara, Prathama-purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The child's eye is twitching.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (Causative), Parasmaipada, Lat-lakara, Prathama-purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: causes to quiver / sets into slight motion
scenarios.example_english: The gentle breeze causes the leaf to quiver.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root spadi is idit, which necessitates the insertion of a canonical num-agama (nasalization), producing the base spand. It denotes subtle movement (kiñciccalana). It is anudattet and therefore belongs to the Atmanepada stream.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes that spadi is idit and means kiñciccalanam (minor agitation or slight pulsing). Forms such as spandate and paspande are formed regularly within the Bhvadi class.

meanings.English: to throb, quiver, twitch, move slightly

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'spardh' means to compete, emulate, or rival someone. Because it is inherently Atmanepada (anudattet), its standard present tense form ends in '-te' (spardhate). In causative forms (Nic), it signifies making someone compete or challenging someone to a contest.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana (standard Atmanepada)
scenarios.example_english: The boy competes with his friend in knowledge.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (Causative), Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The teacher makes the two wrestlers compete against each other.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'spardha' belongs to the Bhvadi class and is read with an anudatta vowel marker signifying Atmanepada. It is glossed as 'sangharshe', which refers to mutual emulation, rivalry, or the desire to excel over another. In sarvadhatuka tenses, the vikaranashap applies, yielding forms like spardhate, spardhete, spardhante.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines 'sangharsha' as 'ahamahamika' (the spirit of asserting oneself over another). Being a set root with initial conjunct 'sp', it takes the regular augment 'it' in ardhadhatuka formations like paspardhe and spardhita.

meanings.English: to compete, to rival, to vie with, to challenge
meanings.Hindi: spardha karna, hod lagana, mukabala karna

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'dṛś' fundamentally means 'to see' or 'to behold'. In general present tense active usage (Kartari Prayoga), it replaces its stem with 'paśya' to mean 'sees'. When used in the causative form (Nic pratyaya), it becomes 'darśayati', altering the action to mean 'shows' or 'causes someone to see'. In the passive voice (Karmani Prayoga), it retains the root form as 'dṛśyate' meaning 'is seen'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga (Present tense active with paśy-ādeśa)
scenarios.example_english: The boy looks at the picture.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic-pratyaya)
scenarios.example_english: The mother shows the moon to the child.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: Madhaviya Dhatuvritti details that 'dṛśir prekṣaṇe' takes the substitution 'paśya' in Sarvadhatuka environments by the Paninian rule 'pā-ghrā-dhmā-sthā-mnā-dāṇ-dṛśy-arti-sarv-arti-śad-sadāṃ piba-jighra-dhama-tiṣṭha-mana-yaccha-paśrchha-dhav-āśīya-sīdāḥ'. Because 'ir' is an It-marker indicating Anit-tva, its Ardhadhatuka forms do not take the augment iṭ, generating forms like draṣṭā, drakṣyati, and adrākṣīt.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes under Kshiratarangini that 'dṛśir' is Sakarmaka and signifies visual perception (prekṣaṇa). He explains the retention of the original guttural-retroflex transformations in Ardhadhatuka paradigms and confirms the elision of the anubandha 'ir' which regulates intermediate aorist and desiderative formations.

meanings.English: to see, to perceive, to observe, to behold

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'ris' means to hurt, tear, or cause injury. In active voice (Parasmaipada), it describes an agent directly causing physical injury or damage to an object. When modified by prefixes or causative affixes (nic), it signifies actively causing harm or inflicting pain upon another.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat-lakara (present tense), prathama-purusha (3rd person singular)
scenarios.example_english: The tiger injures the herd of deer.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (causative), Kartari prayoga, Lat-lakara
scenarios.meaning: causes to be injured or tormented
scenarios.example_english: Bad conduct causes harm to people.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'risa himsayam' belongs to the Bhvadi class. It takes sap-pratyaya with guna of the root vowel (i becomes e in sarvadhatuka contexts, yielding resati/risati based on traditional recensions). In Madhava's exposition, it is glossed identically to rusa in the sense of injuring, destroying, or tearing.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines 'risa' under 'himsayam' (in the sense of harming or violence). It follows the standard phonological derivations of talavya-sha-ending roots of the Bhvadi class, forming parasmaipada forms without optional atmanepada endings.

meanings.English: to injure, to harm, to tear, to hurt
meanings.Hindi: himsan karna, chot pahunchana, kasht dena
meanings.Bengali: hingsa kora, aaghat kora, khoti kora

canonical_dhatvartha: sāmarthye (in the sense of capacity, fitness, or compassion)

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'kṛp' belongs to the First Conjugation (Bhvadi-gana) and regularly uses Atmanepada endings. It conveys being capable, fitting, or experiencing deep compassion/pity. When an affix like the causative (ṇic) is attached, it transforms to 'karpayati', shifting the sense to enabling, preparing, or causing pity.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Lat-lakara (present tense), prathama-purusha (third person), eka-vacana (singular), Atmanepada
scenarios.meaning: is capable, feels compassion, or laments
scenarios.example_english: The compassionate person feels pity for the distressed.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (causative present), prathama-purusha, eka-vacana, Parasmaipada
scenarios.meaning: enables, makes fit, or evokes pity
scenarios.example_english: Knowledge equips the boy for action.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: Krpū sāmarthye. Anudāttetvāt ātmanepadī. Sāmarthyaṁ yogyatvam. Krpate iti rūpaṁ bhavati. Kṣīrasvāmī tu kṛpāyām apīcchati.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kṛpū sāmarthye. Kṛpate sāmarthyaṁ prāpnoti, kṛpāyāṁ vartate vā. Yogyatāyāṁ vā prayogaḥ.

meanings.English: to be capable, to be fit, to pity, to lament
meanings.Tamil: tiran ulladaga iruttal, irakkam kattudal, varundudal
meanings.Hindi: samarth hona, daya karna, kripa karna
meanings.Bengali: samartha haoya, daya kara, kripa kara
meanings.German: fahig sein, taugen, sich erbarmen, Mitleid haben
meanings.French: etre capable, etre apte, avoir pitie

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'gadi~' means to be a part of the face or cheek, or to swell/appear upon the cheek. Because it has an 'i' as an indicator (idit), a nasal 'n' is inserted before the final consonant, transforming 'gad' into 'gand'. In its basic Atmanepada form, it describes something manifesting on the cheek or face, while the causative form denotes causing something to mark or appear on the cheek.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga (Present Indicative, 3rd Person Singular, Atmanepada)
scenarios.meaning: It appears on the cheek / it forms a part of the cheek
scenarios.example_english: A mark or swelling appears on the cheek.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Prerana / Nich-pratyaya, Parasmaipada)
scenarios.meaning: Causes to mark or swell the cheek
scenarios.example_english: The ailment causes swelling on the child's cheek.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'gadi' is categorized under vadanaikadeshe (pertaining to a specific region of the face/cheek). As an idit root, it undergoes the augment num via the Paninian sutra 'idito num dhatoh', resulting in the base 'gand'. It inflects in the Atmanepada to produce forms such as gandate, jagande, and gandita.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin explains 'gadi vadanaikadeshe' as denoting existence or action centered on the facial region (specifically the cheek or temple). From this root, nominal forms such as 'ganda' (cheek, temple, or goiter) are derived through primary affixes.

meanings.English: to be a part of the face, to swell or appear on the cheek
meanings.Tamil: mukattin oru paguthiyaga iru, kannattil tonru
meanings.Hindi: mukh ka ek bhag hona, gal par hona ya dikhna
meanings.Bengali: mukher ekangsho howa, gale prokasito howa
meanings.German: ein Teil des Gesichts sein, an der Wange auftreten
meanings.French: etre une partie du visage, apparaitre sur la joue
meanings.Russian: byt chastiu litsa, proyavlyatsya na shcheke
meanings.Chinese: chengwei lianbu de yibufen, xianyu saibang

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'krakh' signifies injuring, striking, or harming. In primary active voice (Parasmaipada), it describes an agent directly inflicting harm or striking a target. In causative form (krakhayati), it conveys causing someone else to strike, hurt, or destroy.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The warrior strikes the enemy.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nich pratyaya (Causative), Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The king causes the warriors to strike down the enemy.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti places 'krakha himsayam' within the Bhvadi-gana. It is anudattet-rahita, making it Parasmaipadi. Being an idit-free set root with final consonant khakaranta, it forms 'krakhati' in Lat lakara with regular Shap vikaran, and shows gunation or regular intermediate it-agama in ardhadhatuka environments.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines 'krakha himsayam' as denoting harm, violence, or striking down (himsarthaka). The root adheres to standard first-conjugation rules, producing forms like krakhati, cakrakha, krakhita, and krakhitum.

meanings.English: to injure, harm, hurt, strike, kill
meanings.Bengali: aghat kora, himsa kora, bodh kora

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'kṣmāy' primarily means to be motionless, completely steady, or free from trembling. It belongs to the 1st conjugation group (Bhvādi) and strictly takes Ātmanepada endings because the action or state of stillness resides entirely within the subject.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Present tense (laṭ), Third person singular (prathama-puruṣa ekavacana), Active Voice (kartari prayoga)
scenarios.meaning: remains motionless / stays firm and steady
scenarios.example_english: The yogi remains completely motionless in meditation.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (ṇic-pratyaya), Present tense (laṭ), Third person singular
scenarios.meaning: causes to become steady / steadies someone or something
scenarios.example_english: The teacher steadies the restless mind of the student.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: Under 'kṣmāyṛ niṣkampane', Sāyaṇa explains that the indicator letter 'ṛ' (ṛdit) is used for specific grammatical operations in past tense formations. The primary semantic value is 'kampanābhāva' (absence of shaking, motion, or disturbance), denoting unwavering firmness.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kṣīrasvāmin glosses 'kṣmāyṛ niṣkampane' as an Ātmanepada verbal base signifying stability, total stillness, and freedom from trembling or agitation, yielding forms like 'kṣmāyate' and 'cakṣmāye'.

meanings.English: to be motionless, to be steady, to be still without shaking
meanings.Telugu: niścalamugā uṇḍu, sthiramugā uṇḍu, kampamu lēkuṇḍu
meanings.Hindi: sthir rahanā, niścala honā, na kāmpanā
meanings.Bengali: sthir thākā, niścal haoẏā, na kāmpā
meanings.French: être immobile, rester ferme, ne pas trembler
meanings.Russian: byť nepodvižnym, ostavaťsja nepokolebimym, ne drožať

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'dhukṣ' means to kindle, ignite, or revive (such as a fire, energy, or hope). In the 1st conjugation, it takes Atmanepada endings like '-te' to describe something getting kindled or burning up. When used with prefixes like 'sam-' or in the causative form (Nic), it actively means to rekindle, stir up, or inspire enthusiasm in someone else.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga (Present Indicative / Lat Lakara, Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana)
scenarios.example_english: The fire quickly flares up due to the speed of the wind.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative with Upasarga 'sam' (Nic Pratyaya, Parasmaipada, Lat Lakara)
scenarios.example_english: The teacher rekindles the lamp of knowledge in the student's heart.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti states under 'dhukṣa sandīpane' that the root conveys ignition, flaming, or the act of stimulating. Belonging to the Bhvadi class with anudatta characteristics, it takes Atmanepada affixes with the Vikarana 'śap' and follows the seṭ formation rules.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines 'dhukṣa' in the sense of 'sandīpane' (inflaming, making bright, or intensifying illumination). It yields the primary present form 'dhukṣate' and frequentative 'dodhukṣyate'.

meanings.English: to kindle, to ignite, to inflame, to stimulate, to revive
meanings.Hindi: jalana, sulgana, prajvalita karna, uttejit karna

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'kṣap' means to impel, drive, motivate, or send forward. Because it has an anudatta vowel marker in the Dhatupatha, it takes Atmanepada endings in the present active voice. When used with a causative affix (nic), it signifies causing someone to impel or instigate an action.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga (active voice), lat-lakara (present tense), ātmanepada, prathama-puruṣa, eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The charioteer drives the horses on the path.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: ṇic-pratyaya (causative), kartari prayoga, lat-lakara, ātmanepada, prathama-puruṣa, eka-vacana
scenarios.meaning: He/she causes to urge or drive.
scenarios.example_english: The king causes the commander to urge the soldiers forward.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'kṣapā' is read with an anudatta accent indicating Atmanepada ('anudāttettvād ātmanepadī'). It carries the sense of 'preraṇa' (driving, urging, or dispatching). As an anit root ending in a consonant, it does not admit the intermediate i-augment in non-sarvadhatuka forms except where specifically conditioned.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'kṣapā preraṇe' within the bhvadi class as an Atmanepadi root signifying pushing or impelling. Its forms conjugate with the standard sap vikarana yielding kṣapate, cakṣape in lit, and akṣapta in lun.

meanings.English: to impel, urge, drive, send

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'minj' expresses the actions of cleaning/purifying as well as speaking or shining. Because it is an Atmanepadi verb, its standard forms end in '-te' (such as minjate). When converted into the causative form (nic), it uses the affix '-aya-' to indicate causing someone or something to become clean or clear.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga (active voice), lat-lakara (present tense), prathama-purusha, eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The sage purifies his mind.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: nic-pratyaya (causative), lat-lakara, prathama-purusha, eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The mother causes the garment to be washed clean.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti notes that 'miji sauce bhasarthe ca' carries the idit marker which demands the insertion of a canonical num (nasal augment), forming 'minj-'. It takes Atmanepada endings under standard conditions in the Bhvadi class, yielding forms like minjate, miminje, and minjita.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin classifies the root under the set-it group with idit anubandha to indicate nasalization. He glosses the primary sense as shuddhi (purification/cleansing) and shobhana-vachana (pleasing or distinct utterance).

meanings.English: to purify, cleanse, wash, or speak clearly
meanings.Hindi: shuddh karna, manjna, dhona ya bolna
meanings.Bengali: shuddho kora, porishkar kora ba kotha bola

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'bhranś' means to fall down, slip, drop, or deviate from a path. In its basic form (Atmanepada), it denotes the subject itself falling or dropping down. When used in the causative form with 'nic' (bhramśayati), it means to cause something or someone to fall down, dislodge, or remove from a position.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Atmanepada, Lat-lakara (present tense)
scenarios.example_english: The leaf falls down from the tree.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic-pratyaya), Parasmaipada, Lat-lakara
scenarios.example_english: The king removes the enemy from his position.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'bhranśu adhaspadane' belongs to the Bhvadi-gana and is marked with anudatta it (indicatory vowel u), making it an Atmanepadi and Anit dhatu. The nasal (num) is retained in the sarvadhatuka forms like bhranśate according to the anubandha indications, signifying downward motion or moral/physical fall.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes under 'sransu bhransu dhvansu bhranśu adhaspadane' that these roots express falling down or descent (patanarthah). In the non-causative state, the agent undergoes the downward descent, whereas causatives take the Parasmaipada affixes to denote knocking down or overthrowing.

meanings.English: to fall down, slip, drop, deviate, decay
meanings.Bengali: pore jawa, bhrashto howa, khoshiye pora

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'kṣad' primarily means to divide, apportion, or distribute into shares. Being an Atmanepada root, it describes actions where distribution or sharing is carried out for the subject or beneficiary. In causative forms, it conveys having someone else apportion or distribute resources.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: lat-lakāra, prathama-puruṣa, eka-vacana, kartari prayoga
scenarios.example_english: The officer distributes grain in the field.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: ṇic-pratyaya (causative), lat-lakāra, prathama-puruṣa, eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The king causes wealth to be apportioned by the minister.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: kṣadṛ saṃvibhajane. ṛdittvāt ātmanepadī. saṃvibhajanaṃ nāmāṃśīkaraṇam. cakṣade, kṣaditā, akṣadiṣṭa vikalpena aṅ-pratyaye akṣadat iti mādhavīyāyāṃ spaṣṭam.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: kṣadṛ saṃvibhajane. vibhāgo vibhakti-karaṇamityarthaḥ. kṣadate, cakṣade. ṛditvāt aṅ-bhāvaḥ kṣīrataraṅgiṇyām darśitaḥ.

meanings.English: to divide, apportion, distribute, carve into shares
meanings.Bengali: bhāga karā, baṇṭana karā, bibhājana karā

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'sphūrch' means to spread out, expand, or burst into view. In the active voice (Parasmaipada), it describes an object or light naturally expanding or shining forth. When used with a causative affix (ṇic), it means making something spread or expand widely.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti glosses 'sphūrchā vikhāsane' as implying expansion, blossoming, or opening up (vikāsa / vistāra). It follows standard Bhvādi paradigm taking the regular Śap vikarana (sphūrchati, tasphūrcha, sphūrchitā) and takes it-āgama in the periphrastic and future forms.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines 'sphūrchā vikhāsane' as referring to expansion and clear manifestation (vikhāsanaṃ sphītiḥ vistāro vā). It notes morphological parallels with roots like mūrchā and establishes its Parasmaipada classification.

meanings.English: to expand, to spread out, to blossom, to burst forth

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'mruc' describes moving, slipping away, or setting (like celestial bodies). In simple present active voice (Kartari Parasmaipada), the vowel 'u' takes Guna strengthening to form 'mrocati' (he moves or slips away). When used with a causative suffix (Nic), it shifts the meaning to causing someone or something to move or depart.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Lat Lakara, Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana (Kartari Prayoga)
scenarios.example_english: The sun moves away (sets) in the evening.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic Pratyaya (Causative), Lat Lakara, Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The wind causes the cloud to move away.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'mrucu gatibhedanayoḥ' belongs to the Bhvadi class and is marked with an indicatory 'u'. Being anudattopadesha and Parasmaipadi, it undergoes Guna substitution of the penultimate vowel 'u' before Sarvadhatuka affixes having an 'a' augment (Shap), yielding forms like 'mrocati'. In perfect tense (Lit), it reduplicates as 'mumroca'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines 'mrucu' in the sense of 'gatibhedana' (distinct forms of motion, departure, or setting). It follows standard Bhvadi vocalic Guna rules and takes the set augment 'it' in Ardhadhatuka environments, producing forms such as 'amrocit' in Aorist (Lung).

meanings.English: To move, to slip away, to go, to set

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'dhūp' means to heat, to scorch, or to fumigate/burn incense. By a special Paninian rule (3.1.28), the root takes the suffix '-āya' in the sense of the root itself, forming the stem 'dhūpāya-'. It conjugates in Parasmaipada to yield present tense forms like 'dhūpāyati' (he fumigates/burns incense, or it heats up).

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga (active voice), laṭ lakāra (present tense), prathama puruṣa, ekavacana with svārthika āya-pratyaya
scenarios.meaning: Fumigates, burns incense, or heats up
scenarios.example_english: The devotee fumigates the temple with fragrant incense.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga (active voice), laṅ lakāra (past imperfect), prathama puruṣa, ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The sun heated up the earth intensely during the day.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: dhūpa saṃtāpe. 'gupūdhūpavicchipanipaṇibhya āyaḥ' iti svārthe āyapratyayaḥ. dhūpāyati. saṃtāpaḥ jvalanaṃ santāpanaṃ vā.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: dhūpa saṃtāpe. saṃtāpaḥ taptībhāvaḥ santāpanam ca. āyapratyaye kṛte dhūpāyati iti rūpaṃ bhavati.

meanings.Bengali: dhūp deoyā, santapta karā, dhuya deoyā
meanings.French: encenser, fumer, chauffer, tourmenter par la chaleur

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'hlad' means to rejoice, be refreshed, or experience happiness. It is inherently Atmanepada in simple active voice. When used with the causative suffix (Nic), it shifts meaning from 'feeling happy' to 'delighting or refreshing others' (to gladden).

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakara (present tense), prathama purusha, eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: Seeing the moon, the person feels delighted.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (causative), Kartari prayoga, Parasmaipada, Lat lakara
scenarios.example_english: The cool breeze gladdens everyone.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: hlada sukhe ca - sukhanubhave vartate. cakarat kvacit samharshane shabde ca drishyate. idit-tvarahitam set atmanepadi. hladate, jahlade, hladita, ahladishta.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: hlada sukhe - hladate. prahlada ityadi prayogah asmat prasiddhah. antarbhavitanarthatve ca hladayati iti.

meanings.English: to be delighted, to rejoice, to feel happy or refreshed

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'sphur' conveys the action of vibrating, throbbing, flashing, or bursting into view. In its simple active voice (Parasmaipada), it describes something twitching or sparkling on its own. When used in the causative (Nic), it means causing something to tremble, gleam, or manifest brightly.

scenarios.example_english: The eye twitches.

scenarios.meaning: causes to sparkle, causes to vibrate, or manifests
scenarios.example_english: The lamp causes light to flash forth.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: sphura sphuraṇe. sphuraṇaṁ calanam, prakāśanaṁ vā. anit. sphurati, pusphora, sphuriṣyati/sphoriṣyati.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: sphura sphuraṇe. calane prakāśe ca vartate. sphurati vidyut iti calane dīptau ca prayogaḥ.

meanings.English: to throb, twitch, tremble, flash, glitter

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'puṭ' means to connect, combine, or wrap together. In standard active voice (Parasmaipada), it describes an agent bringing parts together or uniting things. When used in the causative (ṇijanta) form, it expresses causing someone or something to unite, roll up, or enclose.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat-lakara (present active), 3rd person singular
scenarios.example_english: The artisan joins the garments together.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (ṇijanta), Lat-lakara, 3rd person singular
scenarios.example_english: The pharmacist wraps the medicine with a leaf.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'puṭa saṁsarge' belongs to the Bhvādi class. It takes guṇa of the radical vowel 'u' before sārvadhātuka affixes, forming poṭati. As an inherently seṭ root, it retains intermediate iṭ in the non-sārvadhātuka forms like poṭitā and poṭiṣyati.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'puṭa saṁsarge' as implying intimate contact, union, or bringing parts into close association. Morphologically, it undergoes standard Bhvādi vikarana śap with guna, yielding poṭati and the reduplicated perfect pupoṭa.

meanings.English: To connect, join together, or wrap

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'char' (chara~) belongs to the First Conjugation (Bhvadi-gana) and means 'to go' or 'to move'. In the basic active form (Kartari Prayoga), it takes Parasmaipada terminations with the thematic vowel 'a' (shap pratyaya), forming 'charati'. In causative (Nic), it signifies making someone move or causing something to move, forming 'charayati'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga (Present Active, 3rd Person Singular, Lat Lakara)
scenarios.example_english: The deer moves in the forest.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic Pratyaya (Causative, Present Active, 3rd Person Singular)
scenarios.example_english: The cowherd causes the cow to move (grazes the cow).

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'chara' is listed under the Bhvadi-gana with the meaning 'gatau' (movement/motion). Being unaccented in Upadesha, it is Anit. It conjugates regularly taking the shap vikarana yielding charati, charatah, charanti in Lat lakara.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'chara gatau' under the dental/palatal aspirate section of Bhvadi. It behaves phonologically in accordance with typical anit roots of the first conjugation, retaining the aspirated ch- sound distinct from un-aspirated car.

meanings.English: to go, to move, to wander

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'dhrsh' means to be bold, to dare, or to venture fearlessly. When used as a simple verb (Kartari), it expresses an individual showing courage or audacity. When used with a causative affix (Nic), it signifies making someone bold or actively challenging and overpowering someone.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga (Present Tense, Active Voice)
scenarios.example_english: The brave warrior dares to confront the enemy.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic Pratyaya (Causative Voice)
scenarios.example_english: The commander emboldens his soldiers.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'dhrshu pragalbhye' belongs to the Bhvadi class. Madhava explains that 'pragalbhya' denotes audacity, bravery, and self-confidence. The vowel 'ri' undergoes Guna to 'ar' before Sarvadhatuka suffixes like 'shap', yielding the primary present-tense form 'dharshati'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines 'pragalbhyam' as 'dharstyam' (boldness, audacity, or lack of fear). It highlights that derived nominals such as 'dharshana' convey bold assertion, confrontation, or assaulting with vigor.

meanings.English: To dare, to be bold, to venture, to overpower
meanings.Bengali: Sahas kora, dharstya dekhano, spardha prakash kora

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'paṇ' means to transact, trade, wager, or praise. When used in daily dealing or betting, it conjugates directly as 'paṇate'. When used in the sense of admiring or praising, it optionally takes the special affix 'āya' yielding 'paṇāyate'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Laṭ Lakāra (Present Tense), Prathama Puruṣa, Ekavacana (Transacting/Wagering)
scenarios.example_english: He wagers wealth in gambling.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Laṭ Lakāra with āya-pratyaya (Praise sense via Pāṇinian rule 3.1.28)
scenarios.example_english: The scholar praises good virtues.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'paṇa' is read in the sense of commercial transaction/wagering (vyavahāra) and laudation (stuti). Under the rule 'gupūdhūpavicchipaṇipaṇibhya āyaḥ' (3.1.28), it receives the affix 'āya' (paṇāya) specifically when expressing praise, leading to Ātmanepada inflection.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kṣīrasvāmin elucidates 'paṇa vyavahāre stutau ca' as governing both fiscal engagement/wagering (as in paṇa/paṇita) and panegyric praise. He distinguishes forms taking the 'āya' suffix from bare thematic conjugations.

meanings.English: to transact, to wager, to stake, to praise
meanings.Hindi: vyavahar karna, daanv lagana, prashansa karna
meanings.Bengali: byabahar kara, baji rakha, prashangsha kara

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'dam' means to be tamed, tranquil, or restrained. In its basic active form (Parasmaipada), it describes becoming calm or tranquil. When used with a causative affix (Nic), it shifts to meaning 'to tame, subdue, or discipline someone or something else'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (Present indicative active 3rd person singular, Bhvadi-gana)
scenarios.meaning: becomes calm / is tranquil / is restrained
scenarios.example_english: The sage becomes tranquil and free from anger.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Prena / Nic-pratyaya)
scenarios.example_english: The king subdues his enemies.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'damU' is read in the sense of 'upaśama' (tranquility, pacification, restraint). It belongs to the Bhvadi-gana and is anit. Its present tense base in the simple active is formed by regular guna and standard vikarana sap, yielding 'damati', and takes lengthening in special parasmaipada contexts or stays standard per gana-sutra classifications.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'damU upaśame' denoting peaceful restraint or pacification. When used in the causal derivation, it signifies the subjugation or taming of senses and external foes ('damana').

meanings.English: to be tranquil, to be tamed, to subdue, to restrain
meanings.Hindi: shant hona, daman karna, vash me karna
meanings.Bengali: shanto howa, domon kora, bosonikrito kora
meanings.German: sich beruhigen, zahm werden, bandigen, unterwerfen

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'svaj' means to embrace or cling to someone. It is inherently used in the Atmanepada voice (e.g., svajate or parishvajate with the prefix 'pari-'). When converted into a causative form, it means to cause someone to embrace or be embraced.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Bhvadi Atmanepada with prefix pari
scenarios.example_english: The mother embraces the son.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (Causative) in Atmanepada
scenarios.example_english: The father makes the two brothers embrace each other.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'svanja' (with initial murdhanya sa-kara undergoing shatva-nivritti to dantya sa) belongs to the Bhvadi class and takes Atmanepada affixes. It denotes 'parisvanga' (embracing, clasping). The nasal drops in sarvadhatuka formations yielding forms like svajate and parishvajate.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes that 'svanja' is read with upadesha-murdhanya 'sa' (shvanj) and signifies clinging or embracing. In non-nasalized environments and standard present-tense conjugation, it appears as svajate.

meanings.English: to embrace, hug, clasp

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'kas' primarily means to go or move. In classical Sanskrit, it is most popularly seen with the prefix 'vi' (vi + kas = vikas), where the meaning becomes 'to bloom', 'to open', or 'to expand'. When used in its regular active form (Parasmaipada), it describes something blooming or going on its own. When an external person causes something to bloom or develop, the causative form (vikasayati) is used.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakara (present tense), prathama purusha (third person singular)
scenarios.example_english: The lotus blooms in the garden.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (causative), Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara (present tense)
scenarios.example_english: The sun causes the lotuses to bloom.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'kasr gatau' belongs to the Bhvadi gana. Being rdit (having an indicatory 'r'), it regulates certain vowel modifications in specific tense formations like the aorist (an-it/set variations). Its primary sense is gati (movement), but in combination with prefixes like 'vi', it denotes sphutikarana (manifestation, opening, or blooming). Standard forms include kasati, cakasa, and kasita.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin lists 'kasr gatau' noting that its canonical sense is movement. He highlights its semantic extension in worldly usage where 'vi-kas' specifically denotes blossoming (vikasane) or wide dispersion. Derivatives such as vikasah and vikasita are formed from this root.

meanings.English: To go, to move, to blossom, to expand
meanings.German: Gehen, sich bewegen, erbluehen, sich entfalten

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'khep' belongs to the 1st conjugation (Bhvadi-gana) and means to shake, tremble, or move unsteady. Because it is marked with an anudatta vowel marker in the Paninian recitation, it takes Atmanepada endings (e.g., khepate). When a causative affix (nic) is added, it switches to indicate making someone or something else shake or move (khepayati).

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat-lakara (present tense), Prathama-purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: When the wind blows, the leaf of the tree shakes.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic-pratyaya), Lat-lakara, Prathama-purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: Causes to move or shakes something
scenarios.example_english: The wind causes the tree branch to shake.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti identifies 'khepṛ sañcalane' as an anudattet, ātmanepadi root of the Bhvadi-gana. The marker 'ṛ' (rit) indicates specific morphological behaviors in certain secondary formations, functioning with standard set properties.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin classifies 'khepṛ' among roots denoting movement and agitation (sañcalana / kampana). Forms such as 'khepate', 'cikhepe', and 'khepitā' are derived strictly in the Atmanepada voice in simplex conjugations.

meanings.English: to shake, to move unsteadily, to tremble

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'hru' expresses bending, going crooked, twisting, or behaving deceitfully. In active voice (Parasmaipada), it describes an agent moving crookedly or acting crookedly. When used causatively, it means to cause someone to go astray, bend, or act deviously.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (Present indicative, 3rd person singular, Parasmaipada)
scenarios.meaning: He/she moves crookedly or acts deceitfully.
scenarios.example_english: The crooked man deviates/falters on the right path.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (Causative, 3rd person singular)
scenarios.meaning: Causes to deviate, twist, or go astray.
scenarios.example_english: Bad company leads the child astray from the right path.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti notes that 'hru kautilye' is primarily used to signify crookedness, twisting, or ethical deviance. Being anit and a parasmaipadi root of the bhvadi-gana, it undergoes regular guna vowel gradation to form 'hvarati' in the sarvadhatuka present tense.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin explains that 'hru' belongs to the group denoting crooked movement and deceitful actions ('kautilye'). It forms its primary present paradigm as 'hvarati' via standard bhvadi vikarana and retains anit properties throughout ardhadhatuka environments.

meanings.English: to bend, to act crookedly, to go astray, to deceive
meanings.Bengali: bainka howa, kutilata kora, pothobhrosto howa
meanings.German: sich kruemmen, krumme Wege gehen, betruegen
meanings.French: se courber, devier, agir avec fourberie
meanings.Russian: iskrivlyat'sya, postupat' kovarolno, sbivat'sya s puti

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'path' means 'to move', 'to go', or 'to tread on a path'. It takes standard Parasmaipada endings in the active voice (pathati = he moves/walks). When turned into a causative (pathayati), it means 'causes to go' or 'leads along a path'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat-lakara, Prathama-purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: He/she walks or travels along a way.
scenarios.example_english: The traveler walks along the path.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (Causative), Kartari prayoga, Lat-lakara, Prathama-purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: Causes someone to go or directs along a route.
scenarios.example_english: The leader directs the person along the right way.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'patha gatau' belongs to the tha-anta section of the Bhvadi-gana. It is anudattet and parasmaibhasha. Its primary sense is physical motion or following a track. Being seṭ, it takes the standard iṭ augment in Ardhadhatuka environments, yielding forms like pathitā and pathiṣyati.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin classifies 'patha gatau' alongside other tha-final roots signifying motion. The dental 'tha' remains unelided. It conjugates regularly as pathati, papātha/petitha, pathitā, and pathiṣyati.

meanings.English: to go, to move, to travel, to walk

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'kṛp' means to be capable, able, or fit for something. Since it has an anudatta marker (u-kara), it naturally takes Atmanepada endings in the present tense (kṛpate). When used in causative forms, it takes the meaning of enabling or making someone capable.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana (Atmanepada)
scenarios.example_english: The learned person is capable in undertaking the work.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (Causative), Lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The teacher makes the student capable in knowledge.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: kṛpū sāmarthye. anudatteta atmanepadinaḥ. sāmarthyaṁ yogyata-bhavanamityarthaḥ. kṛpate, cakṛpe, kṛpta.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: kṛpū sāmarthye. kṛpate. sāmarthyam upayogitvam saktiyogo va.

meanings.English: to be capable, to be fit, to be adequate

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'mrad' means to soften, crush, grind, or rub. As an Atmanepadi verb, the primary action takes the middle voice terminations (e.g., mradate). When used in the causative (Nic), it means to cause something to be rubbed or softened, taking forms like mradayati or mardayati.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana (Simple present indicative, middle voice)
scenarios.example_english: The farmer crushes (rubs/threshes) the grain.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic-pratyaya), Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara (Parasmaipada in causative)
scenarios.meaning: Causes to soften or crushes through an agent
scenarios.example_english: The physician gets the medicinal substance ground/softened.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti notes 'mrada mradane' as an anudattet Atmanepadi root of the Bhvadi class. It undergoes standard gunation/vowel processes where applicable, forming present tense 'mradate' with the vikarana Shap. In lit, it forms mamrade.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin states 'mrada mradane', explaining the semantic scope around mradana (softening, crushing, or tenderizing). It is anit in certain non-sarvadhatuka contexts historically or optionally set, functioning strictly with Atmanepada affixes in primary conjugation.

meanings.English: To rub, crush, soften, or grind

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'sphur' means to throb, twitch, tremble, or flash. In its simple active form (Parasmaipada), it describes an involuntary twitching of a body part (like an eyelid) or the sudden flashing of light. When converted into a causative form (Nic pratyaya), it takes the meaning of causing something to vibrate, brandishing, or manifesting clearly.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga (Present Tense, Lat Lakara, 3rd Person Singular)
scenarios.example_english: The right eye twitches indicating good omen.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic Pratyaya (Causative Active, Lat Lakara, 3rd Person Singular)
scenarios.example_english: The warrior brandishes his bow to frighten enemies.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'sphura' belongs to the Bhvadi class and is read with the meaning of 'sphurane' (throbbing, vibrating, expanding, or shining). As an anit root taking sap vikarana, it forms 'sphurati'. In lit lakara, it becomes pusphora, exhibiting regular guna and abhyasa rules.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines 'sphura sphurane' as expressing quick pulsation, throbbing movement, or radiant manifestation. It forms simple active forms like sphurati and sphuratah without intermediate 'i' in general non-it operations.

meanings.English: to throb, twitch, tremble, flash, vibrate

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root ghur belongs to the first conjugation (Bhvadi-gana) and means to make a frightening sound, snort, or roar terribly. In its standard active form (Parasmaipada), it describes a subject naturally making a fierce or frightening rumble. In the causative form (nic), it expresses causing fright or producing a terrifying noise purposefully.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: lat-lakara (present indicative), prathama-purusha (3rd person), ekavacana (singular), kartari prayoga (active voice)
scenarios.meaning: roars terribly / makes a frightening noise
scenarios.example_english: The lion roars frightfully in the forest.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: nic-pratyaya (causative), lat-lakara, prathama-purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: causes a frightful sound / terrifies with noise
scenarios.example_english: The cloud creates a frightening rumble through its sound.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: ghura bhimarthe. bhimo bhayankarah sabdah tadvacana ityarthah. bhvadi-parasmaipadi set. ghurati, jaghora, ghorita.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: ghura bhimarthe. bhimavaci ghura dhatuh. ghurati, ghorayati ityadi.

meanings.English: to make a frightful noise, snort, roar, or sound terrible
meanings.Hindi: bhayankara dhvani karana, garajana ya ghurrana
meanings.French: emettre un son effrayant, rugir, s'ebrouer

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'kas' primarily expresses the action of opening, blossoming, splitting open, or moving apart. In everyday Sanskrit, it is most commonly combined with the prefix 'vi-' (as in 'vikasati') to mean blooming or developing.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara (present tense), 3rd person singular
scenarios.example_english: The flower opens.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga with 'vi' upasarga, Lat lakara, 3rd person singular
scenarios.example_english: The lotus blooms in the lake.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya explains 'kasa vislesane' as denoting the separation or disjunction of parts, leading to opening or unravelling. It is inflected in Parasmaipada with standard set characteristics in ardhadhatuka affixes (kasisyanti, akasit).
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes that 'kas' denotes separation ('vislesana'), expanding outward from a closed state to an open state, as seen prominently in derived forms like 'vikasa' and 'kaseru'.

meanings.English: to open, bloom, expand, split apart

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root kṣap belongs to the first group of verbs (Bhvadi) and inherently uses middle voice (Atmanepada) endings to mean enduring, tolerating, or showing forbearance (patience). When used in the causative (Nic), it shifts meaning to causing someone to endure, putting to an end, or passing time/destroying, often taking Parasmaipada affixes.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakara (present tense), prathama purusha (third person), ekavacana (singular)
scenarios.example_english: The sage endures distress with patience.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (causative stem), Lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: destroys / spends time / causes to endure
scenarios.example_english: The ascetic spends the night in austerity.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root kṣapa~ is listed under Bhvadi in the sense of kṣānti (forbearance, patience, forgiveness). As an anudatteta, it receives Atmanepada affixes in non-causative active voice. It is anit in primary formations.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes kṣapa kṣāntyām as denoting endurance of hardship (sahanam) and forgiveness. In secondary derived contexts such as causative, it expands semantically to elimination or spending of time (kṣapaṇa/vināśa).

meanings.English: to endure patiently, to forbear, to tolerate

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'bhaṭ' means to hire, nourish, maintain with wages, or speak. In its standard active form (Parasmaipada), it describes maintaining someone or serving for wages. When used in the causative form (ṇic), it signifies causing someone to be maintained or hired.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakara (present tense), Prathama purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: He/She hires, maintains, or serves for wages
scenarios.example_english: The king maintains (hires/pays wages to) the servant.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (ṇijanta), Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: Causes someone to be maintained or hired
scenarios.example_english: The master gets the workers hired/maintained.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti explains 'bhaṭa bhṛtau' in the Bhvadi class. 'Bhṛti' refers to maintenance, wages (vetana), or hiring. In active usage it conjugates as bhaṭati, abhaṭīt, bhaṭitā, taking the augment iṭ across non-sarvadhatuka forms.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes in the Kshiratarangini that 'bhaṭa' denotes 'bhṛti' (supporting by paying wages or sustaining). Derived nominals like 'bhaṭa' (soldier, warrior, mercenary) stem directly from this root meaning of service and maintenance.

meanings.English: to hire, to maintain, to support, to nourish with wages
meanings.Kannada: bhatisu, vetana nidi poshasu, kulige idu
meanings.Hindi: vetan dena, poshan karna, bhruti dena, bhat banana

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'klis' means to suffer, undergo distress, or experience affliction. In the first conjugation (Bhvadi gana), it takes Atmanepada endings in the present tense (klisate), expressing personal suffering or torment. When used in the causative (Nic), it changes to klesayati, meaning 'to cause someone to suffer' or 'to torment'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Bhvādi Ātmanepada, Laṭ-lakāra, Prathama-puruṣa, Eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The sick person suffers from fever.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Ṇic-pratyaya (Causative), Parasmaipada, Laṭ-lakāra, Prathama-puruṣa, Eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The wicked person torments everyone.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti explains 'klisū upatāpe' as an Atmanepadi root in Bhvadi meaning experiencing affliction or torment. The marker ū-kāra denotes optional it-agama (vet) in certain nishtha formations. It conjugates regularly as klisate in the present tense.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes under 'klisū upatāpe' that upatapa signifies internal or bodily suffering (duhkhanubhava). It is grouped with the anudatta-ending Atmanepada section of the Bhvadi class, yielding forms like klisate and cikliṣe.

meanings.English: to suffer, to be distressed, to experience affliction

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'bhṛ' fundamentally means to bear, carry, support, or nourish. Because it has an 'ñ' marker (ñit), it can be used in both Parasmaipada (when the action is intended for another) and Atmanepada (when the benefit of carrying or supporting directly relates to oneself). When used with causative affixes (ṇic), it changes to mean 'causes to bear' or 'causes to support'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara (present tense), Parasmaipada, 3rd person singular
scenarios.example_english: The father supports the family.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara (present tense), Atmanepada, 3rd person singular
scenarios.example_english: The master carries the burden himself.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: bhṛñ bharaṇe - bharaṇaṁ poṣaṇaṁ dhāraṇaṁ ca. ñittvād ubhayapadī. aniṭ. guṇe raparatve ca kṛte bharati bharate iti rūpe bhavataḥ. liṭi babhāra, babhre.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: bhṛñ bharaṇe poṣaṇe ca. ubhayatobhāṣā. aniṭkaḥ. bharati, bharate. bhṛtvā, bhartum.

meanings.English: to bear, to carry, to support, to nourish
meanings.Hindi: poshana karana, dharana karana, bhrana karana
meanings.Bengali: poshana kara, dharana kara, bahana kara

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root jurv means to hurt, injure, or cause distress/destruction. It operates exclusively in Parasmaipada in basic active voice. When used as a causative verb with the suffix nic, it conveys causing another to suffer harm or destruction.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga, Lat Lakara (Active Voice, Present Tense)
scenarios.example_english: The wicked king harms the subjects.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic Pratyaya, Lat Lakara (Causative Active, Present Tense)
scenarios.meaning: Causes to be injured or tormented.
scenarios.example_english: The commander causes the enemies to be overwhelmed and harmed.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root jurvi is designated in the sense of violence, harming, or injury (himsayam). Being a parasmaipadi root with an indicatory long i (ikaranubandha), it forms jurvati in the present tense, jujurva in lit, and jurvita in lut, functioning as a set transitive root.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes jurvi among the set of roots with long medial vowels ending in rv (such as thurv, dhurv, gurv, jurv) which indicate killing, tormenting, or destructive action (himsartha). It inflects uniformly in parasmaipada taking the standard sap vikarana.

meanings.English: to injure, to hurt, to torment, to destroy
meanings.Hindi: chot pahunchana, himsa karna, kasht dena
meanings.Bengali: aghat kora, himsa kora, kshati kora

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The verbal root jamp (from japi~) fundamentally denotes moving or going. Because it is marked with an 'i' indicator (idit), it inserts an 'm' sound (num-agama), resulting in the base jamp-. In its basic active form (Parasmaipada), it simply means 'to go' or 'to move'. When the causative suffix nic is added, it turns into jampayati, meaning 'causes to go' or 'makes someone move'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Lat lakara (present tense), prathama-purusha, eka-vacana, kartari prayoga
scenarios.example_english: The traveler moves along the path.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (causative), Lat lakara, prathama-purusha, eka-vacana
scenarios.meaning: Causes to move or directs someone to go
scenarios.example_english: The leader causes the horse to move.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: Madhaviya Dhatuvritti lists japi~ with the indicator 'i' (idit), which obligates the insertion of the nasal num-agama by the rule 'idito num dhatoh', forming the present stem jampa-. It functions in the primary semantic realm of movement (gatau).
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin in Kshiratarangini treats japi~ in the series of gatyartha (movement) roots of the Bhvadi class, demonstrating regular thematic conjugation with sap to yield jampati, jampatah, jampanti.

meanings.English: to go, to move

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'trap' means to feel shy, ashamed, or embarrassed. It is naturally an Atmanepada verb, expressing an internal feeling experienced by the subject. When modified into the causative form (nic), it means to cause someone to feel ashamed or to embarrass them.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Atmanepada, Lat lakara (present tense), prathama-purusha eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The shy child feels embarrassed in the assembly.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (causative), Lat lakara, prathama-purusha eka-vacana
scenarios.meaning: causes to feel ashamed / embarrasses someone
scenarios.example_english: His misdeed makes him feel ashamed.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'trapus' is read in the sense of lajja (shame, modesty, bashfulness). The anubandha 'u' and 's' indicate relevant morphophonemic markers. It forms 'trapate' in the present indicative as an anudattet-equivalent Atmanepadi root.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'trapus lajjayam' as an Atmanepada root of the Bhvadi class. In the perfect tense it forms tatrape, and in the past participle it yields trapita.

meanings.English: to feel shy, to be ashamed, to blush

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'klad' (kladi) expresses the action of churning, agitating, or stirring liquids. Because it is marked with an 'i' it-marker (idit), an additional nasal 'n' is inserted before the final consonant, producing the basic Atmanepada verb form 'klandate'. In causative constructions, the affix 'nic' creates 'klandayati', meaning to cause to churn or stir.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakara (present tense), prathama-purusha eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The milkmaid churns the yogurt.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (causative), Lat lakara, prathama-purusha eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The mother has the girl stir the milk.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya notes 'kladi vilodane' as an idit root in the Bhvadi gana. Owing to the idit character, num-agama (nasal insertion) applies across all conjugational forms, yielding 'klandate', 'caklande', and 'aklandishta'. The term 'vilodana' denotes 'alodana' (thorough mixing or stirring) and 'prakshobhana' (agitation).
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin states under 'kladi vilodane' that the root takes Atmanepada affixes and an internal nasal, defining the action as the physical agitation, stirring, or churning of fluids.

meanings.English: to churn, to agitate, to stir

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'khaj' belongs to the 1st class (Bhvadi) and uses active voice (Parasmaipada) to express the action of stirring, churning, or agitating. When modified by the causative suffix (Nic), it signifies making someone stir or vigorously agitating something.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga (Present tense, 3rd person singular, Parasmaipada)
scenarios.example_english: The milkmaid churns the curd.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (Causative, 3rd person singular, Parasmaipada)
scenarios.meaning: causes to churn / causes to stir
scenarios.example_english: The mother has the milkmaid churn the curd.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya explains 'khaja sañcalane' as referring to mechanical motion, churning, or vigorous agitating, typically found in contexts like churning curds (manthana) and forming nominal derivatives such as 'khajika' (churning stick).
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines the root as functioning in both intransitive movement (calana) and transitive agitation/churning (mathana), deriving forms like 'cakhaja' in Lit and 'khajita' in Lut.

meanings.English: to churn, to agitate, to stir, to shake

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'luñc' conveys the action of pulling out, plucking, husking, or tearing away. It is primarily used in the Parasmaipada active voice when an agent plucks something directly, and in the causative (Nic) when causing someone else to pull or pluck out.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga (present indicative active 3rd singular)
scenarios.example_english: The ascetic plucks out the hair from his head.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: nic-pratyaya (causative present indicative active 3rd singular)
scenarios.meaning: causes to pluck or tear away
scenarios.example_english: The master makes the servant pluck out the weeds.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti identifies 'luñca apanaye' as an idit or standard seṭ root denoting the removal, extraction, or plucking of items such as hair or husk. Forms derived include luñcati, luloñca, luñcitā, luñciṣyati, and aluñcīt.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines 'luñca' in the sense of 'apanodane' (pulling out/extraction, commonly applied to keśāpanayana or weeding). It is treated as an active transitive root operating under the Bhvadi class rules.

meanings.English: to pluck, pull out, peel, husk, tear away
meanings.Kannada: kithu tege, bīḷisu, kudalannu kittu tege

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'trs' means to feel thirsty or to desire eagerly. In the primary Bhvadi conjugation (Parasmaipada), the vowel 'r' undergoes Guna to become 'ar', forming 'tarsati'. When used in the causative sense (Nic), it signifies making someone thirsty or causing eagerness ('tarsayati').

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Bhvadi-gana, Lat-lakara (Present Tense), Prathama-purusha, Ekavacana, Parasmaipada
scenarios.example_english: In summer, the traveler is thirsty without water.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (Causative), Lat-lakara, Prathama-purusha, Ekavacana, Parasmaipada
scenarios.example_english: The scorching heat makes the traveler thirsty for water.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'trsa pipasayam' belongs to the Bhvadi class and is accented as anudatta. It is primarily akarmaka in the core sense of being thirsty, taking the basic shap vikaran with guna to derive 'tarsati'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes that 'trsa' denotes the physical sensation of thirst (pipasa) as well as psychological craving, exhibiting the standard parasmaipada inflection tarshati, tatarsha, tarshita.

meanings.English: to be thirsty, to crave

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'hreṣ' belongs to the first verb class (Bhvādi Gaṇa) and describes the act of neighing, whinnying, or making an indistinct sound (typically used for horses). In the basic active voice (Kartari Parasmaipada), the simple present tense form is 'hreṣati' (he/it neighs). When used in the causative sense with the suffix 'ṇic', the verb becomes 'hreṣayati' (makes someone or something neigh).

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (Present indicative, 3rd person singular, Parasmaipada)
scenarios.example_english: The horse neighs in the field.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Ṇic pratyaya, Present indicative, 3rd person singular)
scenarios.meaning: causes to neigh / prompts a whinny
scenarios.example_english: The horseman makes the horse neigh with grass.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti glosses 'hreṣa avyakte śabde', explaining that it denotes the emission of indistinct sounds, specifically referring to the neighing of horses. Being a set root with initial conjunct hr, it forms present stem 'hreṣati', perfect 'jahreṣa', and future 'hreṣiṣyati' with standard it-agama.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes under 'hreṣa avyakte śabde' that the root pertains to equine sounds ('aśvasya dhvānaḥ'). It follows standard Bhvadi conjugational rules without irregular sandhi or vocalic shifts, yielding 'hreṣati' and periphrastic perfect 'hreṣāñcakāra' or reduplicated 'jahreṣa'.

meanings.English: to neigh, to whinny, to utter an indistinct sound
meanings.Telugu: hresinchu, gurramu la aruchuta, aspashta shabdamu cheyu
meanings.Tamil: kuthirai pol kural idu, thelivattra oli ezhuppu
meanings.Bengali: heshadhvani kara, ghodar dak deoya, aspashta shabda kara
meanings.German: wiehern, undeutliche Laute von sich geben
meanings.Chinese: ma ming, fa chu bu qingchu de sheng yin

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'mūrcch' primarily means to faint, swoon, or lose consciousness, as well as to grow, thicken, or expand. In its basic active form (Parasmaipada), it describes an individual losing consciousness or an entity expanding. When combined with the causative suffix Ni-c, it expresses the action of causing someone to faint, rendering unconscious, or causing something to solidify/grow.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Active voice (Kartari Prayoga), Present tense (Lat Lakara, Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana)
scenarios.example_english: Afflicted by hunger, the boy faints.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative active voice (Nic-pratyaya, Kartari Prayoga)
scenarios.example_english: The strong smell causes people to swoon.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'mūrcchā' is listed in the senses of 'moha' (stupor, unconsciousness) and 'samucchraya' (growth, expansion, or solidification). It takes standard Guna in relevant environments and takes the 'it' augment (Set), yielding forms like mūrcchati, mamūrccha, and mūrcchitvā.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'mūrcchā mohasamucchrayayoḥ' to mean both the cessation of awareness (moha) and rising or thickening (samucchraya). He explains the formation of forms such as mūrcchati, murcchitaḥ, highlighting standard vocalic and semi-vocalic behavior across tenses.

meanings.English: to faint, to lose consciousness, to grow, to solidify
meanings.Bengali: murccha jaoya, agyana haoya, briddhi paoya
meanings.German: ohnmachtigt werden, das Bewusstsein verlieren, erstarren
meanings.Russian: padat v obmorok, teryat soznaniye, rasti

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root gud means to play, frolic, or engage in amusement. In its basic Parasmaipada form, it indicates the subject actively playing. In the causative form with the nic suffix, it means causing someone else to play or entertaining them.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga, lat lakara (present tense), prathama purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The boy plays with joy.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: nic pratyaya (causative), lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The mother makes the child play in the garden.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti explains guda kridayam as a set root belonging to the first conjugation (bhvadi). It exhibits standard guna strengthening in ardhadhatuka environments without irregular phonological mutations, forming gugoḍa in lit and godita in lut.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin analyzes guda as an intransitive root denoting playful bodily exertion, sport, or recreation, conjugating regularly as gudati, gudatah, gudanti in the sarvadhatuka system.

meanings.English: to play, to sport, to frolic

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'pyāy' means to grow, swell, or increase. In its normal form, it describes a subject expanding or flourishing on its own. When used with a causative affix (ṇic), it means to cause something to swell or to nourish/saturate something.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Laṭ lakāra, prathama-puruṣa, eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The moon waxes (grows) during the bright fortnight.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (ṇic) with ā-upasarga, Parasmaipada, prathama-puruṣa, eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: Milk nourishes and strengthens the body.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: Mādhava notes that 'o~pyāyī~ṅ vṛddhau' has 'o' and 'ṅ' as its markers (anubandhas). The initial 'o' indicates applicability of niṣṭhā forms like pīnaḥ, where the root substitutes to 'pī' under specific grammatical conditions, while 'ṅ' marks it as Ātmanepadī.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kṣīrasvāmin explains that the root operates in the sense of enlargement, swelling, or nourishment (vṛddhi). He details the alternation between pyāy- and pī- in participial formations such as pīna (swollen/fat) and āpīna (udder).

meanings.English: to grow, swell, increase, or nourish

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'maṭh' means to reside, dwell, or live in a place (often a hermitage, cell, or cloister, from which the word 'maṭha' originates). It is conjugated in Parasmaipada in standard usage. When a causative affix (ṇic) is added, it means 'to house' or 'to cause someone to reside'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakara (present tense), 3rd person singular
scenarios.example_english: The ascetic resides in the forest.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (ṇijanta), Lat lakara (present tense), 3rd person singular
scenarios.meaning: Causes to dwell, houses, or lodges someone
scenarios.example_english: The teacher accommodates the student in a hut.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti analyzes 'maṭha nivāse' under the Bhvadi-gana. Being anidit and halanta, it undergoes regular guna of the penultimate short vowel in applicable environments (though 'a' remains unchanged in sarvadhatuka forms) to yield the present stem 'maṭhati'. In kit and it suffixes, it retains seṭ characteristics.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'maṭha nivāse' as referring to the act of settling, residing, or sheltering. It is predominantly used intransitively to express residing peacefully in a fixed abode.

meanings.English: To dwell, reside, inhabit, or lodge

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'nis' fundamentally denotes the physical process of dripping, oozing, or slow trickling. In active voice (Parasmaipada), it describes something oozing or leaking naturally by itself. When paired with causative suffixes (Nic), it shifts meaning to express an agent making a liquid trickle, flow, or drip deliberately.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga (Present tense, 3rd person singular, Lat Lakara)
scenarios.example_english: Sap oozes from the tree.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative form (Nic-pratyaya, Lat Lakara)
scenarios.example_english: The physician makes the medicine drip onto the leaf.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'ṇisa kṣaraṇe' belongs to the Bhvadi class. By the rule 'ṇo naḥ', the initial retroflex ṇ undergoes substitution to dental n in standard forms. The semantic essence is given as 'kṣaraṇam' which signifies 'galanam' (trickling, exuding, or dissolving into a flow). Being Set, it takes the intermediate 'i' augment in relevant ardhadhatuka environments.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'ṇisa kṣaraṇe' with the primary indicative form 'nesati'. The sense 'kṣaraṇa' is explained as slow streaming or continuous dropping (sravaṇam). The guṇa alteration affects the radical vowel 'i' yielding 'nesati' before the sarvadhatuka affix 'śap'.

meanings.English: To trickle, to ooze, to drip, to flow slowly

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'vell' expresses the action of shaking, swaying, swinging, or trembling, similar to a creeper or branch moving in the wind. In standard active voice (Kartari prayoga), it takes Parasmaipada endings ('vellati'). When used causatively with the nic affix, it shifts to 'vellayati' to indicate causing someone or something else to sway or vibrate.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana (Basic active voice)
scenarios.example_english: The branch of the tree sways in the strong winds.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (Causative), Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: causes to swing or moves something
scenarios.example_english: The wind causes the creepers to sway.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti places 'vella calane' in the Bhvadi gana as an idit-free halanta root. It explains that 'calana' here signifies subtle movement, swaying, or trembling. Morphologically, it forms present tense 'vellati', perfect tense 'vivella', and periphrastic future 'vellita', remaining Parasmaipadi and Set throughout all conjugational and non-conjugational tenses.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin interprets 'vella calane' as conveying dynamic motion or oscillation. He notes the formation of standard lakaric patterns such as 'vellati', 'vivellatuh', 'avellit', highlighting that like 'cela' and 'khella', it remains predominantly intransitive denoting physical oscillation or motion without intrinsic object government.

meanings.English: to move, to shake, to sway, to tremble

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The verbal root 'mī' belongs to the first group of verbs (Bhvādi gaṇa) and takes Ātmanepada endings. Its core meaning is to hurt, injure, destroy, or diminish. In the present tense, the vowel undergoes guṇa and changes to 'ay', giving the form 'mayate' (he/she injures or harms).

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakāra (present tense), prathama puruṣa, ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The wicked person always harms the innocent person.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Karmani prayoga (passive voice), Lat lakāra (present tense), prathama puruṣa, ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: is injured, is destroyed, is diminished
scenarios.example_english: Unrighteousness is destroyed by the power of truth.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root mīṅ (ending with anudātta ṅakāra) is classified under hiṃsā (injury/destruction). Being anudāttet, it exclusively takes Ātmanepada terminations. It is anit (does not admit iṭ āgama in general). In Sārvadhātuka environments before the affix śap, the ik-vowel takes guṇa and ay-ādeśa yielding 'mayate'. In perfect tense (Liṭ), it forms 'mamye'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines mīṅ with the semantic domain 'hiṃsāyām' meaning pīḍā (tormenting), vadha (killing), or apacaya (depletion/diminishing). It retains Ātmanepada morphology throughout all primary non-causative tenses and conforms to the standard substitution rules of final īkāra.

meanings.English: to hurt, to injure, to destroy, to diminish, to kill
meanings.Hindi: hiṃsā karnā, mārnā, naṣṭa karnā, ghaṭānā
meanings.Bengali: hiṃsā karā, bināśa karā, khoti karā

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'rat' means to shout, yell, scream loudly, or recite continuously. In simple active voice (Parasmaipada), it describes an agent making a loud noise or crying out. When used in causative (Nic), it means to cause someone to cry out or recite loudly.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga (Present tense, 3rd person singular)
scenarios.example_english: The jackal howls loudly in the forest.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic-pratyaya, Present tense, 3rd person singular)
scenarios.meaning: causes to scream / makes someone howl
scenarios.example_english: Fear causes the child to scream.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti notes that 'rata paribhasane' refers to articulated loud sound, lamentation, shouting, or loud chanting. It forms present 'ratati' in Parasmaipada, taking the intermediate augment 'i' (it) in non-sarvadhatuka forms such as 'ratita' and 'ratitum'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin states under 'rata paribhasane' that 'paribhasana' implies 'visabdana'—clamour, howling, or noisy articulation. The derivation follows standard Bhvadi patterns with Guna-lengthening in specific aorist forms where applicable (aratit / aratit).

meanings.English: to howl, scream, shout, roar, or clamour
meanings.Bengali: chittkar kora, chitkar kora, mukhostho bola

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root dhrākh primarily denotes growing, flourishing, or tasting and enjoying delicious food. It operates in the Atmanepada voice, taking middle-voice terminations like -te in the present tense (dhrākhate). When converted into a causative (nic) form, it expresses helping someone grow, making something prosper, or causing someone to taste food.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, prathama-purusha, eka-vacana (Atmanepada)
scenarios.example_english: The tree grows and thrives well in the field.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (Causative), Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, prathama-purusha, eka-vacana (Parasmaipada)
scenarios.example_english: The farmer causes the crop to flourish with water.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: dhrākhā vṛddhau svāde ca. ātmanepadī, seṭ. dhrākhate, dadhrākhe, dhrākhitā. vṛddhau vartamāno'karmakaḥ, svāde tu sakarmakaḥ.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: dhrākhā vṛddhau svādane ca. dhrākhate iti ātmanepadam. vṛddhyarthe akarmakatvam, svādane sakarmakatvam.

meanings.English: to grow, flourish, increase; to taste, relish
meanings.Tamil: vaḷar, peruku; suvai pār, suvai anupavi
meanings.Hindi: baṛhanā, vṛddhi pānā; svāda lenā, chakhnā
meanings.Bengali: bṛddhi pāoyā, bāṛā; sbāda neoẏā, āsbādana karā
meanings.Russian: rasti, protsvétat', uvelichivat'sya; probovat' na vkus, naslazhdat'sya vkusom

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'caṭ' means to break, split, or fracture. In its normal form (Parasmaipada), it describes something breaking, detaching, or cracking. When the causative suffix (ṇic) is added, it becomes 'cāṭayati', meaning to cause something to break or split into pieces.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat-lakara, Prathama-purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The branch of the tree breaks due to the wind.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic-pratyaya), Lat-lakara, Prathama-purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The carpenter splits the piece of wood.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: caṭa bhedane. Bhvadiradantaḥ parasmaipadī seṭ. Bhedanaṃ viśleṣaṇaṃ dvidhākaraṇaṃ vā. caṭati, cacāṭa, caṭitā, caṭiṣyati, acaṭīt.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: caṭa bhedane. caṭati, cacāṭa, caṭitaḥ. bhedanaṃ vidāraṇam ityarthaḥ.

meanings.English: to break, to split, to crack, to fracture
meanings.Kannada: odedu hogu, bi ಬಿ ಬಿ ಬಿ bidi madu, chedurisu

it_status: Svet (Anit in standard active/Set in certain formations like lrt/san)

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'ruc' fundamentally means to shine, appear bright, or to be pleasing and liked. In simple present tense (Lat), it is conjugated in the Atmanepada as 'rocate'. When someone likes something, the person who is pleased takes the fourth case (caturthi vibhakti) by Panini's rule 'rucyarthanam priyamanah'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara (present tense), prathama-purusha eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The sweet pleases the boy (The boy likes the sweet).

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (Causative), Parasmaipada, Lat lakara
scenarios.meaning: causes to shine / finds pleasant / chooses with delight
scenarios.example_english: The mother makes the milk appealing to the child.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: Ruca diptau abhipritau ca. Anudattetvat atmanepadinam. 'Rocate'. Gunah - o-kara. Diptau shobhayam abhipritau triptau santoshane ca vartate.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Ruca diptau. Rocate dipyate shobhate ityarthah. Abhipritir api grhyate. Karmani tu rucyate.

meanings.English: to shine, to look splendid, to please, to be agreeable to
meanings.Hindi: chamakna, shobha pana, accha lagna, pasand aana
meanings.Bengali: ujjvala howa, shobha paya, bhalo laga, pochondo howa
meanings.French: briller, resplendir, plaire a, etre agreable
meanings.Russian: siyat, blestet, nravitsya, byt po vkusu

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'kṣap' fundamentally means to throw, propel, cast, or spend/pass time. In standard active usage (Parasmaipada), it describes an agent directing or throwing an object, or actively spending time.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga (Present Active, 3rd Person Singular, Lat Lakara)
scenarios.example_english: The brave warrior shoots/casts an arrow.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative / Secondary Present (Nic-pratyaya)
scenarios.meaning: causes to pass, spends (time), or causes to throw
scenarios.example_english: The sage spends the night in austerities.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya identifies 'kṣapa preraṇe' as a Parasmaipada root in Bhvadi gana denoting the act of directing, propelling, or casting forth. It forms regular thematic bases with the Sap-vikarana, generating forms like kṣapati, cikṣāpa, and kṣapsyati.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines 'kṣapa' under the sense of preraṇa (propulsion/dispatch), highlighting its transitive nature in directing objects and passing duration.

meanings.English: to send, to throw, to propel, to pass (time)

canonical_dhatvartha: himsa-samkleshanayoh (to hurt, kill, or cause distress)

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'ghath' belongs to the 1st conjugation (Bhvadi) and means to strike, injure, hurt, or cause physical and mental distress. It takes standard Parasmaipada endings like 'ghathati' (he/she injures or torments). When converted into a causative form (nic), it means to cause someone to torment or hurt another.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga (Active voice), Lat Lakara (Present tense), Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The wicked person hurts living beings.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic Pratyaya (Causative), Lat Lakara, Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: causes someone to hurt / causes distress to
