scenarios.example_english: The demon makes his soldiers distress the people.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'ghatha' is classified under the group 'klatha, katha, gatha, ghatha' meaning 'himsa-samkleshanayoh' (in the sense of injury and tormenting/suffering). Being a set root with middle vowel 'a', it forms 'ghathati' in Lat, taking the standard shap-vikarana of Bhvadi-gana without vocalic guna.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin lists 'ghatha' in the class of roots expressing violence and distress (himsayam, samkleshane ca). It conjugates regularly as Parasmaipadi and Set, yielding present forms such as ghathati, ghathatah, ghathanti.

meanings.English: to injure, to hurt, to torment, to distress
meanings.Hindi: hinsa karna, chot pahunchana, klesh dena
meanings.Bengali: hingsa kora, aghat kora, kleshdana kora

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'spardh' means to compete, vie, or rival with someone to prove excellence. It naturally takes Atmanepada endings (such as -te in present tense). When converted to causative (Nic), it means to cause someone to compete or to organize a contest between parties.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga, lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The boy competes with his friend in running.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: nic pratyaya (causative), kartari prayoga, lat lakara, parasmaipada
scenarios.example_english: The teacher makes the students compete in learning.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'spardhṛ' is read with the meaning 'saṅgharṣe' (rivalry or emulation). The anubandha 'ṛ' indicates specific morphological markers in derivational affixes. Being marked with anubandhas appropriate for Atmanepada, it conjugates as spardhate, paspardhe, spardhitā, spardhiṣyate.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines 'saṅgharṣa' as 'paraspara-jigīṣā' (the mutual desire to overcome or excel over one another). It operates as a seṭ root taking standard Bhvadi vikarana 'śap'.

meanings.English: to compete, to rival, to vie with, to emulate
meanings.Hindi: spardha karna, hod lagana, pratiyogita karna

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'path' belongs to the 1st class (Bhvadi) and inherently means 'to go, move, or travel along a course'. In the active voice (Parasmaipada), it shows a subject walking, moving, or proceeding. Adding the causative suffix (Nic) shifts the action to causing someone to proceed or guiding someone along a path.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana (Active Voice / Kartari)
scenarios.example_english: The traveller walks along the road.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (Causative), Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: causes to go / directs on a path
scenarios.example_english: The leader directs the travelers on the path.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: patha gatau. bhvādiḥ parasmaipado set. pathati, papantha, pathitā, pathiṣyati. panthānam gacchati iti pathati.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: patha gatau. pathati. patha iti sabdasya mārge rūḍhatvāt tad-gatau ayam dhātur vartate.

meanings.English: to go, to move, to travel along a path

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'las' means to shine, flash, frolic, sport playfully, or embrace. In standard active voice (Parasmaipada), it describes an entity glittering or playfully rejoicing. When combined with prefixes like 'vi-' or 'ud-', it vividly denotes shining brightly or blooming with joy.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga (Present Active, 3rd Person Singular, Lat)
scenarios.example_english: Lightning flashes in the row of clouds.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Upasarga 'vi' + Lat Lakara (Active Voice)
scenarios.example_english: The child plays joyfully in the garden with friends.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti explains 'lasa shleshane kridanarthatve ca' indicating adherence, embracing, and playful activity as well as shining. It notes regular Set inflection yielding forms such as lasati, lalasa, lasisyati, and alasit.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin details that 'lasa' conveys sporting (kridana) and embracing (shleshana). It highlights derived nominals and upasarga combinations such as vilasa, ullasa, and lasita denoting splendor and joy.

meanings.English: to shine, to flash, to play, to embrace
meanings.Hindi: chamakana, kridan karna, shobhit hona, gale lagana
meanings.Bengali: jholmol kora, khela kora, shobha pawa

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'bhadi' (pronounced with a nasal as 'bhand' due to the marker 'i') means to be auspicious, happy, or prosperous. It is conjugated exclusively in the Atmanepada middle voice in its basic present form, describing an internal state of welfare or flourishing.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Present tense (Lat), 3rd person singular, Atmanepada
scenarios.meaning: Becomes auspicious or flourishes with happiness
scenarios.example_english: Through righteousness, the entire family flourishes and attains auspiciousness.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic), Present tense (Lat), 3rd person singular, Parasmaipada
scenarios.meaning: Causes to become happy or blesses with auspiciousness
scenarios.example_english: The sage makes the disciple prosperous and joyful through his blessing.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The author Madhava notes that the root 'bhadi' carries the it-marker 'i', which mandates the insertion of num-agama (the nasal 'n') before the final consonant under Panini 7.1.58 (idito num dhatoh), yielding the base 'bhand'. It denotes the semantic realm of kalyana (auspiciousness/good fortune) and sukha (happiness/contentment).
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin comments that the marker 'i' in 'bhadi' results in the medial nasal, generating 'bhandate'. The meaning spans both the attainment of spiritual/material welfare (kalyana) and experiential joy (sukha).

meanings.English: to be auspicious, to be happy, to prosper, to be fortunate
meanings.Hindi: kalyankari hona, mangal hona, sukhi hona
meanings.Bengali: kalyankari howa, mangal howa, sukhi howa

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'krand' means to weep, lament, or to call out distressfully. Because it is marked with an 'i' indicator (idit), it takes a nasal sound 'n' inside the root and inflects in the Atmanepada voice in its basic form. In the causative (Nic), it shifts to Parasmaipada/Ubhayapada to mean 'making someone cry' or 'invoking/calling'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakara (present tense), Prathama purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The distressed child calls out weeping to the mother.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic-pratyaya), Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: causes to weep / brings to tears
scenarios.example_english: The enemy brings the citizens to tears.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'kradi' has the indicatory vowel 'i' (idit), which necessitates the insertion of the internal nasal (num-agama), forming 'krand'. It operates in two principal senses: 'ahvana' (calling out or summoning aloud) and 'rodana' (weeping, lamenting). It takes Atmanepada terminations under general conditions.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes that 'kradi' along with 'kladi' denotes vocal distress—both invoking aid loudly ('ahvane') and shedding tears accompanied by sound ('rodane'). The presence of the 'i' it-marker governs the medial nasal augment across all lakaras.

meanings.English: to weep, to lament, to call out in distress
meanings.French: pleurer, se lamenter, appeler au secours

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'pruṅ' means to move, leap, or glide. Marked with an ītsaṃjñaka 'ṅ', it natively conjugates strictly in Ātmanepada (pravate). When used with specific prefixes like 'pra' or in causative (nic) forms, it can denote propelling forward or causing someone to leap/move.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga (present indicative 3rd person singular ātmanepada)
scenarios.example_english: The deer leaps in the forest.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: ṇic pratyaya (causative present indicative 3rd person singular parasmaipada)
scenarios.example_english: The horseman makes the horse jump.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: pruṅ gatau - ṅittvād ātmanepadī. aniṭ. pravate, pupruve, protā, proṣyate, aproṣṭetyādīni rūpyāṇi bhavanti. gatir ihordhvagamanamapi vivakṣitam.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: pruṅ gatau - ṅitām ātmanepadamiti pravate. anudātta iti kāsmiro na manyate, tena sarvatra aniṭtvam.

meanings.English: to move, to glide, to leap, to jump

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'uṭ' means to gather, assemble, or come together into a group. In simple active voice (kartari prayoga), it takes Parasmaipada endings to show people or things coming together. When used with a causative affix (ṇic), it changes to mean causing things or people to assemble or bringing items together.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat-lakara (present tense), Prathama-purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The person joins the assembly.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (ṇijanta), Lat-lakara, Prathama-purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The leader brings people together.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'uṭa' is listed under the meaning 'samavāye' (in the sense of assembling, aggregate connection, or union). Being in the Bhvādi class, the thematic vowel 'śap' causes guna change of the initial short 'u' to 'o', resulting in present forms such as 'oṭati', 'oṭataḥ', 'oṭanti'. In the perfect tense (liṭ), it takes the reduplicated form 'uvoṭa'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin explains 'uṭa samavāye' as denoting intimate union or aggregation (saṅghāta). It forms standard parasmaipadi sets like 'oṭati', 'auṭīt', and 'oṭitā', indicating entering into an organized aggregation or gathering.

meanings.English: to assemble, to gather, to unite, to come together
meanings.Hindi: ekatr honā, ikaṭṭhā honā, samūhabaddh honā
meanings.Bengali: ekatra haoyā, joṛo haoyā, milito haoyā

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'pluṅ' means to leap, swim, float, or glide. As an Atmanepada root (due to the anubandha 'ṅ'), it takes Atmanepada endings in basic active voice (e.g., plavate - leaps/floats). In the causative (Nic), it can describe causing someone or something to float, bathe, or flood (plavayati / plavayate).

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Active voice (Kartari Prayoga), Lat lakara (present tense), Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The fish swims in the water.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic), Lat lakara, Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: Water inundates the city.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: pluṅ gatau. ṅitvād ātmanepadī. plavate, pupluve, plotā. gatyarthatve 'pi tarana-plavanayor vartate.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: pluṅ gatau. plavate. plutiḥ, plavaḥ. kṣīrataraṅgiṇyām api 'plavate maṇḍūkaḥ' ityādayaḥ prayogāḥ pradarsitāḥ.

meanings.English: to float, jump, leap, swim, overflow

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'mluc' means to go, move, or recede. When the vowel undergoes Guna in the present tense, 'u' becomes 'o', producing forms like 'mlocati'. When combined with the prefix 'ni', it commonly denotes the setting of the sun or sinking downward.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga (Active Voice), Lat Lakara (Present Tense), Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The deer moves toward the forest.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Prefix 'ni' with Kartari Prayoga, Lat Lakara
scenarios.example_english: The sun sets in the evening.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'mlucu' is classified under 'gatau' (in the sense of moving or going). The penultimate 'u' undergoes Guna to 'o' before Sarvadhatuka affixes like Shap, yielding 'mlocati'. In the aorist (Lun), it takes the marker according to standard gatyartha rules.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin categorizes 'mlucu' alongside phonetically related roots of movement (mrucu, brucu, blucu). He notes its specialized usage with prefixes like 'ni' to express the setting or going down of celestial bodies.

meanings.English: to go, to move, to set or sink down

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'raṭ' primarily means to speak loudly, scream, shout, howl, or chant repeatedly. In normal active usage (Parasmaipada), it describes an agent shouting or loudly reciting words. When converted into the causative (ṇic), it expresses making someone shout or causing a text/sound to be loudly recited.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga (Active Voice), Lat Lakara (Present Tense), Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The boy repeatedly recites the lesson out loud.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic Pratyaya (Causative), Kartari Prayoga, Lat Lakara
scenarios.meaning: causes to shout or causes to recite loudly
scenarios.example_english: The teacher makes the student loudly recite the verse.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti comments on 'raṭa paribhāṣaṇe' as denoting distinct or loud vocal expression, noise, clamor, or continuous repeating of sounds. Being ending in a short vowel in anubandha form, it conjugates with the 'śap' vikarana yielding forms like 'raṭati', 'araṭīt', and 'raṭiṣyati' with standard it-agama.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines 'raṭa paribhāṣaṇe' as articulate speech or loud noise ('vyaktāyāṁ vāci śabde ca'). It is treated alongside similar dental/cerebral sounding roots denoting vocative utterance and repetitive chanting.

meanings.English: to shout, howl, scream, or recite loudly
meanings.Tamil: kattuthal, urakka solvathu, manapadam seithu urakka pathithal
meanings.French: crier, hurler, réciter à haute voix

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'jiv' means 'to live' or 'to maintain life'. In its simple active form (Parasmaipada), it describes an individual living, breathing, or surviving. When converted to the causative form with the affix 'nic', it changes to 'jīvayati', meaning 'to make someone live', 'to revive', or 'to sustain/nourish someone'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Lat lakara, prathama-purusha, eka-vacana (Simple Active / Parasmaipada)
scenarios.example_english: The person lives happily.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic-pratyaya) with Lat lakara
scenarios.meaning: Revives / brings back to life / sustains
scenarios.example_english: The physician revives the sick patient.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti analyzes 'jīva prāṇadhāraṇe' as denoting the continuity of vital breath (prāṇadhāraṇa). It takes the standard set vowel augment (it) in forms like jīvitum and jijīviṣati, and forms the present stem regularly with the shab-vikarana as jīvati.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes under 'jīva prāṇadhāraṇe' that the root signifies survival or sustaining the body through vital air. Derivations such as jīvana (life, water, livelihood) and jīvita (lived, life) are illustrated, highlighting its semantic scope extending to subsistence.

meanings.English: to live, to sustain life, to survive
meanings.Hindi: jina, jivit rahna, pran dharan karna

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'kaṣ' primarily means to hurt, scrape, rub, or injure. In active voice (Parasmaipada), the subject performs the act of scraping or hurting directly. When combined with the causative suffix (ṇic), it shifts to causing something to rub against another surface or testing purity by rubbing, as done on a touchstone.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: lat-lakāra, prathama-puruṣa, eka-vacana, kartari prayoga (Parasmaipada)
scenarios.example_english: The hunter grazes or injures the deer with an arrow.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: ṇic-pratyaya, lat-lakāra, prathama-puruṣa, eka-vacana (Parasmaipada)
scenarios.meaning: causes to rub, scrapes against a touchstone to test
scenarios.example_english: The goldsmith rubs the gold on the touchstone to test it.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root kaṣa~ is categorized under the Bhvadi-gana with the meaning 'hiṃsāyām' (injuring, scraping, or hurting). Being anit/set distinctions clarified, it takes the intermediate 'i' affix (seṭ). Its forms include kaṣati in present tense, cakāṣa in perfect (liṭ), and akaṣīt in aorist (luṅ).
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'kaṣa hiṃsāyām' with extensions in physical friction, scraping, and testing. Derivative nouns like 'kaṣaḥ' (touchstone, friction) and 'nikaṣaḥ' arise directly from this root action of severe friction resulting in wearing down or testing.

meanings.English: to injure, to hurt, to scrape or rub harshly

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'gur' means to make an effort, strive, or raise/exert oneself. Because it is exclusively Atmanepada, the action and its internal exertion reside directly within the agent. When used with causative or directional prefixes (such as 'ud-'), it can mean raising a weapon or springing forth vigorously.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, prathama-purusha, eka-vacana (Bhvadi Atmanepada)
scenarios.meaning: He/she strives, endeavors, or makes an effort.
scenarios.example_english: The warrior prepares and exerts himself for the battle.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Upasarga 'ud' + Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, prathama-purusha, eka-vacana
scenarios.meaning: He/she lifts up or raises (in effort).
scenarios.example_english: The warrior raises his weapon to strike.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'gura udyamane' belongs to the Bhvadi class and is anudattet, making it systematically Atmanepada. It conveys the sense of 'udyamana' (initiating exertion, enterprise, or raising oneself). The form in present tense is 'gurate', in perfect 'jugure', and it takes the 'it' augment in non-conjugational tenses yielding 'gorita'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'gura udyamane' as expressing dynamic effort and readiness. In usage, it frequently combines with prefixes like 'ud' ('udgurate') denoting lifting up or threatening with vigor.

meanings.English: to make effort, to strive, to endeavor, to raise up
meanings.Hindi: prayatna karna, udyama karna, tatpara hona

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'skumbh' means to stop, obstruct, prop up, or curb something. In the active voice (Kartari Prayoga), it takes standard Parasmaipada endings to denote holding back or supporting an object.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga (Present Active, Lat Lakara, 3rd Person Singular)
scenarios.example_english: The warrior stops (holds back) the enemy.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic Pratyaya (Causative, Lat Lakara, 3rd Person Singular)
scenarios.meaning: causes to obstruct / causes to support
scenarios.example_english: The leader causes the soldiers to halt.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'skumbhu' belongs to the Bhvadi gana and is listed in the sense of 'pratibandha' (restraint, obstruction, or support). Being anit and parasmaipadi, it forms 'skumbhati' in the present tense (Lat).
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin categorizes 'skumbh' alongside 'stambh', 'stumbh', and 'skambh' as denoting obstruction and propping up ('stambhana-roddhanayoh').

meanings.English: to stop, obstruct, prop up, restrain

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root khad means to be firm, stable, or steadfast. It belongs to the first conjugation (Bhvadi gana) and takes Parasmaipada terminations. When used normally in Kartari prayoga (active voice), it expresses an agent standing firm or enduring. When the causative suffix Nic is added, it means to stabilize, fix, or make something firm.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara (present indicative, 3rd person singular)
scenarios.example_english: The brave person stands firm in crisis.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (causative), Lat lakara (present indicative, 3rd person singular)
scenarios.example_english: The artisan stabilizes the pillar.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: khada sthairye. sthairyam niscalatvam. udattah parasmaibhasa anititi kecit kshirasvami tu sedityaha. khadati. akhadit. khadita.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: khada sthairye. sthiribhave vartate. khadati. khadayati. parasmaipadi sedayam.

meanings.English: to be firm, to stay, to endure, to stabilize
meanings.Hindi: sthir hona, dridh hona, tike rahna
meanings.Russian: byt tvyordym, stoyat krepko, ostavatsya nepokolebimym

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'cṛt' primarily means to tie, bind, connect, or intertwine things together. In normal active voice (Parasmaipada), the subject performs the action of tying or joining an object. In causative form (Nic), it signifies making someone else bind or connecting items together through an intermediary.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Lat (Present Tense), Kartari prayoga (Active Voice), Parasmaipada, Prathama-purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The cowherd binds the cow with a rope.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (Causative), Lat (Present Tense), Kartari prayoga, Parasmaipada, Prathama-purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: causes to tie / has something bound
scenarios.example_english: The master has the load tied by the servant.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti explains 'cṛtī sambandhane' under the Bhvadi-gana with the meaning of linking, joining, or fastening (granthana-bandhana-kriya). The long 'i' marker (ikaranta it) signifies the preservation of standard connecting morphology across periphrastic and derived tenses, taking Guna in Sarvadhatuka environments to form 'cartati'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'cṛtī sambandhane hiṃsayam ca', stating that while its core semantic domain is tying, joining, or weaving together (sambandha), secondary usage in specific contexts extends metaphorically to hurting or capturing by binding. In the Bhvadi class, it conjugates regularly with Sap vikarana yielding cartati, cartatah, cartanti.

meanings.English: to tie, bind, connect, fasten

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root sadh (originally listed as shadhri) means to succeed, be accomplished, or reach completion. In the basic active form (Parasmaipada), it describes a process or effort turning out successfully. When used in the causative form with the -i- (nic) suffix, it shifts the meaning to actively bringing about, proving, or executing a task.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat-lakara (present tense), 3rd person singular
scenarios.example_english: Through diligent effort, the work succeeds.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic-pratyaya), Lat-lakara, 3rd person singular
scenarios.example_english: The student achieves his goal.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti notes that shadhri has an initial murdhanya sha which undergoes replacement by dental sa via 'dhatvadeh shah sah'. The final vowel ri is an it marker. In the sense of samsiddhi (attaining fruition, perfection, or fulfilment), the root conjugates in the Bhvadi-gana with shap to form sadhati.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin explains that the root denotes samsiddhi (complete fruition and accomplishment). Being a shopadesha root, it converts to sadh in classical derivation. It forms primary verbal bases denoting completion of an undertaking.

meanings.English: To succeed, to be accomplished, to attain perfection
meanings.Hindi: Siddha hona, saphal hona, poora hona
meanings.Bengali: Siddha howa, saphal howa, sampanna howa
meanings.Chinese: Cheng gong, wan cheng, da cheng

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'khrāṅkṣ' means 'to desire', 'to crave', or 'to long for'. In the standard active voice (Parasmaipada), it describes an agent desiring an object. When modified into the causative form (khrāṅkṣayati), it conveys causing someone else to desire or aspire after something.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat-lakara, Prathama-purusha, Ekavacana (Simple Active Present)
scenarios.example_english: The boy longs for sweet fruit.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (Causative), Kartari prayoga, Lat-lakara, Prathama-purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: causes to desire / inspires longing in
scenarios.example_english: The mother causes the child to desire good qualities.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: Madhaviya Dhatuvritti identifies 'khrāṅkṣa kāṅkṣāyām' among the group of roots expressive of longing or desire (alongside drāṅkṣ, dhrāṅkṣ, rāṅkṣ). Being accented on the vowel ending with an anudatta-varjita thematic pattern, it takes Parasmaipada and standard set thematic conjugational suffixes yielding khrāṅkṣati.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes under 'khrāṅkṣa kāṅkṣāyām' that this root denotes intense yearning or desiring (abravīt / abhilāṣa). It belongs to the series of roots with guttural and aspirate initial clusters conveying eager expectation and forms normal Bhvadi stems without inner vowel alternation.

meanings.English: to desire, to long for, to crave, to expect eagerly
meanings.Bengali: ichha kora, kamona kora, akankha kora

canonical_dhatvartha: niṣkarṣe (in the sense of extracting, drawing out, or tearing out)

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root kuṣ means to pull out, extract, or tear open something from its place. In simple present tense (kartari prayoga), it takes standard Parasmaipada endings to form kuṣati. When made into a causative with nic, it becomes koṣayati, meaning to make someone extract or cause something to be pulled out.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana (Simple present active)
scenarios.example_english: The doctor extracts the splinter/arrow.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (Causative), Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: causes to extract / gets something pulled out
scenarios.example_english: The king causes the servant to extract the thorn.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti notes kuṣa niṣkarṣe as an udatta-it root belonging to Bhvadi gana. Being a set root with middle vowel u, it undergoes guna in appropriate sarvadhatuka and ardhadhatuka contexts, yielding forms like kuṣati, cokoṣa, and koṣitā.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin analyzes the semantic scope of niṣkarṣa as drawing forth or extracting an embedded object (ākarṣaṇa or bahiṣkaraṇa). It undergoes regular Bhvadi a-vikarana (śap) derivation in the active voice.

meanings.English: to extract, to pull out, to tear asunder

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'khard' means to bite, gnaw, or sting. Because it belongs to the Atmanepada class in the Bhvadi gana, its primary present-tense third-person singular form is 'khardate' (he/she/it bites). When made causative (Nic pratyaya), it becomes 'khardayati' or 'khardayate', meaning 'causes someone or something to bite'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Bhvadi gana, Kartari prayoga, Present tense (Lat lakara), Prathama-purusha, Eka-vacana, Atmanepada
scenarios.example_english: The scorpion stings the man on the foot.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic pratyaya), Kartari prayoga, Present tense (Lat lakara), Prathama-purusha, Eka-vacana, Parasmaipada
scenarios.meaning: Causes to bite or makes sting
scenarios.example_english: The boy causes the dog to bite the stranger.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti lists 'kharda damsane' among the anudatta-it Atmanepadi roots in Bhvadi gana. It takes the thematic affix Sap without guna alteration to the vocalic base due to its consonant structure, forming 'khardate'. In ardhadhatuka tenses it receives the augment it, giving periphrastic future 'khardita' and simple future 'khardisyate'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'kharda damsane' as expressive of biting, pinching, or stinging (damsana-kriya). It is grouped with roots ending in dental clusters expressing specific physical bodily actions or sounds, inflecting regularly in the Atmanepada as 'khardate', perfect 'cakharde'.

meanings.English: To bite, gnaw, or sting

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'khal' means to shake, stumble, agitate, or gather movement. In its simple active form (Parasmaipada), it describes a person or object moving unstably or shaking. When used with a causative suffix (Nic), it changes meaning to cause someone or something to shake, agitate, or sift.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga (Present Active, Lat Lakara, 3rd Person Singular)
scenarios.example_english: The horse stumbles on the road.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic Pratyaya (Causative, Lat Lakara, 3rd Person Singular)
scenarios.meaning: causes to shake or sifts/cleanses by shaking
scenarios.example_english: The farmer sifts the grain.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'khala' is placed in the Bhvadi class with the sense of 'samcalana' (shaking, moving about, gathering agitation). It takes the standard Shap vikarana yielding the present form 'khalati'. In the perfect tense (Lit), it forms 'cakhala' with regular reduplication.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines 'khala samcalane' as agitation or unsteady movement. It is an akarmaka (intransitive) root in its primary sense of movement and stumbling, forming 'khalitah' as the past passive participle.

meanings.English: to shake, to stumble, to agitate, to move about

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'val' primarily means to cover, enclose, or turn around. In basic Atmanepada, it describes an action of moving, turning, or covering. When used with causative affixes (Nic), it shifts the meaning to causing someone or something to turn, wind, or be enclosed.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Lat lakara (Present Tense), Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana (Kartari Atmanepada)
scenarios.example_english: The snake coils and turns around.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (Causative), Lat lakara, Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: causes to turn or winds around
scenarios.example_english: The boy winds the thread around the stick.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: Under the entry 'vala samvarane', Sayana-Madhava glosses the meaning as covering, concealing, or enclosing (achadana). Being anudattet, it takes Atmanepada terminations yielding forms such as valate, vavale, and valita. Common nominal derivatives like 'valaya' (bracelet, circle) originate from this action of encircling.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin interprets 'valate' as 'samvrnoti' (encompasses, encloses, folds). He highlights its application in senses of circular enclosing and folding, giving rise to words such as 'vali' (a fold of skin or wrinkle) and 'valana' (turning or rolling movement).

meanings.English: to cover, to enclose, to turn, to move around

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'dhranksh' expresses movement (going), longing/desiring eagerly, or making a sound (like the cawing of a crow). It operates primarily in Parasmaipada with standard Bhvadi-class conjugational rules (adding intermediate 'a' to form 'dhrankshati'). When causative 'nic' is applied, it means to cause someone to desire or prompt an action.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat-lakara (present tense), prathama-purusha ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: He/she desires eagerly or moves toward something
scenarios.example_english: The child eagerly desires the fruit.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Lun-lakara (aorist tense), kartari prayoga, prathama-purusha ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The youth craved success.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'dhranksha' is listed in the Bhvadi-gana with meanings 'gatau' (moving/going) and 'kankshayam' (wishing or craving), as well as onomatopoeic crowing/cawing in certain usages. It is set and parasmaipadi, taking normal guna and viddhi formations.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines 'dhraṅkṣa' under the sense of desire ('kanksha') and motion ('gati'). It behaves identically to standard gutteral-sibilant cluster roots in the first conjugation, retaining the parasmaipada termination.

meanings.English: to desire eagerly, to crave, to go, to crow/caw
meanings.Bengali: tibrabhabe kamona kora, lalach kora, jawya

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'puth' means to hurt, injure, or crush. Because it is used in Parasmaipada, standard endings like '-ti' are added directly after the thematic stem 'puthati' to describe an action of inflicting harm on an object.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakara (present tense), 3rd person singular
scenarios.example_english: The enemy hurts the warrior.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (causative), Lat lakara (present tense), 3rd person singular
scenarios.meaning: Causes someone to destroy or strike down
scenarios.example_english: The king causes the enemy to be crushed.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti identifies 'putha' in the Bhvadi class under the meaning 'himsayam' (to cause harm or injury). Being an adanta-less consonantal root ending in 'th', it takes the Guna vowel change under specific sarvadhatuka conditions (potheti is not applied in basic present, remaining puthati), and forms standard set forms with it-agama in ardhadhatuka tenses (puputhitha, pothita).
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'putha himsayam' alongside roots like kratha and klatha as verbs denoting violent injury or crushing. It belongs to the Parasmaipada set-class and conjugates regularly with the shappratyaya.

meanings.English: to hurt, injure, kill, crush

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'kaṭ' primarily means to cover, shelter, screen from rain, or encompass. In active voice (Parasmaipada), it shows a subject shielding or screening an object, while in causative form (ṇic), it denotes causing someone to cover or creating a screen/partition.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Active Voice (Kartari Prayoga, Parasmaipada, Lat Lakara, Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana)
scenarios.meaning: He/she covers or protects from rain
scenarios.example_english: The man covers the cottage.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative Form (Prena/Nic, Lat Lakara, Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana)
scenarios.example_english: The master causes the servant to shelter the dwelling.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'kaṭa' is listed in the Bhvādi-gaṇa under the sense of 'varṣe āvaraṇe ca' (raining and screening/covering). It forms 'kaṭati' with standard guṇa-less present stem formation and takes 'iṭ' in relevant non-sarvadhātuka affixes.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'kaṭa varṣāvaraṇayoḥ', signifying rain-shedding, encircling, or covering against elements, deriving forms such as kaṭati, cakaṭa, and participial forms like kaṭitaḥ.

meanings.English: to cover, shelter, screen, or encompass
meanings.Hindi: dhankana, aavaran karna, varsha se bachana
meanings.Bengali: dhaka dewa, aabaran kora, brishti theke banchano
meanings.French: couvrir, abriter, proteger de la pluie

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'śikṣ' inherently belongs to the Atmanepada group and means 'to learn' or 'to acquire knowledge' for oneself. When combined with the causative suffix (Nic), the meaning shifts to 'to teach' or 'to instruct' someone else.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakara (present tense), Atmanepada 3rd person singular
scenarios.example_english: The boy learns good knowledge.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic-pratyaya), Parasmaipada 3rd person singular
scenarios.example_english: The teacher instructs the students in duty.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti notes that 'śikṣa vidyopādāne' is an Atmanepadi Set root indicating the acquisition of knowledge or learning (vidyāgrahaṇa). It forms 'śikṣate' in the present tense, taking the Sap vikarana without root modification.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin in Kshiratarangini explains 'śikṣa' as denoting 'upādāna' (taking/learning) of knowledge, deriving regular forms such as 'śikṣate' and perfect 'śiśikṣe'.

meanings.English: to learn, to study, to acquire knowledge

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'hlad' expresses the feeling of happiness, refreshment, or delight. In its basic Atmanepada form, the subject itself experiences happiness and relief. When used with the causative affix (Nic), it turns into Parasmaipada ('hladayati') and means causing delight or refreshing someone else.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat-lakara (Present Tense), Atmanepada, Prathama Purusha Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The mind feels refreshed and delighted by the moonlit water.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic-pratyaya), Parasmaipada, Lat-lakara, Prathama Purusha Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The cool breeze refreshes and delights the traveler.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'hlada' is listed under the Bhvadi class in the sense of 'sukha' (happiness, delight) and 'ahladana' (rejoicing, causing joy). It takes Atmanepada affixes in non-causative usage, yielding forms like hladate, ahladata, and ahladi.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines 'hlada sukhe', affirming its sense in experiencing bliss, refreshment, or pleasure, behaving identically to other dental-ending roots of this sub-cluster in the Bhvadi gana.

meanings.English: to rejoice, to be delighted, to feel refreshed
meanings.Hindi: prasanna hona, anandita hona, harshita hona
meanings.French: se rejouir, etre ravi, etre soulage

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'dhvans' means to fall down, perish, decay, or crumble. It belongs to the first conjugation group (Bhvadi) and inherently takes Atmanepada endings. In its basic form, it describes something undergoing destruction or falling apart by itself. When used in the causative (Nic), it shifts meaning to 'destroying' or 'causing something to fall to ruin'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakara (present tense), prathama purusha, eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: As time passes, the wicked person perishes.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (causative), Lat lakara, prathama purusha, eka-vacana
scenarios.meaning: causes to fall down or destroys
scenarios.example_english: The storm destroys the cloud / dwelling.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: dhvansu avasramsane. anudatteta atmanepadi. avasramsanam patanam vinasho va. dhatoh idit-tva-abhavat na nityam num, kintu anunasikasya upadhayah dirgha-vyavastha bhavati.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: dhvansu avasramsane. avasramsanam adhobhavah bhranshah vinashashcha. dhvansate, dadhvanse.

meanings.English: to fall down, perish, crumble, decay

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'jarb' fundamentally means 'to go' or 'to move'. In standard active usage (Parasmaipada), it describes the subject moving toward a destination. When used with a causative suffix (Nic), it shifts the meaning to causing or making someone else go or move.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga (Present Active, Lat Lakara, Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana)
scenarios.example_english: The traveler goes along the path.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic-pratyaya, Kartari Prayoga, Lat Lakara, Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana)
scenarios.example_english: The charioteer causes the horses to move forward.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: jarbi gatau. ghatadirayam ityeke. jarbati. ajarbit. ikara anubandhasya vriddhinivrittyarthatvam ityanye. gatyarthatvat dvitvakarmakah sakarmako va.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: jarbi gatau. jarbati. ikaro visheshena svaroopartho vriddhisiddhaye cha. gatisadrisheshu prayogah drishyate.

meanings.English: to go, to move, to march

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'parb' means to go or to move. It is an idit root, which means it takes a nasal (num-agama) insertion before the final consonant in all its forms, resulting in stems like 'parmbati' or 'parvati'. In simple active voice (kartari prayoga), it describes a subject moving toward a location.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), lat-lakara (present tense), prathama-purusha (third person), ekavacana (singular)
scenarios.example_english: The traveler goes to the village.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (causative), kartari prayoga, lat-lakara (present tense), prathama-purusha (third person), ekavacana (singular)
scenarios.meaning: Causes someone to go or march
scenarios.example_english: The king causes the army to march.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti classifies 'parbi' under the Bhvadi class with the sense 'gatau' (movement/motion). Because it is marked with an idit anubandha, it undergoes regular num-agama insertion, yielding forms like parmbati, aparmbit, and parmbita.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin in Kshiratarangini notes that this series of rhyming roots (kharbi, garbi, tarbi, parbi) signifies motion (gatyartha). Being parasmaipadi and set, they follow standard thematic conjugation with nasalization.

meanings.English: to go, to move, to march

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'nādh' belongs to the first conjugation (Bhvādi gaṇa) and takes exclusively Ātmanepada endings. It expresses entreaty (asking for help/begging), distress or torment, exercising authority, or conferring blessings. In causative usage (ṇic), it indicates causing someone to seek help or causing distress.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakāra (present indicative), prathama puruṣa, ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: He/she entreats, seeks help, or suffers distress
scenarios.example_english: The impoverished person entreats the righteous king for help.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (ṇic pratyaya), Lat lakāra, prathama puruṣa, ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: Causes someone to petition or brings distress upon someone
scenarios.example_english: Misfortune causes him to plead for mercy.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: ṇādhṛ yācñopātāpaiśvaryāśiḥṣu. ṇakāro dantaḥ. anudāttetvād ātmanepadam. nādhate. yācñā prārthanā, upatāpaḥ pīḍā, aiśvaryam īśitṛtvam, āśīḥ prayogamiti catvāro 'rthāḥ. ṛkāro 'ṅgābhyāsapratiṣedhārthaḥ.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: ṇādhṛ yācñopātāpaiśvaryāśiḥṣu. nādhate. ṇasya saḥ 'dhātvādeḥ ṣaḥ' itivat 'ṇo naḥ' iti naḥ. arthāḥ prārthanā-santāpa-prabhutva-kalyāṇasaṃśrayāḥ.

meanings.English: to entreat, beg, suffer distress, exercise lordship, bestow blessing
meanings.Kannada: bēḍu, yācisu, santāpagoḷḷu, aiśvarya beḷasu, harasu
meanings.Telugu: yācincu, prārthincu, bādhapaḍu, prabhutvamu celāyincu, āśīrvadincu
meanings.Tamil: yācittal, vēṇṭutal, tunpamuru, āḷukai puri, ācīrvati
meanings.Malayalam: yācikkuka, prārthikkuka, viṣamikkkuka, prabhutvam kāṇikkuka, anugrahikkuka
meanings.Hindi: māṅganā, yācanā karanā, pīṛā pānā, svāmītva dikhānā, āśīrvāda denā
meanings.Bengali: yācñā karā, prārthanā karā, kaṣṭa pāoyā, prabhutva karā, āśīrvāda karā
meanings.Russian: umolyat', prosit', terpet' mucheniya, gospodstvovat', blagoslovlyat'

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'bhASh' means to speak or articulate distinctly in words. Because it has an anudatta vowel marker (A~) in its base form, it naturally takes Atmanepada endings (such as -te, -ete, -nte) in the active voice. When adding the causative suffix (Nic), it changes meaning to making someone else speak.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat-lakara (present tense), prathama-puruSha ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The boy speaks the truth.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic-pratyaya) active form
scenarios.example_english: The teacher makes the silent student speak.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: bhAShA vyaktAyAM vAchi | anudAttettvAd Atmanepadam | vyaktA varNaprakAramayI vAk tasyAM vartate | bhAShate, babhAShe, bhAShitA |
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: bhAShA vyaktAyAM vAchi | vyaktatvaM varNapadAbhivyaktiH | tayA yuktaM vachanameva bhAShaNamityarthaH |

meanings.English: to speak, to utter articulate speech, to say

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'ran' means 'to give' or 'to bestow'. In basic Parasmaipada form (Kartari Prayoga), it describes a subject giving something. When used in the Causative form with the 'nic' affix (ranayati / ranapayati), it shifts the meaning to causing someone to give or making a donation happen.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Lat lakara, Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana (Basic active present tense)
scenarios.example_english: The generous king gives wealth to the scholars.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Lat lakara, Nic pratyaya (Causative present tense)
scenarios.meaning: causes to give / inspires to donate
scenarios.example_english: The spiritual guide causes the wealthy man to give donations.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti treats 'rana dane' alongside 'shrana' and 'bhrana' as roots signifying the act of giving (dana-artha). Conjugational stems are formed with the standard Gana affix 'Shap' (ranati, ranatah, rananti), forming perfect (Lit) forms such as rarana and future (Lrit) forms such as ranishyati with Set vowel augmentation.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes in Kshiratarangini that 'rana dane' belongs to the triplet of 'dana' roots (shrana, bhrana, rana) in Bhvadi gana. It takes the typical parasmaipada inflections and functions transitively where the given object takes the accusative case (dvitiya) and the recipient receives the dative case (caturthi).

meanings.English: to give, to bestow, to donate

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'khag' fundamentally expresses the action of moving, walking, or going (gati). As an intransitive verb in the active voice (kartari prayoga), it takes standard Parasmaipada terminations. When used in the causative (nic) form, it turns transitive to mean 'to cause someone or something to move' or 'to dispatch'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Active Voice (Kartari Prayoga), Present Tense (Lat Lakara), 3rd Person Singular
scenarios.example_english: The deer moves towards the forest.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic-pratyaya), Active Voice (Kartari Prayoga), 3rd Person Singular
scenarios.example_english: The cowherd makes the cow move.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti places 'khaga' in the sequence of guttural and palatal root series indicating motion ('gatau'). It takes the standard Bhvadi vikarana sap, resulting in the present-tense base 'khaga-'. It is classified as set, forming future and periphrastic tense forms with the intermediate i-augment, such as khagisyati and khagita.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin in the Kshiratarangini groups 'khaga' along with similar monosyllabic motion roots (kaga, khaga, gaga, ghaga) denoting pure physical displacement (gatyartha). It conjugate regularly as an unaccented halanta stem taking Parasmaipada affixes: khagati, cakhaga, khagita.

meanings.English: to go, to move, to glide

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'pīv' belongs to the 1st conjugation (Bhvadi) and primarily means to grow fat, gain bulk, or become robust and stout. It takes Parasmaipada terminations. When used in causative (ṇijanta), it changes meaning from 'becoming stout oneself' to 'making someone or something stout/nourished'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The calf grows stout with milk.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (ṇijanta), Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The cowherd fattens the animals with grass.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'pīvṛ~ sthaulye' is interpreted as becoming stout, corpulent, or increasing in bodily strength. Being anit/set classified as set here, it forms standard present tense 'pīvati', perfect 'pipīva', and simple future 'pīviṣyati'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes this root in the sense of 'sthaulya' (density, thickness, or corpulence) and nourishment, conjugating regularly in Bhvadi as Parasmaipada without thematic irregularities.

meanings.English: to grow fat, to become stout, to gain bulk
meanings.Hindi: moṭā honā, puṣṭa honā, sthūla honā
meanings.Bengali: moṭā haoyā, puṣṭa haoyā, bṛddhi pāoyā

canonical_dhatvartha: chedane (in the sense of cutting, splitting, or dividing)

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'chu' means to cut, split, or sever something. Because it carries an indicator letter 'ṅ' (it-samjna), it is strictly an Atmanepada verb in standard active usage, expressing the cutting action. When an agent causes another person to cut or divide something, the causative affix Nic is added, allowing Ubhayapada forms.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat-lakara (present tense), Prathama-purusha (third person), Ekavacana (singular), Atmanepada
scenarios.example_english: The farmer cuts the grass.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (causative), Kartari prayoga, Lat-lakara, Prathama-purusha, Ekavacana, Atmanepada
scenarios.meaning: Causes someone to cut or slice.
scenarios.example_english: The master makes the servant cut the grass.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti analyzes 'chuṅ chedane' as an anudatta, n-it root belonging to the first conjugation (Bhvadi). Due to n-it-samjna, it takes Atmanepada affixes (anudattanita atmanepadam). Guna of the root vowel 'u' produces 'chavate' with Sarvadhatuka affix 'Sap'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes under the cavity/vowel-end series that 'chuṅ' denotes 'chedana' (cutting/division). The radical vowel undergoes normal Guna in Sarvadhatuka environments and av-adesha before vowel-initial affixes, yielding regular Atmanepadi paradigms.

meanings.English: to cut, split, sever, or divide

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root kshmaush expresses the action of shining or emitting radiance. It is conjugated exclusively in the Atmanepada in the active voice. When converted to the causative (nic), it expresses the action of making something shine or illuminating it.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakara (present tense), 3rd person singular
scenarios.example_english: The gem shines brilliantly with light.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (causative), Lat lakara (present tense), 3rd person singular
scenarios.example_english: The lamp illuminates the house.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root kshmaush belongs to the kshmashadi group of roots ending in palatal sibilant denoting dipti (radiance or illumination). It is anudatta-it, taking Atmanepada endings in the active voice with Guna applied to the initial vowel where applicable.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin categorizes kshmaush under the roots signifying dipti (to shine). It follows standard Bhvadi inflection taking Shap vikarana yielding forms like kshmaushate in the present tense.

meanings.English: to shine, to gleam, to radiate light
meanings.Hindi: chamakna, prakashit hona, deepti prapth hona
meanings.Bengali: ujjval haoya, jhikmik kara, alokita haoya

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root mruc means to go, to move, or specifically to set/decline like the sun. In basic usage, it takes Parasmaipada suffixes to describe the natural movement or setting of celestial bodies. When converted to the causative form (Nic), it signifies making someone or something go down, move away, or set.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakara (present tense), 3rd person singular
scenarios.example_english: The sun sets during the evening twilight.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic-pratyaya), Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, 3rd person singular
scenarios.example_english: Time causes the day to decline.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: mrucI gatau. Iditkaraṇam am-pratyayartham. mrocati, mumroca, mrocita. Gativacano'yam dhatuḥ astamayartho'pi bhavati.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: mrucI gatau. Ito'm (7.4.24). mrocati, mumroca, amrocit. Surya-candradinam astagamanam ityeke.

meanings.English: to go, to move, to set or sink down

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root bharts primarily expresses the act of consoling, soothing, or calming someone through gentle words (santvana), though in secondary classical contexts it can mean scolding or threatening. When used in normal active voice (Kartari Prayoga), it takes standard Parasmaipada endings.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara (present tense), Prathama purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The mother soothes the crying child.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lun lakara (aorist tense), Prathama purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The friend consoled his grieving companion.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: Madhaviya clarifies that the root bhartsa belongs to the Bhvadi class and is taught in the sense of santvana (comforting or appeasing with kind words). It takes standard set-aorist forms like abhartsit and forms bhartsita in krdanta participles.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes that bhartsa operates in the sense of pleasing or consoling (santvane), distinguishing its core Dhatupatha meaning from the later derived usage denoting threatening or blaming (bhartsana).

meanings.English: to soothe, console, comfort, appease

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'kṛṣ' fundamentally means to scratch, plow, draw, or pull. In basic active usage (Parasmaipada), it describes an agent drawing a furrow or pulling an object directly. When combined with the causative suffix (ṇic), it shifts to mean causing someone else to pull or cultivate, or to attract/drag someone forcefully.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga, laṭ lakāra, prathama puruṣa, eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The farmer plows the agricultural field.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: ṇyanta (causative), kartari prayoga, laṭ lakāra, prathama puruṣa, eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The landowner causes the servant to plow the field.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: kṛṣa vilekhane. vilekhanaṃ bhūmer vidāraṇam ākarṣaṇaṃ ca. kṛṣa-dhātuḥ aniṭ bhvādi-parasmaipadī. guṇe kṛte karṣatīti rūpaṃ sidhyati.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: kṛṣa vilekhane. vilekhanam ākarṣaṇam ucyate. halādi-sādhana-bhedāt karṣati kṛṣati iti ubhayathā prayogaḥ api dṛśyate.

meanings.English: to plow, to furrow, to pull, to draw, to attract

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'sphur' fundamentally means to throb, twitch, tremble, or flash brightly. In its regular active form (Parasmaipada), it describes an involuntary twitching (like an eye throbbing) or sudden flashing of light. When combined with the causative suffix Nic, it means causing something to shake, reveal, or flash forth.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Active voice (kartari prayoga), Present tense (lat lakara), 3rd person singular
scenarios.example_english: The right eye twitches, indicating good fortune.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative form (nic pratyaya), Present tense (lat lakara), 3rd person singular
scenarios.meaning: causes to vibrate, manifest, or shine brightly
scenarios.example_english: The lightning causes the dark sky to flash brilliantly.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'sphura' is listed with the meaning 'sphurane' (calane, diptau ca). It takes Parasmaipada suffixes and forms 'sphurati' in the present tense (lat). The vritti highlights both mechanical trembling/quivering and luminous flashing as core senses of the dhatu.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines 'sphura sphurane' as movement characterized by subtle vibration (kampana) or manifestation of light (pradarsa). It forms 'pusphora' in the perfect (lit) and exhibits guna in strong conjugational environments.

meanings.English: to throb, to twitch, to tremble, to flash, to manifest
meanings.Bengali: phurphur kora, sphurita haoya, jholse utha

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root phakk means to creep, move slowly, or sneak low to the ground. In the standard active voice (Parasmaipada), it describes an individual creeping or walking at a very slow pace. When used with a causative suffix (nic), it indicates causing someone or an animal to move slowly or crawl.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Lat lakara, prathama-purusha, eka-vacana (Simple Present Active)
scenarios.example_english: The elderly person walks slowly along the path.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya, Lat lakara, prathama-purusha, eka-vacana (Causative Present)
scenarios.meaning: causes to creep or move slowly
scenarios.example_english: The mother gently encourages the child to crawl slowly.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti explains phakka in the sense of nicairgatau (moving slowly, sneaking, or creeping low). Being an adanta/akarantavat-pathita root ending in a consonant, it takes the set-pratyayas (phakkati, paphakka, phakkita, phakkitum). Sayana notes that the sense entails slow, stealthy, or ground-level locomotion.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin glosses phakka nicairgatau as denoting mandagati (sluggish movement) or kshudra-gati (low/creeping motion). It retains Parasmaipada throughout primary active conjugations without medial changes in the present tense.

meanings.English: to creep, to move slowly, to sneak
meanings.Chinese: pa xing, man xing, qiao qiao de zou

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'dhukṣ' primarily means to kindle, ignite, or revive a fire or spirit. It belongs to the Bhvādi class and inherently conjugates in the Ātmanepada voice (dhukṣate). When paired with the prefix 'sam-' and the causative suffix 'ṇic' (sandhukṣayati), it conveys deliberately kindling or instigating enthusiasm, fire, or courage in someone or something.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Bhvādi Ātmanepada, Laṭ-lakāra (Present Tense, 3rd person singular)
scenarios.meaning: Kindles, grows brighter, or is invigorated (for oneself/internally)
scenarios.example_english: The fire slowly kindles.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (ṇic) with upasarga 'sam', Parasmaipada, Laṭ-lakāra
scenarios.meaning: Kindles, revives, or stimulates (an external object/person)
scenarios.example_english: The teacher rekindles enthusiasm in the students.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'dhukṣa~' is defined in the sense of 'sandīpane' (kindling, inflaming, or exciting). Being anudātteta, it takes Ātmanepada endings under normal conditions (dhukṣate, adhukṣiṣṭa). In classical usage, it is frequently seen with the upasarga 'sam' in both base and causative formations.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'dhukṣa sandīpane' as denoting the act of making a flame or faculty burn bright. It is characterized as a set root taking it-āgama in the ardhadhātuka forms such as dhukṣitum and adhukṣiṣṭa.

meanings.English: To kindle, ignite, inflame, revive, stimulate.
meanings.Telugu: Rājeyu, veligincu, utteja parachuta, chalanamu cheyuta.
meanings.Hindi: Sulgana, jalana, sandipita karna, uttejita karna.
meanings.Bengali: Jvalano, pradipita kara, uttejita kara, jagiye tola.

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'gard' means to make a harsh, disagreeable, or unpleasant sound (such as the braying of an animal or a jarring clatter). In its basic active form (Parasmaipada), it describes the subject making the discordant noise directly. When used with the causative suffix (Nic), it signifies making an object or creature emit a harsh, rattling, or dissonant sound.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (Present indicative 3rd person singular, Lat-lakkara)
scenarios.meaning: makes an unpleasant sound / brays / groans
scenarios.example_english: The donkey, separated in the forest, brays harshly.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative form (Nic-pratyaya in Kartari Lat-lakara)
scenarios.meaning: causes to emit a discordant or harsh rattling sound
scenarios.example_english: The boy causes the vessel to rattle disagreeably out of agitation.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti registers 'garda kutsitashabde' under the Bhvadi Parasmaipada section. It explains that the root denotes emitting a disagreeable or corrupted sound. It is classified as an udattopadesha, set root forming gardati, jagarda, and gardita without vocalic lengthening in general sarvadhatuka operations.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin classifies 'garda kutsitashabde' alongside phonetically linked roots like karda and kharda. He glosses the action as 'kutsitadhvani-karanam', referring to defective, grating phonation or discordant animalistic vocalization.

meanings.English: to make a harsh or unpleasant sound, to groan, to bray
meanings.Telugu: karkasha shabdamu cheyuta, asahyamaina dhvani cheyuta
meanings.Tamil: karkasamaana oli elupputhal, asingamaana oli seithal
meanings.Hindi: karkasha dhvani nikalna, kharab aawaz karna, rekna
meanings.Bengali: karkasha shobdo kora, kutsita dhvani kora
meanings.German: einen unangenehmen Laut von sich geben, kraechzen, bloeken
meanings.French: emettre un son desagreable, braire, grincer
meanings.Chinese: fachu nanting de shengyin, sizhu, zaozao

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'plu' means to float, leap, jump, or move swiftly. As an Atmanepadi root in the Bhvadi class, it takes middle endings (e.g., plavate). When converted to causative (nic) or combined with prefixes (upasargas like 'sam-ut' or 'abhi'), its meaning adapts from floating to jumping high, inundating, or overflowing.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakara (present tense), prathama-purusha (third person), eka-vacana (singular)
scenarios.example_english: The fish floats and swims in the water.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (causative), Lat lakara, prathama-purusha, eka-vacana
scenarios.meaning: causes to float, inundates, or submerges
scenarios.example_english: Rainwater inundates the fields.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: pluṅ gatau. anudattetvāt ātmanepadī. plavate, pupluve, plavishyati/plotā. Madhaviya notes that despite having a basic meaning of general movement (gati), it specifically conveys hopping, swimming, floating, or flying through the air.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: pluṅ gatau. plavanam gatih. Kshirasvamin records that 'plu' denotes leaping motion (plutyagatih) or floating upon water, noting standard derivations such as plavah (boat, frog) and plavangamah (monkey).

meanings.English: to float, swim, leap, jump, plunge

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'tuj' means to hurt, strike, push, or dwell. In standard active usage (Kartari Parasmaipada), an nasal infix is inserted due to the 'i' marker (idit), producing forms like 'tunjati' to describe someone hitting or injuring an object.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, prathama-purusa, eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The opponent strikes the enemy.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (Causative), Lat lakara, prathama-purusa, eka-vacana
scenarios.meaning: Causes someone to strike or hurt
scenarios.example_english: The king makes the soldier strike the enemy.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'tuji' is characterized as idit, which necessitates the augment num (nasalization) before the sarvadhatuka affix, forming 'tunjati'. It is glossed in the senses of himsana (harming, striking), balakarana (exerting strength), and niketa (abiding or dwelling).
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'tuji' with the indicative vowel 'i' yielding the nasalized present stem 'tunj-'. In classical and Vedic usage, it also conveys giving or impelling, alongside the primary sense of injury or forceful contact.

meanings.English: to strike, hurt, injure, push, dwell
meanings.Bengali: aghat kora, himsa kora, bas kora

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'dhāv' expresses two primary actions: moving fast ('to run') and making something clean ('to wash' or 'to purify'). Because it has an indicatory vowel marking it as Ubhayapada, it conjugates in both Parasmaipada (dhāvati) and Atmanepada (dhāvate). In the sense of motion, it is intransitive, whereas in the sense of cleansing, it is transitive.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat-lakara, Prathama-purusha, Ekavacana, Parasmaipada
scenarios.example_english: The horse runs swiftly in the field.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat-lakara, Prathama-purusha, Ekavacana, Atmanepada
scenarios.example_english: The boy washes his hands.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: dhāvṛ gatīśuddhyoḥ. svaritetatvād ubhayapadī. dhāvati dhāvate. didhāva didhāve. dhāvitā. dhāviṣyati dhāviṣyate. dhāvanaṃ gatiḥ śodhanamiti dvayorartheṣu vartate. seṭkaḥ.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: dhāvṛ gatau ca śuddhau ca. dhāvati mṛgaḥ iti gatau, vastraṃ dhāvati iti śuddhau. ubhayapadaḥ seṭ.

meanings.English: to run, to glide; to wash, to purify, to cleanse
meanings.Bengali: douṛānō, dhābita haoyā; dhuẏā, pariṣkāra karā

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root kṛṣ means to plough, scratch, furrow, or draw lines upon the earth. When used directly in Parasmaipada, it indicates the action of ploughing a field. When combined with the causative suffix nic, it shifts to mean causing to plough or dragging/pulling.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakara (present tense), 3rd person singular
scenarios.example_english: The farmer ploughs the field.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (causative), Lat lakara (present tense), 3rd person singular
scenarios.example_english: The master causes the farmer to plough the field.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The entry kṛṣa vilekhane explains vilekhana as making furrows or tearing the ground by ploughing. As an anit root of the Bhvadi class, it takes the direct form kṛṣati in the present tense and exhibits the guna form krakṣyati or karkṣyati in the simple future (Lrt).
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines vilekhana as bhedana (breaking or tearing the soil). The root is noted as Parasmaipadi and anit, forming standard active derivatives such as kṛṣati, cakarsa, and kṛṣṭam.

meanings.English: to plough, to furrow, to scratch, to till

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'hras' primarily expresses making a sound (shabda) or diminishing/shortening in size or intensity (alpibhava/kshaya). In its basic form (kartari prayoga), it takes Parasmaipada endings ('hrasati') to indicate that something becomes short, decreases, or resounds. When used with a causative affix (nic), it forms 'hrasayati', meaning to shorten, lessen, or reduce something actively.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga, lat-lakara, prathama-purusha, eka-vacana
scenarios.example_sanskrit: nidaghe divasah vardhate kintu ratih hrasati.
scenarios.example_english: In summer, the day lengthens but the night shortens.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: nic-pratyaya (causative), kartari prayoga, lat-lakara, prathama-purusha, eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: Exercise reduces the bulkiness of the body.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'hrasa' is assigned to the Bhvadi-gana with the meaning 'shabde' (sound-making) and by extension 'alpibhave' (diminution). It is anudattopadesha-parasmaipadi and categorised as set, taking standard it-agama in ardhadhatuka environments (jahrasa, hrasita, hrasishyati).
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'hrasa shabde', illustrating its usage both in the sense of expressing a low sound or murmur and contextual semantic evolution towards diminution/decrease (alpibhava).

meanings.English: to sound, to diminish, to decrease, to shorten
meanings.Bengali: shobdo kora, kshoy howa, choto howa

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'mang' belongs to the first conjugation group (Bhvadi-gana) and means 'to go', 'to move', or 'to step forward'. In standard usage, it takes Parasmaipada endings. When used with causative affixes (Nich-pratyaya), it shifts from moving oneself to causing someone or something else to move.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga, lat lakara, prathama purusha, eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The traveler moves along the path.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: nich pratyaya (causative), kartari prayoga, lat lakara, prathama purusha, eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The leader directs the soldiers forward.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti notes that 'mangi' is an idit root denoting motion ('gatau'). Due to the it-marker 'i', it gains a penultimate nasal (num-agama), forming the stem 'mang-'. It conjugates as mangati in the present tense (Lat-lakara) and is classified as set.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin analyzes 'mangi' under the movement-denoting roots of Bhvadi-gana, confirming the insertion of the nasal before the final consonant and establishing the basic present third-person singular form as mangati.

meanings.English: to go, to move, to step forward

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'luṭh' means to roll, tumble, or wallow on the ground. In basic form (Kartari Prayoga), it takes Parasmaipada suffixes like 'luṭhati' (he/she/it rolls). When combined with the causative suffix Nic, it becomes 'loṭhayati', changing the meaning from rolling by oneself to actively rolling or tumbling an external object.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga, Lat Lakara, Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The horse rolls on the ground.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic), Lat Lakara, Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The boy rolls the ball in the courtyard.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'luṭha' belongs to the Bhvadi gana and is designated in the sense of 'vilolana' (rolling, tossing, or agitation). Being marked with an ending 'a', it takes the sap vikarana in kartari prayoga, forms the present stem 'luṭha-', and follows the standard Parasmaipada paradigm yielding forms like luṭhati, loloṭha, and loṭhita.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'luṭha vilolane', specifying that the verb indicates continuous, unrestrained turning or rolling over surfaces. It is classified as seṭ, taking the intermediate vowel 'i' in non-sarvadhatuka ardhadhatuka environments, producing periphrastic and simple futures such as loṭhitā and loṭhiṣyati.

meanings.English: to roll, to wallow, to tumble

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'mid' fundamentally denotes becoming moist, unctuous, or showing tender love and affection. Because of the 'i' marker (idit), it receives a nasal augment 'num', taking the present-tense form 'mendati'. In causative constructions, it means to moisten, liquefy, or make someone feel affection.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakara (present tense), prathama-purusha ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The mother's heart softens with affection.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (causative), Lat lakara, kartari prayoga
scenarios.example_english: The heat of the sun liquefies the clarified butter.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti notes that 'midi snehane' is an idit root, commanding the insertion of the 'num' augment via the rule 'idito num dhatoh'. This produces the base 'mind-', which undergoes guna to yield 'mendati'. Its semantic core covers both physical unctuousness or softening and emotional affection.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin states in the Kshiratarangini that 'midi snehane' belongs to the idit group in Bhvadi-gana. The marker indicates the invariable presence of nasalization throughout conjugational bases, pointing strictly to affection, fatness, or melting.

meanings.English: to be moist, to liquefy, to soften, to feel affection

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'tuh' means to injure, torment, or cause distress to someone. It belongs to the first group of verbs (Bhvadi-gana) and takes standard Parasmaipada endings. When used as a simple verb (Kartari Prayoga), it describes someone actively causing pain or hurting another person. When converted into a causative verb (Nich-pratyaya), it means causing someone to hurt or afflict another.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Bhvadi-gana standard present tense (Lat Lakara, Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana) with 'shap' affix
scenarios.example_english: The wicked person torments the virtuous person.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative form (Nich-pratyaya) with Guna strengthening of vowel 'u' to 'o'
scenarios.meaning: Causes to torment or instigates hurting
scenarios.example_english: The king causes the enemies to be tormented by the servants.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'tuha' is classified under the Bhvadi-gana with the canonical meaning 'ardane' (causing distress, injury, or pain). It forms simple active verbs with the 'shap' affix yielding 'tuhati'. In the perfect tense (Lit), it undergoes reduplication and Guna yielding 'tutoha'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines 'tuha ardane' as signifying 'himsayam' (violence, harming) and 'pidane' (afflicting). It is an unaccented vowel base behaving as a standard set root in the non-conjugational tenses.

meanings.English: to hurt, torment, afflict, or injure
meanings.Bengali: piran kora, jontrona dewa, aghat kora

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root mlai means to wither, fade, or lose freshness and energy. In its basic Parasmaipada form, it describes a plant drooping or a person losing vigor. When converted to a causative form (nic), it indicates causing someone or something to wither, wilt, or become exhausted.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (Present indicative active, 3rd person singular)
scenarios.example_english: The flower withers due to the heat.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (nic-pratyaya) active, 3rd person singular
scenarios.example_english: The intense heat causes the lotus to fade.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'mlai' is listed under the Bhvadi class in the sense of 'harsa-ksaye' (decay or loss of joy, vitality, or freshness). It is classified as an akarmaka (intransitive) root taking Parasmaipada affixes. Being an adanta-adesha element, it forms 'mlayati' in Lat by substituting the vowel, 'mamlau' in Lit, 'mlasyati' in Lrt, and the past participle 'mlanah' with characteristic 'na'-adesha.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'mlai harsaksaye harsapratighate', indicating the cessation or diminution of lively freshness and cheerful spirit. Forms like 'mlayati', 'mlatah', and 'mlanam' show the standard transformation of final diphthongs to long 'a' in non-sarvadhatuka environments.

meanings.English: to wither, to fade, to languish, to lose freshness
meanings.Bengali: mlan howa, shukiye jaoya, nistej howa

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'svad' means to taste, savor, relish, or to be pleasing/agreeable. In its basic middle voice form (Atmanepada), it denotes the subject relishing an object or pleasing someone directly. In the causative form (svadayati / svadayate), it denotes causing something to become flavorful, making someone savor, or presenting savory food.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat-lakara (present tense), Prathama-purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The boy relishes the sweet fruit.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (causative), Lat-lakara, Prathama-purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: makes palatable, sweetens, or causes to relish
scenarios.example_english: The mother makes the dish savory with salt.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti analyzes 'svadā asvadane' as an Atmanepadi root belonging to the Bhvadi class. It takes the Vikarana shap and forms 'svadate'. In the lit-lakara it yields 'sasvade', and in the aorist (lun) with the it-agama it forms 'asvadiṣṭa'. Its primary semantic scope denotes subjective tasting, experiencing flavor, and agreeable sensation.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes under 'svada asvadane' that the root conveys the cognition of taste (rasana-kriya) as well as the intrinsic capacity of an object to please the palate. As a set root with an anudatta vowel marker, it strictly takes Atmanepada terminations in the non-causative conjugation.

meanings.English: to taste, to relish, to be savory, to please
meanings.Bengali: svad grahan kara, chaka, asvadan kara
meanings.French: gouter, savourer, etre agreable au gout
meanings.Russian: probovat na vkus, naslazhdatsya vkusom, nravitsya

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'hād' means to evacuate the bowels or defecate. It carries an indicatory marker 'ṛ' (ṛkāra anubandha) which directs specific morphological changes and is inherently conjugated in the Ātmanepada (middle voice). In everyday language, it expresses natural bodily excretion or, in causative forms, medicinal purgation.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Active voice (kartari prayoga), Present tense (laṭ), Third person singular
scenarios.example_english: After taking medicine, the patient evacuates the bowels comfortably.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (ṇic-pratyaya), Active voice (kartari prayoga), Present tense (laṭ)
scenarios.meaning: causes to purge / induces bowel evacuation
scenarios.example_english: The physician purges the patient using a laxative.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'hādṛ' is taught in the sense of 'purīṣotsarga' (evacuation of waste/excrement). Being an ṛ-it root, it exhibits specific morphophonemic operations in derived nominals and aorist formations, conjugating in the present tense as 'hādate' with the Śap vikarana in the Ātmanepada.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'hādṛ purīṣotsarge' as an Ātmanepada root having a voiced dental stop ending (dānta). The perfect form is 'jahāde', indicating the biological act of excretion or voiding.

meanings.English: to evacuate the bowels, to defecate, to void excrement

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'vāṣ' means to make a sound, roar, or howl (especially used for animals, birds, or natural sounds). It is an Atmanepada root in basic active use. When converted to the causative (Nic), it means to cause someone or something to make a sound or cry out.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga, laṭ-lakāra, prathama-puruṣa, eka-vacana (ātmanepada)
scenarios.example_english: The bird makes a sound in the tree.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: ṇic-pratyaya (causative), kartari prayoga, laṭ-lakāra, parasmaipada
scenarios.meaning: causes to howl / makes utter a sound
scenarios.example_english: The boy causes the hog to squeal.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: vāṣṛ śabde. ātmanepadī, seṭ. ṛditvād aṅ luṅi. vāṣate, vavāṣe, vāṣitā, vāṣiṣyate, avāṣiṣṭa / avāṣat.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: vāṣṛ śabde. vāṣate. ṛkāra iditkaraṇaṁ luṅi aṅartham. dhvani-karaṇe 'yaṁ vartate.

meanings.English: to make a sound, to roar, to howl, to call

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'kuñj' fundamentally means to emit a rustling or murmuring sound, or to become thick and dense like an arbor or bower (nikuñja). In simple active voice (Parasmaipada), the subject itself makes a rustling sound or grows clustered.
