scenarios.example_english: Time causes all living beings to age.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti analyzes jṝṣa in the sense of vayaḥhāni (loss of youth, growing old, decay). Belonging to the bhvādi class with a dental-sibilant/murdhanya ending, its primary thematic forms undergo guṇa/vṛddhi depending on the context, yielding jarati / jārati in standard derived configurations.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes jṝṣa vayaḥhānau among roots indicating progressive deterioration and exhaustion of life force or material substance, noting its morphological alignment with other aging-related roots.

meanings.English: to grow old, to decay, to wear out
meanings.Bengali: briddha haoyā, jīrṇa haoyā, kshay haoyā

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'krs' primarily means 'to plough', 'to furrow', or 'to pull/drag'. In simple active voice (Parasmaipada), a person directly performs the action of ploughing a field or pulling an object. When modified by the causative affix (nic), it means causing someone else to plough or drag.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Bhvadi class simple present (lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana)
scenarios.example_english: The farmer ploughs the field.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative present (nic pratyaya, lat lakara)
scenarios.meaning: Causes to plough / causes to draw
scenarios.example_english: The master has the field ploughed by the servants.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'krsa vilekhane' belongs to the Bhvadi class. 'Vilekhana' signifies tearing, furrowing the ground, or ploughing. With regular guna substitution of the vowel 'r' to 'ar' before the sarvadhatuka affix 'sap', it forms 'karsati'. Being anit in standard contexts, it follows regular non-it reduplicated and s-aorist patterns.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'krs' in the sense of 'vilekhana' (scratching, furrowing, ploughing with an implement). It takes Parasmaipada terminations when without atmanepada-conditioning markers, distinguishing its basic verbal paradigm across various tense-aspect forms like karsati, cakarsa, and kraksyati.

meanings.English: to plough, to furrow, to drag, to draw

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'mluc' means 'to go', 'to move', or 'to set/sink' (as in the setting of the sun or receding). In standard active voice (Parasmaipada), it describes the subject moving or going down. When prefixed with preverbs like 'ni' (nimlocati), it specifically expresses setting or sinking down. When used in the causative (Nic), it means to cause something or someone to move or set.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Active voice (Kartari Prayoga), Present tense (Lat), 3rd person singular
scenarios.example_english: The sun goes down / sets behind the mountain.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic-pratyaya), Active voice, Present tense, 3rd person singular
scenarios.meaning: causes to move / causes to set
scenarios.example_english: Time causes the sun to set.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'mluca' belongs to the Bhvadi class and is read with the meaning 'gatau' (in the sense of going or motion). It undergoes guna strengthening of the vowel 'u' to 'o' before Sarvadhatuka affixes, forming 'mlocati'. Being an ending in a consonant in the Bhvadi list, it forms perfect forms like 'mamloca'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'mluca gatau' along with 'mruca' as roots denoting motion (gatyartha). It follows standard Parasmaipada inflection of the first conjugation.

meanings.English: to go, to move, to set or sink down

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'mlecch' describes speaking indistinctly, stammering, or talking in an unintelligible, foreign manner. In the basic active voice (Kartari Prayoga), it is conjugated exclusively in the Parasmaipada taking standard suffixes like -ti. When used with a causative affix (Nic), it signifies making someone speak indistinctly.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (present active indicative, 3rd person singular)
scenarios.example_english: Due to fear, the boy speaks indistinctly.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic-pratyaya) active
scenarios.meaning: causes to speak indistinctly or garble words
scenarios.example_english: Intoxication causes the person to speak incoherently.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti explains 'mleccha avyaktayam vaci' as the utterance of speech devoid of clarity or proper articulation (asphuta-bhashanam). It classifies the root as Parasmaipadi and Set, forming the primary present tense base as mlecchati and the perfect as mimleccha.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes in the Kshiratarangini that 'mleccha' refers to articulation that lacks distinct phonemic clarity (aspashtoktau). The derivation undergoes standard guna/sarvadhatuka operations without root-vowel alternation in the present stem, yielding mlecchati and future mlecchishyati.

meanings.English: to speak indistinctly, to utter unintelligibly, to speak a foreign dialect
meanings.Hindi: aspashta bolna, aprasanna ya agamyavani bolna

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'mluc' means to go, to move stealthily, to conceal, or to set (like the sun). When used independently in Parasmaipada, it denotes the subject undergoing the motion or hiding. When combined with the prefix 'ni-' (nimlocati), it specifically refers to the setting of heavenly bodies such as the sun. In the causative form (nic), it means to cause to set or to make someone retreat/hide.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara (present tense), Prathama purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The sun sets toward the western mountain.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nyanta (Causative), Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The cloud conceals (causes to set from view) the sun.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti identifies 'mlucu~' with the meanings of motion ('gati') and theft/concealment ('steya'). Because it has an 'u' as an indicatory letter (udit), the ktva suffix optionally takes the it-agama by 'udito va'. The Guna of the root vowel 'u' yields 'o', forming 'mlocati'. With prefixes like 'ni', it commonly denotes the setting of luminaries ('nimlocati suryaḥ').
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes in Kshiratarangini that 'mlucu' parallels 'mrucu' in meaning and derivation, signifying unobtrusive or curved movement, moving into hiding, or departing. The standard present stem is formed by adding Sap without lengthening the consonant cluster, producing 'mlocati'.

meanings.English: To go, to move secretly, to set (as the sun), to steal
meanings.Hindi: Chalna, chori karna, ast hona, chipna
meanings.Bengali: Jaoa, churi kora, osto jaoya, lukiye thaka
meanings.German: Gehen, sich heimlich bewegen, untergehen (Sonne), stehlen
meanings.French: Aller, se deplacer furtivement, se coucher (soleil), derober

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'hurcch' means to be crooked, bend, stumble, or act deceitfully. In the basic active form (Parasmaipada), it describes a subject moving crookedly, deviating from the straight path, or faltering. When used in the causative form with the affix 'nic', it means making someone or something go astray, bending an object, or causing someone to stumble.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga (present indicative active 3rd person singular)
scenarios.example_english: The elderly person stumbles with his foot on the path.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: nic-pratyaya (causative present active 3rd person singular)
scenarios.meaning: causes to go astray or makes crooked
scenarios.example_english: Evil counsel leads a person astray from the right path.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'hurccha kautilye' is listed in the Bhvadi-gana as ending in the indicatory vowel a-kara. It takes Parasmaipada terminations and is set (takes intermediate i-karana). Forms include the present 'hurcchati', the perfect 'juhurccha', the periphrastic future 'hurcchita', and the simple future 'hurcchisyati'. It denotes crooked motion, deviance, or deceitful behavior.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin analyzes 'hurccha' in the sense of 'kautilya' (crookedness, deceit, or curvature). It conjugates regularly in Bhvadi with the suffix 'sap', yielding 'hurcchati'. Its nominal derivatives express distortion, falling away from rectitude, or staggering.

meanings.English: to be crooked, to bend, to deceive, to stumble or falter
meanings.Bengali: bakra haoya, thokar khaoya, kutilata kara

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root smr fundamentally means to remember, recollect, or long for someone or something. In standard active voice (Parasmaipada), the subject itself performs the action of remembering (smarati). When modified by the causative suffix (Nic), the root takes the form smarayati, meaning to remind or make someone remember.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakara (present tense), prathama-purusha ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The boy remembers the preceptor's advice.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (causative voice), Lat lakara, prathama-purusha ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The mother reminds her son of his lesson.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: smr adhyane. adhyanam utkanthapurvakam smaranam ityarthah. anudatta it, anit, parasmaibhasa. smarati, sasmara, smarta, smarisyati, asmarat, smaret, asmarsit.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: smr adhyane. adhyanam smaranam utkantha ca. smarati. gunah, r-karasya ar-adesha. anit parasmaipadi.

meanings.English: to remember, to recollect, to yearn for

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root jas means to strike, beat, or injure. In standard active voice (Kartari Prayoga), it takes Parasmaipada endings to denote someone striking or subduing an opponent. When combined with the causative suffix (Nic), it signifies making someone strike or causing complete exhaustion.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara (present tense), prathama-purusha, eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The warrior strikes the enemy.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic-pratyaya), Lat lakara, prathama-purusha, eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The king subdues the enemies.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti glosses jasu as tadanarthe (in the sense of beating, striking, or inflicting harm). It notes the base derivation as jasati and discusses the vocalic behaviors and optional it-agama in specific kridanta derivations.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin in Kshiratarangini emphasizes the semantic scope of physical striking and weakening (tadanartha), illustrating its transitive usage in defeating adversaries.

meanings.English: to strike, to beat, to injure, to exhaust
meanings.Hindi: marna, pitna, chot pahunchana, kshin hona
meanings.Bengali: aghat kora, prohar kora, durbal howa

canonical_dhatvartha: himsayam (in the sense of injuring, harming, or hurting)

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'jhas' belongs to the first conjugation (Bhvadi gana) and is conjugated in Parasmaipada to denote inflicting harm or injury upon someone or something. When used in active voice, the subject performs the act of hurting; when combined with causative affixes (nic), it signifies causing someone else to harm or kill.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Active Voice (Kartari Prayoga), Present Tense (Lat lakara), 3rd Person Singular (Prathama Purusha)
scenarios.example_english: The hunter hurts the deer in the forest.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic-pratyaya), Present Tense (Lat lakara), 3rd Person Singular
scenarios.meaning: causes to harm / makes someone strike
scenarios.example_english: The king causes the soldier to strike the enemy.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti analyzes 'jhasi himsayam' as an idit root denoting harm or violence. Because of the anubandha 'i', it takes the augment num in its conjugated bases (though in certain traditional recensions it forms straightforward bases like jhasati), functioning as a parasmaipadi, set transitive verbal root.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes under 'jhasi himsayam' that the root conveys injury and destruction. It follows the standard Bhvadi inflectional paradigm with standard intermediate 'i' in ardhadhatuka environments.

meanings.English: to injure, to harm, to hurt, to strike

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root yup belongs to the first conjugation (Bhvadi gana) and is used in the Parasmaipada voice. It expresses the action of bewildering, confounding, or causing confusion. In ordinary active voice, the subject causes perplexity or acts in a confused manner. When converted to a causative form (yopayati/yopayati), it actively denotes confusing or misleading someone else.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Bhvadi Gana Kartari Prayoga (Present Active)
scenarios.meaning: confounds / acts in a confused or confusing manner
scenarios.example_english: The person gripped by delusion acts in a confused manner.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic Pratyaya (Causative Active)
scenarios.example_english: The illusion bewilders the enemies.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'yupa~ vimohane' is listed under the Bhvadi class as Parasmaipadi and Set. Madhava clarifies its semantic scope as 'vimohana' denoting the obstruction of discernment or delusion (cittavibhrama). In its present tense base, it forms yopati by guna of the vowel u before the sarvadhatuka affix shap.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines 'yupa vimohane' as signifying the state or action of bewildered delusion. It takes standard Bhvadi guna modification (u -> o) yielding yopati, yupitah, and causative forms like yopayati.

meanings.English: to confuse, to bewilder, to stupefy, to confound
meanings.Hindi: bharmit karna, mohit karna, chakkar mein dalna
meanings.Russian: sbivat s tolku, zamorachivat, privodit v zameshatelstvo
meanings.Chinese: shi mihuo, shi kunhuo, mi luan

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'khac' means to inlay, stud, join together, or set stones/jewels closely into something. When used in normal active voice (Parasmaipada), it describes placing or studding gems into an ornament, or being studded/interspersed.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat-lakara (present tense), prathama-purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The craftsman inlays jewels into the bracelet.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Karmani prayoga (passive voice), Lat-lakara, prathama-purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The crown is studded with gems.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti explains 'khaca bhutabimbane' as meaning joining together, combining, or manifesting an inset form (sandarbhana or bimbikarana). Being ending in a consonant, it takes the Guna affix shap in Sarvadhatuka forms resulting in khacati.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines the artha 'bhutabimbane' as setting, embedding, or clustering together into a unified shape, noting forms like khacati and its past participle khacita.

meanings.English: to inlay, stud, combine, set gems

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'mīl' denotes the action of closing or shutting, particularly the closing of eyelids or the folding of flower petals. In basic present tense (kartari prayoga), it takes Parasmaipada endings to mean 'closes/shuts eyes'. When combined with the causative suffix (ṇic), it forms 'melayati', meaning 'causes to close' or 'shuts something (like eyes)'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga (active voice), laṭ lakāra, prathama puruṣa, ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: Due to sleepiness, the child closes his eyes.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: ṇyanta (causative), laṭ lakāra, prathama puruṣa, ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The sage closes both eyes for meditation.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: mīla nimīlane - nimīlanaṃ netrayoḥ saṅkocaḥ. akarmakaḥ, seṭ, parasmaibhāṣā. mīlati, mamīla, melitā, meliṣyati, amīlīt ityādīni rūpāṇi bhavanti.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: mīla nimīlane - cakṣuḥsaṅkocane ityarthaḥ. padmāderapi saṅkoce vartate. mīlati, nimīlati kamalam.

meanings.English: to close the eyes, to blink, to shut, to contract
meanings.Bengali: chokha bojha, chokh bondho kora, mude jaoya
meanings.German: die Augen schliessen, sich schliessen, blinzeln
meanings.French: fermer les yeux, cligner, se fermer
meanings.Chinese: bi yan, he long, zha yan

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'can' primarily expresses the action of giving or donating (and according to some traditions, causing injury). In basic active voice (Parasmaipada), it describes an agent offering a gift or item directly to a recipient. When the causative affix nic is added, it forms 'canayati', meaning causing someone to give or distribute gifts.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana (kartari prayoga)
scenarios.example_english: The king gives wealth to the wise scholar.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: nic pratyaya (causative), lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: causes to give / makes someone donate
scenarios.example_english: The virtuous leader motivates people to give food.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti registers 'cana' in the sense of 'dane' (giving/donation). It records standard Parasmaipada inflection like canati, perfect cacana, and periphrastic forms with the id-agama (canita, canishyati). It also mentions that alternate readings incorporate 'himsayam' (in the sense of harming/hurting).
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'cana dane' within the Bhvadi-gana, confirming the primary semantic classification of gift-making (pradana) along with the morphological regularities of a guttural/dental nasal sequence forming canati and the lit form cacana.

meanings.English: to give, donate, bestow, or injure

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'dhma' means to blow air, kindle fire by blowing, or blow into an instrument (like a conch or flute) to produce sound. In regular present tense forms, 'dhma' changes to 'dhama' before endings, giving 'dhamati' (he/she blows). When used in causative forms with the suffix Nic, it takes the 'puk' augment to form 'dhmapayati' (causes to blow).

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara (present indicative active)
scenarios.example_english: Krishna blows the conch.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (causative active)
scenarios.meaning: Causes to blow / causes to be blown
scenarios.example_english: The teacher makes the student blow the conch.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti explains 'dhma sabdagnisamyogayoh' as denoting both the production of musical or blowing sound (sabda) and blowing onto fire or molten metals (agnisamyoga). By the sutra 'paghradhmasthasadasadam...', the root receives the replacement 'dhama' in Sarvadhatuka environments.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes in Kshiratarangini that 'dhma' belongs to the group of roots ending in long -a that undergo special stem replacement to 'dhama-' before shit-pratyayas, functioning transitively in contexts involving breath, pipes, conches, and forge-fires.

meanings.English: to blow, puff, blow a conch or flute, kindle fire with breath
meanings.Hindi: phumnkana, shankh bajana, aag phumnkakar jalana
meanings.Bengali: phnoka deoya, shankha bajano, agun dhorano
meanings.French: souffler, sonner de la conque, attiser le feu
meanings.Chinese: chui, chui hao jiao, chui huo

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'dhru' refers to going, steady movement, turning, or making firm. When used in Parasmaipada, it highlights an outward or direct action of moving/flowing. When used in Atmanepada, it highlights a deliberate, self-centered, or steady internal motion.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga (Parasmaipada, Lat Lakara, Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana)
scenarios.example_english: Water flows steadily in the forest.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga (Atmanepada, Lat Lakara, Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana)
scenarios.example_english: The traveler takes a turn along the pathway.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: dhrūñ gativalanayoḥ stambhe ca. Ñit-karanad ubhayapadī. Anit. Sarvadhatuke guna-adeshe 'dhravati' 'dhravate' iti rupe bhavatah.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: dhrūñ gatau valane ca. Gatau ca gatipratibandhe ca prayujyate. Dhravati dhravate dudhrāva dudhruve.

meanings.English: to move, to flow, to turn, to steady
meanings.Bengali: chola, probahitoh howa, ghora, sthir kora
meanings.German: sich bewegen, fliessen, sich wenden, festigen

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'klath' means to hurt, injure, harm, or kill. In standard active voice (Parasmaipada), it describes an agent directly causing injury or destroying an opponent. When combined with the causative suffix (Nic), it changes to mean causing someone else to injure or destroy.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (Active voice, Present tense Lat, Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana)
scenarios.example_english: The brave warrior strikes down the enemy on the battlefield.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic-pratyaya, Present tense Lat, Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana)
scenarios.meaning: Causes to hurt, destroy, or injure
scenarios.example_english: The king has the wicked individuals destroyed by his soldiers.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'klatha' belongs to the Bhvadi class and is read in the sense of 'himsayam' (injury or killing). It takes Parasmaipada terminations, is anit/set according to general Gana conventions, and forms 'klathati' by regular Guna-free stem derivation under the Sap vikarana.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin categorizes 'klatha' alongside 'kratha' under 'himsartha' roots (verbs expressing injury and slaughter). The stem undergoes regular thematic 'a' addition to yield forms like 'klathati' and 'chaklatha' in the perfect tense.

meanings.English: to injure, hurt, harm, or kill
meanings.Bengali: himsa kara, aghat kara, hatya kara

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'dhyai' means to meditate, contemplate, or focus the mind upon an object. In active voice (Parasmaipada), it describes an agent directly engaging in continuous and focused thought. When the causative suffix (Nic) is added, it forms 'dhyapayati', which means to cause or guide someone to meditate.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana (Simple active present tense)
scenarios.example_english: The sage meditates upon God in the forest.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (Causative), Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: Causes someone to meditate / Guides in meditation
scenarios.example_english: The teacher guides the disciple to meditate on the ultimate truth.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: dhyai cintayam. dhyayati, dadhyau, dhyata, dhyasyati, adhyasit. dhyanam nama ekagrena manasa satata-cintanam. ayam anit parasmaipadi ca.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: dhyai cintayam. adesho'syaitva-pratisedhe akarah syat. dhyayati. dhyanam eka-vishaya-pravaho manasah.

meanings.English: to meditate, to contemplate, to reflect upon

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'dhrji' means 'to go' or 'to glide/move'. Because it is an 'idit' root (having an 'i' marker in traditional grammar), it inserts a nasal sound 'n' into the base, producing forms like 'dhrñjati'. In the causative form, it means 'to make someone or something move'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice, present tense third-person singular)
scenarios.example_english: The bird moves in the sky.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nich pratyaya (causative voice, present tense third-person singular)
scenarios.example_english: The charioteer causes the horse to move.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: dhrji gatau - iditvān num. dhrñjati. idit-kāryeṇa sarvatra nakārāgamaḥ bhavati. dhrñjitā, didhrñjiṣati.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: dhrji gatau - dhrajādayaścatvāro gatyarthāḥ. iditvān numi dhrñjati. dhrñjitaḥ.

meanings.English: to go, to move, to glide

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root dhyai means to meditate, think deeply, or contemplate. In its simple active form (Parasmaipada), it expresses a person directing their mind toward an object of focus (dhyayati). When used with the causative affix (Nic), it changes to dhyapayati, meaning to guide or cause someone else to meditate.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakara (present tense), Prathama purusha (third person), Ekavacana (singular)
scenarios.example_english: The sage meditates upon God in the forest.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (causative), Lat lakara (present tense), Prathama purusha (third person), Ekavacana (singular)
scenarios.meaning: Causes to meditate / instructs in meditation
scenarios.example_english: The teacher guides the student to meditate.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: dhyai cintayam. Bhvadi-gane pathitah parasmaipadi anit ca. Adeca upadese asiti iti sutrena sit-pratyayebhyo'nyatra akarantatvam bhavati. Sap-sanniyogena dhyayati iti rupam sidhyati. Liti dadhyau, lute dhyata, lrti dhyasyati ityadi rupani bhavanti.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: dhyai cintayam. Cintanam dhyanam ekagrataya smaranam. Anidayam dhatu parasmaipadatmakah. Dhyayati, dadhyau, dhyata, adhyasit iti sarvatra samyag drsyate.

meanings.English: To meditate, to contemplate, to reflect upon, to think deeply
meanings.Hindi: Dhyana karana, cintana karana, dhyan lagana

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'dhāv' has two completely different everyday meanings depending on context: (1) to run/move fast, and (2) to wash/cleanse. When describing movement like running, it requires no direct object (intransitive). When describing washing or cleansing clothes/objects, it takes a direct object (transitive). In causative form (dhāvayati), it means 'makes someone run' or 'causes to wash'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice) in the sense of gati (motion)
scenarios.example_english: The horse runs quickly in the field.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice) in the sense of śuddhi (washing/cleansing)
scenarios.example_english: The washerman cleans the clothes with water.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root dhāvu is taught with two distinct primary meanings: 'gatau' (in movement/running) and 'śuddhau' (in purification/washing). When employed in the sense of gati, the verbal action is intransitive (akarmaka), yielding forms such as dhāvati. When applied in the sense of śuddhi, it is transitive (sakarmaka). Madhava points out the special derivation of the past passive participle: 'dhautaḥ' is formed by irregular vocalic reduction in the sense of purification (dhāvaśca), whereas 'dhāvitaḥ' regularizes in the sense of running.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines the duality of 'dhāvu gatiśuddhyoḥ' by contrasting concrete usages: 'dhāvaty aśvaḥ' (the horse runs) exemplifies rapid locomotion, while 'dhāvati vastram' (cleanses the garment) exemplifies purification. He details that optional id-agama rules apply across tenses and participles, highlighting the differentiation between 'dhāvitaḥ' (one who ran) and 'dhautaḥ' (that which is cleansed or washed).

meanings.English: to run, to move rapidly; to wash, to clean, to purify
meanings.Bengali: dōṛānō, chutē jāoyā; dhuẏē phēlā, pariṣkāra karā
meanings.French: courir, se précipiter; laver, nettoyer, purifier

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'kṛp' means to pity, lament, or show compassion. As a standard First Gana Atmanepada root, it takes middle voice terminations (kṛpate) to denote expressing grief, crying for help, or being compassionate. In the causative (Nic) form, it means causing someone to show mercy or inducing pity.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The poor person pleads for compassion.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (Causative), Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: His words evoke pity in everyone.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'kṛpa kṛpāyām' belongs to the Bhvadi-gana and is marked with anudatta it, taking Atmanepada affixes. It denotes the sense of expressing kindness, showing mercy, lamenting, or petitioning. Forms derived include kṛpate, cakṛpe, kṛpitā, and kṛpiṣyate.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'kṛpa kṛpāyām' as an Atmanepadi root expressing feeling compassion (daya) or pleading. Being set, it takes intermediate 'i' (it-agama) in the non-sarvadhatuka forms like cakṛpe and kṛpitum.

meanings.English: to pity, to show compassion, to lament, to mourn
meanings.Kannada: karunisu, daye toru, kripetoru, rodana madu
meanings.Hindi: daya karna, kripa karna, vilapa karna, gidgidana
meanings.Bengali: doya kora, kripa kora, bilap kora
meanings.German: sich erbarmen, Mitleid haben, klagen, trauern
meanings.French: avoir pitie, faire preuve de compassion, se lamenter

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'kshad' belongs to the first conjugation group (Bhvadi) and primarily functions in the Atmanepada voice. It means to prepare, process, divide, or consume food. When used normally in Atmanepada, it shows the subject performing the act of dressing, carving, or eating food. In the causative (Nic), it expresses making someone else carve, portion, or serve food.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (present indicative, 3rd person singular, Atmanepada)
scenarios.example_english: The cook prepares (or carves) the food.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic) Kartari prayoga (present indicative, 3rd person singular, Parasmaipada)
scenarios.meaning: Causes someone to divide or serve food
scenarios.example_english: The master makes the servant apportion the food.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'kshada' is defined in the sense of 'samskritau' (refining, preparing, or portioning food), as well as distribution and consumption. Being marked as anudattet, it takes Atmanepada affixes in the active voice without the intermediate i-karaka (anit).
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'kshada samskritau' indicates refining, dividing into parts, carving, or eating (samsthane chedanadivyapare bhojane ca). The forms follow the standard bhvadi pattern yielding kshadate.

meanings.English: to prepare, to carve, to divide, to consume food
meanings.Bengali: samskara kara, bhaga kara, bhojana kara

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'mūl' means 'to take root', 'to grow', or 'to sprout'. In simple present active voice (Parasmaipada), it describes a plant or idea taking firm root and growing. When used in the causative form (nic), it changes to mean causing something to take root or planting it firmly.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga (Active Voice), Lat-lakara (Present Tense), 3rd Person Singular
scenarios.example_english: The tree takes firm root in the ground.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nyanta (Causative), Kartari Prayoga, Lat-lakara, 3rd Person Singular
scenarios.meaning: causes to take root / plants / establishes firmly
scenarios.example_english: The farmer establishes the sapling firmly in the field.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'mūla' belongs to the Bhvadi-gana and has the meaning 'rohaṇa' (sprouting, growing, taking root). Being 'seṭ', the intermediate augment 'iṭ' is applied in ardhadhatuka affixes (e.g., molitā, molitum). The radical long 'ū' optionally undergoes guṇa (forming molati or mūlati depending on grammatical tradition) and standard forms in lit include mumola.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin explains 'mūla rohaṇe' as denoting the act of germinating, shooting forth, and establishing base roots ('rohaṇam utpattiḥ vṛddhiśca'). Derived primary nouns like 'mūlam' (root, origin) stem directly from this semantic sense.

meanings.English: To sprout, to take root, to grow, to be firmly established
meanings.Hindi: Jad jamana, ankurit hona, ugna, panapna
meanings.Bengali: Shikor gada, ankurita haowa, gonjano, briddhi paowa
meanings.Chinese: Sheng gen, meng ya, sheng zhang, zha gen

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'hvr' means to be crooked, to bend, to falter, or to deviate from the straight path. In basic active usage (kartari prayoga), it expresses someone bending, faltering, or behaving crookedly. When used with a causative suffix (Nic), it changes to mean making someone or something bend, falter, or go astray.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Lat lakara (present tense), prathama-purusha, eka-vacana, kartari prayoga
scenarios.meaning: He/she falters, deviates, or bends crookedly
scenarios.example_english: The old man falters with his foot on the path.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (causative), Lat lakara, prathama-purusha, eka-vacana
scenarios.meaning: Causes to deviate or leads astray
scenarios.example_english: Bad company causes the youth to deviate from the righteous path.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'hvr kautilye' is listed in the Bhvadi class as a Parasmaipada and Anit dhatu. The primary semantic scope is kautilya (crookedness, deception, or physical/moral bending). It derives present tense forms such as hvarati, perfect jahvara, and causative hvarayati or hvalayati.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'hvr kautilye' as expressing both physical deviation/crookedness and deceptive behavior. The substitution of 'r' to 'l' occasionally observed in related secondary formations reflects phonetic variation in classic grammatical operation.

meanings.English: to be crooked, to bend, to falter, to deviate, to deceive
meanings.Hindi: kutila hona, tedha hona, ladakhadana, bhatakana
meanings.Bengali: kutila haoya, benke jaoya, bhul pathe jaoya
meanings.German: krumm sein, sich biegen, wanken, abweichen
meanings.Chinese: wan qu, pian li, bu zheng, pian xie

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root guñj means to hum, buzz, or make an indistinct continuous low sound, just like bees hovering around flowers. In normal active voice (Parasmaipada), it shows a creature buzzing on its own. In the causative form, it means making a place or instrument echo or resonate with sound.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakara (present tense), prathama purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The black bee hums on the flower.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (causative), Lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The singer makes the hall resonate with his melody.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root guji is classified under the Bhvadi gana with the semantic tag avyakte shabde (indistinct sound). Because it is marked with an indicatory 'i' (idit), it takes the penultimate nasal augment (num-agama) resulting in the base guñj-. It operates strictly in Parasmaipada yielding forms like guñjati, jaguñja, and guñjitaḥ.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines guji as producing low, indistinct acoustic vibration, commonly used to describe the murmuring resonance of bees and swarms. The presence of the it-marker 'i' confirms obligatory nasalization before radical consonants.

meanings.English: To hum, buzz, drone, or murmur indistinctly

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'dṝ' means to experience fear or to be afraid. In the basic first conjugation (Bhvādi gaṇa), it takes Ātmanepada endings to express that someone is frightened. When used in the causative (ṇijanta) form, it changes meaning to scaring or frightening someone else.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Laṭ lakāra (present tense), Prathama puruṣa, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The deer is afraid of the lion.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (ṇijanta), Kartari prayoga, Laṭ lakāra, Prathama puruṣa, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The lion terrifies the deer.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'dṝñ bhaye' belongs to the Bhvādi gaṇa and denotes fear (bhaya). Because it has the 'ñ' anubandha (it-marker), it follows Ātmanepada in the simple present tense taking guṇa to form 'darate'. In the liṭ (perfect), it produces reduplicated forms like 'dāre' or 'dīre'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kṣīrasvāmin notes that 'dṝñ' is classified under Bhvādi with the meaning of fear (bhaya). In universal usage, it forms 'darate' with guṇa of the ṛ-kāra in sārvadhātuka environments before the Śap pratyaya.

meanings.English: to fear, to be afraid, to dread

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'sru' primarily means to flow, drip, or trickle like a liquid. In its basic active form (Parasmaipada), it describes the natural act of flowing. When used with a causative affix (Nic), it shifts from an intransitive state of flowing to actively causing a liquid to flow, discharge, or drain.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana (Basic active present)
scenarios.example_english: Water flows from the mountain.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (Causative), Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara
scenarios.example_english: The farmer drains the water from the field.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'sru' is listed under the Bhvadi class with the sense of movement (gatau), specifically the motion of liquids (prasravana). Being anit and parasmaipadi, the vowel undergoes guna in sarvadhatuka environments to form 'sravati'. In lit lakara, it undergoes regular reduplication yielding 'susrava'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'sru gatau' as referring to liquid movement, discharge, or oozing. It takes standard bhvadi thematic 'sap' leading to guna of the root vowel 'u' to 'o', followed by the av-adesha before vowels, giving forms like 'sravati' and 'prasravati'.

meanings.English: to flow, to trickle, to ooze, to stream

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'drambh' belongs to the first conjugation (Bhvadi gana) and is exclusively conjugated in Atmanepada. It conveys the action of obstructing, hindering, or blocking. When conjugated in active voice (kartari prayoga), the subject performs an obstruction or holds something back. When used in causative (nic), it means causing someone to obstruct or prevent an action.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana (Present indicative active voice with Atmanepada affix)
scenarios.example_english: The soldier obstructs the enemy on the path.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (Causative) in Lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: Causes to obstruct or restrains someone
scenarios.example_english: The king causes the wicked people to be restrained.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: dranbha pratibandhe. anudattet atmanepadi. pratibandhah rodhah vighnakaranam va. drambhate, dadrambhe, drambhita/dranbdha.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: dranbha pratibandhe. dranbhati iti na bhavati kintu anudattettvad drambhate. pratibandho nishedhah avarodhashca.

meanings.English: to obstruct, to block, to hinder, to restrain
meanings.Hindi: rokna, baadha daalna, avarodha paida karna
meanings.Bengali: badha deoya, atke rakha, pratirodh kara

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'kath' means to live with difficulty or struggle for subsistence (scraping by). In basic active voice (Parasmaipada), it describes an individual surviving hardship or living an austere life. When converted into the causative (Nic), it signifies putting someone in difficult living conditions or compelling them to endure hardship.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: lives with difficulty / survives an austere life
scenarios.example_english: The poor person lives with great difficulty.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic pratyaya), Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: causes to endure hardship / subjects to a difficult livelihood
scenarios.example_english: The famine subjects the people to difficult living conditions.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti analyzes 'katha kricchrajivane' under the Bhvadi class. It notes that the root denotes enduring life under severe scarcity, poverty, or austere circumstances. Being marked with an anudatta accent on an it-marker, it forms its present stem as kathati via the standard Bhvadi vikarana sap, functioning primarily as an intransitive verb in Parasmaipada.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin in Kshiratarangini identifies 'katha' within the class of roots expressive of bodily and economic states of survival ('kricchrajivana'). It emphasizes the semantic nuance of 'duhkhena vartanam' (existing with sorrow or deprivation) and confirms its set nature with standard guna/sandhi applications in ardhadhatuka environments.

meanings.English: to live with difficulty, to scrape by, to survive hardship
meanings.Telugu: kashtamuto jivincuta, braduku teruvu koraku kashtapaduta
meanings.Hindi: kathinai se jivan bitana, kashtapurvak jina
meanings.Bengali: koshter shonge jibon dharon kora, tana-porane bacha
meanings.German: in Not leben, sich mühsam durchschlagen
meanings.French: vivre difficilement, vivoter dans la gêne

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root stebh expresses the action of stopping, blocking, arresting, or fixing firmly in place. It operates in the Parasmaipada voice in classical active constructions, taking a direct object for the obstacle or the entity being halted.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga, lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The soldier stops the enemy in the middle of the path.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga, lun lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The dam blocked the flow of water.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti analyzes stebhu as belonging to the Bhvadi class, carrying the sense of stambha (blocking, arresting, stiffening, or rendering motionless). It conjugates with the standard shap vikarana yielding stebhati, stebhitum, and takes standard set i-agama additions in periphrastic and future tenses.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin in Kshiratarangini notes stebhu stambhe, classifying it as a root denoting obstruction and fixing. It forms its primary present stem regularly as stebhati without vowel alteration in the general sarvadhatuka environment.

meanings.English: to stop, to obstruct, to block, to support firmly

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'jhas' means to hurt, strike, or injure. As a regular first-conjugation Parasmaipada root, it directly attaches verbal endings with the standard vowel thematic marker 'a', becoming 'jhasati' (he/she hurts or strikes). In causative forms (Nic), it signifies making someone strike or causing injury.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Lat lakara (present tense), prathama-purusha, eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The hunter hurts the deer in the forest.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (causative present tense)
scenarios.meaning: causes to hurt / causes to strike
scenarios.example_english: The master makes the servant strike the enemy.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya gloss confirms 'jhasa himsayam' belongs to the Bhvadi class, taking Parasmaipada affixes and Set augment. It expresses the semantic action of injuring, hurting, or striking.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines 'jhasa' as functioning specifically in the sense of violence, affliction, or bodily harm (himsarthaka).

meanings.English: to hurt, injure, or strike

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'shudh' means to become clean, pure, or free from blemish. In the primary Bhvadi conjugation, it takes Parasmaipada endings (shodhati) to express becoming pure. When used with causative affixes (shodhayati), it becomes transitive, meaning to cleanse, purify, or correct something.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Bhvadi Parasmaipada Lat-lakara (kartari prayoga)
scenarios.example_english: The mind becomes pure through knowledge.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (Causative Parasmaipada)
scenarios.example_english: The teacher corrects the flaw of the student.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'shudha~ shuddhau' is placed in the Bhvadi class. It is anit and Parasmaipada. In the sarvadhatuka environment, guna of the root vowel 'u' occurs by 'pugalghupadhasya ca', yielding the base 'shodh-'. Its forms are shodhati, shoshodha, shoddha, shotsyati.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin glosses 'shudh shuddhau' as attaining purity and cleanliness. Being anit, it takes dental substitutions in relevant past participles and ardhadhatuka forms without the intermediate 'i' augment (e.g., shuddhah, shoddhum).

meanings.English: to be pure, to become clean, to be purified

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'ras' expresses the action of tasting, relishing, savoring, or producing liquid/sound. In basic Parasmaipada usage, an agent directly experiences or relishes a taste. When combined with the causative suffix (Nich), it denotes making someone else taste or experience something delicious.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana (Simple Present Active)
scenarios.example_english: The child tastes (relishes) the sweet fruit.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nich-pratyaya (Causative), Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: Causes to taste / feeds to savor
scenarios.example_english: The mother makes the baby taste the sweet milk.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti classifies 'rasa asvadane' under the Bhvadi class as a standard set Parasmaipada root. The text analyzes its primary forms such as 'rasati' in present, 'rarasa' in perfect (lit), 'rasita' in periphrastic future, and 'arasit' in aorist (lun). It notes the semantic domain of experiencing flavors and poetic sentiment, connecting the verbal action to the creation and enjoyment of rasa.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin in Kshiratarangini remarks that 'rasa' primarily indicates tasting (asvadana) and affectionate experiencing (snehana/drava-bhava). He records forms like 'rasati', 'rarasitha', and highlights nominal derivatives like 'rasa' (essence, taste, juice) that stem directly from the act of savored perception.

meanings.English: to taste, to relish, to savor, to express juice or sentiment
meanings.Russian: probovat na vkus, smakovat, naslazhdatsya vkusom
meanings.Chinese: pin chang, ti wei, chang shi

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'śloś' fundamentally means 'to shine' or 'to glow'. Because it belongs to the Atmanepada class, the action of glowing or shining is viewed as centered within or belonging to the subject itself. When used in the causative form with the affix 'nic', it changes its meaning from 'shining on its own' to 'causing something else to shine' or 'illuminating'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana (Atmanepada)
scenarios.example_english: The jewel shines in the darkness.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (Causative), Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana (Parasmaipada)
scenarios.example_english: The lamp illuminates the entire house.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'ślośṛ' is read with the anubandha 'ṛ' indicating optional 'an' substitution in aorist (lun lakara). It is grouped among roots expressing brilliance (diptyarthah) and conjugates in the Atmanepada due to its traditional anudatta status.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes this root among the cluster of phonologically close verbs denoting illumination (bhras-bhraj-bhlas-bhlaj-srus-slos-hrus-hles diptau), indicating simple inward radiant manifestation.

meanings.English: to shine, to be radiant, to glow

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'khyā' fundamentally means to tell, narrate, or declare. When used by itself or with prefixes like 'pra' (prakhyā), it conveys announcing, celebrating, or making something widely known. Adding the causative suffix (khyāpayati) shifts the action to causing information to be proclaimed or published to others.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Parasmaipada, Lat lakāra (present tense), prathama puruṣa, ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The poet narrates the heroic deeds in the assembly.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (ṇic pratyaya), Lat lakāra, prathama puruṣa, ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: Causes to be known / proclaims / announces
scenarios.example_english: The king proclaims the royal order in the city.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root khyāñ is categorized under the meaning 'prakathana' (clear narration or detailed declaration). Marked with the anubandha 'ñ', it historically exhibits ubhayapada characteristics. In classical usage, its primary non-causative forms are often complemented by or integrated with roots like cakṣ (via cakṣiṅaḥ khyāñ), expressing complete verbalization of facts or events without intermediate vowel augment (aniṭ).
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin states that 'khyā prakathane' denotes making an occurrence known explicitly to listeners. The commentary highlights its common combinations with preverbs such as 'pra' (celebrated/proclaimed), 'vi' (renowned), and 'ā' (recounting in detail).

meanings.English: To tell, narrate, declare, recount, proclaim
meanings.Hindi: Kahna, batana, varnan karna, prakhyat karna

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'dhran' means to make a sound, to ring, or to reverberate. In simple present tense (kartari prayoga), it takes Parasmaipada endings to mean 'makes a sound'. When a causative suffix (Nic) is added, it forms 'dhranayati', meaning 'causes something to sound or ring'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara (simple present), prathama-purusha ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The bell rings.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic-pratyaya), Lat lakara, prathama-purusha ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: Causes to sound / strikes to ring
scenarios.example_english: The priest rings the bell.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: Dhraṇa viśabde. Viśabdaḥ viśiṣṭaḥ śabdaḥ dhvaniḥ ityarthaḥ. Anudāttetaḥ paraḥ sa-setkaḥ parasmaipadī.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Dhraṇa viśabde. Dhraṇati. Dhvani-viśeṣārthe vartate.

meanings.English: to sound, to make a distinct noise, to ring

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'dhrañj' (dhraji~) means 'to go, glide, fly, or move smoothly'. Because it has an 'i' as an indicative marker (idit), it inserts a nasal 'n/ñ' before the final consonant in all its conjugations, forming 'dhrañjati' in the active present tense. In the causative (Nic), it signifies making someone or something move or glide rapidly.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakara (present tense), prathama-purusha ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The bird glides in the sky.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic-pratyaya), Lat lakara, prathama-purusha ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: causes to move or makes glide
scenarios.example_english: The wind causes the flags to flutter and move.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'dhraji' belongs to the Bhvadi-gana and denotes locomotion ('gatau'). Being marked with the anubandha 'i' (idit), it takes the augment 'num' by the rule 'idito num dhatoh', yielding the present form 'dhrañjati'. It takes Parasmaipada terminations regularly in the active voice.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'dhraji gatau' within the group of verbs signifying motion along with mruc and mluc. Due to the idit marker, the medial nasal insertion is mandatory across all relevant tenses and derivatives (e.g., dhrañjati, dadhrañja).

meanings.English: to go, move, glide, fly

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root cṛt means to bind, connect, or string together. In its simple active voice (Parasmaipada), it describes an agent physically or conceptually connecting or fastening objects. In its causative form (nic), it denotes causing someone to tie or make a connection.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat-lakara, Prathama-purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The garland-maker binds flowers together with a thread.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic-pratyaya), Lat-lakara, Prathama-purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: Causes to bind or tie together
scenarios.example_english: The teacher makes the student bind the leaves together.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root cṛtī is classified under the Bhvadi-gana carrying the semantic sense of saṃbandha (connection, unification, or tying together). Due to the anubandha mark ī, specific rule operations apply during the formation of perfect and desiderative stems, yielding forms like cṛtati, cacarta, and cartitā.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines cṛtī in the sense of saṃbandhana (binding/fastening). It is accented as an udātta set root within this sub-group of Bhvadi, operating transitively when binding distinct elements into a whole.

meanings.English: to tie, bind, fasten, connect

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'tuj' means to hurt, strike, injure, or urge forward. In the simple active voice (Parasmaipada), it describes a subject directly hitting, harming, or impelling someone or something. When used with causative affixes (Nic), it signifies making or inciting someone else to attack, urge, or strike.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Lat-lakara, Prathama-purusha, Ekavacana (Kartari Prayoga)
scenarios.example_english: The enemy strikes the warrior with a weapon.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Lat-lakara, Prathama-purusha, Ekavacana (Nic / Causative)
scenarios.meaning: causes to strike / incites to harm
scenarios.example_english: The commander incites the soldiers to strike the enemies.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti glosses 'tuji himsayam', noting its application in the sense of causing injury, imparting force, or striking. Forms generated include tujati, tatoja, and tojita, treated as an active transitive verbal root.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin in Kshiratarangini observes 'tuji himsayam', confirming its classification under the Bhvadi class taking Parasmaipada endings and governing an accusative object representing the entity subjected to injury or force.

meanings.English: To strike, injure, hurt, or urge forward
meanings.Hindi: Chot pahunchana, prahar karna, prerit karna
meanings.Bengali: Aghat kara, himsa kara, prerana deya

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'klp' means to be fit, capable, suitable, or to transform/result into something. In standard usage, it takes Atmanepada endings (kalpate) to express that a situation or condition is conducive or develops into a certain outcome. When used in the causative (canta, with nic), it becomes 'kalpayati' (Parasmaipada) meaning to arrange, shape, design, or make something capable.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara (present indicative), prathama-purusha ekavacana, Atmanepada
scenarios.meaning: is capable of / results in / serves for
scenarios.example_english: Knowledge accompanied by humility leads to true happiness.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (causative), Lat lakara, prathama-purusha ekavacana, Parasmaipada
scenarios.example_english: The architect designs a beautiful building.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti highlights 'klpu samarthye' under the Bhvadi-gana as an Atmanepadi root. In the general tenses it forms 'kalpate' via guna of the vocalic r-vowel to ar/al. It details specific phonological options in the future and desiderative stems where alternate l/r operations apply according to Paninian sutras such as 'krlpo ro li' and related rules.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes in Kshiratarangini that 'klpu' denotes capacity, suitability, readiness, and transformation. He discusses the specific vikarana interaction in non-conjugational tenses, the anubandha 'u' indicating optional it-augment in certain ardhadhatuka environments, and the shift to transitive meaning ('to formulate' or 'to allot') in causative constructions.

meanings.English: to be capable of, to be fit, to lead to, to result in
meanings.Hindi: samartha hona, yogya hona, siddha hona
meanings.Bengali: samartha haoya, upajukta haoya, parinata haoya
meanings.German: fahig sein, taugen zu, fuhren zu, gelingen

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'hval' denotes physical stumbling, shaking, or mental wavering. When used in normal active voice (Parasmaipada), it describes an individual losing balance or moving unstably. When converted to the causative form (Nich), it conveys the action of making someone or something stumble, falter, or waver.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakara (present tense), 3rd person singular
scenarios.example_english: The foot stumbles on the road.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nich-pratyaya), Lat lakara, 3rd person singular
scenarios.example_english: The strong wind causes the traveler to stumble.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti classifies 'hvala' under the Jvaladi gana ('jvala dīptau, hvala calane...'). By Paninian sutra 'jvalātibhyo ṇaḥ' (3.1.140), it takes the 'na' affix to derive nominal agent forms such as 'hvalana' (that which falters or shakes). The basic present-tense derivation is formed with the Shapa affix as 'hvalati'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin glosses 'hvala calane' as expressing dynamic instability, erratic motion, or falling off course. It is grouped closely with related motion-roots such as 'hmal' and 'sval', indicating slight variations of physical and moral deviating motion.

meanings.English: to stumble, to waver, to shake, to falter
meanings.Bengali: thotmoth khawa, tolmol kora, bicholito howa

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'dru' primarily means to run, speed, flow, or melt. In normal active usage (Parasmaipada), it describes an agent moving rapidly, flowing, or softening. When used with the causative marker (Nic), it shifts to 'causing to run' or 'melting/liquefying' an object.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, prathama-purusha ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The horse runs swiftly.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (Causative), Lat lakara, prathama-purusha ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: Heat melts the gold.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti notes that 'dru gatau' undergoes standard guna to 'o' and av-adesha before the sarvadhatuka vikarana shap, forming 'dravati'. In the perfect tense (lit), reduplication yields 'dudrava', and in the aorist (lun), it takes the anit aorist marker yielding 'adrut'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin states that 'dru' signifies motion (gati) as well as the transition into a liquid state (dravibhava). It forms 'dravati', 'droshyate' in lrt, and 'drutah' in the kta-pratyaya, illustrating swift motion or dissolution.

meanings.English: to run, to flow, to melt

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'kṣmā' expresses the action of trembling, shaking, or vibrating. Since it is marked with an anubandha 'ṅ' (ṅit), it is inherently Atmanepadi, taking middle-voice endings such as '-te' in the present tense (forming 'kṣmāyate'). When used with the causative suffix (ṇic), it means 'to cause to tremble' or 'to shake something', taking the form 'kṣmāpayati'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (Primary agent, Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana)
scenarios.example_english: The boy trembles out of fear.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic pratyaya, Lat lakara, Parasmaipada)
scenarios.example_english: The strong wind causes the tree to shake.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: kṣmāṅ kampane. ṅitvād ātmanepadam. anidantatvād anit. kṣmāyate. cakṣme. kṣmātā. kṣmāsyate. akṣmāsta.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: kṣmāṅ kampane. kṣmāyate. calanārthe vartate. cakṣme, kṣmāteti rūpāṇi.

meanings.English: to tremble, to shake, to quiver

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'rah' means to leave, forsake, abandon, or part from someone or something. In standard active voice (Parasmaipada), it shows a subject abandoning an object. When modified into causative forms, it means making someone leave or causing something to be deserted.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (Present active 3rd person singular with Sap vikarana)
scenarios.example_english: The sage leaves the village.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (Causative active)
scenarios.example_english: The king causes the enemy to leave the kingdom.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'raha' is listed in the Bhvadi class with the semantic indication 'tyaage' (in the sense of abandonment/quitting). It forms 'rahati' in the present tense and exhibits the 'Set' character across relevant non-sarvadhatuka affixes, forming participles like 'rahita' (deprived, bereft, or abandoned).
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines 'raha tyaage', explaining its derivation as an unaugmented dental-aspirate-ending root indicating cessation of association or relinquishment. It forms standard Parasmaipada inflections such as 'rahati', 'araheet', and participial derivations denoting absence or abandonment.

meanings.English: to abandon, leave, forsake, or separate from

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root bhreṣ means to strive, make an effort, or to slip and waver. In standard usage, it takes Ātmanepada affixes to denote moving, tottering, or exerting effort. When used causatively, it means to cause someone to waver, deviate, or stumble.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga, laṭ lakāra, prathama puruṣa, ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The traveler slips on the path.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: ṇic-pratyaya (causative), kartari prayoga, laṭ lakāra, prathama puruṣa, ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The wind causes the tree branch to waver.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root bhreṣṛ is listed in the Bhvādi gaṇa in the senses of endeavor (yatna) and motion or shaking (calana). It is an anudāttet root and therefore takes Ātmanepada endings under normal conditions, forming bhreṣate, bibhreṣe, and bhreṣiṣyate with the iṭ augment.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes bhreṣṛ in the semantic field of movement and striving (bhreṣa yatne calane ca). It conjugates in the first conjugation as an Ātmanepada verb yielding the base form bhreṣate.

meanings.English: to slip, waver, stumble, or strive

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root katth belongs to the first conjugation (Bhvadi-gana) and takes Atmanepada terminations. It primarily expresses self-praise, bragging, boasting, or flattering. In basic kartari prayoga, it takes Atmanepada markers to form katthate ('he boasts'). In causative usage (nic-pratyaya), it takes Parasmaipada or Atmanepada to convey causing someone to boast or praising actively.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga, lat-lakara, prathama-purusha, eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The foolish person vainly boasts of his own qualities.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: nic-pratyaya (causative), lat-lakara, prathama-purusha, eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: He makes his friend boast (or praises his friend) in the public assembly.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti analyzes katth as 'kattha slaghayam'. Being marked as anudattopadesha in traditional recital streams, it yields standard Atmanepada forms like katthate, cakatthe, katthita, katthishyate. The vritti highlights its primary sense of atmaprashamsa (self-laudation or vaunting).
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes under 'kattha slaghayam' that the root conveys both positive praise and conceited bragging. Derived nouns like katthana (boaster, braggart) stem from this root, and it admits the augment it (set) in ardhadhatuka environments, giving forms such as katthitum and katthitavan.

meanings.English: to boast, brag, praise, flatter
meanings.Tamil: thannai pugazh, perumai pesu, tharpukazhchi sei
meanings.Hindi: shekhi bagharana, atmaprashamsa karana, dinga hakana
meanings.Bengali: atmaprashangsa kara, ahankara kara, barai kara
meanings.Chinese: kua yao, chui xu, zi zan

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'tam' primarily signifies desiring, longing, or craving something intensely. When used in the normal present tense (Kartari Prayoga), it takes Parasmaipada endings to mean 'desires' or 'longs for'. When used in the causative form with the suffix Nic, it means 'causes someone to long for' or 'makes someone yearn'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga (Present Tense, Lat Lakara, 3rd Person Singular)
scenarios.example_english: The deer yearns for water.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nich-pratyaya, Lat Lakara, 3rd Person Singular)
scenarios.meaning: causes to yearn / makes someone long for
scenarios.example_english: Remembrance makes the heart yearn.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: tamU kankshayam. uditakarah. tamati, tatama, tamita/tanta. kanksha abhilashah, tatra vartate.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: tamU kankshayam. uditktvo va vet bhavati. tamati, tatama. kanksha iccharthah.

meanings.English: to desire, to yearn, to long for
meanings.Bengali: iccha kora, kamona kora, akankkha kora

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'gluñc' denotes moving in a crooked, zigzag, or curved path. As a standard Parasmaipada root of the Bhvadi class, it directly takes suffixes like '-ati' to describe a subject moving along an indirect or curving trajectory.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The snake moves along a winding path in the forest.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (Causative), Lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: Causes to move crookedly or diverts along a detour
scenarios.example_english: The charioteer causes the horse to move through a detour on the uneven road.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti places 'gluñca' in the Bhvadi class in the sense of 'gatikautilya' (crooked motion). The penultimate nasal is retained throughout regular Sarvadhatuka forms yielding 'gluñcati', with perfect 'jugluñca' and periphrastic future 'gluñcitā'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin categorizes 'gluñca' within the cluster of movement-verbs denoting deviance, winding, or crooked displacement (kruñca, kluñca, gluñca). It is marked as set with uniform Parasmaipada inflection.

meanings.English: to move crookedly, to wind along, to curve
meanings.Hindi: ṭēṛhī cāl calnā, kutil gati karnā
meanings.French: se déplacer de manière tortueuse, serpenter

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'dhruk' conveys the primary action of moving, going, or walking. It functions exclusively in Atmanepada in standard non-causative usage, with the vowel 'u' strengthening to 'o' (guna) before the thematic affix 'a' in present tense (sarvadhatuka) forms to produce 'dhrokate'. When used causatively with the suffix 'nic', it denotes causing someone or something to move.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga (active voice), lat lakara (present tense), prathama purusha (third person), ekavacana (singular)
scenarios.example_english: The horse moves on the path.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: nic pratyaya (causative), lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The charioteer causes the chariot to move.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'dhruka' belongs to the Bhvadi class and is read in the sense of motion (gatau). Due to its designation as an anudatteta root, it assumes Atmanepada affixes by default. In the presence of sarvadhatuka suffixes, guna of the radical vowel occurs, giving the base 'dhroka-'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'dhruka gatau' among the roots indicating motion. He explains the morphophonemic strengthening of the core vowel 'u' to 'o' in the present system, forming 'dhrokate' with anit characteristics in ardhadhatuka environments.

meanings.English: to move, to go

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'maś' means to make a sound, buzz, hum, or murmur. As an Ātmanepada root in the first conjugation, it takes middle endings (e.g., maśate). When used in the causative (ṇijanta), it conveys causing someone or something to make a buzzing sound or humming tone (māśayati/māśayate).

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat-lakara (present tense), prathama-purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: makes a humming or buzzing sound
scenarios.example_english: The bee hums in the forest.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (causative), Lat-lakara, prathama-purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: causes to buzz or produce a sound
scenarios.example_english: The boy causes the string of the lute to hum.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'maśu' belongs to the Bhvadi class and is read with the meaning 'śabde' (in the sense of producing sound or buzzing). Due to the anudatta anubandha on the vowel 'u', it takes Atmanepada affixes in kartari prayoga (maśate, mamaśe, maśitā).
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'maśu śabde' as an inarticulate sound producer (such as the humming of insects or low resonant vocalizations). It follows the standard Bhvadi conversion with guna-strengthening in non-sarvadhatuka environments and takes the 'it' augment (set).

meanings.English: to sound, to hum, to buzz, to murmur
meanings.Telugu: dhvani cheyu, jhumkarinchu, runajhuna dhvani cheyu
meanings.Bengali: dhvani kara, gunjan kara, bhonbhon kara

canonical_dhatvartha: gatau (in the sense of flowing or movement)

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'sru' describes the action of liquid or fluid motion—such as flowing, trickling, or oozing. In the basic active form (Kartari), it takes standard Parasmaipada endings where the vowel 'u' undergoes guna to become 'o' and then turns into 'av' before the present affix, forming 'sravati' (it flows). When modified by the causative affix (Nic), it shifts to 'sravayati', meaning to cause to flow, shed, or pour out.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakara (present tense), prathama-purusha eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: Cool water flows continuously from the mountain.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (causative voice), Lat lakara (present tense), prathama-purusha eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The sorrowful man sheds tears from his eyes.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti glosses 'sru gatau' as indicating fluid motion and continuous stream-like movement. Being an anit root, it rejects the augment 'it' in standard ardhadhatuka environments, giving classical forms like 'srotum' (infinitive) and 'sasrava' (perfect tense). Under the sarvadhatuka affix shap, the root vowel undergoes regular guna to form 'sravati'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin categorizes 'sru' among roots denoting directional fluid progression (dravatva-vishishta-gatih). He highlights its anit status in derivation, its regular un-augmented simple past/aorist forms, and its clear differentiation from non-liquid locomotion roots.

meanings.English: to flow, to stream, to trickle, to ooze

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'dhṝ' belongs to the 1st Gana (Bhvadi) and primarily signifies oozing, dripping, or flowing downwards (avasravana). When used as a basic active verb in Parasmaipada, it means something is trickling or flowing down. When a causative suffix (Nic) is added, it turns into 'dhārayati', meaning 'causes to trickle or pour down'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Bhvadi-gana kartari prayoga (Parasmaipada, Lat lakara, prathama-purusha, eka-vacana)
scenarios.example_english: The sap oozes from the tree.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic-pratyaya) in kartari prayoga
scenarios.example_english: The cloud pours down water.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'dhṝ' with the canonical meaning 'avasravane' signifies downwards trickling, oozing, or secretion. Guna substitution applies to the radical vowel 'ṝ' resulting in 'ar' before the Sarvadhatuka class affix 'śap', yielding 'dharati'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'dhṝ avasravane' in the collection of ṝkārānta roots of the Bhvadi-gana. It denotes the act of flowing or dripping down slowly ('avasravaṇaṃ kṣaraṇam').

meanings.English: to trickle, to ooze, to flow down
meanings.French: suinter, couler goutte à goutte, dégouliner

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'trap' means to feel shy, to be ashamed, or to blush. In standard usage, it takes Atmanepada endings (e.g., trapate). When transformed into a causative (Nic) form, it takes both padas (trapayati / trapayate) and means 'to cause someone to feel ashamed' or 'to embarrass someone'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana (Atmanepada)
scenarios.example_english: The dull-witted boy feels ashamed in the assembly.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic), Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana (Parasmaipada)
scenarios.example_english: The ill-behaved son embarrasses his father.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'trapuṣ' is listed in the Bhvadi-gana with the meaning 'lajjāyām' (in the sense of shyness, shame, or modesty). It is anudattet and therefore strictly Atmanepadi in primitive conjugations, yielding 'trapate', 'tetrape', 'traptā', and 'trapsyate'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'trapuṣ lajjāyām' as an intransitive root signifying modest behavior or the inward shrinking of mind caused by embarrassment or conscience, taking the 'trap-' base after the elision of the it markers 'u' and 'ṣ'.

meanings.English: to feel shy, to be ashamed, to blush, to be embarrassed

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'drph' means to distress, nauseate, or cause discomfort to someone. Because it contains an indicator 'i' (idit), it inserts an 'm' sound into its base form, becoming 'drmphati' in simple present tense.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The pungent taste distresses the weak stomach.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Lun lakara (aorist), parasmaipada, kartari prayoga
scenarios.example_english: Impure food caused nausea in the boy.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti notes that 'drphi utklesane' belongs to the Bhvadi class. Being idit (possessing the it-marker 'i'), it takes the num-augment (n/m) unconditionally across sarvadhatuka formations, yielding forms like drmphati, adrmphit, and dardrmphiti in yan.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin explains that 'utklesana' refers to causing internal distress or physical nausea (jatharotklesa/hrdayotklesa). He highlights that as an idit root, the nasal insert produces the present base drmpha- in Parasmaipada.

meanings.English: to distress, to disgust, or to cause nausea

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'svard' means to taste, savour, relish, or make something agreeable. In the normal Atmanepada form (svardate), the person doing the action enjoys or tastes the food. When converted to the causative form with Nic (svardayati), it means to sweeten or make food delicious for someone else.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara (present tense), Prathama purusha, Ekavacana, Atmanepada
scenarios.example_english: The boy relishes the sweet fruit.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic-pratyaya), Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana, Parasmaipada
scenarios.meaning: Makes delicious, sweetens, or causes to taste
scenarios.example_english: The mother makes the pudding delicious.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'svarda asvadane' is categorized in the Bhvadi group as an Atmanepadi root with an 'it' augment (set). The primary meaning 'asvadana' signifies the perception and enjoyment of culinary flavor. Its base forms include svardate in present tense, sasvarde in lit, and svardita in lut.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin glosses 'svarda asvadane' as tasting or experiencing rasa (svado rasah tasyanubhavah). The derivation follows the standard Bhvadi formation with Sap vikaranana, yielding svardate without vowel lengthening because of the conjunct consonant ending.

meanings.English: To taste, to relish, to savour, to be agreeable or delicious
meanings.Bengali: Svad grohon kora, chaka, asvadan kora
meanings.Russian: Probovat na vkus, naslazhdatsya vkusom, degustirovat
meanings.Chinese: Pin chang, xiang shou, pin wei

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'krath' belongs to the 1st conjugation (Bhvadi gana) and is conjugated in the Parasmaipada voice. Its primary meaning is to injure, harm, or torment. When used in the simple active present tense, it takes the form 'krathati' (he/she hurts or kills). When converted to the causative (nic) form, it becomes 'krathayati' (he/she causes someone to harm or kill).

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, prathama purusha, eka-vacana (Active voice present indicative)
scenarios.example_english: The warrior's sword strikes and injures the enemy.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (Causative), Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, prathama purusha, eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The king causes the wicked people to be punished and harmed.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'kratha' is listed under the Bhvadi-gana with the meaning 'himsayam' (to kill, injure, or cause pain). Being an anudattet-free root with Parasmaipada inflection, it receives the thematic vikarana shap and exhibits the base form 'kratha-' in Sarvadhatuka affixes, forming 'krathati'. In Ardhadhatuka forms, it takes the intermediate 'i' (it-agama) as a set root.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'kratha himsayam', classifying it among roots denoting violence and physical harm. The derivation runs regular across tenses: krathati in present indicative, cakratha in the perfect (lit), and krathita as the past participle, meaning harmed, struck, or injured.

meanings.English: to injure, harm, kill, or torment
meanings.Bengali: himsa kara, aghat kara, badha deya

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'khañj' belongs to the first conjugation (Bhvadi) and means to limp or walk with an impaired gait. It takes Parasmaipada terminations. When used in its causative form (Nich), it changes from intransitive to transitive, expressing the act of causing someone or something to limp.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakara (present tense), prathama-purusha (third person), ekavacana (singular)
scenarios.example_english: The wounded-footed old man walks slowly with a limp.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic-pratyaya), Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara (present tense), prathama-purusha, ekavacana
