scenarios.grammar_trigger: Ņic (Causative), Laṭ, Prathama puruṣa, Ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: causes to pull out / makes extract
scenarios.example_english: The king makes the servant extract the thorn.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root kuṣa belongs to the Bhvādi class ending in a consonant, taking Parasmaipada. The primary sense is niṣkarṣa (pulling out, tearing apart, or extracting forcefully). It undergoes guṇa to form koṣati in sārvadhātuka contexts and is seṭ.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes kuṣa niṣkarṣe in the sense of ākarṣaṇa (drawing or extracting out). It is marked as seṭ and forms koṣati, kukoṣa, koṣitā.

meanings.English: to extract, to tear out, to pull out
meanings.Malayalam: parichu kalayuka, veliyil edukkuka, valichu thurakkuka

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'skambh' means to support, prop up, hold firmly, or obstruct. In the active voice (Parasmaipada), the subject performs the action of holding up, bracing, or stopping something from falling or moving. When used with causative or preverbs, it highlights making something firm, stationary, or obstructed.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga (Present tense, 3rd person singular, Parasmaipada)
scenarios.example_english: The pillar supports the building.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Lan Lakara (Past imperfect, 3rd person singular, Parasmaipada)
scenarios.example_english: The warrior held up the falling chariot.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'skambhu' belongs to Bhvadi Gana and denotes 'pratibandha' (obstruction, holding, or bracing). The terminal 'u' is an it-marker. In active conjugation with sap-pratyaya, the nasal is retained or dropped according to specific phonological rules, yielding forms like skambhati and caskambha.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'skambhu pratibandhe' as denoting the act of stopping motion, supporting, or establishing stability. It shares close semantic and morphological traits with root stambh, occasionally alternating in Vedic and classical usage.

meanings.English: to support, prop, hold fast, obstruct, make firm
meanings.Hindi: sahara dena, rokna, thambhna, sthira karna

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'smr' means to remember, recollect, or keep in mind. In basic active forms (Parasmaipada), it describes the subject actively remembering or recalling something from memory. When the causative suffix (Nic) is added, it turns into 'smarayati', which means 'to remind someone' or 'cause someone to remember'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (Present active 3rd person singular, Lat lakara)
scenarios.example_english: The boy remembers the lesson he studied.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (Causative active 3rd person singular)
scenarios.example_english: The mother reminds her son of the rule.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti identifies 'smr cintayam' as operating in the sense of memory, mental focus, and contemplation. In the active voice with Sap pratyaya, guna applies to the root vowel producing the present stem 'smara-', yielding 'smarati'. In lit, reduplication gives 'sasmara', and in lut, 'smarta'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines 'smr cintayam' as encompassing both past recollection (anudhyanam) and present contemplation (cintanam). It takes anit characteristics in general conjugational markers while retaining regular guna and vriddhi progressions.

meanings.English: to remember, recollect, recall, contemplate

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'has' inherently conveys the act of smiling or laughing. In its standard active form (Parasmaipada), it is intransitive and denotes the subject laughing on their own. When the causative suffix (Nic) is added, it transitions into a transitive verb, meaning to cause someone else to laugh or to entertain.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga, lat lakara, prathama purusha, eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The child laughs while playing.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: ṇic pratyaya (causative), lat lakara, prathama purusha, eka-vacana
scenarios.meaning: causes to laugh / makes someone laugh
scenarios.example_english: The jester makes everyone laugh with his story.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: hasṛ hasane. hasanaṃ mukhādivikāsaḥ ullāsakhyāpanam. seṭ ayam. hasati, jahāsa, hasitā, hasiṣyati, ahasīt. ṛditvāt caṅi hrasvādiviśeṣa-niyamaḥ.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: hasṛ hasane. hasanaṃ prasannatā-lakṣaṇo vikāsaḥ. seṭ parasmaipadī. hasati, jahāsa, hasitā.

meanings.English: to laugh, to smile, to bloom

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'tvakṣ' means to carve, pare, slice, or make something thinner and smoother (tanūkaraṇa). In the active voice (Parasmaipada), the agent performs the action of shaping or carving wood/materials. In the middle voice (Atmanepada), it denotes the action done for oneself or an internal craft process, and when converted into causative (Nic), it means to cause someone else to plane or carve an object.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga, Lat Lakara, Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana, Parasmaipada
scenarios.meaning: He/she pares, carves, or thins down.
scenarios.example_english: The carpenter pares the wood.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga, Lat Lakara, Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana, Atmanepada
scenarios.meaning: He/she carves or crafts for himself/herself.
scenarios.example_english: The craftsman carves the timber for himself.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti discusses 'tvakṣū' alongside 'takṣū' under the sense of 'tanūkaraṇe' (reducing in thickness, peeling, cutting fine). The anubandha 'ū' indicates optionality in certain reduplicated forms and past participles, taking standard set viddhi across the lakaras with guna in sarvadhatuka affixes.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'tvakṣū tanūkaraṇe' as denoting the mechanical reduction, paring, or sculpting of wood or materials into slender shapes, forming tvakṣati and tvakṣate uniformly in the Bhvadi class.

meanings.English: to pare, to carve, to slice thin, to peel, to reduce

canonical_dhatvartha: diiptau (to shine, to glitter, to appear radiant)

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'bhaas' means to shine, glow, or appear bright. In standard everyday speech, it takes Atmanepada endings ('bhaasate') to describe an object shining naturally by its own light. When modified by the causative affix (nic), it forms 'bhaasayati' (or 'bhaasayate'), shifting the meaning to actively illuminating or causing another object to become bright.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara (Present tense, Atmanepada, 3rd person singular)
scenarios.example_english: The moon shines with a white radiance in the sky.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic-pratyaya), Lat lakara, Parasmaipada
scenarios.example_english: The sun illuminates the entire world with its brilliance.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti classifies 'bhaasa' under the diipti-artha (radiance/shining) group of Bhvadi. Due to its anudatteta nature, it exclusively takes Atmanepada terminations in active voice (kartari). It is anit (devoid of the augment it in non-sarvadhatuka forms like babhaase), retaining the long root-vowel 'aa' systematically throughout its conjugational paradigms.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin interprets 'bhaasa diiptau' as manifest illumination and visible brilliance. He records regular nominal derivatives such as 'bhaasa' (lustre/splendour) and 'bhaasvara' (radiant/luminous), highlighting the inherently stative and intransitive nature of the primary action.

meanings.English: to shine, glitter, radiate, appear bright or evident

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'dhvan' means to sound, echo, or make a noise. In the basic active voice (Parasmaipada), it describes something emitting a sound or ringing. When used in the causative (Nic), it means to cause something to sound or to play an instrument/ring a bell.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga (Present Active, Lat Lakara, 3rd Person Singular)
scenarios.example_english: The bell sounds loudly in the temple.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic Pratyaya, Kartari, 3rd Person Singular)
scenarios.meaning: causes to sound / rings / strikes a musical sound
scenarios.example_english: The musician sounds the conch shell.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'dhvana shabde' belongs to the Bhvadi class. It is categorized under roots indicating sound production (shabda-kriya). Since it has an intermediate short vowel ending with an 'a' in upadesha, it forms dhvanati in Lat and admits the augment it (it-agama) in ardhadhatuka affixes, forming adhavanit in Lun and dhvanita in the past passive participle.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines dhvan as 'dhvan ghoshe shabde ca'. It signifies audible acoustic resonance or the emission of musical/natural tones. It follows standard Bhvadi inflection with 'shap' vikarana taking the active endings exclusively.

meanings.English: to sound, to ring, to murmur, to echo
meanings.Chinese: fa chu sheng yin, ming xiang

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'kuc' means to make a shrill, high-pitched, or loud sound (screeching, whistling, or calling out shrilly). It takes Parasmaipada endings in the active voice and Seṭ augment (i) in non-conjugational tenses.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga (Active Voice), Lat-lakara, Prathama-purusha, Eka-vacana
scenarios.meaning: makes a high-pitched or shrill cry
scenarios.example_english: The bird screeches shrilly on the tree.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (Causative), Kartari Prayoga, Lat-lakara, Prathama-purusha, Eka-vacana
scenarios.meaning: causes to emit a shrill sound / makes sound shrilly
scenarios.example_english: The boy causes the flute to sound shrilly.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'kuca' is glossed as 'śabdatārāyām' indicating making a high-pitched or shrill sound (tāre uccaiḥ śabde). It belongs to the Bhvadi-gana, receives guna in universal sarvadhatuka contexts producing 'kocati', and is seṭ (taking 'it' in ardhadhatuka affixes like kukocitha, kocitā).
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'kuca śabdatārāyām' as distinct from 'kuca saṅkocane', emphasizing its specific sense of sharp, piercing, or high-register vocalization (tāra-śabda).

meanings.English: to make a high-pitched sound, to screech, to utter a shrill cry
meanings.German: einen schrillen Laut von sich geben, kreischen

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'cukk' belongs to the 1st conjugation (Bhvadi-gana) and takes Parasmaipada endings to convey the action of erring, missing, slipping, or making a mistake (pramada). When converted to causative (nic-pratyaya), it takes the form 'cukkayati', expressing the sense of causing someone to err or leading someone to make a slip.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat-lakara (present tense), prathama-purusha, eka-vacana
scenarios.meaning: Errs, makes a mistake, or slips
scenarios.example_english: A careless pedestrian makes a mistake or slips along the path.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (nic-pratyaya), Kartari prayoga, Lat-lakara, prathama-purusha, eka-vacana
scenarios.meaning: Causes to err, leads into error, or misleads
scenarios.example_english: The confused person causes him to err through misleading words.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti registers 'cukka pramade' in the Bhvadi class. Being accented as an unaccented vowel base in the general list of roots ending in consonant clusters (kk-anta), it is marked as Parasmaipada and takes the intermediate augment 'it' (set). Forms: cukkati, cucukka, cukkita.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines 'cukka pramade' as signifying lapse, heedlessness, or making a blunder (pramada). It conjugates regularly in the Bhvadi class with the shab-vikarana, retaining the guttural geminate throughout the conjugational tenses (cukkati, acukkat).

meanings.English: to err, to blunder, to slip, to make a mistake, to be heedless
meanings.Tamil: tavaru ceytal, maratiyaka iruttal, vali tavarutal
meanings.Hindi: chookna, bhool karna, galti karna, pramad karna
meanings.Bengali: bhul kora, chuke jaowa, promad kora
meanings.German: irren, einen Fehler machen, straucheln, versaumen
meanings.French: se tromper, commettre une erreur, faillir, tre negligent

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'chad' primarily means to cover, conceal, or screen. In its regular simple form, it expresses the action of covering or hiding an object. When modified into the causative structure, it highlights actively covering up or enveloping something using an instrument or garment.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga, parasmaipada, lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The cloud covers the sun.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga, nic-pratyaya, atmanepada, lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The boy covers his body with a garment.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'chada' is classified under bhvadi-gana in the sense of apavarana (covering or hiding). In its standard derivations, it takes guna or vriddhi in suitable lakaras and forms both mittva-based and regular causative forms conveying concealment or enveloping.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'chada apavarane' as belonging to the covering semantic group, identifying apavarana with achadana and samvarana, resulting in forms like chadayati and chadati denoting concealment.

meanings.English: to cover, conceal, veil, shelter

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'sul' (shul) primarily means to ache, pierce, or cause acute sharp pain (just like the sharp point of a 'shula' or trident/spike). In the simple active present tense, it describes an organ or wound throbbing or aching. In causative forms, it denotes the action of inflicting sharp torment or piercing someone with pain.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga (Present Active, 3rd Person Singular)
scenarios.example_english: His stomach aches sharply due to indigestion.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (Causative, 3rd Person Singular)
scenarios.meaning: Causes acute pain to someone / torments with sharp pain
scenarios.example_english: The severe illness torments the patient with sharp pain.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'sula rujayam' is listed in the Bhvadi class as a Parasmaipada, Set root. It denotes intense distress or bodily affliction ('ruja'). In the present tense, it forms 'sulati', in the perfect 'susula', and in the aorist 'asulit'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes under 'sula rujayam' that the semantic core of 'sula' is sharp, stabbing pain akin to being struck by an iron dart or spit ('sula-ruja'). Derivations like 'sulam' (colic or trident) trace directly to this sense of sharp torment.

meanings.English: To ache, to pain, to cause acute sharp pain, to pierce
meanings.Kannada: Novu madu, tivra novu baru, kuttu
meanings.Telugu: Noppi kaliginchu, shula noppi kalugu, guchu
meanings.Hindi: Dard hona, shul uthna, chubhana, dukhana
meanings.Bengali: Batha kora, bedona dewa, shul batha howa
meanings.French: Faire mal, élancer, tourmenter par une vive douleur

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'ī' (īṅ) belongs to the Bhvādi class and exclusively takes Ātmanepada endings. It signifies the action of going, approaching, or moving. In the present tense, the root vowel undergoes Guṇa to form 'ayate'. In causative forms with the suffix ṇic, it means to cause someone to go or to direct.

scenarios.example_english: The boy goes to the city.

scenarios.example_english: The father makes his son go to school.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: īṅ gatau. ṅiditvād ātmanepadam. sārvadhātuke guṇe 'ayate' iti rūpam sidhyati. aniṭ.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: īṅ gatau. ayate, āyāñcakre, etā. ṅit-kāraṇād ātmanepada-pratyayāḥ bhavanti.

meanings.English: to go, to move towards, to attain

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'bhlāś' denotes shining, glowing, or radiating light. In standard active voice (Kartari Prayoga), it is conjugated in Atmanepada (bhlāśate), indicating the subject naturally shines or possesses radiance. When the causative suffix (Nic) is added, it transitions to meaning 'to illuminate' or 'to cause something to shine' (bhlāśayati).

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga, Lat Lakara, Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The moon shines brightly in the sky.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic Pratyaya (Causative), Kartari Prayoga, Lat Lakara, Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The lamp illuminates the entire house.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The author notes bhlāśa in the context of 'dīptau' (to illuminate, to shine). It follows the morphological pattern of bhrāśa, forming the present third-person singular 'bhlāśate' with Śap pratyaya, and taking the augment iṭ optionally in non-sarvadhatuka forms per specific Paninian rules applicable to the bhrāś-adi group.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin categorizes 'bhlāśa dīptau' alongside bhrāśa, signifying lustrous brightness and brilliance (prakāśa-vistāra). He outlines standard derivational patterns highlighting the phonetic interchangeability and parallel behaviour between the 'ra' and 'la' variants.

meanings.English: to shine, to beam, to glow, to radiate light
meanings.Bengali: ujjvala haoya, jvaljval kara, shobha paoya
meanings.Chinese: fa guang, zhao yao, shan yao, fang guang

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'psā' means to eat, devour, or consume food. In standard present tense (Kartari Prayoga with the Shyap affix), it operates in the Parasmaipada taking the form 'psāyati' (or 'psāti' in classical usages under related rules). Adding the causative affix (Nic) transforms it into 'psāyayati' or 'psāpayati', meaning 'causes someone to eat' or 'feeds'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga (Present Active, 3rd Person Singular, Lat-lakara)
scenarios.example_english: The child eats the sweetmeat.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic-pratyaya, 3rd Person Singular, Lat-lakara)
scenarios.example_english: The mother feeds milk to the infant.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'psā' is classified under Bhvadi-gana with the meaning 'bhakṣaṇe' (eating/consumption). It is anudātta-it, Parasmaipadi, and anit. In the present tense, taking the universal shap-pratyaya, it yields the base psāya- (psāyati) as well as the uncontracted forms, having parallel existence in Adadi-gana with luk of shap (psāti).
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'psā bhakṣaṇe' as an adanta root denoting consumption. Its perfect tense (Lit) forms reduplicated base 'papsau' (papsatuḥ, papsuḥ), and in simple aorist (Lun) it realizes 'apsāsīt' under the s-aorist rules for anit adanta roots.

meanings.English: to eat, to consume, to devour

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'vicch' primarily signifies going, moving, or seeking. By the special Paninian rule 'gup-dhup-vicch-pani-panibhyah ayah' (3.1.28), it obligatorily takes the 'aya' suffix in non-causative present conjugations, resulting in forms like 'vicchayati' (he/she goes or approaches). When prefixed or used transitively, it can convey seeking, begging, or shining.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Lat lakara (present tense), prathama-purusha, eka-vacana with the obligatory 'aya' pratyaya (Panini 3.1.28)
scenarios.example_english: The traveler on the road goes towards the village.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Lun lakara (aorist tense), prathama-purusha, eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The traveler went to the forest.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti discusses 'viccha gatau' along with the special svarthe aya-pratyaya prescription by the sutra 'gup-dhup-vicch-pani-panibhyah ayah'. It notes that it denotes motion (gati) and, according to various commentators, also encompasses seeking (bhiksa), succession (santana), or beauty/lustre (sobha).
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin analyzes 'viccha' under the Bhvadi-gana roots taking the aya affix. He explains the morpho-phonemic integration where the penultimate short and root-final combination undergoes regular guna/vriddhi restrictions governed by the aya affix, deriving the standard present stem 'vicchaya-'.

meanings.English: to go, to move, to seek, to shine
meanings.Hindi: jana, gati karna, mangna, shobhit hona
meanings.Bengali: jaoya, chola, bhiksha kora, shobha paoya

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The verbal root ghaj expresses making a sound/noise or gathering/condensing items together. In basic active voice (Parasmaipada), it simply describes the action of sounding or assembling. In the causative form (ghajayati), it indicates causing someone or something to make sound or bringing elements together.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (Present active, 3rd person singular)
scenarios.meaning: sounds, makes a noise, or gathers
scenarios.example_english: A sound resonates in the cave due to the force of wind.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (Causative active, 3rd person singular)
scenarios.meaning: causes to sound or collects together
scenarios.example_english: The teacher gathers the students together in one place.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: In the Madhaviya Dhatuvritti, the root ghaja is glossed in the senses of shabda (making sound) and sanghata (assembling or compacting). It conjugates in the first class with standard shab-vikarana to form ghajati in the present tense.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines ghaja under sound and collection (shabde sanghate ca), noting its parallel phonetic structure with other guttural Bhvadi roots and regular unaugmented thematic inflections.

meanings.English: to sound, to make noise, to collect, to assemble
meanings.Hindi: dhvani karna, aavaj karna, ekatra karna
meanings.Bengali: shobdo kora, awaj kora, jotola kora

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'cas' expresses the act of eating, consuming, or narrating/telling. In simple active voice (kartari prayoga), it takes standard Parasmaipada endings like 'casati' to show someone eating or recounting something. When made causative with 'nic', it takes the form 'casayati', meaning to cause someone to eat or to have something narrated.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Simple present tense (lat lakar), active voice (kartari prayoga), 3rd person singular
scenarios.example_english: The boy eats the fruit.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative present tense (nic-pratyaya, lat lakar), active voice
scenarios.example_english: The mother feeds the child.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'casa~' is listed in the Bhvadi gana with the meanings of 'bhakshana' (eating/consuming) and according to some traditions 'kathana' (telling/narrating). It takes the standard sap vikarana yielding the simple present form 'casati' with anit/set distinctions observed in ardhadhatuka environments.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'casa bhakshane kathaane va', taking Parasmaipada affixes. The canonical present third-person singular is 'casati', forming derived forms regularly in the first conjugation without internal vowel lengthening in general sarvadhatuka contexts.

meanings.English: to eat, to consume, to narrate, to tell
meanings.Bengali: khaoa, bhakshan kara, bala, barnana kara

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'nat' means to dance, act, or make artistic bodily movements. In its basic Parasmaipada active form (natati), the performer is directly dancing or acting. When used with a causative affix Nic (natayati), it means to cause someone else to dance, direct an actor, or stage a dramatic performance.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakara (present tense), prathama-purusha ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The dancer dances on the stage.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (causative), Lat lakara (present tense), prathama-purusha ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: causes to dance / directs a dramatic representation
scenarios.example_english: The stage director makes the actors perform.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'nata' is listed in the Bhvadi-gana with the sense of nritti (dancing, dramatic movement). Being anudatta-it-rahita and ending in a consonant, it takes Parasmaipada terminations. Forms like natati, nanata, natita, and natisyati are derived with it-agama.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines 'nata nrittau' as artistic bodily movement or rhythmic dance (avaspandana). The root forms the primary nominal derivative 'nata' (actor/dancer) and follows standard bhvadi set conjugation.

meanings.English: to dance, act, represent dramatically, move rhythmically
meanings.Bengali: nach kora, natok kora, obhinoy kora

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'smal' belongs to the Bhvadi class and fundamentally conveys physical movement, wavering, or staggering. In standard active voice (Kartari Parasmaipada), it simply denotes a subject moving or shaking on its own. When used in the causative form with the affix Nic, the meaning transforms to making someone or something stagger, shake, or oscillate.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (present active indicative, 3rd person singular, Lat lakara)
scenarios.example_english: The old man staggers along the path.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic-pratyaya, Lat lakara, 3rd person singular)
scenarios.meaning: causes to shake or makes stagger
scenarios.example_english: The fierce wind causes the tree to shake.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'smalṛ calane' belongs to the jvalādi-group within Bhvadi-gana. Being marked with an irit-anubandha (ṛ), it indicates that the root takes the affix 'ṇa' in the sense of the agent under the rule 'jvalitikasantevyo ṇaḥ' (Pāṇini 3.1.140), forming nominal derivatives like 'smālaḥ' (one who staggers/moves). It is akarmaka, parasmaipadi, and takes standard set augment in ardhadhatuka operations.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'smalṛ calane' alongside 'hvalṛ' and 'hmalṛ' as expressing unsteadiness or motion ('calana'). As part of the jvalādi subset, it exhibits vowel lengthening to vṛddhi when the kṛt-affix 'ṇa' is applied, retaining standard a-thematic conjugation smalati in sarvadhatuka tenses.

meanings.English: to move, stagger, waver, shake

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'dhvans' means to perish, crumble, fall down, or be ruined. Being an Atmanepada root in the Bhvadi gana, it takes the 'te' ending (dhvamsate) to describe an entity collapsing or disintegrating. When combined with the causative suffix nic, it shifts to Parasmaipada/Ubhapadapada (dhvamsayati) meaning 'causes to destroy' or 'demolishes'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The old palace crumbles due to the passage of time.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (Causative), Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The force of the wind destroys the tree.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: dhvansu gatau avadhvamsane ca. anudatteta atmanepadino bhabhavah. dhvamsate. dhvamsisyate. adhvamsta. avadhvamsanam paribhutasya ksanikah patanam nastata ca.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: dhvansu gatyavadhvamsanarthah. anudattet. dhvamsate. avadhvamsanam vinasah adhahpatanam va.

meanings.English: to perish, crumble, fall down, disintegrate

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'bhrāmṛ' means to shine, flash, or radiate light. Because of the special 'ṛ' marker, it can optionally take both Parasmaipada and Atmanepada endings as well as the 'śyan' affix in the present tense, producing forms like 'bhrāmyati' or 'bhrāmate'. When used in the causative (Nic), it means to cause something to shine or illuminate.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakara (present tense)
scenarios.example_english: The golden ornament gleams in the assembly.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Prakriti-pratyaya with Nic (causative)
scenarios.meaning: causes to illuminate or makes radiant
scenarios.example_english: The sunlight causes the entire world to shine.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti identifies 'bhrāmṛ' in the meaning of dīpti (illumination, brightness). Due to the sutra 'bhrāśa-bhlāśa-bhramu-kramu-klama-trasi-truṭi-laṣaśca', this root takes the optional 'śyan' vikarana in the Sarvadhatuka present system along with optional voice switches.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes under the group of radiant roots (dīptāvubhayatodantāḥ) that 'bhrāmṛ' belongs to the specific cluster sharing phonological and morphological alternations of stem vowel and conjugational class options.

meanings.English: to shine, gleam, flash, or be radiant

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'svañj' means 'to embrace', 'to clasp', or 'to hug'. It is primarily conjugated in the Atmanepada voice (svajate). When prefixes like 'pari-' are added (parisvajate), it means to embrace warmly or completely. In the present tense, its nasal 'n' is dropped according to Paninian rules, giving the smooth form 'svajate'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: lat-lakāra (present indicative), prathama-puruṣa, eka-vacana, kartari prayoga
scenarios.example_english: The mother lovingly embraces the child.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: upasarga 'pari' + lat-lakāra, prathama-puruṣa, eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: Having seen his friend, he warmly embraces him.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: Madhava analyzes 'ṣvañja pariṣvaṅge' as an aniṭ, ātmanepadī root belonging to the bhvādi gaṇa. By the rule 'daṃśasvañjaṣvañjāṃ śapi' (6.4.25), the internal nasal is dropped before the śap pratyaya in sārvadhātuka contexts, resulting in 'svajate'. The initial dental 'sa' arises from mürdhanya 'ṣa' via dhatvādeḥ ṣaḥ saḥ.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines the root in the sense of 'āliṅgana' (embracing/clasping). He notes its status as aniṭ in the ātmanepada series, detailing its nominal and participial derivations such as 'svaṅktaḥ' and 'svajiḥ'.

meanings.English: to embrace, to hug, to clasp, to cling to

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'mi' belongs to the first conjugation (Bhvadi-gana) and means 'to harm, injure, destroy, or hurt'. Because it carries the silent marker 'n' (nit), it operates in the Atmanepada voice, focusing the result of the action on the grammatical framing. When used in the causative (Nic), it shifts to 'to cause to harm' or 'to cause destruction'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat-lakara (present indicative), Prathama-purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The wicked person harms the righteous one.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic), Lat-lakara, Prathama-purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The king causes the enemy to be harmed by others.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'min himsayam' is classified under the Bhvadi class. Being marked with 'n' (nit/anudanveta traits), it takes Atmanepada endings. The present form develops as 'mayate' through guna (e) followed by ay-adesha before the 'shap' affix. Forms include perfect 'mamye', periphrastic future 'mata', and simple future 'masyate'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'min himsayam' as an aniṭ root signifying injuring, hurting, or causing decay. It takes 'shap' vikarana yielding 'mayate' in Kartari.

meanings.English: to harm, to injure, to destroy
meanings.Hindi: himsa karna, nuksan pahunchana, vinash karna
meanings.Bengali: himsa kora, khoti kora, binash kora

canonical_dhatvartha: saṃbandhane (in the sense of tying, connecting, or binding together)

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'chṛt' means to tie, string together, or connect objects. In basic active voice (Kartari Prayoga), it takes standard Parasmaipada endings to denote the action of fastening or linking. When used with a causative affix (Nic), it signifies making someone else bind or connect items together.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga (Present Active, Lat Lakara, Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana)
scenarios.example_english: The garland-maker binds the flowers together with a thread.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic-pratyaya, Lat Lakara, Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana)
scenarios.meaning: Causes someone to tie or bind together
scenarios.example_english: The teacher causes the student to bind the book.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'chṛtī' is listed in the Bhvadi class under the meaning of saṃbandhana (binding/connecting). It belongs to the set of roots with an indicatory long i (īkaranirdesha) which conditions specific morphophonological behaviors in derived nominals and verbal paradigms, operating as an active transitive root.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines 'chṛtī saṃbandhane' as the action of tying, joining, or fastening things into a unified whole. It forms 'chṛtati' in the present indicative and undergoes regular guna strengthening in non-sarvadhatuka environments.

meanings.English: To tie, bind, connect, or string together

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The verbal root 'svai' means 'to go' or 'to move'. Because it possesses the marker 'ṅ' (ṅit) in Paninian grammar, it inherently conjugates in the Atmanepada (self-oriented middle voice), forming 'svāyate'. When a causative suffix (ṇic) is added, it expresses making another person or entity move.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Active Voice (Kartari Prayoga), Atmanepada, Present Tense (Lat lakara), Third Person Singular
scenarios.example_english: The traveler moves along the path.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Prena / Nijanta), Parasmaipada, Present Tense (Lat lakara), Third Person Singular
scenarios.example_english: The leader causes the person to move forward.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti identifies 'ṣvaiṅ' with initial retroflex ṣakāra ('dhatvadeh sah sah' applies to make it svaiṅ) under the meaning 'gatau' (in the sense of movement). As an anudattedit/ṅit root, it takes Atmanepada affixes exclusively in the non-causative base, deriving forms like 'svāyate' via the application of the relevant vikaraṇa and vowel changes.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin classifies 'ṣvaiṅ gatau' sequentially along with 'śyaiṅ' and 'styaiṅ'. It is treated as anit and anudattedit, forming 'svāyate' in the present tense (sarvadhatuka) through standard a-karanta modification rules.

meanings.English: to go, to move

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'trap' expresses feeling shy, bashful, or embarrassed. Because it is inherently Ātmanepada, the action of feeling bashful or ashamed reflects directly within the person experiencing the emotion.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga (present indicative, 3rd person singular)
scenarios.example_english: The soft-spoken girl feels shy in the assembly.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: ṇic pratyaya (causative present indicative)
scenarios.meaning: causes someone to feel embarrassed or ashamed
scenarios.example_sanskrit: gurur anucitaṁ kāryaṁ dṛṣṭvā śiṣyaṁ trāpayati.
scenarios.example_english: Seeing improper conduct, the teacher makes the student feel ashamed.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'trapūṣ' is cataloged under Bhvādigaṇa in the sense of lajjā (modesty, shyness, or embarrassment). Being anudātteta, it takes Ātmanepada affixes (trapate, trape). In non-conjugational tenses, it operates as an aniṭ root.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'trapūṣ lajjāyām' as an Ātmanepada aniṭ root. Its primary sememe denotes inward hesitation, bashfulness, or modesty (lajjā-vṛtti), contrasting with aggressive or bold attitudes.

meanings.English: to be shy, to feel bashful, to be ashamed or embarrassed
meanings.French: avoir honte, être timide ou embarrassé

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root kag means to move, proceed, or go. In its standard active form (Parasmaipada), it describes an agent moving or advancing. When converted to the causative form with the affix nic (kag + nic = kagaya), it means to drive, impel, or make someone or something move.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Lat-lakara, prathama-purusha, eka-vacana (Simple Present Active)
scenarios.example_english: The traveler moves toward the path.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (Causative), Lat-lakara, prathama-purusha, eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The charioteer causes the horse to move.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: kaga gatau - ayam parasmaipadi set ca. asya dhatoh prayogah gatyarthe bhavati. rupani - kagati, cakaga, kagita, kagisyati.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: kaga gatau - bhvadau parasmaipadisu pathitah. gati-kriyayam vartate, nitvam nirasya savarana-dhatu-vargesu kathyate.

meanings.English: to go, to move, to march, to advance

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root kṛṣ means to plough, furrow, draw, or drag. Because it is an Ubhayapada root, it can take Parasmaipada endings (karṣati) when the action is directed outwards, and Atmanepada endings (karṣate) when the fruit of the action is intended for oneself. When used with the causative affix (karṣayati), it means to cause someone to plough or to drag something.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga, lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana (Parasmaipada)
scenarios.example_english: The farmer ploughs the field.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: upasarga 'āṅ' + lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The magnet attracts iron towards itself.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'kṛṣa vilekhane' belongs to the Bhvādi class. The canonical artha 'vilekhana' signifies making furrows, scratching, or drawing lines. Being anit and svaritet, it admits both Parasmaipada and Atmanepada endings. In sārwadhātuka environments before the affix shap, guna of the root vowel ṛ occurs, forming karṣati and karṣate.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes that 'kṛṣ' is primarily glossed in the sense of tilling the ground (vilekhana) and dragging/pulling. The root exhibits guna in the present tense (karṣati/karṣate), and forms the past passive participle kṛṣṭa by transformation of the final retroflex sibilant and dental ta-pratyaya.

meanings.English: to plough, till, furrow, draw, drag, or pull
meanings.Hindi: jotna, hal chalana, kheenchna, aakarshit karna
meanings.Bengali: chash kora, langal deoa, tana, aakorshon kora

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root mlai means to wither, fade, or lose vigor. In simple everyday Sanskrit, you use it whenever something fresh—like a flower, leaf, or face—wilts or droops. In basic active voice (Kartari Prayoga), it takes Parasmaipada endings yielding 'mlayati'. When used in the causative sense (Nic), it shifts to 'mlapayati' meaning 'causes to wither' or 'dries out'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga (Present Active, Lat Lakara, 3rd Person Singular)
scenarios.example_english: Due to the intense heat, the flower withers quickly.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (Causative, Lat Lakara, 3rd Person Singular)
scenarios.example_english: Disrespect wilts the face of a friend.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: mlai glanau harsaksaye ca pathyate. adeca upadeshe ashiti ityattve shyo dhyangvornayiti vatve krte mlayatiti rupam bhavati. liti mamlau mamlatuh mamluh. lut-adi prayogesu mlata ityadi. nisthayam tu phulla-ksiba-krsa-ullagha-mlana ityadinipatanat mlana iti rupam siddham bhavati.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: mlai glanau. glanirutsahasya ksayah saityam ca. mlayati. atah ksayarthe vartate. mamlau. mlatavya iti tavyadadi. mlano vriksah. ksitabhimardat padmam mlayati.

meanings.English: to wither, to fade, to wilt, to languish
meanings.Bengali: mlana howa, murjhe jaoya, shukiye jaoya

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'taksh' means to chisel, plane, cut, or fashion wood/stone into a desired shape. In simple present tense (Kartari Prayoga), it takes Parasmaipada endings ('takshati'). When someone causes someone else to carve or chisel, it takes the causative affix Nich ('takshayati').

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga (Present Active, 3rd Person Singular, Lat)
scenarios.example_english: The carpenter carves/planes the timber.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Prayojaka Vyapara (Causative, Lat, 3rd Person Singular)
scenarios.example_english: The master makes the carpenter plane the wood.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: Taksa tvaksane tanukarane ca. The root taksh denotes peeling, scraping, chiseling, and thinning down materials such as wood or stone. It takes the thematic affix Shap in Bhvadi and behaves as a standard Set Parasmaipada verbal stem forming takshati, tataksha, takshita.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Taksayati tanukaranam karoti. Kshiraswamin emphasizes the primary sense of reducing bulk or paring outer layers to refine an object, noting identical phonological behaviour with roots expressing surface shaping.

meanings.English: to chisel, carve, pare, plane, cut or fashion

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'kṣai' means to decay, waste away, diminish, or wane. In standard active voice (Kartari Prayoga), it takes Parasmaipada endings and changes to 'kṣāyati' in the present tense. When used in the causative form (adding the suffix Nic), it means to cause to decay or to consume/destroy, taking the form 'kṣāpayati'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga (Present Tense, 3rd Person Singular)
scenarios.example_english: With the passage of time, wealth diminishes.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic (Causative, Present Tense, 3rd Person Singular)
scenarios.example_english: Fire consumes and destroys everything.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'kṣai' belongs to the Bhvadi-gana and is listed in the sense of 'kṣaya' (waning, destruction, or exhaustion). Being anit and a-denta equivalent under derivation via 'ādeśa' to a-kara before sarvadhatuka affixes, it undergoes substitution of ai to a by 'adeca upadese'asiti' giving forms like kṣāyati, cakṣau, and akṣāsīt.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'kṣai kṣaye', denoting reduction or gradual destruction. In the non-causal primary conjugation, it behaves as a parasmaipadi anit root showing regular a-vowel replacement patterns.

meanings.English: to decay, to wane, to diminish, to waste away

canonical_dhatvartha: utsāhe (in the sense of enthusiasm, exertion, striving)

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'dhreks' describes exerting oneself with great enthusiasm or striving boldly toward a goal. As an active Parasmaipada verb, it expresses personal effort and initiative in undertaking difficult tasks.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga (active voice), lat-lakara (present tense), prathama-purusha, eka-vacana
scenarios.meaning: he/she strives enthusiastically or exerts effort
scenarios.example_english: The brave hero exerts himself enthusiastically in his task.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga (active voice), lun-lakara (aorist tense / past), prathama-purusha, eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The youth strove enthusiastically for victory.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti analyzes 'dhreksr utsahe' as belonging to the Bhvadi class. The ending 'ri' marker indicates specific phonological treatments in certain derivational contexts. It denotes bold effort, energy, and resolute initiative.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes under 'dhreksa utsahe' that the root conveys exertion accompanied by mental vigor and zeal, forming present stem 'dhreksati' with standard shap vikaranas.

meanings.English: to strive enthusiastically, to exert oneself, to be eager or bold
meanings.Hindi: utsaha dikhana, prayatna karna, utsuk hona
meanings.French: s'efforcer avec enthousiasme, faire des efforts avec zèle

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root mna means to study, repeat, or memorize through repeated recitation. By Paninian rule (pa-ghra-dhma-stha-mna...), the root substitutes 'mana' in sarvadhatuka tenses, conjugating as manati. In causative forms with nic, it becomes mnapayati, meaning to teach or cause someone to memorize.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The student memorizes the Vedic hymn.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (Causative), Lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: causes to learn or memorize, teaches
scenarios.example_english: The teacher causes the disciple to memorize the scripture.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: mna abhyase. abhyasah punah punah pathanam anushilanam va. paghradhmashthamnadandrishyarcchasritsadshadityadina manadeshe krite manati manatah mananti iti rupani bhavanti. ayam anit parasmaipadi ca.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: mna abhyase. abhyasah punah punar uccaranam. manati, mamnau, amnat. anit parasmaibhashah.

meanings.English: to practice, to repeat, to memorize, to learn by heart
meanings.Kannada: abhyasa madu, manana madu, punaravartane madu
meanings.Tamil: thirumba thirumba payil, mananam sei, ninaivil kol
meanings.Hindi: abhyas karna, manan karna, dohrana, ratna
meanings.Bengali: abhyas kora, manan kora, path kora

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'dhṛ' means to hold, sustain, bear, or wear. Being an Ubhayapadi root (marked with 'ñ'), it can take both Parasmaipada (dharati) and Atmanepada (dharate) endings in active voice with identical core meanings. When used with the causative affix (ṇic), it forms 'dhārayati', which commonly means 'to wear' clothes/ornaments or 'to owe' a debt to a creditor.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara (present indicative active), Parasmaipada third-person singular
scenarios.example_english: The earth sustains the moving and non-moving world.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (ṇijanta) form in Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara
scenarios.example_english: The boy wears new clothing.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: Sayana notes in Madhaviya Dhatuvritti that dhṛñ is ñit, which triggers ubhayapada inflection under Panini 1.3.72. The root undergoes guna strengthening to 'ar' (forming dharati/dharate) before sarvadhatuka affixes like sap. As an anit root ending in vocalic r, it rejects the augment it in general ardadhatuka environments. In causative construction, the creditor takes sampradana (dative case) under the special rule 'dhāreruttamarṇaḥ' (1.4.35).
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin categorizes dhṛñ under the concluding Ubhayapada group of Bhvadi gana. He highlights the semantic range covering holding, maintaining, and supporting. The reduplicated perfect forms include dadhāra (Parasmaipada) and dadhre (Atmanepada), illustrating standard anit behavior across tenses.

meanings.English: To hold, to bear, to sustain, to support, to wear

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'khañj' means to limp or walk with an impaired gait. In basic Parasmaipada form, it describes the subject walking lamely due to pain or injury. When used with a causative suffix (Nic), it shifts the meaning to causing someone or an animal to limp.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga (Present Active, Parasmaipada, Lat Lakara, Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana)
scenarios.meaning: He/she/it limps or walks with a limp
scenarios.example_english: The old man limps along with the help of a stick.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic Pratyaya (Causative Active, Parasmaipada, Lat Lakara, Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana)
scenarios.meaning: Causes to limp / makes one walk lamely
scenarios.example_english: The sharp stone makes the horse limp.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The author glosses 'khañji gativaikalye' indicating the cessation of normal uniform movement due to physical impediment. Because it is marked with an idit (or retaining the nasal), the nasal is preserved across major conjugational forms such as khañjati, cakhañja, khañjitā, and khañjiṣyati.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin explains 'gativaikalyam' as 'padadoṣeṇa calanam' (walking with foot affliction). The root follows standard first conjugation paradigms with an intermediate iṭ augment in Ardhadhatuka forms due to its Set classification.

meanings.English: to limp, to walk lamely, to falter in movement
meanings.Telugu: kuṇṭu, kaalu noppitho naḍucu, vaṅkaga naḍucu
meanings.Malayalam: kuṇṭuka, noṇṭuka, kaalinu doṣam uṇṭāyi naḍakkuka
meanings.Hindi: laṅgaḍānā, pair meṁ doṣa hone se aṭaka-aṭakakar calanā
meanings.Chinese: bo xing, que bu, po jiao zou lu

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'khyā' means to narrate, declare, or tell a story clearly. In simple language, whenever you relate an event or tell someone about something that happened, you use this root. When prefixes (upasargas) are added, it takes on specialized nuances: 'ā-khyā' means to recount a tale or story (ākhyāna), while 'pra-khyā' means to become famous or well-known.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Sārvadhātuka Laṭ Lakāra (Present Tense), Prathama Puruṣa, Ekavacana, Ātmanepada / Karmaṇi Prayoga
scenarios.meaning: It is narrated / It is declared
scenarios.example_english: The ancient story is narrated by the sage.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga with Upasarga 'ā', Laṭ Lakāra, Prathama Puruṣa, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The teacher explains dharma to the student.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root khyāñ is designated in the sense of prakathana (elaborate narration or declaration). As a root with marker ñ (ñit), it takes Ātmanepada markers in its primary assignment, though in classical usage and secondary formations with upasargas it actively surfaces across both padas. It acts as an anit root.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'khyāñ prakathane' indicating clear exposition and narration of facts. He highlights its role as an ādeśa (substitute) for root cakṣiṅ under Paninian rule 'cakṣiṅaḥ khyāñ' in specific non-sarvadhatuka contexts.

meanings.English: to narrate, to declare, to recount, to make known
meanings.Bengali: katha bala, barnana kara, prakasha kara

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'kru' belongs to the Bhvadi class and fundamentally means to produce a loud sound, cry, or scream. In its basic form (kartari prayoga), it takes standard Parasmaipada endings with guna strengthening (kravati). When used in the causative sense with the affix Nic, it denotes causing someone or something to make a sound or cry out (kravayati).

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Lat lakara, prathama-purusha, eka-vacana (Kartari)
scenarios.example_english: The bird cries out loudly in the forest.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (Causative), Lat lakara, prathama-purusha, eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: Fear makes the child cry out.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'kru' is classified under 'shabde' (sound production). Being devoid of anudatta or svarita markers that trigger Atmanepada, it is strictly Parasmaipadi and Anit in the primary conjugations. Guna replacement takes place before Sarvadhatuka affixes, yielding forms like kravati and cakrāva.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'kru shabde' among the u-karanta roots in the Bhvadi-gana. It forms its present stem regularly via Shap (a) with Av-adesha as 'kravati', sharing phonetic behavior with similar acoustic roots like ru and shru.

meanings.English: to make a sound, cry out, scream

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'bhlāś' means to shine, flash, or blaze with light. By default, it takes Atmanepada endings in the present tense (bhlāśate). By a special Paninian rule (3.1.70), it can optionally take the Shyan affix (bhlāśyate/bhlāśyati) in active usage without changing its essential meaning of shining brightly.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga (active voice), standard bhvādi-gaṇa sap-pratyaya (Atmanepada)
scenarios.example_english: The lightning shines brightly in the sky.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: ṇic-pratyaya (causative), kartari prayoga (Parasmaipada)
scenarios.example_english: The lamp illuminates the room.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: bhlāśṛ dīptau. ṛditvāt caṅi vā hrasvaḥ. 'vā bhrāśa-bhlāśa-bhramu-kramu-klamu-trasi-truṭi-laṣaḥ' iti vā śyan. bhlāśate, bhlāśyate.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: bhlāśṛ dīptau. ṛdit tvād dīrghābhāvaś caṅi. bhlāśate, bhlāśyate vā śyan-pakṣe.

meanings.English: to shine, to beam, to blaze, to radiate light
meanings.Bengali: ujjval haoya, jhikmikiye otha, alokita haoya

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root klam means to become tired, fatigued, or exhausted. In the basic active present tense, it elongates its vowel and can take either the standard Bhvadi affix or the special Divadi-like affix, giving forms like klamati and klamyati. When transformed into the causative (Nic), it becomes klamayati, shifting the meaning from 'becoming tired' to 'tiring someone out' or 'exhausting someone'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakara (present tense), prathama purusha, eka-vacana with Sap vikarana and dirgha
scenarios.example_english: The traveler becomes weary from the long journey.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (causative), Lat lakara, prathama purusha, eka-vacana
scenarios.meaning: causes someone to be exhausted / exhausts
scenarios.example_english: The intense heat exhausts the traveler.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: Under klamu glanau, Madhava explains that glani indicates the depletion of energy or bodily strength (utsahahani or sarirasaithilya). By the sutra 'samam astanam dirghah syan ca', the penultimate vowel undergoes lengthening to 'a' along with optional Syan vikarana, yielding the dual present forms klamyati and klamati.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin analyzes klamu as signifying bodily fatigue and languor (glanih sariravasadah). He confirms its anit classification and illustrates the phonological elongation of the base vowel in the sarvadhatuka environment.

meanings.English: to grow weary, to fatigue, to exhaust, to languish
meanings.Hindi: thakna, glani hona, shithil hona, klanta hona
meanings.Bengali: klanto howa, obosonno howa, klanti bodh kora

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The verbal root 'mnā' means to practice, repeat, or memorize by continuous recitation. In the active present tense (kartari prayoga), Paninian rules replace the root 'mnā' with 'mana-' before standard verb endings. Therefore, instead of 'mnāti', it conjugates as 'manati' (he/she memorizes or recites). With prefixes like 'ā-', it forms 'āmnāya' (traditional sacred instruction or revelation).

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat-lakara (Present tense active voice), prathama-purusha eka-vacana with 'mana' substitution via sutra 7.3.78
scenarios.meaning: Recites, practices, or commits to memory through repeated study.
scenarios.example_english: The student memorizes the Vedic mantra in the morning.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Karmani prayoga (Passive voice), Lat-lakara with upasarga 'ā'
scenarios.meaning: Is traditionally taught, handed down, or mentioned in sacred lore.
scenarios.example_english: This meaning is traditionally handed down in the sacred scriptures.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'mnā' is classified under Bhvadi-gana in the sense of 'abhyāsa' (repeated practice, rehearsal, memorization). In Sarvadhatuka environments, 'mnā' undergoes regular substitution to 'mana' by the specific sutra 'pā-ghrā-dhmā-sthā-mnā...', yielding the primary finite forms like 'manati', 'manataḥ', and 'mananti'. In Ardhadhatuka forms, where this substitution is blocked, the root preserves its original form as an Anit base (e.g., mnatum, mnātaḥ).
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'mnā abhyāse' as referring to repeated vocalization and internal contemplation ('punaḥ punaḥ uccāraṇam śīlanaṁ vā'). From this root, critical traditional nouns such as 'āmnāya' (authoritative transmission or canon) and 'samāmnāya' (traditional enumeration or compendium) are derived.

meanings.English: to repeat, memorize, recite, study diligently
meanings.Tamil: payirci sei, mananam sei, thirumba solli paḍi
meanings.Bengali: abhyāsa karā, mukhastha karā, ābṛtti karā

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'dhāv' carries two distinct primary meanings: to run/glide (motion) and to wash/cleanse (purification). When used intransitively to express running, it is commonly conjugated in Parasmaipada. When conveying cleansing or self-directed action, it takes either Parasmaipada or Atmanepada. Adding the causative suffix -nic- forms 'dhāvayati', meaning 'to cause to run' or 'to cause to wash'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Parasmaipada, Lat lakara, prathama-purusha ekavacana (Motion / Running)
scenarios.example_english: The horse runs swiftly in the field.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Atmanepada, Lat lakara, prathama-purusha ekavacana (Cleansing / Purifying for oneself)
scenarios.example_english: The person washes his face.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti analyzes 'dhāvῡ gatiśuddhyoḥ' as possessing the anubandha long 'ū', which marks it as taking both sets of endings (Ubhayapada) and optionally taking specific nistha forms. It clarifies that in the sense of motion ('gatau') the root is primarily intransitive, whereas in the sense of cleansing ('śuddhau / mārjane') it is transitive.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes under 'dhāv gatiśuddhyoḥ' that the root manifests dual semantic scopes: physical kinetic movement ('dhāvati vegena') and scouring or wiping away impurities ('dhāvati vastraṃ mārjati').

meanings.English: to run, to glide, to wash, to purify

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'bhrans' means to fall down, slip, or drop from a place. In the standard active voice (Kartari), it takes Atmanepada endings ('bhransate') to describe an object naturally slipping or falling. When converted into the causative form (producing an action), it takes the 'Nic' affix and becomes Parasmaipada ('bhransayati') to describe causing something to fall or knocking it down.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga (Present tense / Lat lakara, 3rd Person Singular, Atmanepada)
scenarios.example_english: The leaf falls down from the tree.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic-pratyaya, Lat lakara, 3rd Person Singular, Parasmaipada)
scenarios.example_english: The wind causes the leaves to fall from the tree.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'bhransu' belongs to the Bhvadi gana with the canonical sense 'avadhramsane' (falling down or decaying). It is anudattopadesha and idit/anudattet, taking Atmanepada terminations inherently (bhransate, bhabhranse). Madhava explains 'avadhramsanam' as the act of falling, slipping, or loss of position (patanam / bhranshah).
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines 'bhransu avadhramsane' as signifying 'patane' (in the sense of dropping or falling down). The nasal 'n' is retained in non-kit/git configurations and the root conjugates in the Atmanepada yielding forms like 'bhransate' and perfect 'babhranse'.

meanings.English: to fall down, to drop, to slip, to decay
meanings.Bengali: niche pora, bhrashta howa, poton ghotano

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'svi' primarily means to swell, grow, or move. In normal Parasmaipada usage (svayati), it describes an entity expanding in size or moving forward. When used in causative forms (svayayati), it indicates causing something to expand or inflate.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat-lakara (present tense), prathama-purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The wound swells over time.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lit-lakara (past perfect tense), prathama-purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: His joy swelled due to the festival.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'tuosvi' belongs to Bhvadi gana with 'tu' and 'o' as anubandhas, leaving 'svi'. It denotes movement (gati) and growth or swelling (vriddhi). The marker 'o' signifies that it takes the nistha affix 'na' under special conditions (e.g., suna) and the 'tu' marker indicates the addition of 'athu' for making primary nouns (e.g., svayathu).
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes that 'tuosvi' signifies expansion and locomotion (svayati vriddhau gatau ca). It undergoes samprasarana in certain kit-affixes resulting in forms like 'sunam' and nominal derivatives like 'svayathuh' meaning inflammation or swelling.

meanings.English: to swell, to grow, to increase, to move

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'vyeñ' means to cover, wrap, or conceal. As an Ubhayapada verb, it can take Parasmaipada endings when the action is directed outwardly, or Atmanepada endings when the action is done primarily for or upon oneself (such as wrapping a garment around oneself).

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Parasmaipada (Kartari Prayoga, Lat, Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana)
scenarios.example_english: The mother covers the child with a cloth.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Atmanepada (Kartari Prayoga, Lat, Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana)
scenarios.example_english: He wraps the upper garment around himself.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'vyeñ samvarane' belongs to the Bhvadi-gana. Marked with 'ñ' it is Ubhayapada. It indicates 'samvarana' (covering, enclosing, concealing). In lit lakara, it undergoes samprasarana in specific environments and doubles, producing forms such as vivyaya and vivyatu.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'vyeñ samvarane' as denoting the act of wrapping, enveloping, or covering up. It is an anit root ending in 'e' which undergoes standard ay-adesha before sarvadhatuka affixes (vyayati, vyayate).

meanings.English: to cover, wrap, veil, conceal, envelop

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'srañj' denotes the action of moving, going, slipping, or flowing forward. In basic Parasmaipada usage, it describes a subject moving or gliding. When transformed into the causative (Nic), it shifts to mean causing someone or something to move or advance.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga (Present Active, 3rd Person Singular)
scenarios.example_english: The river flows/moves rapidly.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic Pratyaya, Kartari Prayoga)
scenarios.example_english: The charioteer drives/causes the horse to move forward.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'srañji~' belongs to the Bhvadi class and is read with an 'i' it-marker indicating obligatory internal nasalization (num-agama), yielding the base form 'srañj-'. It expresses the sense of motion (gatyam) and follows the standard Parasmaipada inflection.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin classifies 'srañji' among roots of movement (gatyarthah). Being idit (having 'i' as an anubandha), the insertion of penultimate nasal is constant across all conjugational tenses and moods.

meanings.English: to go, to move, to glide

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'kṛṣ' primarily means to plow, furrow, or drag/pull. In the basic active voice (Kartari Prayoga), it uses either Parasmaipada or Atmanepada endings to describe someone plowing a field or pulling an object. When made causative with the 'ṇic' affix (karṣayati), it means to cause someone to plow or to attract/drag someone forcefully.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat-lakara, Prathama-purusha, Ekavacana (Parasmaipada)
scenarios.example_english: The farmer plows the field.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nyanta (Causative), Kartari prayoga, Lat-lakara, Prathama-purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The magnet attracts iron.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'kṛṣa vilekhane' is enumerated in the Bhvādi-gaṇa. It denotes furrowing, tilling, or dragging ('vilekhanaṁ halādinā dāruṇam'). It forms both 'karṣati' (with guṇa) and 'kṛṣati' (with tudādivat śa-pratyaya in alternate usages), admitting both padas and functioning without an intermediate 'iṭ' vowel (aniṭ).
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'kṛṣa vilekhane' as signifying breaking or scratching the earth through implements like a plow. It takes aniṭ character in primary conjugations and undergoes vocalic guṇa 'ar' before sārvadhātuka affixes to yield 'karṣati' and 'karṣate'.

meanings.English: to plow, to furrow, to drag, to attract

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'styai' means to congeal, solidify, collect, or thicken into a dense mass. When used in active voice, it describes substances like milk, ghee, or clouds gathering density or thickening naturally. When paired with prefixes or used in causative constructions, it shows making something condense or form a cluster.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (Present indicative active third-person singular, Lat lakara)
scenarios.example_english: During the cold season, ghee solidifies.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Upasarga 'sam' (intensive prefix showing complete consolidation)
scenarios.meaning: completely gathers together / becomes fully dense
scenarios.example_english: In the sky, a cluster of clouds gathers densely together.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: Madhaviya glosses 'styai sanghate' as the action of dense accumulation, aggregation, or hardening into a compact mass (sanghibhave). It undergoes the replacement of ai to a (adeca upadeshe'shiti) before non-shit suffixes, and forms styayati in standard active conjugation.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines the root in the sense of 'sanghatah samhananam' (cohesion, condensation, or compact grouping). It belongs to the ai-ending set of roots within the Bhvadi class and is noted as anit.

meanings.English: to congeal, to solidify, to accumulate, to thicken into a mass
meanings.Bengali: jomat badha, ghonibhuto howa, joro howa
meanings.French: se figer, se coaguler, s'amasser, se densifier

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'śas' means to hurt, cut, or injure. In standard simple present tense (Parasmaipada), it is conjugated as 'śasati' to mean someone cuts or injures something. When used in the causative (Nic), it becomes 'śāsayati', meaning to cause someone to cut or destroy.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga (present tense active voice)
scenarios.example_english: The hunter slays the deer in the forest.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: nic pratyaya (causative active voice)
scenarios.meaning: causes to cut / causes to injure
scenarios.example_english: The king causes the enemy to be struck down.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'śasṛ' belongs to the Bhvadi class and is read in the sense of 'hiṁsā' (violence, injuring, or cutting). Being marked with an 'ṛ' it marker, it behaves systematically in derivation, forming forms like 'śasati' in the present and 'śaśāsa' in the perfect.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'śasṛ hiṁsāyām' as conveying injuring or slaughtering, noting its nominal derivation 'śastra' (a cutting weapon or instrument used for injury).

meanings.English: to injure, to hurt, to kill, to cut down

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'tij' primarily means to sharpen or make keen, and with the mandatory svarthe-san affix, it means to endure or tolerate with patience. In regular usage, it appears with the desiderative affix as 'titiksate' to express enduring hardship, while in its causative form 'tejayanti/tejayati', it means to sharpen, incite, or kindle enthusiasm.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: svarthe san-pratyaya (atmanepada)
scenarios.example_english: The wise person tolerates cold and heat patiently.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: nic-pratyaya (causative, parasmaipada)
scenarios.example_english: The teacher sharpens the intellect of the student.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'tiji' is listed in the bhvadi-gana under the gupprabhrti group with the meaning 'nisane' (sharpening/whetting) and 'ksamayam' (forbearance). By the sutra 'gup-tij-kidbhyah san', it obligatorily takes the 'san' suffix in the root sense to form 'titiksate' meaning 'ksamate' (he tolerates or endures).
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'tiji nisane' as belonging to the gupadi class taking the svarthe san affix, yielding the form 'titiksate' in the sense of enduring or forbearance, as well as regular causative formations like 'tejayati' in the sense of sharpening or exciting.

meanings.English: to sharpen, whet, endure, tolerate, bear patiently
meanings.Hindi: teja karana, dhar lagana, sahana karana
meanings.Bengali: dhar dewa, teja kora, sojhyo kora

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'mruc' primarily expresses motion, specifically descending, setting, or going into hiding. In its basic active form (Parasmaipada), it describes the subject moving down or setting (like the sun). In the causative form (nic), it means causing someone or something to descend or hide.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga, lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: goes down / sets / moves into hiding
scenarios.example_english: The sun sets toward the mountain.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: nic pratyaya (causative), lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: causes to set / causes to go down
scenarios.example_english: Time causes the day to decline.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti places 'mruca' under the Bhvadi class with the meaning of gati (movement/setting). It undergoes guna of the vowel 'u' to 'o' in sarvadhatuka environments, yielding forms like mrocati, amrocat, and mamroca.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'mruca gatau', associating it with downward motion, slipping away, or fading, structurally parallel to mluc and gruc.

meanings.English: to go, move, set (as the sun), disappear

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'vah' means to carry, bear, convey, or flow. In simple present active voice, it takes Parasmaipada (vahati) when someone is carrying something for another, and Atmanepada (vahate) when the action directly benefits or belongs to the carrier. When made causative with 'nic' (vahayati), it means 'makes someone carry' or 'drives/guides a cart'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga (Present Active, Parasmaipada, 3rd Person Singular)
scenarios.example_english: The horse carries the load.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga (Present Active, Atmanepada - self-benefiting action)
scenarios.example_english: He carries the burden upon his own shoulder.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (Causative, Parasmaipada, 3rd Person Singular)
scenarios.example_english: The charioteer drives the chariot.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'vaha prapane' belongs to Bhvadi and is svaritet, thus taking both Parasmaipada and Atmanepada terminations. It is anit (does not take intermediate 'i' in general non-sarvadhatuka ardhadhatuka environments). The meaning 'prapana' signifies conveying, carrying, moving an object from one location to another, or naturally flowing as in streams.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'vaha prapane' as an anit dhatu signifying transportation, carrying of loads, or leading. In reduplication and samprasarana forms (such as uvaha, uhyate), standard sandhi and phonological rules apply to the semi-vowel 'va' converting into vowel 'u'.

meanings.English: to carry, to convey, to bear, to flow
meanings.Bengali: bohon kora, boye niye jaowa, probahito howa

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'ad' means 'to eat'. In standard active voice (Parasmaipada), it describes the subject performing the act of eating. When using causative or specific prefixes, the meaning can shift to feeding or consuming fully.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga (present active third person singular)
scenarios.example_english: The boy eats a fruit.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: ṇijanta (causative present active third person singular)
scenarios.example_english: The mother feeds the child a fruit.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root ada~ is placed first in the Adadi gana with the sense of bhakṣaṇa (eating or consuming). In sarvadhatuka affixes, the augment śap is elided by 'adi-prabhṛtibhyaḥ śapaḥ' (luk), yielding forms such as atti, attaḥ, adanti. In certain non-sarvadhatuka environments, 'ghasḷ' substitution applies.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes ada~ bhakṣaṇe as the heading root of Adadi gana. The elision of vikarana śap is characteristic, and morphological changes like the dental assimilation in 'atti' (from ad + ti) define its primary conjugation.

meanings.English: to eat, to consume

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'han' fundamentally means to strike, kill, or move toward. In standard active voice (Parasmaipada), it describes directly hitting, destroying, or slaying an object. When modified with causative affixes (ṇic), it transforms into 'ghātayati', meaning to cause someone else to strike or execute.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: lat-lakara (present tense), prathama-purusha (3rd person), ekavacana, parasmaipada
scenarios.example_english: The warrior strikes the enemy.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: nic-pratyaya (causative), lat-lakara, prathama-purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: causes to be killed / causes to strike
scenarios.example_english: The king causes the wicked person to be executed.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'haṇa' belongs to the Adadi class and is read with the meaning of injury/violence (hiṃsā) and movement (gati). It is inherently Anit and takes Parasmaipada terminations under normal operation, undergoing substitution to 'vadh' or 'ghna' in specific grammatical environments.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes that 'hana hiṃsāgatyoḥ' denotes both inflicting harm/destruction and locomotion. In non-causative conjugation, it conjugates directly without intermediate Vikarana vowels in strong forms (hanti, hataḥ, ghnanti).

meanings.English: to strike, injure, kill, destroy, or go
meanings.Hindi: marna, vadh karna, chot pahunchana, jana
meanings.Bengali: aaghat kora, bodh kora, binash kora, jaoya

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'iṇ' fundamentally signifies the action of going, motion, or approaching. As an Adādi class root, it drops the intermediate conjugation sign (sap) and directly joins personal endings. When combined with prefixes (upasargas), its motion nuance shifts predictably: with 'anu' it means 'to follow', and with 'prati' it means 'to return' or 'to trust'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga, lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana (base form)
scenarios.example_english: The boy goes home.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: upasarga 'anu' + kartari prayoga, lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The disciple follows the teacher.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti specifies 'iṇ gatau' as an anit, parasmaipadi root belonging to the Adadi group. Because of its membership in Adadi, 'luk' of sap takes place. In singular strong conjugational forms (pit-pratyayas), it takes guna resulting in 'eti', 'eṣi', 'emi', whereas in weak plural forms 'yanti' occurs through the application of yan-sandhi.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin analyzes 'iṇ' under gatyartha roots, outlining its principal inflections across tenses: 'eti' in present, 'iyāya' in perfect (lit), 'etā' in periphrastic future (lut), and 'eṣyati' in simple future (lrt), emphasizing the regular phonological change before vowels.

meanings.English: to go, to move, to attain, to approach

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'duh' belongs to the Adadi class (Class 2) and fundamentally means to milk, draw out, or extract. As an Ubhayapada and Dvikarmaka (doubly transitive) verb, it can take both Parasmaipada and Atmanepada endings and govern two accusative objects (the source from which extraction happens and the substance extracted). In Parasmaipada, it highlights the general act of milking, while in Atmanepada, it often signifies milking for one's own benefit.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana, parasmaipada
scenarios.example_english: The cowherd milks milk from the cow.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana, atmanepada
scenarios.example_english: The farmer milks the cow at his home for his own use.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti notes 'duha prapurane' as an Adadi Ubhayapadi Anit root. It explains that 'prapurana' denotes the drawing forth or full yielding of nourishing fluid like milk. In phonological derivations, the initial 'd' becomes 'dh' (dhatosthadha-gho-dhoh) when followed by consonant affixes, yielding forms like dogdhi, dugdhah, duhanti, and atmanepada forms like dugdhe, dhukshe.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin analyzes 'duh' as conveying the release and accumulation of milk or essential essence. He highlights its dvikarmaka nature governed by the sutra 'akathitam ca', allowing both the cow (avadhi) and the milk (pradhana-karma) to take the dvitiya vibhakti (accusative case).

meanings.English: to milk, extract, yield, draw forth
meanings.Chinese: ji nai, zha qu, huo de

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'bhā' belongs to the 2nd conjugation (Adādi gaṇa) and means 'to shine' or 'to look splendid/appear radiant'. Because it is in the 2nd group, it attaches personal endings directly to the root in the present tense without inserting intermediate 'a' (śap-luk), giving forms like 'bhāti' (it shines) and 'bhānti' (they shine). When made causative (ṇic), it changes to 'bhāsayati' meaning 'causes to illuminate' or 'makes bright'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga (Present tense active / Laṭ Lakāra, 3rd person singular)
scenarios.example_english: The moon shines in the sky.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative form (Ṇic-pratyaya, Kartari Prayoga)
scenarios.example_english: The sun illuminates the entire world.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: Bhā dīptau. Dīptiḥ prakāśaḥ. Adādiḥ parasmaipadī anit. Śapo luk. Bhāti, bhātaḥ, bhānti. Babhau, babhatuḥ, babhuḥ. Bhātā, bhāsyati. Abhāt, abhātām, abhan.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Bhā dīptau. Prakāśane vartate. Anudātta-itvat anit. Luk śapaḥ. Bhāti, bhānti. Babhau. Bhāyāt, bheyāt.

meanings.English: to shine, illuminate, appear radiant, look bright
meanings.Bengali: alokito howa, shobha pawa, deep ti pawa

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'vid' means 'to know' or 'to understand'. In simple present tense (Lat lakara), it drops the intermediate conjugational vowel -a- because it belongs to the Adadi group (Class 2), giving forms like 'vetti' (he knows). It can also take ancient perfect endings in the present tense to form 'veda' (he knows). When made causative (Nic), it becomes 'vedayati' meaning 'makes someone know' or 'informs/teaches'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara (simple present), prathama-purusha eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The student knows the truth.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic pratyaya), Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara
scenarios.example_english: The teacher informs the student about righteous duty.
