vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti analyzes 'vida jnane' as an Adadi Parasmaipada root denoting perception, awareness, and direct cognition. In the present tense, it uniquely allows the replacement of standard personal endings with the affix forms of Lit lakara (via 'vidah kurvan parasya'), generating alternate synonymous forms like 'veda', 'vittah', 'vidanti'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes under Kshiratarangini that 'vida jnane' refers to knowledge and consciousness. It takes Guna of the penultimate vowel in Sarvadhatuka strong affixes (vetti), while weak affixes retain the short vowel (vittah, vidanti). It is classified as an Adadi root with set character in secondary derivations.

meanings.English: to know, to understand, to perceive, to experience
meanings.Bengali: jana, upalabdhi kara, gyan lav kara

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'su' belongs to the Adadi class and inherently takes Atmanepada endings to denote bringing forth life or giving birth. In its simple form, it expresses the natural act of giving birth, whereas adding prefixes like 'pra' (as in prasute) emphasizes the active process of producing, generating, or procreating.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Lat (Present Indicative), Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana, Atmanepada
scenarios.meaning: She gives birth to / brings forth
scenarios.example_english: The mother gives birth to a son.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Upasarga 'pra' + Lat, Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana, Atmanepada
scenarios.example_english: The earth yields abundant crops.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'shung' is listed in the Adadi gana with the semantic value of pranigarbhavimocana (parturition/childbirth). Because of the it marker 'nga', it is exclusively Atmanepadi. As an Adadi root, it drops the intervening sap affix in sarvadhatuka contexts and undergoes guna/uvang substitution where morphologically applicable.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'shung praniprasave', defining it as the physical delivery of offspring or yielding creation. It is characterized by anit status in ardhadhatuka operations and follows standard non-thematic Adadi conjugation patterns.

meanings.English: to give birth, bring forth, deliver, produce
meanings.Hindi: janma dena, prasava hona, paida karna

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'prā' belongs to the 2nd conjugation (Adādi gaṇa) and primarily means 'to fill', 'to make full', or 'to satisfy'. In regular active voice (Parasmaipada), it describes a subject directly filling a container or satisfying a desire. When used with causative affixes (ṇic), it changes to mean 'to cause someone or something to fill or be fulfilled'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Laṭ (Present Tense), Kartari prayoga, Prathama puruṣa, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The water fills the pot.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Ṇic) Laṭ, Kartari prayoga, Prathama puruṣa, Ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: causes to fill / makes full through another
scenarios.example_english: The mother causes the child to fill the vessel.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'prā pūraṇe' is categorized under Adādi gaṇa as an anit, parasmaipadī root. It forms 'prāti', 'prātaḥ', 'prānti' in the present tense by elision of the 'śap' vikarana. In the perfect tense (liṭ), it forms 'paprau', 'paprathuḥ', 'papruḥ'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'prā' in the semantic sense of pūraṇa (filling up or completing). It retains its long vowel in sārvadhātuka strong forms and drops the vikarana per the characteristic luk rule of Adādi.

meanings.English: to fill, to replenish, to complete

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'ik' means to remember, recall, or contemplate. Belonging to the Adadi class (class 2), it drops the typical intermediate -a- vowel before standard Parasmaipada endings. When someone remembers a fact, teacher, or instruction, this root conveys that mental recall.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Lat lakara, prathama-purusha ekavacana (Present tense, 3rd person singular)
scenarios.example_english: The practitioner remembers the mantra taught by the spiritual teacher.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Lat lakara, prathama-purusha bahuvacana (Present tense, 3rd person plural)
scenarios.example_english: The students recall the ancient instruction.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: ika smarane. ayam anudatta-it parasmaipadi adadishu pathitaḥ. ikah kit-tvat gunabhavah kvacit, kintu sarvadhatuke 'iṇo yaṇ' ityadikam apekshya roopani prasidhyanti.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: ika smarane. smaranam anusamdhanam. adadih anit parasmaipadi. eti itah yanti ityadi roopani bhavanti.

meanings.English: to remember, to recall, to mind

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'vā' primarily means 'to blow' or 'to move' (used often for wind) and secondarily 'to diffuse scent' or 'to perceive odor'. Because it belongs to the second class (Adādi gaṇa), the present tense conjugational suffix (śap) is dropped, so the personal endings attach directly to the root (e.g., vā + ti = vāti). When used causatively with the suffix 'ṇic' and 'puk' augment, it takes the form 'vāpayati' or 'vāyayati', meaning 'causes to blow' or 'fans'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Laṭ lakāra (Present Tense), Prathama Puruṣa, Ekavacana, Kartari prayoga (Direct root without śap)
scenarios.example_english: The gentle breeze blows softly.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (ṇic pratyaya with puk-āgama), Laṭ lakāra, Prathama Puruṣa, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The attendant fans (causes breeze to blow) with a fan.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: vā gatigandhanayoḥ. Adādiḥ parasmaipadī aniṭ. 'gatiḥ' prasaraṇaṃ calanaṃ ca, 'gandhanaṃ' tu sauśīlya-sūcana-hiṃsā-sauganvhyādayaḥ. Śapo luk. Vāti, vātaḥ, vānti. Lit-prayoge 'vavau'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: vā gatigandhanayoḥ. Adādau parasmaipadiṣu paṭhitaḥ. Vāti vātaḥ. Gandhane vartamāno'yaṃ sakarmakaḥ, gatau tu akarmakaḥ. Aniṭtvena ktādiviṣaye 'vātaḥ' iti rūpam.

meanings.English: to blow, to move, to diffuse fragrance, to emit scent
meanings.Bengali: boye jaowa, batash boha, sugondho chhorano

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'sva' means to go (gati) or to move with agitation/pant/sound (vidhvanana). In the Adadi gana, it is conjugated in Parasmaipada without an intermediate thematic vowel in basic tenses (lati snoti/svati). When converted to causative (nic) form, it expresses causing someone or something to move swiftly or agitate.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Simple present indicative (lat, prathama-purusha, eka-vacana)
scenarios.example_english: The horse moves swiftly.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative present (nic, lat, prathama-purusha, eka-vacana)
scenarios.example_english: The wind causes the dry leaves to stir.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti analyzes 'sva gatividhvananayoh' under the Adadi-varga as an anit Parasmaipada root denoting both physical motion (gati) and distinct sound or agitated vibration (vidhvanana). In sarvadhatuka affixes, special phonological sandhi operations apply.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes in Kshiratarangini that 'sva' signifies directional motion accompanied by rapid oscillation, panting, or rushing sound (vidhvananam gatikshepah). It belongs to the akaranta subgroup of the second class.

meanings.English: to go, to move swiftly, to pant, to agitate with sound
meanings.Kannada: calisu, vegavagi hodu, sphurisu, shabda madu
meanings.Telugu: velluta, vegamu ga kadaluta, shabdamu cheyuta
meanings.Tamil: selluthal, viraivaga selgai, osaiyudan asaiyum nilai
meanings.Hindi: jana, teji se chalna, hilna, shabda karna
meanings.Bengali: gamana kara, druta chala, shabda sahita chalana
meanings.German: sich schnell bewegen, rauschen, keuchen, gehen
meanings.French: se deplacer rapidement, bruire, haleter, aller
meanings.Russian: dvigat'sya bystro, shumet', tyazhelo dyshat', idti
meanings.Chinese: kuaisu yidong, qichuan, fachu xiangsheng, qianwang

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'pā' belongs to the Adadi class (class 2) and signifies protecting, guarding, or governing. In simple present tense (Parasmaipada), it conjugates directly with suffixes without an intermediate thematic vowel 'a' (unlike Bhvadi roots), giving forms like 'pāti' (he/she protects). When transformed into the causative (Nic), it becomes 'pālayati', conveying 'causes to be protected' or 'rules/sustains'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: lat lakāra, prathama puruṣa, eka vacana (kartari prayoga)
scenarios.example_english: The king protects the citizens.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: ṇic pratyaya (causative), lat lakāra, prathama puruṣa, eka vacana
scenarios.example_english: The king upholds (sustains) righteousness.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: Madhaviya Dhatuvritti notes that 'pā rakṣaṇe' is an anidit, aniṭ root of the adādi class. Unlike 'pā pāne' (bhvādi, which takes piba- substitution in sarvadhatuka), this root retains its original 'pā' base throughout sarvadhatuka affixes in the sense of preservation and guarding, yielding 'pāti', 'pātaḥ', 'pānti'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin in Kshiratarangini explains 'pā rakṣaṇe' as an adādi root taking direct personal endings. He emphasizes the distinct semantic boundary from 'pā pāne' (to drink), noting that 'pā' preserves its vowel lengthening and does not undergo the pib-ādeśa rule in the meaning of rakṣaṇa (protection).

meanings.English: to protect, guard, preserve, defend

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'lā' fundamentally signifies the act of taking, receiving, or grasping an object. Because it is in the Adadi gana, it drops the standard conjugation sign 'a' (sap-luk), resulting directly in forms like 'lāti' (he/she takes) in the active present tense (Parasmaipada). When combined with causative affixes (nic), it changes from simply taking to causing someone else to take or accept something.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (Active Voice, Lat Lakara, Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana)
scenarios.example_english: The boy takes the book from the teacher's hand.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic-pratyaya, Lat Lakara, Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana)
scenarios.meaning: causes to take / makes one receive
scenarios.example_english: The father makes the son take the sweet.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: Madhaviya Dhatuvritti classifies 'lā ādāne' as an anit, anudātta Parasmaipada root of the Adādi gaṇa. The semantic field 'ādāna' denotes receiving, accepting, or appropriating ('ādānam grahaṇam parigraho vā'). Due to the elision of the affix 'śap' by 'adiprabhṛtibhyaḥ śapaḥ', the root attaches endings directly: lāti, lātaḥ, lanti.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin states 'lā ādāne grahaṇe', glossing it as receiving or holding. He highlights the anit character of the root across classical derivations (e.g., participial lātaḥ) and remarks on its straightforward non-guna Adadi paradigm.

meanings.English: to take, to receive, to grasp, to obtain

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'dā' (dāp) belongs to the Adadi class and signifies the act of cleansing, pruning, or purifying. In simple terms, it means to clear away impurities, weeds, or unwanted parts from an object. It directly takes an accusative object (the item being cleansed or pruned) in standard active voice.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga (active voice, present tense, 3rd person singular)
scenarios.example_english: The farmer weeds the grass in the field.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: ṇic-pratyaya (causative active voice, present tense, 3rd person singular)
scenarios.meaning: causes to cleanse / causes to prune
scenarios.example_english: The master makes the servant prune the field.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: dāp śodhane. dāp iti pāṭhaḥ ukāra-lopa-niṣedhārthaḥ. śodhanaṁ chedanaṁ pavitrīkaraṇaṁ vā. luk-vikaraṇaḥ parasmaipadī aniṭ.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: dāp śodhane. dāti dātaḥ dānti. śodhanaṁ nirmalīkaraṇaṁ lavanaṁ vā.

meanings.English: to purify, cleanse, prune, cut away

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'pa' in the Adadi gana means 'to protect' or 'to guard'. Unlike the Bhvadi root 'pa' which means 'to drink' and changes into 'piba-', this Adadi root retains its form directly taking class-2 endings without the intermediate 'a' (sap-luk), conjugating as 'pati', 'patah', 'panti'. When used with causative or voice markers, it conveys protecting, ruling, or guarding someone or something.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: lat-lakara, prathama-purusha, eka-vacana, parasmaipada
scenarios.example_english: The king protects the citizens righteously.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: nic-pratyaya (causative/svarthe), lat-lakara, prathama-purusha, eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The father protects and takes care of the family.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: pa rakshane. Adadi parasmaipadi anit. Shapah luk. Pati patah panti. 'Pati rakshati' iti arthavisheshah. Pano luk (7.3.37 iti anivaryatvat) akarantatvat yathasvam rupa-siddhih.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: pa rakshane. Adadih. Pati, patah, panti. Pane tu bhvadau pibatih, iha tu rakshane patih ity ubhayor bhedah.

meanings.English: to protect, guard, govern, rule

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'ksnu' means to sharpen, whet, or hone weapons and tools. In active voice (Parasmaipada), it describes an agent directly grinding or sharpening an instrument. When combined with the causative suffix (-nic-), it means making someone sharpen a blade or tool.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Active Voice (Kartari Prayoga), Present Indicative (Lat lakara), Parasmaipada 3rd person singular
scenarios.example_english: The blacksmith sharpens the weapon on the whetstone.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic), Present Indicative (Lat lakara), Parasmaipada 3rd person singular
scenarios.meaning: causes to sharpen or gets sharpened
scenarios.example_english: The warriors get their swords sharpened by the craftsman.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'ksnu' belongs to Adadi gana and is defined in 'tejane' (sharpening/whetting). Being an u-karanta adadi root, it takes vriddhi before sarvadhatuka strong affixes (such as tip, tas, jhi) by the rule 'arto vriddhir luk ca' or standard guna/vriddhi mechanics, yielding forms like ksṇauti, ksṇutaḥ, ksṇuvanti. It is anit.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'ksnu tejane' as a monosyllabic u-ending root signifying the act of keen sharpening or providing a fine edge. In the reduplicated perfect (Lit), it forms cuksnāva / cuksnūve depending on pada usage in secondary formations.

meanings.English: to sharpen, whet, hone, grind, make keen

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'pā' belongs to the Adadi class (class 2) and specifically means 'to protect' or 'to guard' (distinct from the Bhvadi root pā which means 'to drink'). In standard active voice (Parasmaipada), it forms 'pāti' (he/she protects). When used with causative or passive affixes, it indicates causing someone to protect or being protected respectively.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: lat lakara (present tense), prathama-purusha (3rd person), ekavacana (singular), parasmaipada
scenarios.example_english: The king protects the citizens righteously.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: nic-pratyaya (causative/extended secondary base), lat lakara, prathama-purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The father always protects and nurtures the son.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: pā rakṣaṇe - adādi parasmaipadī aniṭ. luk-vikaraṇa-bhāvaḥ. pāti, pātaḥ, pānti. apāt, apātām, apan.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: pā rakṣaṇe - pāti bhuvanaṃ hariḥ. adāditvāt śapo luk. rakṣaṇārthe'yaṃ dhātuḥ.

meanings.English: to protect, to guard, to preserve

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'vā' primarily signifies blowing (movement of wind or air) and diffusing fragrance or scent. In the active voice (Parasmaipada), it describes natural motion such as the blowing of a breeze. When prefixed with preverbs like 'pra-' or 'nir-', it denotes blowing forcefully or being extinguished, respectively.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: lat-lakāra (present indicative), prathama-puruṣa, eka-vacana, parasmaipada
scenarios.example_english: The gentle breeze blows softly.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: upasarga 'nir' + lat-lakāra (extinction / going out)
scenarios.example_english: The lamp goes out due to the wind.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti explains 'vā gatigandhanayoḥ' as functioning in two semantic domains: 'gati' (movement, typically of air) and 'gandhana' (injury, revealing, or scent diffusion). As an Adadi root, it drops the intervening sap affix (luk) in Sarvadhatuka conjugations, yielding forms like vāti, vātaḥ, vānti.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes in Kshiratarangini that 'vā' is anit and parasmaipadi. The sense of 'gandhana' implies diffusing odor or fragrance (gandhasūcane). In past participial formation, with the kta pratyaya, it takes the form 'vātaḥ' (blown) by special nipatana rules.

meanings.English: to blow, to move as wind, to diffuse fragrance, to emit scent
meanings.Bengali: batasa baha, boye jaoya, sugandha charano

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'khyā' means 'to tell', 'to narrate', or 'to proclaim'. When used in its regular transitive sense, it denotes expressing or describing a fact or story. In causative (ṇijanta) formations, it means causing someone to proclaim or making something well known (renowned).

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga, lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana (parasmaipada)
scenarios.example_english: The sage narrates the story.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: karmani prayoga with upasaraga 'ā', lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The text is recounted in detail by Vyasa.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: khyāñ prakathane - ayaṃ ādānikaḥ ubhayapadī aniṭ sakarmakaśca. prakathanaṃ prakaṭīkaraṇapūrvakaṃ kathanam. asya ca chādayaterapratyaye cakṣiṅaḥ sthāne 'khyāñ' ityādeśa-vidhānepi viśeṣaprayogāḥ siddhyanti.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: khyāñ prakathane - khyāti khyāte. prakathanam vistarābhidhānam prakaṭīkaraṇaṃ vā. luk ślukaraṇeṣu ādānikatvam.

meanings.English: to tell, narrate, declare, proclaim, make known
meanings.Hindi: batanā, kahanā, prakhyāt karnā, varnan karnā

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'rud' belongs to the Adadi class and means to weep or shed tears. Uniquely in the present tense, it adds an 'i' sound before consonant endings (like roditi instead of roddhi). When used in the causative form (rodayati), the meaning shifts from 'crying oneself' to 'making someone else cry'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana (active voice)
scenarios.example_english: The child cries out of hunger.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: nic pratyaya (causative), lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: causes to weep / makes someone cry
scenarios.example_english: Sorrow makes everyone cry.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: rudi~r aśruvimocane. adādiḥ parasmaibhāṣā. 'rudādibhyaḥ sārvadhātuke' iti valādyoḥ sārvadhātukayoḥ iḍāgamo bhavati. roditi, ruditaḥ, rudanti.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: rudi~r aśruvimocane. roditi, ruroda, roditā, rodiṣyati. rudāditvād iṭ. guṇaprāptau roditīti rūpam sidhyati.

meanings.English: to weep, to cry, to shed tears

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'prā' means 'to fill' or 'to make full'. In the Adādi gaṇa, it directly takes verbal endings without an intervening vowel in simple present tense (e.g., prāti = fills). When used with a causative suffix (ṇic), it forms prāpayati/pūrayati, meaning 'causes someone or something to fill'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga (active voice), laṭ lakāra (present tense), prathama puruṣa, ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The cloud fills the water reservoir.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: laṅ lakāra (past imperfect), prathama puruṣa, ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The sun filled the universe with light.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'prā pūraṇe' is an anit parasmaipadi root belonging to the Adādi gaṇa. Being an ākārānta root, it retains its direct root structure in sārvadhātuka affixes (e.g., prāti, prātaḥ, prānti). In the liṭ lakāra, it forms paprau, papratuḥ, papruḥ.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines 'prā pūraṇe' as denoting the action of filling or satiating (pūraṇam āpyāyanam). In luṅ (aorist), it takes the sici vṛddhi forms like aprāsīt or the parasmaipada luk-substitutions.

meanings.English: to fill, to satiate, to complete

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The verbal root 'śās' primarily means to instruct, govern, teach, or advise. In its basic Parasmaipada form, it indicates directing, advising, or ruling over subjects. When combined with the prefix 'āṅ' (ā-śās), the voice switches to Ātmanepada to convey wishing, blessing, or hoping.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara (present indicative), prathama-purusha, eka-vacana without prefixes
scenarios.example_english: The king governs the citizens righteously.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga with prefix 'āṅ' triggering Ātmanepada, Lat lakara, prathama-purusha, eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The mother wishes for the well-being of her son.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti clarifies 'śāsu anuśiṣṭau' as instructing, advising, or commanding (śikṣaṇam ājñāpanaṃ vā). It highlights key morphophonemic rules such as 'śāsa id aṅhaloḥ', where the radical 'ā' changes to 'i' before consonant-initial weak affixes and the aṅ-aorist, yielding forms like 'śiṣṭaḥ' and 'aśiṣat'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin in Kshiratarangini notes that 'anuśiṣṭi' denotes disciplined guidance and governing (praśāsanam). It emphasizes the transformation of the sibilants and the special third-person plural inflection 'śāsati' under the rule 'śāsa ubhayeṣām'.

meanings.English: to instruct, to govern, to command, to teach, to punish
meanings.Hindi: shasan karna, aadesh dena, sikhana, danda dena
meanings.Bengali: shashon kora, upadesh deoa, shiksha deoa, dondo deoa

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'snu' means to ooze, drip, or trickle out. In the basic present tense, it directly describes a liquid trickling or dripping on its own (snoti). When used with a causative affix (Nic), it shifts meaning to causing liquid to drip or flow forth (snavayati / snavyayati).

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga (active present tense, 3rd person singular, Lat lakara)
scenarios.example_english: Sap trickles from the tree.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: nic pratyaya (causative present tense)
scenarios.example_english: The mother yields milk.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The author specifies 'snu prasrave' as an anit, parasmaipadi root belonging to the Adadi class. It undergoes guna substitution in sarvadhatuka strong affixes (e.g., snoti, snutaḥ, snavanti) and denotes the natural outflow or dripping of fluids.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin analyzes 'snu' under the Adadi list indicating 'prasravaṇa' (oozing or trickling). He points out the dental 's' replacement from initial murdhanya 'ṣ' per 'dhatvadeh sah sah' and notes vowel changes before various tense-mood affixes.

meanings.English: to ooze, to trickle, to drip, to flow forth

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'rā' belongs to the Adadi group (class 2) and fundamentally means 'to give' or 'to bestow'. In active voice (Parasmaipada), it attaches verb endings directly to the stem because the intermediate affix 'śap' is dropped. In the causative form with the affix 'ṇic', the augment 'puk' is added to produce 'rāpayati', meaning 'causes someone to give'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: lat lakāra (present tense), prathama puruṣa, eka-vacana, parasmaipada
scenarios.example_english: The deity bestows a boon upon the devotee.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: ṇic pratyaya (causative), lat lakāra, prathama puruṣa, eka-vacana
scenarios.meaning: Causes to give / Makes someone bestow
scenarios.example_english: The king causes the treasurer to give wealth.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: rā dāne. adādiḥ parasmaipadī aniṭ. rāti, rātaḥ, rānti. ādantatvāt śapo luk. arāt, arātām, aruḥ iti lani.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: rā dāne. rāti dravyam. dānakriyāyām vartate. adāditvāt śapo luk bhavati.

meanings.English: To give, bestow, grant, yield

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'kshu' belongs to the Adadi gana and means 'to sound' or specifically 'to sneeze'. Because it belongs to the 2nd class of verbs, it takes direct personal endings without the thematic vowel 'a' in the strong forms (taking vriddhi like 'kshauti'). As an intransitive verb, it does not govern a direct object.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Lat lakara (present tense), prathama-purusha (3rd person), ekavacana (singular), Parasmaipada
scenarios.meaning: He / she sneezes or makes a sound
scenarios.example_english: Due to the touch of cold wind, the child sneezes.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (causative), Lat lakara (present tense), 3rd person singular
scenarios.example_english: Black pepper dust makes everyone sneeze.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti records 'kshu shabde' under the Adadi gana. In Sarvadhatuka strong forms, it takes guna or vriddhi leading to forms such as 'kshauti', dual 'kshutah', plural 'kshuvanti' due to 'uvang' adesha before vowels. It is anit in Ardhadhatuka formations.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'kshu shabde kshavane ca', establishing both sounding and the physiological act of sneezing as primary imports. It is aniṭ and conjugates like 'ru' in Parasmaipada.

meanings.English: To sneeze, to sound, to cough

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'śās' fundamentally means to teach, command, rule, or discipline. In the basic present tense, it takes Parasmaipada endings with special stem alterations (such as becoming 'śāsti' in singular and 'śiṣ-' before certain consonants). When prefixed with 'ā' and used in the sense of wishing or praying, it generally shifts to Atmanepada ('āśāste'). When used in the causative form ('śāsayati'), it means to cause someone to govern or give instruction.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat-lakara (Present tense), Prathama-purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The king rules the kingdom righteously.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Upasarga 'ā' + Atmanepada, Lat-lakara, Prathama-purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The mother wishes for the well-being of her son.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'śāsu' belongs to Adadi Gana and denotes 'anuśiṣṭi' (instruction, correction, governance). Paninian sutras trigger specific changes: 'śāsa id aṅhaloḥ' (6.4.34) causes the vowel 'ā' to become 'i' before consonant-initial kit/ṅit affixes and aṅ-pratyaya, yielding forms like 'śiṣṭaḥ' and 'aśiṣat'. The root drops 'n' in the third-person plural yielding 'śāsati' under the Jakṣityādi class.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'śāsu anuśiṣṭau' as belonging to the Jakṣityādi sub-group of Adadi. It is recognized as halanta, aniṭ, and takes Parasmaipada by default. When joined with the upasarga 'ā', it takes Atmanepada in the sense of expressing a desire or benediction ('āśāsa icchāyām').

meanings.English: to instruct, command, govern, punish, or wish
meanings.Hindi: shasan karna, sikhana, aagya dena, aashirvad dena
meanings.Bengali: shason kora, upadesh dewa, adesh kora

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'kṣṇu' means to sharpen, whet, or hone a blade or weapon. As an Adādi root, it drops the intervening conjugational vowel 'a' (luk of śap), causing the root vowel 'u' to take vṛddhi before strong endings (like -ti in the singular) and regular guṇa/uv-ādeśa before weak vowel endings. In the causative (ṇijanta), it takes the meaning of causing someone to sharpen or having an instrument polished.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga (Present Indicative 3rd Person Singular, Parasmaipada, Lupta-vikaraṇa)
scenarios.example_english: The blacksmith sharpens the sword with a hard whetstone.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Ṇic, Parasmaipada, Present Indicative 3rd Person Singular)
scenarios.example_english: The warrior gets the arrows sharpened by the artisan.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: kṣṇu tejane - adādiranudāttaḥ parasmaibhāṣaḥ. tejanaṁ niśānam ucyate. kṣṇauti kṣṇutaḥ kṣṇuvanti. sārvadhātukārdhadhātukayoriti vṛddhau kṣṇautīti rūpam. hrasvasya guṇaḥ prāptaḥ 'sārvadhātukārdhadhātukayoḥ' iti guṇavṛddhī bādhate.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: kṣṇu tejane. tejanaṁ śātanākhyaṁ tīkṣṇīkaraṇam. kṣṇauti kṣṇutaḥ kṣṇuvanti. anit kṣṇāva kṣṇāvayitumityādayaḥ.

meanings.English: to sharpen, to whet, to hone, to polish
meanings.Hindi: dhār lagānā, painā karnā, tej karnā

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'sna' means to bathe, wash, or purify. In its primary form (Adadi class, Parasmaipada), it drops the vikaranana affix 'shap' via 'luk' before Sarvadhatuka suffixes, directly yielding forms like 'snati' (he/she bathes). In the causative form, it takes 'puk' augment yielding 'snapayati' (causes to bathe or bathes someone/something).

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara (present indicative), prathama-purusha eka-vachana
scenarios.example_english: The sage bathes in the river in the morning.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nich-pratyaya (causative), Lat lakara, prathama-purusha eka-vachana
scenarios.meaning: He/she gives a bath to someone / bathes an object
scenarios.example_english: The mother bathes the baby.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'shna shauce' belongs to Adadi gana and is anit. The initial dental sa takes cerebralization in upadesha (shna). Being an adanta root in Adadi, shap luk applies in Sarvadhatuka environments without stem modification in the present tense, giving snati, snatah, snanti. In causative (nich), it undergoes the rule 'arti-hri-vli-ri-knayi-kshmi-shnam puki' to obtain the puk-agama, producing snapayati.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'shna shauce' in the sense of purification and physical ablution. As an Adadi root, it is parasmaipadi and anit. In perfect (lit), it forms sasnau, sasnatuh, sasnuh. In aorist (lun), it takes the 'sich' or 'an-adeshah' variations appropriately according to Paninian sutras.

meanings.English: to bathe, to cleanse, to purify

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'kshu' means to make a sound or sneeze. Beloging to the Adadi group (2nd class), it drops the typical conjugational infix '-a-' before basic endings. In its standard active form (Parasmaipada), it describes an individual performing the act of sneezing or making a sneezing sound. When converted to the causative form (adding '-nic-'), it expresses making someone sneeze.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Active voice (Kartari Prayoga), Present tense (Lat Lakara), 3rd person singular
scenarios.meaning: He/She sneezes or makes a sound
scenarios.example_english: The boy sneezes because of dust.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Prerana / Nic-pratyaya), Present tense (Lat Lakara), 3rd person singular
scenarios.example_english: The strong odor causes everyone to sneeze.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'kshu' is assigned the sense of 'shabde' (sound/noise, particularly sneezing). Being an anit root ending in an u-kara in the Adadi gana, the radical vowel undergoes vriddhi before sarvadhatuka strong affixes (kshauti, kshautah, kshuvanti).
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin interprets 'kshu shabde' primarily in the sense of sneezing-induced sound (kshuta). It drops the intermediate vikarana and forms its present indicative paradigm directly with primary endings: kshauti, kshutos, kshuvanti.

meanings.English: to sneeze, to make a sound

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root cakās belongs to the 2nd conjugation (Adadi Gana) and means to shine, appear radiant, or look splendid. As an intrinsically Parasmaipada root, it expresses the state of radiant shining. When used with causative affixes (Nic), it shifts from an intransitive state of shining to an active causative meaning 'to cause to shine' or 'to illuminate'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, prathama-purusha, eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The sun shines in the sky with divine radiance.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (causative), Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, prathama-purusha, eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The lamp of knowledge illuminates the entire heart.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: cakāsaṛ dīptau. adādiḥ parasmaipadaprakaraṇe paṭhitaḥ seṭ ca. cakāsti cakāstaḥ cakāsati. liṭi cakāsāñcakāra. anāsika ṛkāra it-saṃjñakaḥ. dīptir nāma prakāśaḥ śobhā ca.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: cakāsaṛ dīptau. cakāsti, cakāstaḥ, cakāsati. cakāsāñcakāra, cakāsitā. dīptir ujjvalatvaṃ prakāśanam ityarthaḥ.

meanings.English: to shine, to be bright, to illuminate, to look splendid
meanings.Bengali: ujjvala haoya, shobha paoya, alokita haoya

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'śās' belongs to the 2nd class (Adadigaṇa) and means to teach, instruct, advise, or rule over. In simple present tense (kartari parasmaipada), it conjugates irregularly as 'śāsti' in singular and 'śiṣṭaḥ' in dual because the vowel 'ā' changes to 'i' when combined with weak consonant endings. When combined with prefixes like 'anu-' (anuśāsti), it emphasizes regular discipline or systematic instruction.

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root caks belongs to the second group of verbs (Adadi gana) and takes Atmanepada endings. It fundamentally means to speak clearly or articulately, and in classical usage it often means to see, observe, or declare. In non-Sarvadhatuka tenses like the perfect or future, Paninian rules replace it with the substitute root khya.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: Caksin vyaktayam vaci. By the rule caksah khyan, in ardhadhatuka environments, it gets substituted by the root khya, retaining the semantic property of clear narration and description.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes caksing in the sense of vyaktavacana (distinct vocal expression) and darsana (seeing/beholding). He remarks upon the elision of the intermediate marker in sarvadhatuka forms like caste and cashe, noting its inherent Atmanepada character due to the anubandha ing.

meanings.English: to speak distinctly, tell, narrate, perceive, see

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'an' means to breathe, to live, or to respire. In its basic form (Parasmaipada), an extra vowel 'i' is inserted before consonant-initial endings in the present tense because it belongs to the Rudadi sub-group, producing forms like 'aniti' (he/she breathes). When combined with the prefix 'pra-', it forms 'praniti' meaning 'he lives' or 'he breathes'. In the causative form (nic), it changes to 'anayati' or 'pranayati', meaning 'to cause to breathe' or 'to revive/animate'.

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root śās belongs to the Adadi group (Class 2) and fundamentally means to instruct, discipline, or rule. In standard Parasmaipada without prefixes, it means to govern or teach (e.g., śāsti). When prefixed with the upasarga 'āṅ' and used in the Atmanepada, its meaning specifically shifts from commanding/governing to hoping, blessing, or wishing (e.g., āśāste).

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: Sayana explains 'śāsu anuśiṣṭau' as teaching, chastising, and governing. The root is aniṭ and parasmaipadi. It exhibits vowel weakening ('śās' to 'śiṣ') before kit/ṅit suffixes (e.g., śiṣṭaḥ, śiṣyaḥ) by special sutras ('śāsa id aṅhaloḥ'). In lot-lakara it uniquely derives the imperative singular form 'śādhi'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes that 'anuśiṣṭi' denotes both pedagogical guidance (upadeśa) and administrative ruling (rājya-śāsana). He highlights the peculiar paradigm alterations such as 'śāsti', dual 'śiṣṭaḥ', plural 'śāsati', and the suppletive/allomorphic imperative form 'śādhi'.

meanings.English: to instruct, to teach, to govern, to discipline

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'khyā' belongs to the second verb group (Adādi Gaṇa) and means 'to tell', 'to narrate', or 'to declare'. When used on its own or combined with prefixes (upasargas) like 'ā' (forming ākhyāti - to narrate/recount) or 'pra' (forming prakhyāti - to make well-known/celebrated), it conveys the act of speaking out clearly or making something known.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: Mādhavīya-dhātuvṛtti identifies 'khyā prakathane' in Adādi-gaṇa as an ādanta aniṭ root taking Parasmaipada endings. 'Prakathanam' is explained as detailed exposition and communication (prakaṭatayā kathanam). In the non-conjugational tenses (ārdhadhātuka), the root undergoes specific morphological replacements and operations governed by sūtras such as 'khyañ ādeśa' where applicable.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kṣīrataraṅgiṇī defines 'khyā prakathane' as the act of speaking forth, recounting, or declaring publicly. It highlights that the root maintains its vowel structure in basic Adādi conjugation (khyāti, khyātaḥ, khyanti) and frequently combines with prefixes like ā, sam, and vi to express narration, enumeration, and renown.

meanings.English: to tell, to narrate, to declare, to make known

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'vā' belongs to the Adadi group (Class 2) and fundamentally means 'to blow' or 'to diffuse fragrance'. In Class 2, the conjugational sign (śap) is dropped, so personal endings attach directly to the root, forming 'vāti' (it blows). When used in the causative (ṇic), it acquires the augment 'puk' to become 'vāpayati', shifting the meaning to 'causes to blow' or 'fans'.

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root śās belongs to the 2nd class (Adādi-gaṇa) and means to instruct, discipline, or govern. As an Adādi root, it takes verbal terminations directly after the root without an intermediate vowel 'a' in strong forms, and undergoes a vowel change from 'ā' to 'i' (śās -> śiṣ) before consonant-initial weak affixes (yielding forms like śiṣṭaḥ). In the active voice (Parasmaipada), it expresses the act of teaching, commanding, or ruling.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root śāsu anuśiṣṭau belongs to Adādi-gaṇa and is aniṭ. Madhava highlights its unique phonological behavior: under Paninian rule 'śāsa id aṅhaloḥ' (6.4.34), the vowel 'ā' is replaced with short 'i' before aṅ-pratyaya and consonant-initial kniti affixes (e.g., śiṣṭaḥ, śiṣanti vs. śāsati). With the preverb 'āṅ', it optionally or idiomatically assumes Ātmanepada in the sense of wishing/blessing (āśāste).
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes that śāsu is employed in the sense of discipline, governance (anuśāsana), and instruction. He observes the allomorphic reduction of the root to 'śiṣ-' before weak consonant-initial sarvadhatuka and ardhadhatuka affixes, forming standard derivatives such as śiṣya, śāstra, and śāsana.

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'ās' belongs to the Adadi group (class 2) and means 'to sit', 'to remain', or 'to dwell'. It is strictly used in Atmanepada, where personal endings attach directly to the root without an intervening vowel (e.g., āste). When combined with the causative suffix (ṇic), it shifts to Parasmaipada/Atmanepada as 'āsayati' to mean 'causes someone to sit' or 'seats someone'.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti defines 'āsa upaveśane' as an anit, Atmanepada root of Adadi gana. In Sarvadhatuka tenses, the Sap vikarana is dropped by 'adiprabhṛtibhyaḥ śapaḥ' resulting in forms like 'āste', 'āsāte', 'āsate'. In lit lakara, it compulsorily takes the am-pratyaya (ām-pratyayavat), yielding 'āsāñcakre'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes under 'āsa upaveśane' that the root denotes the physical act of sitting or maintaining a static posture. Being anit and svara-adi, it exhibits regular sandhi with personal terminations, forming 'āsiṣṭa' in lun and 'āsiṣyate' in lrit.

meanings.English: to sit, dwell, abide, remain

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'śās' (typically used with the prefix 'ā-') means to wish, bless, or pray for good fortune. Being an Adādi gana Ātmanepada root, the verbal terminations attach directly to the base without adding intermediate thematic vowels, expressing a personal wish or benevolent prayer.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'śāsaँ icChāyām' is read in the Adādi class as an Ātmanepadī root. It drops its nasal/vowel modifications according to standard Adādi rules and follows aniṭ inflection in non-sarvadhātuka environments.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes that 'śās' here carries the specific sense of 'icChā' (desire, seeking, praying for). Governed by the Adādi luk-vikaraṇa mechanism, it forms 'āśāste' in the singular and 'āśāsate' in the plural, retaining its unaccented aniṭ status.

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'ya' belongs to the Adadi class (Class 2) and fundamentally means 'to go' or 'to reach/attain'. Because it belongs to the second conjugation, verb endings attach directly to the root in the present tense (e.g., ya + ti = yati) without adding an extra thematic vowel 'a'. When used with prefixes like 'pra', it means 'to set out', and in the causative form with affix 'nic' (yapayati), it shifts the meaning to 'to cause to go' or 'to spend/pass time'.

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'ir' primarily means to move, rise, or shake. Because it is an Atmanepada root of the second class (Adadi), it directly takes personal endings without an intermediate 'a' vowel in strong positions (forming 'irte'). When used with prefixes like 'pra-' or when combined with the causative suffix (-aya-), it shifts into the meaning of 'urging', 'motivating', or 'sending forward' (prerayati).

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'ira' belongs to the Adadi class and is read in the sense of motion and vibration (gatau kampane ca). Being anit and Atmanepadi, it undergoes lengthening/guna mechanisms before sarvadhatuka affixes, yielding standard forms such as irte, irate, and iramcakre in literature.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin analyzes 'ira' as expressive of going (gati) and agitation or trembling (kampa). He highlights its lack of an it-augment (anittva) and details its morphological transitions when joined with directional upasargas like pra, sam, and ud.

meanings.English: to move, to go, to shake, to rise

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'īś' belongs to the Adadi class and is conjugated exclusively in the Atmanepada. It means to rule, possess mastery over, govern, or command. Because it is in the Adadi gana, verb endings attach directly to the root in the present tense without inserting the intermediary 'a' (sap) vowel, resulting in forms like 'īṣṭe' (he/she rules).

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti designates īśaँ under the meaning aiśvarya (sovereignty, dominion, and mastery). It notes the retention of Atmanepada by default. By the elision of the sap vikarana (luk) due to being an Adadi dhatu, the combination of root final palatal 'ś' followed by dental 'ta' undergoes transformation via 'vrajabraśca...' to cerebral 'ṣ' and 'ṣṭhutva', yielding 'īṣṭe'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin analyzes īśaँ aiśvarye as a root expressive of absolute lordship and governance. He highlights the genitive or accusative government in syntactic constructions involving sovereignty, observing the phonological development into īṣṭe, īśāte, īśate in the present tense.

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root jakṣ belongs to the Adadi group (Class 2) and carries two distinct meanings: eating (when transitive) and laughing (when intransitive). Because it heads the special jakṣityādi group, its third-person plural present form ends in -ati rather than -anti (for example, jakṣati instead of jakṣanti).

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: jakṣa bhakṣahasayoḥ. This root is placed at the head of the jakṣityādi group. Under Paninian sutra 'jakṣityādibhyaḥ ṣaḍbhyaḥ' (6.1.6), roots of this class obtain abhyasta designation, triggering 'adabhyastāt' (7.1.4) to replace the plural affix 'jhi' with 'at', resulting in 'jakṣati'. It functions transitively in the sense of eating (bhakṣaṇa) and intransitively in the sense of laughing (hasana).
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes: 'jakṣa bhakṣahasane'. Leading the six roots starting with jakṣ, it takes special reduplicated behavior (abhyasta-saṃjñā) without an actual reduplication step in the present stem. Its primary usages encompass physical mastication and vocal mirth.

meanings.English: to eat, to laugh, to consume

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'srA' belongs to the Adadi group (Class 2) and signifies clumsy, improper, or blameworthy motion (such as stumbling or wandering aimlessly). Because it drops the intervening vowel -a- (shap-luk), basic endings attach directly to the root in Parasmaipada (e.g., srAti). When converted to causative (Nic), it uses the augment puk to form srApayati, meaning 'causes to wander or move awkwardly'.

vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin categorizes 'srA' alongside other AkArAnta roots in Adadi indicating contemptible movement. It is treated as anit in primary conjugations and follows standard rules for roots ending in long -A.

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root vevī belongs to the Adadi group and is used exclusively in Atmanepada due to the marker letter 'ṅ'. It carries multiple potential meanings including going, pervading, conceiving/giving birth, glowing/desiring, throwing/resting, and consuming. As an Adadi root, it connects directly to tense endings without taking the intermediate thematic vowel 'a', taking forms like vevīte in the present tense.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root vevīṅ is listed under Adadi-gana with multiple semantic connotations: gati (movement), vyāpti (pervasion), prajana (generation/bearing), kānti (beauty/splendor/desire), asana (hurling/sitting), and khādana (eating). It is ṅit, making it obligatorily Atmanepadi, and behaves analogously to dīdhīṅ in dropping or altering semi-vocalic properties under special Paninian sutras like 'dīdhīvevīṭām'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes vevīṅ as a root conveying multi-directional actions (anekārthatva) including moving, pervasive presence, and consuming. It conjugates without the shab-vikarana (luk) in the non-conjugational or Sarvadhatuka environments, taking standard Atmanepada personal terminations.

meanings.English: to go, pervade, conceive/bear, shine/desire, throw, eat
meanings.Hindi: gati karnā, vyāpta honā, janma denā, kānti/icchā honā, khānā
meanings.Bengali: gaman karā, byāpta haoyā, janma deoyā, dīpti pāoyā, khāoyā

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'svap' belongs to the Adadi class (specifically the Rudadi group), which inserts the augment 'iṭ' before sarvadhatuka consonant affixes (forming 'svapiti' instead of 'svapti'). In its primary form, it is intransitive and means 'to sleep'. When the causative suffix 'ṇic' is added, it forms 'svāpayati', turning the verb into a transitive action meaning 'to put to sleep' or 'to lull'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Rudadi augment 'iṭ' in Lat lakara (present tense, 3rd person singular, Parasmaipada)
scenarios.example_english: The child sleeps on the bed.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative affix (ṇic) with vriddhi vowel gradation
scenarios.meaning: causes to sleep / puts to sleep
scenarios.example_english: The mother puts the baby to sleep.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti explains 'ñiṣvap śaye' within the Rudadi sub-division of the Adadi class. It details the operation of the sutra 'rudādibhyah sārvadhātuke' which enjoins the augment 'iṭ' before valadi consonant-beginning sarvadhatuka endings, deriving 'svapiti'. It also notes the samprasarana changes in past participial and weak environments ('suptaḥ', 'suṣvāpa').
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin in Kshiratarangini clarifies the it-markers: initial 'ñi' indicates the formation of action nouns with 'kta' without gender change rules, while 'ṣ' converts to dental 's' via dhatvadeḥ sah. It highlights the semantic boundary of 'śaye' as quiet slumber or rest, and lists samprasarana phonological operations occurring across non-guna formations.

meanings.English: to sleep, slumber, repose

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'pra' belongs to the Adadi group and means 'to fill' or 'to replenish'. Since it is an Adadi root, it connects the verbal endings directly to the stem without inserting the extra 'a' vowel. In active usage (Parasmaipada), it shows a person or thing performing the action of filling an object or space.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, prathama-purusha, eka-vacana (Present Active 3rd Singular)
scenarios.example_english: The potter fills the pot with water.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, prathama-purusha, bahu-vacana (Present Active 3rd Plural)
scenarios.example_english: The clouds fill the water reservoirs.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'pra' is cataloged in the Adadi gana with the canonical meaning 'purane' (to fill). Being an anit root, it rejects intermediate 'i' (it-agama) in Ardhadhatuka environments where applicable. In Sarvadhatuka affixes, the vikaranapratyaya shap undergoes elision (luk) per the rule 'adadibhyah shapah', yielding the standard present forms prati, pratah, pranti.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines 'pra purane' within the second conjugation. He notes that the root preserves its long 'a' in strong forms (prati) and contrasts its simple non-reduplicated Adadi paradigm with roots like 'pri' (palanapuranayoh) from other classes.

meanings.English: To fill, to complete, to replenish

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'īś' means to rule, command, possess supreme power, or be the lord/master of something. Because it belongs to the Adadi class (Class 2) and takes Atmanepada endings, the personal suffixes attach directly to the root without the intermediary 'a' vowel, causing sound changes like 's' turning into 'ṣ' and 't' turning into 'ṭ'. It frequently governs the genitive case (showing mastery over someone or something).

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga (Present tense 3rd person singular, Atmanepada)
scenarios.example_english: The Supreme Lord rules over the entire universe.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Lṛṭ Lakāra (Future tense 3rd person singular, Atmanepada with 'iṭ' augment)
scenarios.example_english: A righteous king will rule over the kingdom.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'īśa' is stated in the sense of 'aiśvarya' (sovereignty, mastery). Being an Adādi root, the conjugational affix 'śap' is elided by 'adiprabhṛtibhyaḥ śapaḥ'. When followed by a dental consonant suffix like 'ta', it undergoes retroflexion (ṣṭutva) to form 'īṣṭe'. In Ardhadhātuka tenses, it takes the 'iṭ' augment according to standard rules, yielding forms such as 'īśitā' and 'īśiṣyate'. In syntactic usage, its object often takes the genitive case by the rule 'adhīgartha-dayeśāṁ karmaṇi'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes that 'īśa aiśvarye' belongs to the Atmanepada division of the Adādi group. It denotes uncontested supremacy, divine lordship, and the capacity to govern. The phonetic modifications across different suffixes follow the regular patterns of root-final palatal sibilants transforming before dental inflections.

meanings.English: To rule, govern, possess mastery, command, be lord of
meanings.Hindi: Shasan karna, svamitva rakhna, prabhutva hona
meanings.Bengali: Shason kora, probhutwo kora, odhikari howa
meanings.French: Regner, commander, dominer, etre maitre de

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'śās' means to teach, govern, rule, or instruct. In standard Parasmaipada forms, it indicates an authority or teacher giving discipline or governing subjects directly. When used in the causative (Nic), it shifts the meaning to causing someone to instruct or govern.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Parasmaipada, Lat lakara (Present tense), Prathama purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The king governs the subjects righteously.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Parasmaipada, Vidhiling lakara (Potential mood), Prathama purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The teacher should always instruct the disciple.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti analyzes 'śāsu anuśiṣṭau' under the Adadi class as an Anit root. It details the operational changes like the substitution of 'i' for 'ā' before consonants (śāsa id aṅhaloḥ), yielding forms like śāsti, śiṣṭaḥ, and śāsati.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes that 'śāsu' denotes discipline, instruction, and governance. He highlights the special elision and vocalic changes that occur before non-sarvadhatuka and consonant-initial affixes, producing distinctive forms such as 'aśāt' and 'śiṣyāt'.

meanings.English: to instruct, to govern, to rule, to discipline
meanings.Bengali: shashon kora, upadesh dewa, shikha dewa

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'yā' means to go, to reach, or to attain. In Class 2 (Adādigaṇa), it directly takes standard Parasmaipada endings without an intermediate thematic vowel 'a' in present tense (e.g., yā + ti = yāti). When a causative suffix (ṇic) is added, it becomes 'yāpayati', meaning 'causes to go' or 'passes/spends (time)'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Simple present tense (laṭ, prathama-puruṣa, ekavacana) in active voice (kartari prayoga)
scenarios.example_english: The traveler goes to the city.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative present (ṇic-pratyaya, laṭ, prathama-puruṣa, ekavacana)
scenarios.example_english: The sage spends his time in the forest.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'yā' belongs to the Adādi class and carries the primary sense of 'prāpaṇa' (attaining, reaching, or moving towards a destination). Being anit and ākārānta, the root takes luk of the sap affix in sārvadhātuka forms, yielding forms like yāti, yātaḥ, yanti.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'yā prāpaṇe' as an adādi parasmaipadi root signifying motion directed towards an objective or destination. In lit-lakāra, reduplication yields yayau, yayatuḥ, yayuḥ.

meanings.English: to go, to travel, to attain, to reach

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'jaks' uniquely holds two distinct meanings: 'to eat' (sakarmaka / transitive) and 'to laugh' (akarmaka / intransitive). Beloging to the special 'jaksityadi' sub-group in Class 2, it receives the technical designation 'abhyasta', which causes the third-person plural ending to take 'ati' (jaksati) instead of 'anti'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Lat lakara (present tense), Prathama purusha (third person), Ekavacana (singular)
scenarios.example_english: The boy eats a fruit.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Lat lakara (present tense), Prathama purusha (third person), Bahuvacana (plural) with abhyasta elision of nasal
scenarios.example_english: The children laugh out of joy.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti explains 'jakṣa bhakṣahasitayoḥ' as functioning in both eating and laughing. It highlights the sutra 'jakṣityādayaḥ ṣaṭ' which assigns the technical designation of abhyasta to this root and five others in the Adadi class, triggering specific phonological behaviors such as the jhi-adesha replacement by ati (adas/at).
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin in Kshiratarangini notes that 'jakṣ' encapsulates both bhakṣaṇa (consuming) and hasana (smiling/laughing). He mentions the etymological view that this root originated as a blended or onomatopoeic development connected with ghas (eating) and has (laughing).

meanings.English: to eat, to laugh

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'mā' means to measure, gauge, or encompass. Since it is an Ātmanepada root in the Adādi class, it takes middle endings directly (such as 'māte' or 'mimīte' in standard conjugational forms). Adding a causative suffix turns it into 'māpayati' meaning 'causes to measure' or 'constructs/builds'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The craftsman measures the plot of land with his hands.

vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: māṅ parimāṇe. māte, mimīte. paricchinatti arthaḥ. upasargavaśāt pramāṇa-nirmāṇa-anumānādi-bhāve vartate.

meanings.English: to measure, mete out, limit, delineate

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'śās' means to instruct, govern, command, or punish. In standard active voice (Parasmaipada), it describes a teacher instructing students or a king ruling citizens ('śāsti'). When combined with the prefix 'āṅ' in the meaning of wishing or blessing, it switches by rule to Atmanepada ('āśāste').

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Active voice (Kartari Prayoga), Lat lakara, Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The king governs the subjects righteously.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'śāsu anuśiṣṭau' is explained in the sense of 'anuśiṣṭi' (instruction, correction, governance). In the present tense, it conjugates as śāsti, śāstaḥ, śāsati (with the elision of the nasal by 'śāsor didhi-vevyor nityam'). In the aorist and before certain consonantal weak affixes, the vowel undergoes substitution to 'i' by 'śāsa id aṅ-haloḥ', producing forms like aśiṣat and śiṣyate.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines 'anuśiṣṭiḥ śikṣaṇam' (instruction and discipline). It is illustrated as 'śāsti rājā pṛthivīm' (the king governs the earth). It undergoes root-vowel mutation to 'i' before haladi kit/ṅit affixes, giving non-finite and participial forms like śiṣṭaḥ and śiṣṭavān.

meanings.English: to govern, to rule, to instruct, to command, to punish
meanings.Hindi: shasan karna, upadesh dena, danda dena, nirdeshit karna
meanings.Bengali: shason kora, upadesh deoya, aadesh kora

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'kshu' primarily means to make a sneezing sound or to sneeze. Being in the Adadi class (Class 2), the base verbal suffix 'Shap' is deleted (luk), giving forms like 'kshauti'. When used in the causative (Nich), it changes meaning to causing someone to sneeze or sound.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakara (present tense), Prathama purusha (3rd person singular)
scenarios.example_english: The sick child sneezes repeatedly.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nich pratyaya), Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, 3rd person singular
scenarios.example_english: The pungent powder makes the man sneeze.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'kshu shabde' belongs to Adadi Parasmaipada. In Sarvadhatuka non-aprikt-hal contexts, Guna of the root vowel 'u' takes place to yield 'o' which before vowels undergoes Av-adesha, resulting in kshauti, kshutaH, kshuvanti. It is anit (devoid of it-agama in nishtha etc.).
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'kshu shabde kshauti' indicating audible expulsion or sound emission, categorised as anit among the u-ending roots of the Adadi group.

meanings.English: to sneeze, to make a sound

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'dra' means to run away, flee, or move in a contemptible or wretched manner. Belonging to the Adadi group (class 2), it drops the conjugational infix 'sap' before basic endings, yielding forms like 'drati' directly from the root.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Lat lakara (Present Indicative), Prathama Purusha (3rd person), Ekavacana, Parasmaipada
scenarios.example_english: The terrified enemy flees from the battlefield.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'dra' is listed under Adadi-gana with the meaning 'kutsitayam gatau' (wretched motion or running away). Being an akaaraanta root, luk of sap takes place in Sarvadhatuka environments without additional guṇa, forming 'drati', 'dratah', 'dranti'. In lit it reduplicates to produce 'dadrau'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines 'dra' in the sense of 'kutsita gati' (bad or cowardly motion / flight). It is anit and parasmaipadi, taking standard luk of vikaranas in the second conjugation.

meanings.English: to run away, to flee, to move contemptibly

canonical_dhatvartha: nidrākṣaye (to awaken, to stay awake, cessation of sleep)

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'jāgṛ' belongs to the Adadi group (Jakṣādi class) and means 'to wake up' or 'to remain alert'. It is primarily used in Parasmaipada for normal intransitive actions of staying awake. When used in the Causative (Ṇic) form, it changes to 'jāgarayati' meaning 'to cause someone to awaken' or 'to awaken someone', becoming transitive.

scenarios.meaning: He/she wakes up or remains awake

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic Pratyaya (Causative), Kartari Prayoga, Lat Lakara, Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The mother wakes up the child in the morning.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'jāgṛ' belongs to the Jakṣādi gaṇa within Adādi. The semantic assignment 'nidrākṣaye' denotes the end of sleep or vigilance. In Sarvadhatuka non-piti affixes, it maintains a unique guna/guna-blocking behaviour and guna replacement before consonantal strong affixes (jāgarti, jāgṛtaḥ, jāgrati).
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes that 'jāgṛ' expresses the elimination of slumber ('nidrā-vināśa'). Being part of Jakṣādi, abhyastasañjñā rules apply, yielding 'jāgrati' in the 3rd person plural present.

meanings.English: to wake up, to be awake, to watch

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'jāgṛ' fundamentally denotes being awake, waking up, or keeping vigil. In simple active voice (Parasmaipada), it describes a person staying awake or watching vigilantly. When used with a causative suffix (ṇic), it changes to mean causing someone else to wake up or awakening someone.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana (simple present active)

vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: jāgṛ nidrākṣaye nidrātyāge vartate. jakṣityāditvād abhyastatvam. jagarti, jagratah, jagrati iti rupasiddhaḥ.

meanings.English: to be awake, to watch, to awaken

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root svap means to sleep or recline in rest. Because it belongs to the special Rudadi subgroup inside the second conjugation (Adadi Gana), it takes an extra 'i' augment before consonant-initial endings, producing 'svapiti' instead of 'svapti'. In the causative form (nic), it turns into an active transitive action 'svapāyati' meaning 'puts to sleep'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana (Rudadi-it augment applied)
scenarios.example_english: The child sleeps comfortably on the bed.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root ñiṣvap is listed in the Rudadi section under the Adadi class with the meaning of lying down or sleeping (śaye). By the rule 'rudādibhyaḥ sārvadhātuke', it receives the it-agama before valadi sarvadhatuka affixes, forming svapiti, svapitaḥ, svapanti. In asarvadhatuka, samprasarana operates regularly under designated conditions yielding forms like suṣvāpa and suptaḥ.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes that svap belongs to the class of five roots starting with rud (rud, svap, śvas, an, jakṣ) which take the special augment i/ī in sarvadhatuka conjugations. The root takes samprasarana (va changing to u) before kit and nit suffixes, generating forms such as supta and supti.

meanings.English: to sleep, slumber, repose

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'ḍī' specifically denotes flying or moving through the air. Because it carries the marker 'ṅ' (ḍīṅ), it takes Atmanepada endings. It is most commonly seen in literature joined with the prefix 'ut' to form 'uḍḍayate' or 'uḍḍīyate' (to fly up). When used in the causative (Nic), it shifts to Parasmaipada/Ubhayapada to mean 'causing to fly' or 'launching into flight'.

scenarios.example_english: The bird flies in the sky.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic-pratyaya) with prefix 'ut', Parasmaipada

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: Madhaviya Dhatuvritti glosses ḍīṅ as 'vihāyasā gatau' meaning aerial movement (ākāśe gamanam). It notes that by virtue of the anudatta-it marker 'ṅ', it takes Atmanepada terminations. It details the stem transformations when compounded with preverbs such as 'ut' leading to 'uḍḍayana' and standard conjugation.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin highlights that ḍīṅ is strictly akarmaka (intransitive) representing the specialized motion of birds and winged beings soaring through the atmosphere, forming ḍayate and undergoing class-specific shifts when applied with different affixes.

meanings.English: To fly, to soar in the air
meanings.French: Voler, s envoler dans l air

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'dīdhī' belongs to the 2nd conjugation (Adādi gaṇa) and is used in Ātmanepada to mean 'to shine', 'to glow', 'to be bright', or 'to play/gambol'. Because it is an anubandha-ṅ root (dīdhīṅ), it exclusively takes Ātmanepada suffixes (such as -te, -āte, -rate). In causative and derived forms, it signifies causing someone or something to illuminate or shine.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: dīdhīṅ dīptidevanayoḥ - The root dīdhīṅ is read in the Adādi gaṇa having the senses of dīpti (illumination, brightness, splendor) and devana (play, shining, movement). It is an Ātmanepada root characterized by an it-letter 'ṅ'. Special grammatical sutras like 'dīdhīvevīṭām' (1.1.6) define its vowel behavior where its final ī is treated uniquely with respect to guṇa and vṛddhi prohibitions.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: dīdhīṅ dīptau devane ca - In Kshirasvamin's analysis, the root denotes radiating light and playful movement. It forms dīdhīte in the present singular without taking the standard sap-vikarana, following the luk elision characteristic of the Adādi gaṇa.

meanings.English: to shine, to glow, to radiate light, to play
meanings.Bengali: ujjvala haoyā, dīpti pāoyā, prakāśita haoyā

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root vevī belongs to the second conjugation group (Adadi Gana) and conveys the meanings of weaving threads, moving, or expanding/pervading. Because it carries the indicator tag 'ṅ' (ṅit), it takes only Atmanepada endings. In the present tense, endings attach directly to the root without the connecting vowel 'a', producing forms like 'vevīte'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga, laṭ lakāra, prathama-puruṣa (3rd person), eka-vacana

scenarios.example_english: The artisans weave garments.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti classifies vevīṅ in the Adadi gana with the semantic tags 'tantusantāna' (extension of woven threads) and 'gativyāpti' (motion and pervading). As a ṅit root, it is strictly Atmanepadi. Sārvadhātuka suffixes directly follow the root, and before vowel-affixes, standard iyan-ādeśa applies according to regular Paninian sandhi rules.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes vevīṅ in the context of continuous expansion and weaving (tantusantāne). He highlights its structural similarity to the root dīdhīṅ, noting that both are treated with specific reduplicative and vowel-replacement characteristics across diverse conjugational tenses.

meanings.English: to weave, to stretch threads, to pervade, to move

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'ru' means to make a sound, to cry out, or to roar. Belonging to the 2nd class (Adadi Gana), it directly adds endings to the root. In the present tense, it shows two alternative singular forms: 'rauti' (with guna/vriddhi change) and 'ravīti' (with an intermediate 'ī' vowel). Adding a causative suffix changes it to 'rāvayati', meaning 'causes to produce sound' or 'makes roar/cry'.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti categorizes 'ru' under Adadi Parasmaipada with the sense of 'śabda' (sound-making). It details the operation of the sutra 'īd ruto dhātoḥ', which optionally introduces the augment 'ī' before sarvadhatuka consonant endings, giving parallel forms such as 'ravīti' alongside 'rauti'. The lit forms are 'rurāva' and 'ruruvatuḥ'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'ru śabde' as an intransitive root denoting vocalization, roaring, or natural resonance. He highlights regular participial and nominal derivations including 'ruta' (sound/chirp of birds) and 'rava' (noise/roar), conforming to the standard anit-akarmaka phonological behavior.

meanings.English: to make a sound, to roar, to cry out, to resound, to hum
meanings.Tamil: oli eḻuppu, kattu, kaṟjikkai cey, koo
meanings.Bengali: śabda karā, cītkar karā, garjan karā, ḍākā

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'brū' means to speak clearly, declare, or tell. Because it is an Ubhayapada root, it can take Parasmaipada terminations (bravīti, brūtaḥ, bruvanti) or Atmanepada terminations (brūte, bruvāte, bruvate). In Paninian grammar, 'brū' is counted among the 16 dvikarmaka (two-object) verbs, meaning it can take both a primary object (what is said) and a secondary object (the person spoken to) in the accusative case (dvitiya vibhakti).

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Parasmaipada, Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana, Lat Lakara
scenarios.meaning: He/She speaks or tells (action directed generally)
scenarios.example_english: The teacher tells the student about dharma.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Atmanepada, Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana, Lat Lakara
scenarios.meaning: He/She speaks or professes for oneself
scenarios.example_english: The sage speaks the truth of the Self.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'brūñ' is marked with the anubandha 'ñ', signifying Ubhayapada status. Its primary meaning is 'vyaktāyāṃ vāci' (articulate and clear speech). Madhava notes the special augment 'īṭ' applied in sarvadhatuka strong forms (e.g., bravīti, bravīṣi, bravīmi via 'bruva īṭ') and its characteristic dvikarmaka behavior where both the listener and the message take the accusative case.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin highlights that 'brū' takes an irregular substitution of 'vac' (vaci-adesha) before certain ardhadhatuka affixes like Lit (uvāca) and Lrt (vakṣyati). In its unaugmented forms before consonantal endings, it retains its base (brūte, brūtaḥ), and is classified under anit roots.

meanings.English: To speak, tell, declare, articulate

transitivity: Both Intransitive and Transitive (Dvipadi/Ubhayakarmaka depending on specific sense: shine/glow, desire, reflect)

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'dīdhī' belongs to the Adadi class and is used in the Atmanepada voice. It means to shine, glow, reflect, or desire. In everyday use and classical Vedic-style expressions, it shows a subject glowing or shining by itself, or deeply meditating/reflecting internally.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Lat lakara (present tense), prathama purusha (third person), ekavacana (singular), Atmanepada
scenarios.example_english: The sage shines/glows through meditation.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (causative stem) + Atmanepada
scenarios.meaning: Causes to glow or makes radiant
scenarios.example_english: Knowledge illuminates and makes the self radiant.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'dīdhīṅ' is listed under the Adadi gana with the meaning 'dīptikāntigatiṣu' (illumination, affection/desire, and motion/comprehension). The 'ṅ' marker indicates that it exclusively takes Atmanepada terminations. In classical and Vedic forms, roots like dīdhī and vevī have special morphophonemic behaviors under sutras such as 'dīdhīvevīṭām' regarding vowel replacement and syllable treatment.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin categorizes 'dīdhīṅ' in the Adadi gana under the shades of dīpti (splendor/radiance) and devana (play, shining, movement). It is classified as anit and anubandha-marked for Atmanepada, showing forms such as dīdhīte, adīdhīta, and dīdhīṣyate.

meanings.English: to shine, glow, reflect, meditate, admire
meanings.Bengali: ujjval howa, shobha pawa, dhyan kora

it_status: Ananiṭ (Seṭ in certain ardhadhatuka environments with idiṭ-lakshana)

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'didhi' means to shine, glow, or engage in divine play/worship. Being an Atmanepada root (due to the marker 'n'), its verb forms reflect the state or action residing inherently within the subject, showing how an entity naturally radiates light or rejoices.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Lat (Present Tense), Prathama Purusha (3rd Person), Ekavacana (Singular)
scenarios.example_english: The radiance of the sun shines brightly in the sky.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Lan (Past Tense / Imperfect), Prathama Purusha (3rd Person), Ekavacana (Singular)
scenarios.example_english: The star shone during the night.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti outlines didhin under Adadi gana with the semantic scope of dipti (luminosity) and devana (play, brilliance, or desire). Because it bears an anubandha 'n', it takes Atmanepada affixes. Special deletion and substitution sutras govern its forms in combination with sarvadhatuka and ardhadhatuka affixes (e.g., 'didhivevibhyam it' for specific ardhadhatuka operations).
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes didhin along with vevin as unique Adadi Atmanepada roots ending in dirgha-ikara. Its central meaning encompasses glowing, sporting, and expressing radiant effulgence, with technical luk-vikarana procedures characteristic of the Adadi class.

meanings.English: to shine, to glow, to sport, to rejoice
meanings.Hindi: chamakna, prakashit hona, deepti prapth karna
meanings.Bengali: ujjval haoya, jvalajvala kara, prakasita haoya

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'vevī' belongs to the Adadi group (class 2) and is an inherently Atmanepada root. It signifies radiating, shining brightly, moving gracefully, or sporting. In primary usage, it takes direct middle voice terminations (vevīte, vevāte, vevate). When used with a causative suffix (vevayati/vevayate), it means causing something to shine, illuminate, or manifest radiance.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Lat lakara (present tense), prathama-purusha (third person), ekavacana (singular), Atmanepada
scenarios.example_english: The radiance of the sun shines everywhere.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (causative), Lat lakara, prathama-purusha, ekavacana, Parasmaipada
scenarios.example_english: The lamp illuminates the hall.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti places 'vevīṅ' in the Jakṣityādi (abhyasta) section of the Adadi class. It marks the root as anit and anubandha 'ṅ' denotes exclusive Atmanepada inflection. In Sarvadhatuka environments without intermediate augment, abhyasa operations apply leading to forms such as vevīte and vevate.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'vevīṅ dīptau devane ca' as a root expressing illumination and celestial activity or movement. It belongs to the non-vikarana class alongside dīdhīṅ, behaving uniquely in euphonic vowel treatments before Atmanepada endings.

meanings.English: to shine, to radiate, to move gracefully, to sport
meanings.Hindi: chamakna, prakashit hona, deepti purna hona

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root kṣṇu means to sharpen, whet, or polish an edge such as a blade or weapon. In the basic Parasmaipada form, it indicates the direct action of sharpening a tool. In the causative form, it signifies getting an implement sharpened by someone else.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Lat lakara (present tense), prathama-purusha, eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The blacksmith sharpens the sharp weapon.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic-pratyaya), Lat lakara, prathama-purusha, eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The army chief causes the swords to be sharpened by the blacksmiths.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti analyzes 'kṣṇu tejane' as referring to tīkṣṇīkaraṇa (the act of sharpening or honing). Being an u-ending root of Adadi gana without an it-augment (Anit), it exhibits vriddhi in the singular strong forms (kṣṇauti) and uvaṅ-adesha before vowel endings in weak forms (kṣṇuvanti).
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin classifies kṣṇu among the u-ending roots of the Adadi gaṇa signifying tejana (sharpening or making keen). The vritti highlights core conjugated forms including kṣṇauti, cikṣṇāva, kṣṇotā, and note its anit nature in ardhadhatuka environments.

meanings.English: to sharpen, whet, hone, make keen

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root cakāś means 'to shine' or 'to appear radiant'. In the basic Parasmaipada form, it describes a subject naturally glowing or shining with beauty and light. When used with the causative affix (ṇic), it shifts to mean 'illuminating' or 'causing something to shine brightly'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Laṭ lakāra, prathama-puruṣa, eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The sun shines brightly in the sky.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Ṇijanta (causative), Laṭ lakāra, prathama-puruṣa, eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The lamp illuminates the house.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root cakāśṝ is placed in the Adādi gaṇa in the sense of dīpti (illumination). Being marked with anubandha ṝ, it allows the optional aṅ pratyaya in the aorist (luṅ lakāra), yielding the form acakāśat alongside the standard seṭ form. Its present tense conjugation drops the intermediate vikaraṇa śap, resulting in forms like cakāsti, cakāstaḥ, and cakāsati.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes cakāśṝ as inherently possessing a reduplicated appearance yet functioning as a primitive root belonging to the Adādi class. It denotes luminous appearance, brilliance, and self-manifestation.

meanings.English: to shine, to glitter, to be radiant, to appear bright
meanings.Bengali: prokasheto howa, ujjwal howa, jholmol kora

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root dīdhi belongs to the Adadi group (class 2) and is an Atmanepada verb indicating shining, illuminating, or contemplating. Since it has an anubandha 'ṅ', it takes middle-voice personal endings in the present tense (e.g., dīdhīte).

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The sun shines in the sky.
