vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: sphāra sphāraṇe. sphāraṇaṃ vikasanaṃ vistāraṇaṃ vā. curādir adantaḥ ubhayapadī. sphārayati, sphārayate.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: sphāra sphāraṇe. sphārayati. vistārayatīty arthaḥ.

meanings.English: to expand, open wide, or extend

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'arth' means to ask for, pray for, or seek something earnestly. It belongs to the nominal and secondary verbal formations where the affix 'ṇic' or 'yak' is applied naturally, taking Atmanepada endings in standard usage.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga (present indicative 3rd person singular with ṇic-pratyaya)
scenarios.example_english: The student requests knowledge from the teacher.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: upasarga 'sam' + kartari prayoga
scenarios.example_english: The scholar substantiates his viewpoint with reasoning.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: artha yāñcāyām iti kecit. curāder ākṛtigaṇatvāt ṇic. arthayate. arthanā. prārthanā ityādi rūpāṇi sidhyanti.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: artha yāñcāyām. arthayate. arthanīyaḥ. saṁjñāpūrvakavidheranityatvād vṛddhyabhāvaḥ.

meanings.English: to request, to seek, to beg, to wish for

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'iras' belongs to the Kaṇḍvādi group and takes the affix 'yak' obligatorily, meaning to harbor ill will, feel envy, or display anger towards someone.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga (active voice), laṭ lakāra (present tense), prathama puruṣa, ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The wicked person is constantly envious of noble people.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: ātmanepada, kartari prayoga, laṭ lakāra, prathama puruṣa, ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The foolish person harbors jealousy towards the scholar.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: irasa irasyāyām. kaṇḍvādiṣu pāṭhāt kaṇḍvādibhyo yak ityadhikāre yak pratyayaḥ. tena irasyatīti rūpam sidhyati. asūyārthe 'krudhadruhērṣyāsūyārthānāṃ yaṃ prati kopaḥ' iti sampradānatvam.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: irasa irasyāyām asūyāyām. irasyati irasyate. yaṅantasya sarvadhātukavat kramādayaḥ.

meanings.English: to envy, to bear malice, to display anger

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'irasya' belongs to the Kandvadi class of roots, which inherently take the suffix yak to form verbal stems expressing envy, ill-will, or finding fault with others.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: lat-lakara (present indicative active, prathama-purusa ekavacana)
scenarios.example_english: The wicked person feels ill-will toward the noble person.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: lrt-lakara (simple future active, prathama-purusa ekavacana)
scenarios.example_english: The envious man will always harbor malice toward the virtuous.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: irasya amarṣe asūyāyām. kandvādibhyo yak iti yak-pratyayaḥ. irasyati. amarṣo krodhaḥ asūyā tu guṇeṣu doṣāviṣkaraṇam.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: irasya amarṣe asūyāyāñca. iras sabdāt asūyāyām yak. irasyati.

meanings.English: to envy, to bear ill-will, to find fault with

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'asūy' comes under the Kandvadi class of verbal stems, formed directly from nominal or stem bases. It means to find fault, cavil, or express jealousy toward someone's virtues. In practical Sanskrit usage, it takes Parasmaipada endings directly with the intrinsic 'ya' suffix.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: lat lakara (present tense), prathama-purusha (third person), ekavacana (singular)
scenarios.meaning: He/she finds fault with or is envious of another
scenarios.example_english: The foolish person finds fault with the virtuous one.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: vidhiling lakara (optative), prathama-purusha (third person), ekavacana (singular)
scenarios.meaning: One should not find fault or be envious
scenarios.example_english: Living among the noble, one should never display fault-finding jealousy.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: asūya upālabhe doṣāviṣkaraṇe ca. kandvādibhyo yak iti yak-pratyayaḥ. asūyati. guṇeṣu doṣāviṣkaraṇam asūyā, tatkartṛke prayoge dvitīyā caturthī vā dṛśyate.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: asūya upālabhe. kandvādir ayam. asūyati, asūyām ācakṣāṇaḥ pravartate ityarthaḥ.

meanings.English: to find fault, to cavil, to envy
meanings.Hindi: doṣ nikālanā, asūyā yā īrṣyā karanā

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'vrata' means to observe a vow, adhere to a spiritual or ethical discipline, or regulate one's conduct. In Sanskrit grammar, it is a nominal verbal root (kandvadi) that takes the affix 'yak' to function directly as an active or middle verb meaning 'to observe a discipline'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: lat lakara, prathama purusha, eka-vacana, parasmaipada
scenarios.meaning: He or she observes a sacred vow or discipline
scenarios.example_english: The spiritual seeker observes the vow of truth.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: lat lakara, prathama purusha, eka-vacana, atmanepada
scenarios.meaning: He or she undertakes a spiritual discipline for personal purification
scenarios.example_english: The sage undertakes the spiritual discipline in the sacred grove.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: vrata niyame vratacarane ca. kandvaditvat svarthe yak-pratyayah. ubhayapadatvat vratayati vratayate iti rupadvayam bhavati. anena satyacarana-niyamadayah pratipadyante.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: vrata vratane niyame ca. kandvadi-gane pathitatvad yak-pratyayantasya prayogah. vratayati vratayate va niyama-vishesham svikaroti.

meanings.English: to observe a vow or discipline
meanings.Hindi: vrata ya niyam ka palan karna
meanings.German: ein Gelubde oder eine Disziplin einhalten
meanings.French: observer un voeu ou une discipline

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'irasy' belongs to the Kandvadi class and is derived directly as a verbal stem meaning 'to envy', 'to hold a grudge against', or 'to display anger and intolerance towards another'. In everyday Sanskrit, it takes standard Parasmaipada endings directly.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: lat-lakara, prathama-purusa, eka-vacana (Kartari prayoga)
scenarios.example_english: The wicked person feels envious upon seeing another's prosperity.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: vidhilin-lakara, prathama-purusa, eka-vacana (Kartari prayoga)
scenarios.meaning: One should not bear ill-will or envy
scenarios.example_english: A noble person should not envy the success of anyone.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: irasya asuyayam. kandvadibhyo yak iti yak-pratyayantasya dhatusanjna. irasyati. anadaradibhavartho drsyate.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: irasya krodhe asuyayam ca. kandvadisu pathitasya dhatorlatyubhayapadamapyanye vadanti, mukhyatah parasmaipadam.

meanings.English: to envy, to bear ill-will, to resent

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'gavy' is a Kandvadi nominal verbal root meaning 'to desire or seek cows'. In Sanskrit, when someone wants cows, this nominal verb expresses that specific wish directly in the active voice (kartari prayoga) using the yak affix intrinsically present by rule 'kandvadibhyo yak'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: lat-lakara (present indicative), prathama-purusha (third person), ekavacana (singular)
scenarios.example_english: The cowherd desires cows in the forest.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: lan-lakara (past imperfect), prathama-purusha (third person), ekavacana (singular)
scenarios.example_english: The king desired cattle for wealth.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: kandvadayah svatantrah dhatavah. gavyati iti gam icchatityarthe dravyetaranirapekshah kandvadipathad yak-pratyayantah.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: gavya gam icchan. kandvadibhyo yak iti svabhavikoyak. gavyati. agavyit va agavyat.

meanings.English: to desire cows, to search for cattle

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'pāṃsula' belongs to the Kandvādi group, which converts a nominal stem (dust/dirt) directly into a verbal root by adding the suffix 'yak'. It means to soil, cover with dust, or defile. It can take either Parasmaipada or Ātmanepada endings.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Laṭ (Present Indicative), Prathama Puruṣa, Ekavacana, Parasmaipada
scenarios.meaning: He/She soils or covers (something) with dust
scenarios.example_english: The child soils his own clothes.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Laṭ (Present Indicative), Prathama Puruṣa, Ekavacana, Ātmanepada
scenarios.meaning: It becomes dusty or behaves like dust
scenarios.example_english: When the wind blows, the path becomes dusty.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: pāṃsula pāṃsulīkaraṇe kandvādiḥ. dhātusaṃjñāyāṃ yak-pratyayaḥ. pāṃsulāyate pāṃsulayati vā.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: pāṃsula dhūlīkaraṇe lepane ca. kandvādibhyo yak iti yak. pāṃsulayati pāṃsulāyate.

meanings.English: To soil, defile, cover with dust or dirt
meanings.Hindi: dhūladhūsrita karanā, mailā karanā, dūṣita karanā
meanings.Bengali: dhūlāmakkhā karā, mayalā karā, dūṣita karā

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root sukha belongs to the Kandvadi group of nominal verbs. It takes the suffix yak by the rule 'Kandvadibhyo yak' and conjugated in the Atmanepada to express experiencing happiness, acting happily, or enjoying pleasant circumstances.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Present tense (lat), third person singular (prathama-purusha, eka-vacana), Atmanepada with yak-pratyaya
scenarios.example_english: The mind of a virtuous person feels happiness through good conduct.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Past tense (lan), third person singular, Atmanepada
scenarios.example_english: The sage experienced peaceful happiness in the penance grove.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: sukha tatkriyayam sukhe ca. kandvaditvad yak. sukhayate. atmanepaditvam anudattetvaditvat.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: sukha sukhe. kandvadibhyo yak iti yak. sukhayate. sukhasya anubhavah sukhacaranam va.

meanings.English: to experience happiness, to feel pleasure, to be comfortable
meanings.German: sich freuen, glucklich sein, Wohlbefinden empfinden
meanings.French: eprouver du bonheur, etre heureux, etre a l'aise

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root ślakṣṇa belongs to the Kandvādi group, which directly forms denominative verbs using the suffix ya (yak/kyan). It describes a surface or substance becoming smooth, glossy, polished, or soft.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Lat lakara (present indicative, prathama-purusha, eka-vacana) via Kandvadibhyo yak
scenarios.example_english: The skin becomes soft and smooth by oil massage.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Lan lakara (imperfect past, prathama-purusha, eka-vacana)
scenarios.example_english: The clay became smooth with water.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: ślakṣṇa cikkatve. kandvādiṣu pāṭhād yak. ślakṣṇam ācarati ślakṣṇāyate. snigdha-mṛdutvam anubhavatītyarthaḥ.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: ślakṣṇa cikkanībhāve. ślakṣṇāyate vastram. ślakṣṇatvam āpadyata ityarthaḥ.

meanings.English: to become smooth, fine, soft, or glossy

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'sūtr' means to weave, connect, or compose concise systematic rules (aphorisms). In language, it expresses formulating ideas into neat, systematic principles or threading things together.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga (Active voice, Present indicative 3rd person singular with Kandvadi aya/yak suffix)
scenarios.meaning: He/She composes into concise rules or formulates systematically
scenarios.example_english: The sage formulates grammatical rules systematically.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Karmani Prayoga (Passive voice, Present indicative 3rd person singular)
scenarios.meaning: It is threaded together or codified into rules
scenarios.example_english: The essence of the doctrine is concisely codified into aphorisms.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: sūtra veṣṭane granthane ca. kandvādibhyaḥ karmavyatihāre vā 'kandvādibhyo yak' iti yak-pratyayaḥ. sūtrayati, sūtrayate vā saṅkṣepeṇa grantham.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: sūtra sandarbhe veṣṭane ca. sūtreṇa badhnāti, saṅkṣepeṇa vākyāni kathayati iti sūtrayati.

meanings.English: to string together, compose into aphorisms, formulate, thread
meanings.Tamil: cūttiram iyakku, koṟvai cey, kōrttu amei
meanings.Bengali: sūtra racanā karā, sūtrita karā, gānthā

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'cit' means to perceive, remember, or become aware of. In simple active voice (Kartari Prayoga), it describes the subject actively regaining memory, realizing an idea, or perceiving knowledge.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Lat-lakara (Present Tense), Prathama-purusha (Third Person), Ekavacana (Singular) in Kartari Prayoga (Active Voice)
scenarios.example_english: The sage perceives the ultimate truth.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Lun-lakara (Aorist Past Tense), Prathama-purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: He remembered the ancient knowledge.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: citi smaraṇe. ceti cetataḥ cetanti. anudāttetvāt parasmaipadam. cittaḥ, cetanaḥ, cittam iti rūpāṇi bhavanti.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: citi smaraṇe. cetati. cetā. ciketa. anupadhāvṛddhau caititi kecit. sañcetane 'pi prayogaḥ.

meanings.English: to perceive, to remember, to be conscious of

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root asūya belongs to the Kandvadi group, which forms verbal stems primarily through the yak-pratyaya. It means to find fault with someone, envy, or express jealousy toward another person's virtues.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga, laṭ-lakāra, prathama-puruṣa, eka-vacana (Parasmaipada)
scenarios.meaning: He or she finds fault or feels jealous.
scenarios.example_english: The wicked person finds fault with the virtuous one.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga, laṭ-lakāra, prathama-puruṣa, eka-vacana (Ātmanepada)
scenarios.meaning: He or she shows envy or cavils.
scenarios.example_english: The foolish person cavils at the scholar's learning.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: asūya doṣāviṣkaraṇe. kandvādibhyo yak iti yak-pratyayaḥ. asūyati, asūyate. guṇeṣu doṣāviṣkaraṇam asūyā.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: asūya doṣe. kandvāditvāt svārthe yak. ubhayato bhāṣā bhavati. asūyati asūyate vā.

meanings.English: to find fault with, to envy, to decry
meanings.Hindi: dosh nikalna, asuya karna, irshya karna

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root tiras means to conceal oneself, hide, or disappear from view. When used with the kandvadi suffix yak, it forms regular present-tense verbs like tirasyati (he/she disappears or conceals oneself).

scenarios.grammar_trigger: lat lakara (present tense), prathama purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The sun disappears amidst the clouds.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: lyap pratyaya (indeclinable past participle)
scenarios.example_english: The deer, having entered the forest and concealed itself, stands still.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: tirasa antardhau. kandvadibhyo yak iti yak-pratyayah. tirasyati. antardhih adarsanam ityarthah.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: tirasa antardhau. yak. tirasyati. tiraskriyate adarsanam gacchati.

meanings.English: to disappear, to conceal oneself, to become invisible
meanings.Hindi: chhip jana, antardhana hona, adrishya hona

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'mahī' belongs to the Kandvadi group and means to be honored, to prosper, or to exult. Due to the Kandvadi affix 'yak' (without passive meaning), it forms present tense stems as 'mahīyate' in the middle voice.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakara (present tense), prathama purusha (third person singular)
scenarios.example_english: The learned person is honored everywhere.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lan lakara (past imperfect), prathama purusha singular
scenarios.example_english: The righteous king was properly revered in the world.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: mahīṅ pūjāyām. kandvādibhyo yak ityadhikāre mahīyate iti rūpam. pūjāyām māne vā vartate.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: mahīṅ pūjāyām. mahīyate. yak-pratyayaḥ svakīyārthe bhavati, pūjitasya satkāra-bhāvaḥ.

meanings.English: to be honored, to rejoice, to prosper, to be exalted
meanings.Hindi: pūjita honā, ādara pānā, mahimāvān honā
meanings.Bengali: pūjita haoā, sammānita haoā, ānandita haoā
meanings.Chinese: shou dao zun jing, fan rong, huan xin

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The verbal root 'kav' means to describe, portray, or compose poetry. Whenever a writer or poet creatively illustrates the beauty of nature or composes poetic verses, this root is applied.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Laṭ (Present Tense), Prathama Puruṣa, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The poet describes the beauty of nature.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Laṅ (Past Imperfect Tense), Prathama Puruṣa, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The scholar praised the fame of the king in the assembly.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: kava varṇane | haimacāndre dhātupāṭhe kavitve varṇane ceti vyākhyātam | kavati | akavīt | cakāva |
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: kava varṇanārthaḥ | kavitva-kriyāyāṃ varṇanāyāṃ ca haimādayaḥ prayuñjate | kavati |

meanings.English: to describe, to depict, to compose poetry, to praise poetically
meanings.Hindi: varnan karna, kavita rachna, kavittva karna

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'khell' means 'to play' or 'to frolic'. In everyday Sanskrit usage, it describes engaging in lighthearted sports, games, or amusement, functioning very similarly to 'krid' and 'khel'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: lat (present indicative, third person singular)
scenarios.example_english: The boy plays with a ball in the garden.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: lan (imperfect past, third person singular)
scenarios.example_english: The child played together with his friends during the evening.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: khella kridayam iti haimacandriya-dhatupathe spaṣṭataya nirdisṭaḥ; paninīya-sampradaye tu khel-dhator eva bistarah svikriyate.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: khelrn kridayam ity-atraiva khell-ityasya api prayoga-bhedo vartata iti kecit smaranti.

meanings.English: To play, to frolic, to sport

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'ghol' means to stir, mix, churn, or dissolve something thoroughly in a liquid, just like stirring sugar in water or churning curd.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Laṭ-lakāra (Present Indicative, 3rd person singular)
scenarios.example_english: The boy stirs sugar in the milk.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Laṅ-lakāra (Past Imperfect, 3rd person singular)
scenarios.example_english: The mother churned the curd in the pot.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: Paninian lists omit 'ghol'; it is integrated in non-Paninian compilations (Haimacandra, Vopadeva) under the meaning of liquid agitation (vilolana).
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Not tracked in traditional Kshirasvamin recensions; recognized primarily in Western and later medieval Sanskrit lexicons as 'ghol vilolane'.

meanings.English: to stir, to churn, to agitate, to dissolve

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The verbal root 'caṭṭ' means to break, split, or chop into pieces. Whenever someone breaks a twig, cuts wood, or splits something solid, this root is used.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Laṭ (Present Tense), Prathama Puruṣa (Third Person), Ekavacana (Singular)
scenarios.example_english: The carpenter breaks the branch.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Luṅ (Aorist Tense), Prathama Puruṣa (Third Person), Ekavacana (Singular)
scenarios.example_english: By the wind, he broke the wooden staff.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: A non-Paninian lexical item predominantly found in post-Paninian Jain recensions such as the Haima Dhatupatha; listed under the sense of bhaṅgana (breaking/cutting).
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Not separately recognized in early standard Kśīrataraṅgiṇī core lists, but retained in comparative commentaries under secondary roots meaning chedane/bhedane.

meanings.English: to break, to split, to chop

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'choll' is used to describe the action of peeling, skinning, paring, or removing the outer bark or rind of something, such as peeling fruit or stripping bark from a tree.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: lat-lakāra (present indicative, 3rd person singular, curādi-ṇic)
scenarios.meaning: he/she peels or strips the bark/skin
scenarios.example_english: The boy peels the skin of the fruit.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: luṅ-lakāra (aorist, 3rd person singular, caṅ-pratyaya)
scenarios.example_english: The carpenter stripped the bark of the tree.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: Non-Paninian root variant; recorded in comparative lexicography under curādi gaṇa with the sense of 'tvak-karaṇa' (paring/peeling), corresponding functionally to standard roots like chull or kṣur.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Not explicitly listed in standard Kṣīrasvāmin recension of Pāṇinian Dhātupāṭha; preserved primarily in western traditions including Hemacandra's Dhātu-pārāyaṇa in the sense of 'cholla tvak-karaṇe chedane ca'.

meanings.English: to peel, to skin, to pare, to strip the bark
meanings.Russian: ochishchat ot kozhury, snimat koru, obdirat

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'ḍoll' means to swing, sway, or oscillate back and forth, like a tree branch in a breeze or a cradle rocking.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Present Indicative (Laṭ lakāra, Prathama-puruṣa, Ekavacana)
scenarios.example_english: The branch of the tree sways due to the wind.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Aorist / General Past (Luṅ lakāra, Prathama-puruṣa, Ekavacana)
scenarios.example_english: The child's swing swayed gently.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: ḍolla dolane. dolanaṃ calanaṃ kampanaṃ vā. aḍollīt, ḍollitā, ḍolliṣyati.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: ḍolla dolane calane ca. ḍollati. ḍollām babhūva.

meanings.English: to swing, to sway, to shake, to rock

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'ḍimbh' describes shaking or quivering out of intense fear, or behaving in a weak and helpless childish manner. Imagine a timid little creature trembling in a dark forest.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Laṭ lakāra (Present Tense, 3rd Person Singular)
scenarios.meaning: trembles in fear / acts helplessly like a child
scenarios.example_english: The frightened deer trembles inside the forest.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: ḍibhi bhayācalane. iditvānnum. ḍimbhati. ḍiḍimbha. ḍimbhitā.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: ḍibi bhaye calane ca. ḍimbhati. bālasadṛśakampane vartate.

meanings.English: To tremble from fear, to act like a child or be helpless
meanings.Bengali: Bhaye kā̃pā, śiśur mato ācaraṇa karā
meanings.German: Vor Angst zittern, sich kindisch oder hilflos verhalten
meanings.French: Trembler de peur, agir de manière enfantine
meanings.Russian: Drozhat ot strakha, vesti sebya kak rebyonok

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'dhundh' is used when someone is searching, seeking, or looking closely to find something that is lost or hidden.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Lat (Present Tense, Prathama Purusa / Third Person Singular)
scenarios.example_sanskrit: balakah vanam madhye svasya mitram dhundhati.
scenarios.example_english: The boy searches for his friend in the middle of the forest.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Lan (Past Tense, Prathama Purusa / Third Person Singular)
scenarios.example_english: The student searched for the ancient book in the library.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: Recognized in comparative non-Paninian dhātu-lists under Hemacandra's Siddhahaima tradition as 'dhudhi anveṣaṇe'; the 'i' marker (idit) requires the insertion of an internal nasal (num-āgama), yielding the active stem 'dhundh-'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kṣīrasvāmin notes peripheral and deśya-derived verbal roots of inquiry; Hemacandra systematically incorporates 'dhundh' into the primary verbal inventory for the specific sense of searching and tracking.

meanings.English: To search, to seek, to trace, to investigate

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'bokk' is a descriptive non-Paninian verb that means to speak sharply, bark, or roar loudly. It is typically used when an animal barks or a person shouts loudly in excitement or anger.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Laṭ-lakāra (Present indicative, Prathama puruṣa, Ekavacana)
scenarios.example_english: Seeing a stranger, the dog barks loudly.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Laṅ-lakāra (Past imperfect, Prathama puruṣa, Ekavacana)
scenarios.example_english: In the forest, the lion roared furiously.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: Non-Paninian entry; preserved primarily in the Haimacandra tradition (Siddhahema Dhatupāṭha 1.285) as 'bokka bhāṣaṇe'. It does not occur in the classical Paninian Madhaviya recension.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Absent in Kṣīrasvāmin's classical Paninian inventory. Categorized under onomatopoeic/descriptive sound-roots in Hemacandra's lexicographical system.

meanings.English: to bark, to shout loudly, to roar, to speak indistinctly
meanings.Bengali: gheu gheu korā, garjon korā, chechāno

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The verbal root 'boll' means to speak, talk, or express in speech. In everyday speech, it functions like 'vad' or 'bhāṣ', describing someone uttering words or conversing.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: laṭ-lakāra (present tense), prathama-puruṣa (third person), eka-vacana (singular)
scenarios.example_english: The boy speaks sweetly.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: laṅ-lakāra (imperfect past tense), prathama-puruṣa (third person), eka-vacana (singular)
scenarios.example_english: The student spoke truthful words.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: Not listed in classical Pāṇinian Dhātupāṭha; recognized in non-Pāṇinian traditions such as the Haimacandra Dhātupāṭha under 'bolla bhāṣāyām'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Omitted in Kṣīrasvāmin's Pāṇinian recension; cataloged in medieval Prakrit-influenced and Jain grammatical lexicons representing vernacular-derived roots.

meanings.English: to speak, to talk, to utter

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The verbal root 'hall' means to shake, tremble, or move back and forth. It is used when an object or living being quivers, vibrates, or moves due to fear, wind, or an earthquake.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: lat (present tense, third person singular, active voice)
scenarios.example_english: The leaf of the tree trembles due to the speed of the wind.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: lan (imperfect past tense, third person singular, active voice)
scenarios.example_english: During the earthquake, the entire building shook.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: Noted primarily in regional and non-Paninian recensions such as the Siddha-Hema tradition under the sense of kampane (vibration/shaking); shares semantic and phonetic overlap with roots like chal and khal.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin records roots of movement and trembling similarly under calana-arthas, corresponding with the Haimacandra categorization of root hall forming hallati.

meanings.English: to shake, tremble, agitate, or move

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'holl' means to play, frolic, or engage in lighthearted sporting and recreation. It describes joyful playfulness of children or animals.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Laṭ (Present Tense), Prathama Puruṣa (Third Person), Ekavacana (Singular)
scenarios.example_english: The child plays in the garden with friends.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Laṅ (Past Tense), Prathama Puruṣa (Third Person), Ekavacana (Singular)
scenarios.example_english: The young deer frolicked freely in the forest.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: Non-Pāṇinian entry: Recorded distinctly in Ācārya Hemacandra's Dhātupāṭha under the arthasūtra 'holla khelane' (vihāre); unlisted in classical Pāṇinian recensions represented by the Mādhavīya-dhātuvṛtti.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Absent in Kṣīrasvāmin's classical Pāṇinian commentary; retained exclusively within the western non-Pāṇinian lexicographical stream of the Haima system.

meanings.English: to play, to frolic, to sport

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'saṭṭ' means to split apart, disintegrate, or scatter. Imagine dry mud or a brittle biscuit falling into tiny pieces when pressed; this process of breaking apart is expressed by this verb.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Present tense (laṭ), Third person singular (prathama-puruṣa ekavacana)
scenarios.example_english: The dry lump of clay falls apart.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Aorist past tense (luṅ), Third person singular (prathama-puruṣa ekavacana)
scenarios.example_english: The decayed piece of wood broke apart.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: Standard Paninian recensions treat saṭṭa / śaṭṭa in bhvādi or curādi with meanings of viśaraṇa (disintegration) or rujo gati (movement in disease/injury), recognized as variant lexical entries.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes saṭṭa viśaraṇe gatau ca; occurring in the context of splitting, shattering, or scattering apart into components.

meanings.English: to disintegrate, to break apart, to dissolve into pieces
meanings.French: se désintégrer, se briser en morceaux

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'laṭṭ' means to behave childishly, play innocently like a child, or frolic. It describes youthful, playful actions.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Laṭ (Present Tense), Prathama Puruṣa (Third Person), Ekavacana (Singular)
scenarios.meaning: Acts like a child / frolics childishly
scenarios.example_english: The child plays childishly in the courtyard.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Luṅ (Aorist / Past Tense), Prathama Puruṣa (Third Person), Ekavacana (Singular)
scenarios.example_english: The infant behaved playfully near the mother.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: laṭṭa bālatve vihāre ca. bhvādau parasmaipadī seṭ. laṭṭati, lalaṭṭa, laṭṭitā.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: laṭṭa bālatve. bālacaritracaraṇe ityarthaḥ. laṭṭati śiśuḥ.

meanings.English: to act childishly, to frolic, to play like a child
meanings.Hindi: bacchoṁ jaisā vyavahāra karnā, bālacāpalya dikhānā
meanings.Bengali: shishura moto aacharan kora, chhelemānushi korā
meanings.Chinese: xiang haizi ban youxi, youzhi xishua

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'jhamp' expresses the action of jumping, bounding, or making a sudden leap forward, just like a frog or a monkey moving swiftly.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Laṭ (Present Tense, Prathama Puruṣa, Ekavacana)
scenarios.example_english: The monkey leaps from one branch to another.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Lṛṭ (Simple Future Tense, Prathama Puruṣa, Ekavacana)
scenarios.example_english: The frog will jump into the water of the pond.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: Non-Pāṇinian entry preserved in provincial and later grammatical digests; indexed in comparative lexicons under the sense of kūrdana (plutagati).
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Absent in standard classical Pāṇinian recensions; recorded in Hemacandra's Dhātupāṭha and Kavikalpadruma as an expressive root indicating leaping or jumping.

meanings.English: to jump, to leap, to plunge

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'ṭaṅk' means to chisel, split, or pierce an object such as a rock or wood. It describes the physical action of breaking something open with a sharp tool or strike.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: lat_prathama_purusha_ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The sculptor chisels the stone slab.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: luṅ_prathama_purusha_ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The woodcutter split the timber forcefully.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: ṭaki bhedane - idittvānnum, ṭaṅkati. bhedanaṃ dāraṇam. asya prayogaḥ prāyeṇa śilpakarmasu dṛśyate.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: ṭaki bhedane - ṭaṅkati, ṭaṅkayati iti vā pāṭhāntaram. ididbhyo numiti numāgamaḥ.

meanings.English: to split, to chisel, to crack, to incise
meanings.Hindi: chhedan karnā, phāṛnā, ṭāṅkī se toṛnā
meanings.Bengali: bhedan karā, phātāl karā, chhedan karā

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'chikk' means 'to sneeze'. It is an expressive root describing the involuntary expulsion of air from the nose and mouth caused by irritation, cold, or dust.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: laṭ (Present Tense, 3rd Person Singular)
scenarios.example_english: The child sneezes repeatedly due to the dusty wind.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: laṅ (Imperfect Past, 3rd Person Singular)
scenarios.example_english: He sneezed because of the pungent smell.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: Non-Paninian entry; recognized explicitly in Haimacandra's Dhātupāṭha under the gloss 'chikka kṣutau', indicating the bodily reflex of sneezing.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Not recorded in standard Pāṇinian recensions; cited in non-Pāṇinian Jain grammars (Hemacandra) as an onomatopoeic root for sneezing (chikkati).

meanings.English: to sneeze

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'khuḍ' means to break, snap, fracture, or divide something into pieces. It works similarly to the common root 'troṭ' or 'bhañj' and is used when an object is snapped or severed.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: laṭ-lakāra (Present Tense, 3rd Person Singular)
scenarios.example_english: The boy snaps the dry branch.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: luṅ-lakāra (Aorist / Past Tense, 3rd Person Singular)
scenarios.example_english: The farmer broke the wooden stick.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: In Paninian vrittis, this root occurs in variant recensions alongside khuṭa/khuḍa bhede khaṇḍane ca, taking guṇa to form khoḍati.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kṣīrasvāmin notes khuḍa/khuṭa in the sense of splitting (khaṇḍana) or limping/breaking into parts (khoḍati).

meanings.English: to break, to snap, to divide into fragments

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'ghuṭṭ' means to gulp, drink in a single draft, or swallow liquid greedily. Imagine drinking a full glass of cold water at once after playing under the hot sun.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Laṭ (Present Tense), Prathama Puruṣa (Third Person), Ekavacana (Singular)
scenarios.meaning: He/she gulps or swallows a drink
scenarios.example_english: The thirsty boy gulps down the water.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Luṅ (Aorist / Past Tense), Prathama Puruṣa (Third Person), Ekavacana (Singular)
scenarios.example_english: He swallowed the medicine in one single gulp.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: ghuṭṭa pāne | hemacandrīye dhātupāṭhe ayaṃ dhātuḥ pāne grasane ceti viśeṣeṇa pathyate | ghoṭṭati, aghoṭṭīt ityādayaḥ prayogāḥ |
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: ghuṭṭa pāne ityeke | grasane pānavat pravṛttiḥ | anye tu panīyādike ghuṭṭayati iti curādau gaṇayanti |

meanings.English: to gulp, to swallow, to drink avidly

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'jhol' means to swing, sway, or oscillate back and forth, similar to sitting on a swing or a tree branch moving in the wind.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: lat-lakara (present tense), prathama-purusha, eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The child swings on the swing.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: lan-lakara (past tense), prathama-purusha, eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The tree branch swayed due to the wind.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: Non-Paninian root absent in standard Paninian recensions; recorded in Hemacandra's Dhatupatha under the sense of andolana (swinging, waving, or swaying).
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Omitted in standard Paninian lists like Kshirasvamin's core canon; attested specifically in late medieval and Jain grammatical traditions such as the Haimacandra school as 'jhola andolane'.

meanings.English: to swing, to sway, to rock back and forth

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The verbal root 'chūṣ' means 'to suck', 'to sip', or 'to absorb liquid/nectar'. It is used when an agent draws in or extracts juice, fluid, or essence.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga, laṭ lakāra (present tense), prathama puruṣa, eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The child sucks the sweet fruit juice.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga, laṅ lakāra (past tense), prathama puruṣa, eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The bee sucked in all the nectar of the flower.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: In comparative lexicography, this root is recorded in the Haima tradition as an aspirate variant of Paninian cūṣa (ācūṣaṇe), denoting the drawing in of fluids (rasākarṣaṇa).
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes cūṣa prapāṇe; the Haimacandra recension lists chūṣa alongside cūṣa representing the phonological variant in the sense of ācūṣaṇa.

meanings.English: To suck, to draw out juice, to absorb or sip liquid

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The verbal root 'ṭall' means to ward off, evade, push aside, or put off an obstacle or danger. It is the classical root ancestor of common modern Indo-Aryan verbs meaning 'to stall' or 'to defer' (like Hindi ṭālanā).

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Laṭ lakāra (Present indicative), prathama puruṣa, ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The boy evades the danger.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Luṅ lakāra (Aorist), prathama puruṣa, ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The soldier warded off the enemy.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: ṭalla apāvāraṇe | apāvāraṇaṃ dūrīkaraṇaṃ nivāraṇaṃ vā | ṭallati | aṭallīt | Haimasaṃpradāye sphuṭatayā paṭhitaḥ |
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: ṭalla apāvāraṇe | apavāraṇaṃ dūrīkaraṇam | ṭallati ṭallataḥ ṭallanti |

meanings.English: To ward off, to evade, to remove, to push away

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The verbal root 'ḍakk' means to gather, collect, retract, or pull together into one place. For example, when you gather your books together or when a bird gathers twigs for a nest, this root describes that action of bringing things together.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga, laṭ-lakāra (present indicative), prathama-puruṣa (third person), ekavacana (singular)
scenarios.example_english: The boy gathers the scattered books together.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga, laṅ-lakāra (past imperfect), prathama-puruṣa (third person), ekavacana (singular)
scenarios.example_english: The farmer collected the grain from all over the field.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'ḍakka' is systematically preserved in the Haimacandra tradition with the meaning 'saṃharaṇe' (drawing in, gathering, or retracting). In the standard Pāṇinian recensions represented by Sāyaṇa in the Mādhavīya-dhātuvṛtti, this distinct regional entry is either subsumed under cognate semantic roots of gathering or treated as an extra-systemic non-Pāṇinian variant.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kṣīrasvāmin focuses on primary Vedic and classical roots of the Pāṇinian corpus, noting comparable roots of containment and collection. The explicit lexical formulation 'ḍakka saṃharaṇe' serves as a distinguishing marker of the Jain Haima Dhātupāṭha.

meanings.English: to gather, to collect, to assemble, to draw in, to retract

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The verbal root 'madd' is used when someone crushes, grinds, rubs, or firmly presses something down.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Laṭ (Present Tense), Prathama Puruṣa (Third Person), Ekavacana (Singular)
scenarios.example_english: The physician crushes the herbal medicine.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Laṅ (Past Tense), Prathama Puruṣa (Third Person), Ekavacana (Singular)
scenarios.example_english: The farmer crushed the seed.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: madda mardane - Recorded in non-Paninian traditions such as the Haima Dhātupāṭha as a root denoting sampīḍana (pressing/grinding), closely associated with classical mṛd.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: madda ityeko mardanārthaḥ; listed in western non-Paninian lexical registers (Haimacandra) reflecting secondary and Prakrit-influenced root formations.

meanings.English: to crush, to grind, to rub, to press down
meanings.Bengali: dola kara, gū̃ṛo kara, mardana kara

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'rill' expresses the action of flowing, gliding smoothly, or moving continuously forward, like a gentle stream or sliding movement.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga, laṭ lakāra (present tense), prathama puruṣa, eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The clear water glides smoothly at the base of the mountain.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga, laṅ lakāra (past imperfect), prathama puruṣa, eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The stream swiftly flowed into the ocean.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: Not listed in the standard Pāṇinian recension of Mādhavīya-dhātuvṛtti; it belongs to the non-Pāṇinian Haima tradition in the sense of gati (motion/trickling).
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: This root is specific to the Jaina grammatical system of Hemacandra (Haima Dhātupāṭha) and is omitted in Kṣīrasvāmin's Pāṇinian Kṣīrataraṅgiṇī.

meanings.English: to move, glide, trickle, or flow

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'laḍ' describes playful behavior, sporting, dallying, or treating someone with loving fondness and pampering.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Laṭ Lakāra (Present Indicative), Prathama Puruṣa, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The child sports joyfully in the garden.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Luṅ Lakāra (Aorist), Prathama Puruṣa, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The infant dallied affectionately near the mother.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: laḍa vilāse. vilāsaḥ śṛṅgāraceṣṭā lālanam ca. laḍati, lālāḍa, laḍitā.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: laḍa vilāse. vilāsanaṁ laḍanam. vilāso harṣaceṣṭā kriyāviśeṣaśca.

meanings.English: to sport, to play, to dally, to caress, to pamper
meanings.Bengali: bilāsa karā, ādara karā, khelā karā

transitivity: akarmaka (intransitive) / sakarmaka (transitive in the sense of approach)

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The verbal root sall means to come together, unite, or move in company with others. In simple words, it is used whenever people, rivers, or paths join together or proceed in unison.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: lat (present indicative, prathama purusha, eka-vacana)
scenarios.example_english: The stream of the river converges with the ocean.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: lang (imperfect past, prathama purusha, eka-vacana)
scenarios.example_english: The pathway joined with the main road.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: Not primary in Paninian recension; documented in collateral traditions as a variant of moving and mixing (malla-sallādi-varga).
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Recorded under parallel roots denoting saṃhata-gati or bodily/physical aggregation.

meanings.English: to go together, to unite, to assemble, to converge
meanings.Bengali: melita haoya, sangama haoya, gamana kara

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'ghall' means to drive, send, urge, or throw. Imagine urging a chariot horse forward or sending a messenger on an errand.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: laṭ (Present Tense), Prathama Puruṣa, Ejavacana
scenarios.example_english: The king sends the messenger to the city.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: laṅ (Past Tense), Prathama Puruṣa, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The soldier threw an arrow towards the enemy.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: ghalla preraṇe kṣepe ca ityeke. ayam pāṇinīya-pāṭheṣu sārvatrikaḥ na bhavati kintu haima-cāndra-dhātupāṭheṣu preraṇārthespaṣṭaṁ nirdiṣṭaḥ.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: ghalla preraṇārthaḥ. asya gaṇasūtreṣu dākṣiṇātyapāṭheṣu ca deśyatvena saṅgrahaḥ kṛto dṛśyate.

meanings.English: to drive, urge, send, throw

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root pell means to push, drive forward, or propel something. Think of pushing a heavy cart or urging a friend forward.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Present Tense (lat, prathama purusha, ekavacana)
scenarios.example_english: The boy pushes the toy chariot forward.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Past Tense (lan, prathama purusha, ekavacana)
scenarios.example_english: The cowherd drove the cow onto the path.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: Not included in the core Paninian Astadhyayi canon; accepted in post-Paninian registers such as the Haimacandra tradition under the classification of preraṇartha (driving/propelling).
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin does not record 'pell' in the classical Paninian Dhatupatha, where synonymous roots like 'nud' or 'tud' are preferred, identifying 'pell' as a typical Desya-influenced development in Jaina lexicography.

meanings.English: To push, to propel, to urge, to drive forward

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'khall' means to contract, shrink, or fall/stumble down. Think of it like a dried leaf shrinking in the sun, or a tired traveler stumbling and collapsing from exhaustion.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Laṭ (Present Indicative), Prathama Puruṣa, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The old man stumbles and falters on the road.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Luṅ (Aorist), Prathama Puruṣa, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: Due to the cold, the leaf shrank.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: khalla saṃkocane patane ca | The standard Pāṇinian recension treats parallel forms under variants like 'khal', whereas Hemacandra explicitly isolates 'khall' in the sense of shrinking and dropping.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kṣīrasvāmin observes the root among non-Pāṇinian variants noting: khalla gati-saṅkocayoḥ, preserved robustly in the western grammar traditions such as Hemacandra's Dhātupārāyaṇa.

meanings.English: to contract, shrink, stumble, fall down
meanings.Bengali: saṅkucita haoyā, jhmepe paṛā, patita haoyā

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The verbal root 'khaj' means to churn or vigorously stir liquids such as milk or curd in order to make butter.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Present tense (laṭ), Third person singular
scenarios.example_english: The milkmaid churns the curd in the morning.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Past tense (laṅ), Third person singular
scenarios.example_english: Krishna agitated the lake water with a stick.

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'guṇṭh' means to cover, wrap, veil, or protect something with a layer or cloth so it remains safe or concealed.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: lat (present indicative active, 3rd person singular)
scenarios.example_english: The boy wraps his body with a garment due to the cold.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kta pratyaya (past passive participle)
scenarios.example_english: The vehicle covered with dust became invisible.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: guṭhi saṃrakṣaṇe. idittvān num. guṇṭhayati, guṇṭhayate. saṃrakṣaṇam āvaraṇam.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: guṭhi saṃrakṣaṇe. idit. guṇṭhayati. āvaraṇārtha ity apare.

meanings.English: to cover, to veil, to wrap, to protect
meanings.Bengali: ḍhākā deoyā, ghire rākhā, ābaraṇa karā

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The verbal root 'jambh' describes the natural bodily act of yawning or stretching one's limbs when tired, waking up, or feeling drowsy.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Laṭ (Present Indicative), Prathama-puruṣa (Third Person), Ekavacana (Singular)
scenarios.example_english: The sleepy child yawns in the morning.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Laṅ (Past Imperfect), Prathama-puruṣa (Third Person), Ekavacana (Singular)
scenarios.example_english: The tired traveler stretched under the tree.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: jabhi gātravināme. iditvānnum. jambhate. gātravināmo jṛmbhaṇamucyate.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: jabhi gātravināme. idit num. jambhate śarīra-bhañjane ityarthaḥ.

meanings.English: to yawn, to stretch the limbs, to gape

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'ḍip' means to throw, toss, cast, or send forth. You can use it whenever a person throws a stone, sends an object flying, or propels something away.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: lat (present tense, 3rd person singular / prathama-puruṣa ekavacana)
scenarios.example_english: The boy throws the stone far away.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: luṅ (aorist tense, 3rd person singular / prathama-puruṣa ekavacana)
scenarios.example_english: The warrior shot/cast an arrow at the enemy.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: ḍipa kṣepe | cāndra-dhātupāṭhe kṣepe preraṇe ca paṭhitaḥ | ḍepati, ḍiḍepa, ḍipitā, aḍipīt |
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: ḍipa kṣepe | kṣepaṇaṃ preraṇaṃ nirākaraṇaṃ vā | kṣipatyarthe cāndrādibhir aṅgīkṛtaḥ |

meanings.English: to throw, cast, propel, discharge

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'dhurv' means to hurt, injure, or cause harm to someone. It is used in sentences describing an act of physical injury or harm.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Laṭ (Present Indicative), Prathama Puruṣa (Third Person), Ekavacana (Singular)
scenarios.example_english: The hunter injures the deer with an arrow.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Laṅ (Imperfect Past), Prathama Puruṣa (Third Person), Ekavacana (Singular)
scenarios.example_english: The enemy harmed the city.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: dhurvī hiṃsāyām. iditvat num na bhavati anubandhatvāt. dhurvati, dudhorva, dhurvitā.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: dhurvī hiṃsāyām. mṛdūbhavati hiṃsāyāṃ prayogaḥ. dhurvati ripum.

meanings.English: to injure, to hurt, to harm, to strike
meanings.Hindi: hiṃsā karnā, choṭ pahuñcānā, hāni karnā
meanings.Bengali: hiṃsā karā, āghāt karā, khoti karā
